papers.title: Analyzing Learned Convnet Features with Dirichlet Process Gaussian Mixture Models
papers.abstract: Convolutional Neural Networks (Convnets) have achieved good results in a range of computer vision tasks the recent years. Though given a lot of attention, visualizing the learned representations to interpret Convnets, still remains a challenging task. The high dimensionality of internal representations and the high abstractions of deep layers are the main challenges when visualizing Convnet functionality. We present in this paper a technique based on clustering internal Convnet representations with a Dirichlet Process Gaussian Mixture Model, for visualization of learned representations in Convnets. Our method copes with the high dimensionality of a Convnet by clustering representations across all nodes of each layer. We will discuss how this application is useful when considering transfer learning, i.e.\ transferring a model trained on one dataset to solve a task on a different one.
papers.summary: Visualizing what convolutional neural networks (Convnets) learn is hard because internal representations are high-dimensional and deep layers are highly abstract. The proposed technique **clusters a Convnet's internal representations with a Dirichlet Process Gaussian Mixture Model, pooling across all nodes of each layer**, and uses the resulting clusters to visualize what the layer has learned. The authors also discuss how the approach can inform transfer learning, where a model trained on one dataset is reused for a task on another.

papers.title: Improved Convergence Rates for Stochastic Multi-Gradient Descent which Close the Gap: A Proof by AI
papers.abstract: For smooth nonconvex stochastic multi-objective optimization, stochastic multi-gradient descent (SMG) computes an approximate steepest common descent direction of the objectives from stochastic gradients. Under standard assumptions, this note establishes a new convergence rate for SMG in terms of the squared Pareto-stationarity (PS) measure. With a constant stepsize and linearly growing mini-batches, the expected squared empirical PS measure at the algorithm's output is $\tilde{O}(T^{-1})$ after $T$ iterations. This improves on the $\tilde{O}(T^{-1/4})$ bound obtained by Chen et al. (JMLR, 2024) for linearly growing batches, without requiring bounded gradients. Here, $\tilde{O}(\cdot)$ suppresses logarithmic factors. The key to the rate improvement is to exploit the Lipschitz continuity of the PS measure, defined by the norm of the multi-gradient descent algorithm (MGDA) direction, rather than the $(1/2)$-H\"older continuity of the MGDA direction used by Chen et al. (2024). For variants of MoCo and MoCo+ with exact MGDA updates and constant batch sizes, the analysis gives expected squared empirical PS rates of $O(T^{-1/2})$ and $\tilde{O}(T^{-2/3})$, respectively. These bounds match the corresponding single-objective momentum rates up to logarithmic factors. The proof was accidentally discovered while the author was preparing homework for a graduate course: ChatGPT 5.4 Thinking Extended generated the initial proof strategy for the main SMG result in response to an author-written homework-solution prompt; the author then verified and reorganized the resulting argument. The appendices document the prompt, summarize the student submissions with LLM disclosures, and present additional proofs and results on momentum-based stochastic MGDA.
papers.summary: For smooth nonconvex stochastic multi-objective optimization, this note proves a faster convergence rate for stochastic multi-gradient descent (`SMG`), measured by the squared Pareto-stationarity (PS) measure. With a constant stepsize and linearly growing mini-batches, the expected squared PS measure falls at **roughly 1/T up to logarithmic factors, versus the earlier T^(-1/4) bound of Chen et al. (2024)**, and without assuming bounded gradients; the gain comes from using the Lipschitz continuity of the PS measure rather than the Hölder continuity of the multi-gradient descent algorithm (`MGDA`) direction. Variants of `MoCo` and `MoCo+` with constant batch sizes get rates of T^(-1/2) and about T^(-2/3), matching single-objective momentum rates up to log factors. The initial proof strategy was generated by `ChatGPT 5.4 Thinking Extended` in response to a homework-solution prompt and then verified and reorganized by the author.

papers.title: Continual-ARC: Measuring Skill Acquisition over a Working Lifetime
papers.abstract: Agent harnesses have emerged as a promising mechanism for continual learning, alongside test-time parametric learning. However, the current benchmarks have several limitations: they generally focus on a single applied domain, serve each instance only once, and assume a single family of learner, so memory-based and weight-based systems are rarely compared on the same scale. We propose Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream built from the three ARC-AGI editions, whose tasks need no domain knowledge. The same tasks return after dormant gaps with fresh instances, while new tasks keep arriving. On each instance, the learner may pay for demonstrations, submit answers, or act inside the harness, with retries permitted on incorrect submissions, which are paid for. Each instance is scored based on the share of this feedback budget consumed. Since a learner may keep anything between instances, memory-based and weight-based systems are scored on the same scale. After the stream, the learner is frozen and tested on fresh instances of the tasks it met, which measures memorization, and on unseen tasks, which measures generalization. We run an agent harness with frozen weights, with and without persistence, on Qwen3.5-9B and GLM-5.3 Flash, comparing them with two prompting floors, a program-induction method and Qwen3.5-9B's weights trained to imitate GLM-5.3 Flash. Persistence in the harness generally does not improve memorization unless provided with explicit expert guidance. Most harness-based methods still learn less than a floor that simply caches each task's demonstrations, across all models we tested. Harness-based methods gain little or nothing on unseen tasks, whereas weight-based learning shows substantial gains. This opens the door to future weight-based continual learning that could teach models to drive harnesses in new domains.
papers.summary: Existing continual-learning benchmarks tend to cover one applied domain, serve each instance once, and assume one kind of learner, so memory-based agent harnesses and weight-based learning are rarely compared on the same scale. `Continual-ARC` builds a lifelong stream from the three `ARC-AGI` editions in which tasks return after dormant gaps with fresh instances, scores each instance by the share of a feedback budget (demonstrations, retries, harness actions) consumed, and then tests the frozen learner on both seen and unseen tasks. Experiments with `Qwen3.5-9B` and `GLM-5.3 Flash` find that harness persistence generally does not improve memorization without explicit expert guidance, and that **most harness-based methods learn less than a baseline that simply caches each task's demonstrations**. Harness-based methods gain little or nothing on unseen tasks, while weight-based learning shows substantial gains.

papers.title: Marimba: A System One Model for Speech
papers.abstract: Speech applications require decisions about term presence, turn completion, and language within an audio window. We present Marimba, an interface for typed speech decisions built on frozen Qwen3-ASR 0.6B features. Lexical questions use zero-shot scoring of ASR transcripts; non-lexical questions use a question-conditioned head and a separate layer-18 turn-end readout. Language identification uses the ASR model's own language scores. On private conversational test sets, decoder AUROC is 0.80-0.92; on public read speech it is 0.92-0.97. Speech Commands four-way accuracy is 0.93; binary lexical ECE is at most 0.08. Personal-information detection, which passes the greedy transcript to a private, curated PII pipeline, reaches item-level F1 0.904 on synthetic Brazilian Portuguese speech (1.000 on reference transcripts). Layer-12 speaker readouts detect speaker change with AUROC 0.966-0.980 on AMI and VoxConverse, above an ECAPA baseline, and count speakers (0, 1, 2, or 3+) more accurately than pyannote 3.1. The turn-end readout reaches AUROC 0.930 versus Smart Turn v3.2 at 0.982 on Smart Turn's own test set. On a subset of ICSI meetings labeled by next speaker, AUROC is 0.716 versus 0.712; the paired confidence interval includes zero.
papers.summary: Speech applications need quick decisions about an audio window, such as whether a term was said, whether a turn has ended, and which language is spoken. `Marimba` answers such typed questions on top of frozen `Qwen3-ASR 0.6B` features, using zero-shot scoring of transcripts for lexical questions, a question-conditioned head for non-lexical ones, and separate layer readouts for turn-end and speaker cues. Decoder AUROC is 0.80-0.92 on private conversational sets and 0.92-0.97 on public read speech, and **speaker-change detection reaches AUROC 0.966-0.980 on `AMI` and `VoxConverse`, above an `ECAPA` baseline**, with speaker counting more accurate than `pyannote 3.1`. Its turn-end readout trails `Smart Turn v3.2` on that model's own test set (0.930 versus 0.982) and is statistically indistinguishable from it on a subset of `ICSI` meetings.

papers.title: CrisisBench: an evaluation suite for crisis counseling AI
papers.abstract:
Background: Crisis helplines are essential to mental health systems but are often understaffed and underfunded. LLMs could support counselors, but existing benchmarks do not capture the escalation, risk assessment, and de-escalation central to crisis conversations, while privacy restrictions limit use of real transcripts.
Methods: We present CrisisBench, a privacy-preserving suite for single- and multi-turn crisis counseling evaluation. It includes 1,085 single-turn tasks from 200 de-identified conversations and 1,185 patient LLMs derived from hotline metadata. Patient models and a 23-item LLM judge were calibrated against expert counselors.
Results: We evaluated five GPT models plus draft-then-edit and retrieval-augmented generation. All systems underperformed human counselors on excessive empathy and questioning in single-turn evaluation. The rubric achieved human-human Krippendorff's $\alpha$ = 0.51 and LLM-human $\alpha$ = 0.54 (Pearson r = 0.80). In multi-turn evaluation, retrieval-augmented generation scored highest overall (0.961), with all systems within 0.058. Microskills and style/tone were near ceiling, while productivity and safety/risk accounted for most between-system variation. Counselors rated patient LLMs realistic (86%) and useful (92%).
Conclusion: CrisisBench enables scalable, privacy-preserving evaluation of crisis counseling. Current systems perform strongly on core structural competencies but still diverge from experts on important response-level failure modes. We release the rubrics, judge prompts, and evaluation tasks.
papers.summary: Existing benchmarks do not capture the escalation, risk assessment, and de-escalation central to crisis helpline conversations, and privacy rules restrict the use of real transcripts. `CrisisBench` offers 1,085 single-turn tasks drawn from 200 de-identified conversations plus 1,185 simulated patient LLMs derived from hotline metadata, with the patient models and a 23-item LLM judge calibrated against expert counselors. Across five GPT models plus draft-then-edit and retrieval-augmented generation variants, **all systems underperformed human counselors on excessive empathy and questioning in single-turn evaluation**, while multi-turn scores were tightly clustered, with retrieval-augmented generation highest at 0.961 and all systems within 0.058. The judge agreed with humans about as well as humans agreed with each other (Krippendorff's alpha 0.54 versus 0.51), and counselors rated the patient simulations realistic in 86% of cases.

papers.title: Fragmented Markers, Mixed Results: A Systematic Review of AI Coding Assistants and Developer Productivity
papers.abstract:
AI coding assistants are increasingly embedded in software engineering practice, yet the literature still offers no cumulative, easily interpretable picture of their effects on software developer productivity. The central problem is not a lack of studies, but a lack of comparability: prior work operationalizes productivity through heterogeneous markers, settings, and reporting styles, making cross-study conclusions difficult. To address this, we conduct a staged systematic literature review. In the first stage, we synthesize studies that explicitly examine developer productivity. In the second, we extend the scope to productivity-related developer outcomes using SPACE as a theory-informed lens, capturing human-centered evidence that explicit productivity studies often omit. Across both stages, we analyze how productivity is operationalized, which confounding factors are discussed, and how reported effects are distributed.
  We identify 187 unique productivity and productivity-related markers, while individual studies typically only use five, revealing a broad but highly fragmented evidence base. Explicit productivity research is dominated by time-, output-, and artifact-oriented proxies, whereas the broader SPACE-aligned corpus makes satisfaction, psychological aspects, and well-being substantially more visible. Reported effects are often positive, but this pattern is stronger in perceived and tendency-based findings than in objective or statistically evaluated ones. Overall, the literature suggests that AI coding assistants can support productivity, but current evidence does not yet support simple, context-independent conclusions. The key contribution of this review is therefore a structured basis for making productivity evidence more interpretable, multidimensional, and comparable across studies.
papers.summary: Studies of AI coding assistants measure developer productivity in such different ways that their results are hard to compare or combine. A two-stage systematic literature review first synthesizes studies that explicitly examine productivity and then widens to productivity-related outcomes through the `SPACE` framework, analyzing how productivity is operationalized, which confounders are discussed, and how effects are distributed. It identifies **187 unique productivity markers, while individual studies typically use only five**, with explicit productivity research dominated by time, output, and artifact proxies. Reported effects are often positive, but more so in perceived and tendency-based findings than in objective or statistically evaluated ones, so the evidence does not support simple context-independent conclusions.

papers.title: Measuring Human-AI Alignment as an Early Indicator for Effective Collaboration in Hybrid SE Teams
papers.abstract: As AI agents increasingly integrate into software engineering (SE) processes, ensuring effective collaboration in these hybrid teams becomes a critical challenge. While existing metrics focus on observing dynamic run-time performance, there is a lack of systematic, static measurements for early human-AI alignment -- the degree to which an AI's actions and granularity map to human expectations. This position paper proposes a research agenda to develop an SE-specific alignment metric suite drawing principles from software architecture, organizational psychology, and human-computer interaction. Furthermore, it outlines a validation methodology using concepts and techniques from business process monitoring (BPM) and introduces static assessment tools leveraging declarative BPM languages to ensure agents adhere to specific project constraints.
papers.summary: As AI agents join software engineering (SE) teams, existing metrics observe run-time performance but offer no static, early measure of human-AI alignment, defined here as how well an agent's actions and granularity map to human expectations. This position paper **proposes a research agenda for an SE-specific alignment metric suite** drawing on software architecture, organizational psychology, and human-computer interaction. It also outlines a validation methodology based on business process monitoring (BPM) and static assessment tools that use declarative BPM languages to check that agents adhere to project constraints.

papers.title: Can AI Help Explain AI? Effects of Multimodal LLM-Generated Explanations on Perceived Understanding and Perceived Trust in XAI Visualizations
papers.abstract: Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) aims to make machine learning models understandable, yet many XAI visualizations remain difficult for end-users to interpret. Here, we evaluate whether augmenting XAI outputs with textual explanations from multimodal LLMs improves perceived understanding and perceived trust. We conducted a pre-registered within-subject experiment ($N = 128$) across seven decision scenarios and five XAI methods, with and without LLM generated explanations. The explanations improved perceived understanding and perceived trust by 0.35 and 0.26 points on five-point scales (both $p < .001$). The gain appeared in all seven scenarios, did not differ between local and global explanations, and was largest for participants with the least prior XAI exposure. A mediation analysis indicates an indirect effect on perceived trust through perceived understanding. These results suggest that multimodal LLMs can provide a useful interpretive layer for XAI beyond expert audiences.
papers.summary: Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) visualizations are often hard for end-users to interpret, so the authors test whether adding textual explanations written by multimodal LLMs helps. In a pre-registered within-subject experiment with 128 participants across seven decision scenarios and five XAI methods, the explanations **raised perceived understanding by 0.35 and perceived trust by 0.26 points on five-point scales**. The gain appeared in every scenario, did not differ between local and global explanations, and was largest for participants with the least prior XAI exposure. A mediation analysis indicates that part of the trust effect runs through perceived understanding.

papers.title: ClearTalk: Data-Driven Mandarin Articulation Analysis and Personalized Communication Support for Children with Dysarthria
papers.abstract: Children with dysarthria may experience reduced intelligibility and difficulty expressing everyday needs. ClearTalk is a smartwatch-based system that converts Mandarin speech-recognition differences into interpretable articulatory profiles for personalized practice and staged communication. Target and recognized utterances are aligned at the syllable level, summarized across seven articulatory positions, and ranked by a count-sensitive asymmetric heuristic. For 13 dysarthric speakers from the Mandarin Dysarthria Speech Corpus, system syllable-level accuracy showed a Pearson correlation of 0.908 with expert intelligibility, with an R-squared value of 0.824 and a p-value below 0.001. The system-selected priority targets achieved an 86.7 percent overlap with the consensus of three blinded speech-language pathologists; across 210 target consonants, automated labels achieved 86.7 percent agreement, a Cohen's kappa of 0.76, and a macro-F1 score of 0.81. In a balanced single-session pilot with 15 children, mean pre/post gains were 14.4, 29.4, and 27.7 percentage points for mild, moderate, and severe groups, while communication-round completion rates were 81.3, 66.7, and 48.0 percent. These findings support the feasibility of using interpretable patterns of speech errors to guide wearable articulation practice and communication assistance.
papers.summary: Children with dysarthria often have reduced speech intelligibility and difficulty expressing everyday needs. `ClearTalk` is a smartwatch-based system that aligns target and recognized Mandarin utterances at the syllable level, summarizes the differences across seven articulatory positions, and ranks practice targets with a heuristic. On 13 speakers from the `Mandarin Dysarthria Speech Corpus`, the system's syllable-level accuracy showed a **Pearson correlation of 0.908 with expert intelligibility ratings**, and its priority targets overlapped 86.7 percent with the consensus of three blinded speech-language pathologists. A single-session pilot with 15 children reported mean pre/post gains of 14.4, 29.4, and 27.7 percentage points for mild, moderate, and severe groups.

papers.title: RAW: Refusal Aversion in the Wild, A Causal Measurement Method for Deployed LLMs
papers.abstract: Deployed LLMs field hundreds of millions of conversations a day and refuse a non-trivial fraction of user requests, yet the user-side cost of refusal, whether users disengage and by how much, is unmeasured on any production model: a blind spot for the consumer-facing platforms built on them. A/B-testing refusal is ethically and operationally constrained on frontier-lab products and unavailable to third-party platforms deploying these models through a fixed API. We introduce RAW, a method that uses LLM stochasticity as a natural experiment: at near-identical prompts in any existing log, the same model sometimes refuses and sometimes does not, and that variation identifies the causal user-side effect of refusal. Applying the method to 15 deployed LLMs in LMSYS-Chat-1M and WildChat, with user-clustered inference, we find that for about half of the models we can measure precisely, a refusal costs 3 to 17 pp of subsequent re-engagement; the rest show no distinguishable effect, among them one deployment whose positive point estimate we trace to persistent users retrying the refused request. Our contribution is the measurement method, which runs on any deployed model from logs alone for about \$0.30 per 1,000 conversations. We release labels, moderation scores, prompt embeddings, and pipeline code.
papers.summary: How much users disengage after a deployed LLM refuses a request has not been measured on production models, and A/B-testing refusals is constrained for labs and unavailable to third parties using a fixed API. `RAW` treats model stochasticity as a natural experiment: at near-identical prompts in existing logs the same model sometimes refuses and sometimes does not, which identifies the causal effect of refusal on the user. Applied to 15 deployed LLMs in `LMSYS-Chat-1M` and `WildChat`, it finds that for about half of the precisely measurable models **a refusal costs 3 to 17 percentage points of subsequent re-engagement**, while the rest show no distinguishable effect. The method runs from logs alone at about $0.30 per 1,000 conversations, and the labels, embeddings, and pipeline code are released.

papers.title: Sleep2Word: Peripheral-to-EEG Translation via Duration-Aware Wordization
papers.abstract: Estimating full-night electroencephalography (EEG) spectrograms from peripheral measurements could extend EEG-informed sleep analysis to recordings acquired without EEG. This task requires compact representations of signals with different temporal structures. We introduce Sleep2Word, a framework for translating respiration, electrocardiography (ECG), or photoplethysmography (PPG) into EEG spectrograms through duration-aware physiological words. Building on context-dependent chunking, Sleep2Word groups physiological embeddings into variable-duration chunks and jointly quantizes their content and duration into modality-specific wordbooks. A block-autoregressive translator then predicts target EEG word identities and occurrence-specific duration refinements within fixed-duration blocks. This design accommodates independent source and target wordbooks, limits temporal drift, and shortens the autoregressive decoding path. Trained on over 20K PSG cases across 9 datasets, Sleep2Word consistently outperforms existing spectrogram generation baselines in EEG spectrogram reconstruction, sleep staging, arousal detection, and survival prediction. Compressing full night sequences by up to 69.7%, the learned words yield a favorable accuracy-compute trade-off. Sleep event analysis further shows that the learned words capture physiologically plausible associations across modalities, suggesting their potential for interpretable cross-modal analysis.
papers.summary: Estimating full-night electroencephalography (EEG) spectrograms from peripheral signals would extend EEG-informed sleep analysis to recordings made without EEG. `Sleep2Word` translates respiration, electrocardiography (ECG), or photoplethysmography (PPG) into EEG spectrograms by grouping physiological embeddings into variable-duration chunks, quantizing content and duration into modality-specific wordbooks, and predicting target EEG words with a block-autoregressive translator. Trained on more than 20K cases across 9 datasets, it outperforms existing spectrogram generation baselines on reconstruction, sleep staging, arousal detection, and survival prediction while **compressing full-night sequences by up to 69.7%**.

papers.title: MInfoVisQA: A Multilingual Benchmark for Information-Rich Visual Question Answering
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) excel in vision-language tasks; yet, whether they maintain consistent understanding of information-rich visuals (InfoVis) when the surface language changes remains unclear. To quantify this capability, we introduce MInfoVisQA, a parallel benchmark with 8,960 QA configurations derived from 128 seed instances across 24 languages. We construct seed-matched, language-parallel visuals and QA pairs by disentangling numerical-structural data from text and programmatically synchronizing translated labels. We evaluate 25 MLLMs under two settings: Language-Aligned QA (LQA, matching visual-text languages) and Cross-Language QA (XQA, fixed QA language with varying visual languages). The results show that aggregate accuracy masks substantial robustness gaps: two models with comparable mean LQA accuracy (80.4\%) exhibit performance spreads of 7.8 and 20.3 percentage points across languages. Moreover, all 25 models score lower with non-English visuals under fixed English QA, underscoring the need for cross-language sensitivity metrics.
papers.summary: Whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) understand charts and other information-rich visuals consistently when the language of the visual changes is unclear. `MInfoVisQA` is a parallel benchmark of 8,960 question-answer configurations built from 128 seed instances across 24 languages, with translated labels synchronized programmatically so that the underlying data stays identical. Testing 25 MLLMs with matched visual and question languages (LQA) and with a fixed question language over varying visual languages (XQA) shows that average accuracy hides robustness gaps: two models with the same 80.4% mean LQA accuracy differ in cross-language spread, 7.8 versus 20.3 percentage points. In addition, **all 25 models score lower on non-English visuals when questions stay in English**.

papers.title: Asking What Matters: Disagreement-Guided Ambiguity Detection for Interactive Text-to-SQL
papers.abstract: Interactive text-to-SQL requires an LLM agent not only to generate executable SQL, but also to decide which uncertainty to clarify within a limited interaction budget. However, current clarification policies have three limitations: (i) they target surface ambiguity without testing its SQL impact; (ii) they miss ambiguities implicit in schema routes or domain knowledge; and (iii) they spend limited turns on unfocused or redundant questions. These limitations expose a critical challenge: identifying SQL-impacting ambiguity before the intended SQL is known. In this paper, we propose DisGuAD, a Disagreement-Guided Ambiguity Detection framework that specializes clarification selection. DisGuAD treats disagreement among plausible SQL interpretations as direct evidence of which uncertainty matters to the final query. Specifically, it constructs a query-term inventory, elicits contrastive SQL interpretations through complementary probe families, compares their canonical SQL components, and attributes recurring differences to user-facing clarification targets. A lightweight prioritization and dialogue-state mechanism then selects one high-impact unresolved target for clarification. Experiments on BIRD-Interact Lite and Full with two LLM backbones demonstrate consistent improvements in task success and clarification quality. Compared with the original interaction policy, DisGuAD improves normalized Reward by 4.40--8.97 points and raises overall critical-ambiguity coverage from 48.62% to 82.75% and from 45.76% to 85.14%. Its clarification signals further improve two independently designed static text-to-SQL frameworks by up to 13.97 Reward points while keeping their SQL generators fixed. These results demonstrate that disagreement among plausible SQL queries provides actionable evidence for selecting clarification targets that matter to downstream generation.
papers.summary: In interactive text-to-SQL, an LLM agent has a limited budget of clarifying questions, and current policies tend to ask about surface ambiguity that may not change the query, miss ambiguity hidden in schema routes or domain knowledge, and repeat themselves. `DisGuAD` generates several contrasting SQL interpretations of a request, compares their canonical components, and treats recurring disagreements as evidence of which ambiguity actually affects the final query, then asks about one high-impact unresolved target per turn. On `BIRD-Interact` Lite and Full with two LLM backbones, it improves normalized reward by 4.40-8.97 points over the original interaction policy and **raises critical-ambiguity coverage from 48.62% to 82.75% and from 45.76% to 85.14%**. Its clarification signals also improve two static text-to-SQL frameworks by up to 13.97 reward points without changing their SQL generators.

papers.title: Limite 1B - Violetto: Technical Report
papers.abstract: We present Limite 1B - Violetto, a one-billion-parameter model designed for high-throughput mathematical reasoning. Limite is trained from scratch on 237 billion tokens from a carefully curated, mathematics-centric corpus and supports context lengths of up to 131k tokens. Its architecture and training recipe were developed together to maximize reasoning capability while keeping training and inference costs low. Post-training combines knowledge distillation, targeted supervised fine-tuning, and RLVR on a curated curriculum. Limite achieves 94.01% on AIME 2026 and 74.25% on BeyondAIME, placing it among models many times its size on our evaluation suite. The model is deliberately only lightly instruction-tuned: it is intended primarily as a single-turn mathematical solver and as a fast, parallel component of larger systems, rather than as a general-purpose assistant. We release the model, its base and value checkpoints, and an optimized serving implementation under the Apache 2.0 license.
papers.summary: `Limite 1B - Violetto` is a one-billion-parameter model built for high-throughput mathematical reasoning, trained from scratch on 237 billion tokens of a mathematics-centric corpus with context lengths up to 131k tokens. Post-training combines knowledge distillation, targeted supervised fine-tuning, and RLVR on a curated curriculum. It scores **94.01% on `AIME 2026` and 74.25% on `BeyondAIME`**, which the authors report places it among models many times its size on their evaluation suite. The model is only lightly instruction-tuned and intended as a single-turn solver or a fast parallel component of larger systems; weights, base and value checkpoints, and a serving implementation are released under Apache 2.0.

papers.title: FieldGuide: A Corpus Map for Token-Efficient Agentic Document Exploration
papers.abstract: Generative AI agents can help journalists explore large document collections. But exploratory workflows can require substantial token use and time, especially when the task is broad and the relevant subquestions are not yet known. This paper introduces FieldGuide, an agent-facing corpus map that organizes a document collection into a topic hierarchy and exposes tools for corpus orientation, scoped search, and bounded reading. I evaluate FieldGuide on five journalistic document-exploration tasks using 38 Chicago Police Department public-records documents, comparing it with raw-file access and retrieval-augmented generation. Across the five tasks, FieldGuide used 27% fewer tokens and 41% less elapsed time than raw-file access; relative to RAG, it used 38% fewer tokens and 21% less elapsed time. An accuracy audit identified four minor issues in FieldGuide's responses, comparable to the other conditions. In blind ratings of generated reporting leads, FieldGuide's mean ratings were higher than RAG's and lower than the raw-file condition's. These descriptive results suggest that corpus orientation may reduce runtime token use and elapsed time without severe accuracy failures. They also motivate further study of whether selective access limits broad, cross-document discovery.
papers.summary: Agents exploring large document collections for journalists can spend many tokens and much time when the task is broad and the relevant subquestions are not yet known. `FieldGuide` gives the agent a corpus map that organizes the documents into a topic hierarchy, with tools for orientation, scoped search, and bounded reading. On five exploration tasks over 38 Chicago Police Department public-records documents, it used **27% fewer tokens and 41% less elapsed time than raw-file access**, and 38% fewer tokens and 21% less time than retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). An accuracy audit found four minor issues, comparable to the other conditions, while blind ratings of the generated reporting leads placed it above RAG but below raw-file access.

papers.title: Can an LLM dream? Testing the overfitted brain hypothesis on an agent with text memory
papers.abstract: Hoel (2021) proposed that dreams distort replayed experience so that the brain does not overfit to recent events. We test this hypothesis on an LLM agent (Claude Opus 5.5) that stores what it learns in a text memory and rewrites that memory each night from the day's conversation transcript. The agent goes through ten simulated days of conversation built from LongMemEval. We corrupt 5, 10, 20 or 40 percent of the transcript's turns before each nightly rewrite in one of two ways. Detail corruption changes one or two details in a turn to plausible wrong ones, or replaces the turn with one by the same speaker from an earlier day. Random-text corruption replaces half of the selected turns with a passage of Moby-Dick and inserts Moby-Dick words into the other half. A size limit on the memory, rising from 19,500 to 117,000 tokens over ten nights, set from human free-recall data, forces it to forget. We learned that corruption did not help the agent apply what it learned in earlier conversations to new tasks in any of 30 runs (ten conditions, three different conversation histories). Replacing details in 40 percent of turns lowered recall from 76 to 60 percent. Random text had no consistent effect on recall, with a paired difference of 0 $\pm$ 2 points at 40 percent, because the model recognized it as corrupted and left it out of memory. Replaced details were stored as fact even when another turn held the correct value, and the agent answered 40 percent of those questions correctly, compared with 75 percent without corruption. These results suggest that a pretrained model can separate corrupted text from real events, so a fair test needs a learner that cannot make this separation as easily, such as a model fine-tuned on the corrupted days or an agent whose days take place in an invented world.
papers.summary: Hoel's overfitted brain hypothesis holds that dreams distort replayed experience to prevent overfitting to recent events. The authors test it on a `Claude Opus 5.5` agent that rewrites a size-limited text memory each night from the day's transcript, across ten simulated days built from `LongMemEval`, corrupting 5 to 40 percent of turns with either plausible wrong details or random `Moby-Dick` text before each rewrite. **Corruption did not improve the agent's transfer of earlier learning to new tasks in any of 30 runs**; replacing details in 40 percent of turns lowered recall from 76 to 60 percent, while random text had no consistent effect because the model recognized it and left it out. Wrong details were stored as fact even when another turn held the correct value, and the authors conclude a fair test needs a learner that cannot separate corrupted text from real events so easily.

papers.title: Literary Language Mashup: Curating Fictions with Large Language Models
papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose an alternative approach to human evaluation of literary fictions by employing LLMs themselves as evaluators within the GrAImes framework. We apply this methodology to assess human-written and AI-generated microfictions in Spanish, to five PhD professors in literature and sixteen literary enthusiasts, and to short stories in both Spanish and English. By comparing the evaluations performed by LLMs with those of human judges, we examine the degree of alignment and divergence between both perspectives, thereby assessing the feasibility of LLMs as auxiliary literary evaluators. Our analysis focuses on the alignment of responses from LLMs with those of human evaluators, providing insights into the potential of LLMs in literary assessment. The conducted experiments reveal that while LLMs cannot be regarded as substitutes for human judges in the evaluation of literary microfictions and short stories, with a Krippendorff's alpha reliability coefficient less than 0.66, they can serve as a valuable tool that offers an initial perspective on the editorial quality of the texts in question. Overall, this study contributes to the ongoing discourse on the role of artificial intelligence in literature, underlining both its methodological constraints and its potential as a complementary resource for literary evaluation.
papers.summary: Whether LLMs can stand in for human judges of literary fiction is tested by having LLMs evaluate texts within the `GrAImes` framework. Human-written and AI-generated microfictions in Spanish, along with short stories in Spanish and English, are assessed by LLMs and compared with ratings from five literature professors and sixteen literary enthusiasts. Agreement is limited, with **Krippendorff's alpha below 0.66**, so the authors conclude LLMs cannot replace human judges but can give an initial view of a text's editorial quality.

papers.title: From Preference Data to Personalization: Tracing Sycophancy in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Sycophancy in large language models is often measured as agreement with the user, yet agreement can be appropriate when the user's claim is valid, their preference is genuine, or their experience warrants acknowledgment. We study sycophancy as inappropriate agreement: validating a claim, preference, or self-assessment when the context calls for correction, qualification, or resistance. We introduce a validity-aware sycophancy grader and SycoDrift, a persona-targeted evaluation set of 3,298 validity-annotated probes with controlled annotations for user openness and stakes. We use this framework to analyze three sources of agreement pressure: human preference data, automated judge specification, and in-context personalization. First, preference for validating responses in human datasets (Chatbot Arena, HH-RLHF, Community Alignment) is weak and concentrated where agreement is often appropriate. Second, in a selected-value, single-model experiment, emphasized judge rubrics produce consistent but modest increases relative to paired suppressed rubrics, demonstrating a plausible mechanism for training-time amplification. Third, in off-policy evaluations across 14 models, inference-time personalization increases inappropriate agreement, with the largest effect from matched user profiles placed directly before the query.
papers.summary: Sycophancy is usually measured as agreement with the user, but agreement is sometimes appropriate, so the authors define it as inappropriate agreement: validating a claim, preference, or self-assessment when the context calls for correction or resistance. They introduce a validity-aware grader and `SycoDrift`, a set of 3,298 validity-annotated probes with controlled user openness and stakes, and use them to examine three sources of agreement pressure. Human preference data (`Chatbot Arena`, `HH-RLHF`, `Community Alignment`) shows only a weak preference for validating responses, concentrated where agreement is often appropriate, and judge rubrics that emphasize validation produce consistent but modest increases in a single-model experiment. Across 14 models, **inference-time personalization increases inappropriate agreement, most strongly when a matched user profile sits directly before the query**.

papers.title: Consistency Is Not Correction: Separating Confidence, Abstention, and Recovery in LLM Agents
papers.abstract: A controller that resamples an answer, escalates to a larger model, or abstains is usually justified by a confidence signal. Three claims about such a signal do not follow from one another: it ranks answers (discrimination), it supports withholding some of them (selective prediction), and it changes an answer for the better (correction utility). We give an exact decomposition of the third into gated recoveries minus gated harms, which bounds whether a comparison can succeed before it is run: a gate that only replaces a proposal can act only where the base policy was already wrong, so the initial error count caps the discordant pairs any correct gate can produce. When that cap falls below the count a paired test needs, the experiment cannot return a positive result for a working mechanism, nor distinguish one from a gate that never fired. We measure all three targets on two model scales and find the bound binds. In a small-model suite a perturbation-agreement verifier reaches within-policy AUROC 0.990 (95% interval [0.95, 1.00]) while every episode outcome matches single-sample decoding at 4.32 times the call count. In a controlled 840-episode study no verifier replaced the proposal on any of the 60 GSM8K decisions, so that comparison tested nothing; the entire GSM8K gain across six controllers is one task, and it is the task whose identical temperature-zero repeats disagreed, making it the one answer the service does not reproduce. On the diagnostic set the gate could reach four errors while the test needed six, so even a perfect gate had no significant result available. We report two checks that would have caught this before any budget was spent, and show that tie handling in rankings, tied selection cutoffs, and unequal output limits each move a headline number in the same dataset. The binding constraint on this literature is measurement resolution, not the choice of signal.
papers.summary: Agent controllers that resample, escalate to a larger model, or abstain rely on a confidence signal, but ranking answers well, supporting abstention, and actually improving answers are three separate claims. The authors decompose correction utility exactly into gated recoveries minus gated harms, which shows that the base policy's initial error count caps how many outcomes any gate can change and therefore whether an experiment can detect an effect at all. In a small-model suite, **a perturbation-agreement verifier reached AUROC 0.990 while every episode outcome matched single-sample decoding at 4.32 times the call count**, and in an 840-episode study no verifier replaced a proposal on any of the 60 `GSM8K` decisions. They offer two checks that would flag such underpowered comparisons before budget is spent and show that tie handling and unequal output limits each shift headline numbers.

papers.title: Evaluating Semantic Insensitivity in Financial Sentiment Analysis: Implications for Sustainable Financial Decision-Making
papers.abstract: Financial sentiment analysis is critical for automated trading, portfolio management, and risk assessment, heavily relying on models like FinBERT. Despite high benchmark accuracy, these models remain vulnerable to subtle adversarial text modifications, threatening the integrity of algorithmic decision-making. In this paper, we propose Agent-driven Semantic Inversion (ASI), a novel adversarial attack framework targeting financial sentiment models through domain-specific semantic manipulation. Utilizing an LLM-powered multi-agent pipeline, our approach identifies eligible financial news sentences and applies targeted lexical substitutions. We empirically evaluate ASI against FinBERT, one of the most widely deployed financial sentiment models. Our results reveal a striking vulnerability: the attack successfully deceived FinBERT in 90.85% of eligible cases, with the model frequently maintaining its original sentiment prediction despite the fundamental inversion of financial performance indicators. Through qualitative analysis and token-level investigation, we demonstrate that FinBERT critically over-relies on contextual keywords and syntactic patterns rather than true logical comprehension of financial semantics. Our findings highlight the urgent need for logic-aware, robust financial NLP models to ensure the reliability of automated decision-making systems.
papers.summary: Financial sentiment models such as `FinBERT` feed automated trading and risk assessment, yet may be vulnerable to subtle adversarial edits to text. Agent-driven Semantic Inversion (`ASI`) uses an LLM-powered multi-agent pipeline to pick eligible financial news sentences and apply targeted lexical substitutions that invert the reported financial performance. The attack **deceived `FinBERT` in 90.85% of eligible cases**, with the model frequently keeping its original sentiment prediction despite the inverted meaning. Token-level analysis indicates that it over-relies on contextual keywords and syntactic patterns rather than the logic of the financial statement.

papers.title: Depth-Aware Activation Steering via Attention Residuals
papers.abstract: Activation steering is a simple, training-free way to modulate LLM behavior, yet existing methods typically inject vectors at a single layer and lack mechanisms for depth-aware propagation or internal verification. We combine two recent ideas - Attention Residuals (AttnRes) providing learnable cross-layer pathways, and Jacobian-lens (J-space) concept readout - into a lightweight depth-aware steering pipeline. On two small open models (Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3.5-0.8B), distributing a persona vector according to AttnRes-style depth weights yields stronger internal alignment (deeper-layer concept cosine and rank, p<0.0001) and stronger behavioral shifts than single-layer injection. The effect is sign-specific: reverse vectors invert all six metrics, random directions degrade alignment (p<0.0001), and a short LoRA fine-tune erases the imprint. Injection rewires attention strictly downstream of the injection point (upstream JS = 0.00000). Three practical findings follow. First, a layer-wise geometric decomposition of cosine readouts: at the injection layer 123% of the increase is arithmetic, while 5-11 layers downstream 100% is dynamical. Second, an intensity window: effects are monotone over 0.3-0.7, then generation collapses (617 to 306 to 25 chars). Third, metric discipline: keyword-rule metrics fail LLM-judge validation (kappa <= 0.09), and two rule-based conclusions were retracted. Training the depth weights on a steering objective (200 steps, frozen backbone) raises final alignment 10x on held-out prompts. Cross-persona vectors retain 96-99% of the effect: specificity holds against random, not semantic, directions. We contribute a practical, low-overhead depth-aware steering method with a careful evaluation protocol. Code and data are released.
papers.summary: Activation steering usually injects a vector at a single layer, with no mechanism for spreading it across depth or checking its internal effect. The authors distribute a persona vector across layers using Attention Residuals (`AttnRes`) style depth weights and verify it with a Jacobian-lens (`J-space`) concept readout on `Qwen3-0.6B` and `Qwen3.5-0.8B`, obtaining stronger internal alignment and behavioral shifts than single-layer injection. Training the depth weights for 200 steps on a frozen backbone **raises final alignment 10x on held-out prompts**, while generation collapses above an intensity of about 0.7. Keyword-rule metrics failed LLM-judge validation (kappa at most 0.09), and cross-persona vectors retained 96-99% of the effect, so specificity holds against random but not semantically related directions.

papers.title: Token Commitment as a Control Surface for Steering Masked Diffusion Generation
papers.abstract: Masked diffusion models repeatedly predict provisional tokens before a sampler decides which predictions become permanent. Existing inference-time steering methods primarily modify activations, logits, or denoising trajectories, while treating this commitment policy as a fixed decoding detail. We instead study token commitment as a diffusion-specific control surface and separate it into two decisions: which tokens to commit and how many tokens to commit at each step. For the first, we introduce counterfactual target-aware commitment, which ranks unresolved positions by a mixture of model confidence and leave-one-token-out target contribution. For the second, we introduce calibrated adaptive budgets driven by target progress and confidence. Across language and vision-language settings in the LLaDA family, multiple targets, two activation-steering methods, and an unsteered control, both mechanisms yield empirically monotonic target-quality trade-offs in every configuration we evaluate. Adaptive schedules also recover competitive operating points relative to scorer-free stochastic schedules matched in average denoising cost. Because both mechanisms require only a scalar score evaluated on a provisional completion, they apply unchanged when the target is an automatic proxy for task success rather than an output attribute: NLI entailment for dialogue summarization and CLIPScore for captioning, neither of which corresponds to a single reusable steering direction. We reproduce the behavior of both mechanisms on a second masked-diffusion family, Dream-7B, for one control target and one task-success target. These results characterize commitment--which provisional predictions become irreversible, and how rapidly--as an interpretable control surface for steering masked diffusion generation under the conditions we test.
papers.summary: Masked diffusion language models predict provisional tokens and a sampler then decides which become permanent, a step that steering methods normally treat as a fixed decoding detail. The authors turn this commitment policy into a control mechanism with two parts: counterfactual target-aware commitment, which ranks positions by model confidence mixed with leave-one-token-out target contribution, and calibrated adaptive budgets for how many tokens to commit per step. Across language and vision-language settings in the `LLaDA` family, **both mechanisms yield monotonic target-quality trade-offs in every configuration evaluated**, and the behavior is reproduced on `Dream-7B`. Because only a scalar score on a provisional completion is needed, the same mechanisms work with task-success proxies such as NLI entailment for summarization and `CLIPScore` for captioning.

papers.title: Improving Early Detection of Scientifically Interesting Radio Sources Using Enhanced Isolation Forest
papers.abstract: The rapid growth of radio astronomical surveys has created a major challenge in identifying scientifically interesting sources from large populations of observed objects. This study investigates whether enhanced Isolation Forest (iForest) methods can improve the early detection and ranking of scientifically interesting radio sources. Four iForest variants, Standard Enhanced, Pooled Gain, Kurtosis-based, and Hypervolume, are evaluated using 1,031 extended radio sources from the MeerKAT Galaxy Cluster Legacy Survey (MGCLS). Each source is represented by a 52-dimensional feature set derived using Bootstrap Your Own Latent (BYOL) self-supervised learning and principal component analysis (PCA), while expert scientific-interest ratings are used to define the ground-truth labels. The methods are evaluated using Average Precision (AP), receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC AUC), Precision@10, Precision@50, and cumulative anomaly detection. Pooled Gain achieves the highest Average Precision (AP = 0.201) and the strongest early-stage ranking performance (P@10 = 0.600), identifying six expert-validated anomalies among the ten highest-ranked sources. Standard Enhanced and Kurtosis-based achieve the highest ROC AUC (0.677), while the AUC values of the four variants range from 0.653 to 0.677. These results indicate that feature-aware isolation strategies can improve the prioritization of scientifically interesting sources at the top of the ranked list, although overall discrimination remains comparable across the evaluated variants. The findings support the use of enhanced Isolation Forest methods as an initial ranking mechanism within human-in-the-loop systems for large-scale radio astronomical surveys.
papers.summary: Large radio astronomy surveys produce more sources than experts can inspect, so the study tests whether enhanced Isolation Forest (`iForest`) variants can rank scientifically interesting ones near the top. Four variants (Standard Enhanced, Pooled Gain, Kurtosis-based, and Hypervolume) are evaluated on 1,031 extended sources from the MeerKAT Galaxy Cluster Legacy Survey (`MGCLS`), using 52-dimensional features from Bootstrap Your Own Latent (`BYOL`) self-supervised learning and principal component analysis, with expert ratings as ground truth. `Pooled Gain` gives the best early ranking, with **six expert-validated anomalies among its ten highest-ranked sources** and an Average Precision of 0.201. Overall discrimination is similar across variants, with ROC AUC between 0.653 and 0.677.

papers.title: RTLReviewBench: LLM Hardware Reviewers Rarely Miss Bugs but Routinely Reject Correct RTL
papers.abstract: Hardware teams increasingly ask large language models (LLMs) to review register-transfer level (RTL) code, yet it is unclear whether a model can tell a correct module from a buggy one without simulating it. We introduce RTLReviewBench, a benchmark of 114 matched pairs of buggy and correct Verilog modules. Each pair shares one specification, most buggy modules are real failures of LLM code generators, and every label is confirmed by simulation. Evaluating 12 commercial and open-weight models, we find a consistent asymmetry: reviewers rarely accept buggy code but often reject correct code, producing more than five false rejections for every missed bug. Synthetic mutants hide part of the problem: on the same designs, models miss far fewer injected bugs than real ones. Asking a model to reason before it commits to a verdict sharply reduces false rejections for weaker reviewers, and a controlled ablation shows that where the reasoning appears in the output matters more than the instruction to reason, whereas sampling and majority voting do not help. A blinded audit further shows that some correct "buggy" verdicts rest on false technical claims. We release the benchmark, a harder split for future models, all model responses, and the evaluation code at https://github.com/yasirmahmud/RTLReviewBench
papers.summary: Whether large language models (LLMs) can tell correct register-transfer level (RTL) hardware code from buggy code without simulating it is tested with `RTLReviewBench`, a benchmark of 114 matched pairs of buggy and correct Verilog modules sharing one specification, with every label confirmed by simulation. Across 12 commercial and open-weight models, reviewers rarely accept buggy code but often reject correct code, producing **more than five false rejections for every missed bug**. Models miss far fewer synthetic injected bugs than real ones on the same designs, and a blinded audit finds that some correct buggy verdicts rest on false technical claims. Having a model reason before committing to a verdict sharply reduces false rejections for weaker reviewers, with the position of the reasoning in the output mattering more than the instruction itself, whereas sampling and majority voting do not help.

papers.title: FCP: Formal Context Protocol for Verifying LLM-Generated Artifacts
papers.abstract: When a language model writes both an artifact and the tests meant to check it, a passing test is weak evidence: one misreading of the request yields a faulty artifact and a check that accepts it. We present the Formal Context Protocol (FCP), which checks AI-generated artifacts against the request itself. FCP separates conformance (does the artifact satisfy a formal reading of a requirement?), which model checkers and SMT solvers decide, from fidelity (does the reading mean what the prose means?), which has no decision procedure but is refutable by a concrete witness. Eight ways a proof can falsely certify a requirement each become a mechanical check that returns a witness, and what no machine can settle becomes concrete questions for the request's author. Adapters place hardware, text, agents and code on the same engines. On four hardware designs, trusting AI-written assertions certified 23% of violated requirements, and FCP certified none. On ten code tasks, code from three language models passed its own tests and violated the request every time. Trusting the tests certified all 33 violations, and FCP certified three. Agreement among models, readings or tests did not imply correctness.
papers.summary: When a language model writes both an artifact and its tests, one misreading of the request can produce a faulty artifact and a check that accepts it. The Formal Context Protocol (`FCP`) checks artifacts against the request itself, separating conformance to a formal reading of a requirement, decided by model checkers and SMT solvers, from fidelity of that reading to the prose, which is refutable by a concrete witness. Eight ways a proof can falsely certify a requirement become mechanical checks, and what no machine can settle is turned into questions for the request's author. On ten code tasks where code from three models passed its own tests yet violated the request every time, **trusting the tests certified all 33 violations while `FCP` certified three**; on four hardware designs, trusting AI-written assertions certified 23% of violated requirements and `FCP` certified none.

papers.title: Edge-Adaptive Hiera-Seg Model for Building-Integrated Photovoltaic Power Forecasting
papers.abstract: Building integrated photovoltaic power forecasting is challenging because facade orientation, rooftop geometry, nearby buildings, vegetation, cloud movement, module temperature, inverter status and edge device reliability jointly affect power generation. This paper proposes an edge-adaptive HieraSeg model for short term BIPV power forecasting with multi-orientation visual-irradiance fusion. RGB facade images, optional thermal cues, irradiance measurements, module temperature, facade orientation, rooftop masks, shading labels, sky condition, historical power and edge device state are aligned into synchronous forecasting windows. HieraSeg extracts hierarchical regions from facade, rooftop, sky, shadow and background images, while the edge-adaptive module changes feature weights under missing frames, latency shifts and local shading changes. The segmentation branch identifies occluded module areas and separates facade, rooftop, sky and background evidence before the forecasting head estimates future BIPV output. Experiments are designed on a simulated multibuilding BIPV dataset with unseen building and unseen orientation tests. The model reports predicted power, confidence interval, dominant evidence, occlusion contribution, orientation contribution and energy-management review priority. This output is intended to show whether the forecast is driven by irradiance change, visible shading, orientation response, stale edge information or recent power history. The framework supports local forecasting at edge controllers with limited communication delay and computing resources, linking visual occlusion, irradiance dynamics and power history to traceable forecasting results for building energy management, microgrid scheduling and BIPV operation planning.
papers.summary: Short-term power forecasting for building-integrated photovoltaics (BIPV) is complicated by facade orientation, shading from nearby structures, cloud movement, and unreliable edge devices. The proposed edge-adaptive `HieraSeg` model fuses facade images, irradiance, module temperature, orientation, and power history, segments occluded module areas, and reweights features under missing frames, latency shifts, and local shading changes. Its output pairs each power forecast with a confidence interval and an attribution of the dominant evidence, such as shading, orientation, or stale edge data. Experiments are **designed on a simulated multi-building dataset, and the abstract reports no quantitative results**.

papers.title: NEBench R1: a Reasoning Benchmark for Evaluating Nuclear Domain Competence in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being explored for knowledge-intensive and safety-critical applications in nuclear engineering. However, existing nuclear-domain benchmarks provide limited content coverage or focus primarily on answer accuracy without systematically evaluating the quality of the underlying reasoning. This study introduces NEBench R1, a reasoning-oriented benchmark comprising 7,546 unique multiple-choice questions extracted from U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) reactor operator licensing examinations covering 18 nuclear facilities. Each question is classified according to the NRC Knowledge and Abilities catalogs and accompanied by an official explanation serving as a reference for reasoning evaluation. Six LLMs were evaluated, with overall accuracy ranging from 34.0% to 73.9% across three distinct performance tiers. To assess reasoning quality, an LLM-based judge evaluated correctly answered responses using a multidimensional rubric. Although responses generally demonstrated strong problem comprehension, they scored lower in factual and procedural accuracy and distractor analysis, indicating that correct answers were not necessarily supported by technically sound justifications. Response clarity was also weakly indicative of technical quality. Furthermore, longer reasoning traces were associated with lower accuracy in both frontier reasoning models, suggesting that reasoning length may reflect question difficulty rather than improved problem-solving performance. Reasoning-token consumption may therefore provide an additional signal for identifying potentially unreliable responses. NEBench R1 establishes a benchmark for evaluating both answer accuracy and reasoning quality, providing a foundation for assessing the domain competence and reliability of LLMs in nuclear engineering.
papers.summary: `NEBench R1` evaluates large language models (LLMs) on nuclear engineering using 7,546 multiple-choice questions from U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) reactor operator licensing exams covering 18 facilities, each paired with an official explanation for judging reasoning. Six models reached **overall accuracy between 34.0% and 73.9%**, falling into three performance tiers. An LLM judge scoring correctly answered responses found strong problem comprehension but weaker factual and procedural accuracy and distractor analysis, so correct answers were not always backed by sound justifications. Longer reasoning traces were associated with lower accuracy in both frontier reasoning models, suggesting reasoning-token consumption could flag unreliable responses.

papers.title: DeltaHarness: Self-Evolving Harnesses for Resource-Adaptive Tool Execution
papers.abstract: Tool-using agents rely on execution harnesses to organize and schedule tool operations. The same task and resource description can conceal runtime conditions that reverse the latency ordering of valid execution plans. Resolving this uncertainty requires firsthand execution in the target setting. We introduce DeltaHarness, an execution-guided policy-search method that adapts agent harnesses from cold-start measurements. Its QHI loop uses the observed response to update runtime dispatch, revise physical plans, and select experiments for later proposals. An independent confirmation panel controls policy replacement. With fixed dispatch, a revised materialization policy reduces complete-delivery latency by 30.0% on one video-editing task across three fresh pairs. On held-out tasks, the evolved policies reduce latency by 8.2% relative to the best fixed plan in one seed and by 4.6% relative to the initial proposal in another.
papers.summary: Tool-using agents depend on execution harnesses to schedule tool operations, but runtime conditions not visible in the task or resource description can reverse which valid execution plan is fastest. `DeltaHarness` adapts the harness through execution-guided policy search from cold-start measurements: its `QHI` loop uses observed responses to update runtime dispatch, revise physical plans, and choose later experiments, while an independent confirmation panel controls policy replacement. With fixed dispatch, a revised materialization policy **reduces complete-delivery latency by 30.0% on one video-editing task** across three fresh pairs. On held-out tasks the evolved policies cut latency by 8.2% relative to the best fixed plan in one seed and by 4.6% relative to the initial proposal in another.

papers.title: EgoLink: Egocentric Language-Vision Interactive Network Knowledge Challenge Summary
papers.abstract: The EgoLink Challenge at ACM Multimedia 2026 benchmarks egocentric multimodal intelligence linking first-person perception, social reasoning, and interactive action. Unlike benchmarks centered on visible objects and activities, EgoLink evaluates whether models can interpret emotional and social cues, resolve visually grounded references, and convert user requests into verified tool-mediated actions. Its two tracks cover social reasoning in egocentric video and interactive agents that complete service tasks through dialogue, tool use, and closed-loop execution. Together, they test whether perception, reasoning, and decision-making remain coupled under both offline question answering and state-changing interaction. We highlight a multi-stage Track 1 data pipeline for multiple-choice question (MCQ) generation, chain-of-thought generation, automatic quality grading, and video-contribution filtering. We summarize the task design, evaluation metrics, rules, leaderboards, and representative solutions. The benchmark combines objective answer scoring with process- and result-based evaluation, enabling analysis of both final correctness and execution quality. The best Track 1 system achieved 0.9263 accuracy, while the best Track 2 system achieved 0.844 joint success and 0.916 micro accuracy. Participant reports reveal a shared principle: strong systems make intermediate evidence explicit through candidate verification, option-robust reasoning, scenario-aware planning, tool canonicalization, and state-aware correction before answering or acting. These findings highlight the importance of process verification and evidence-grounded reasoning for reliable egocentric multimodal intelligence.
papers.summary: The `EgoLink` Challenge at ACM Multimedia 2026 benchmarks first-person multimodal systems on two tracks: social and emotional reasoning over egocentric video, and interactive agents that complete service tasks through dialogue, tool use, and closed-loop execution. The summary covers the task design, a multi-stage pipeline for generating and filtering multiple-choice questions, the metrics, the leaderboards, and representative solutions. The best Track 1 system reached 0.9263 accuracy, and the best Track 2 system reached **0.844 joint success** with 0.916 micro accuracy. Top entries shared a pattern of making intermediate evidence explicit through candidate verification, scenario-aware planning, tool canonicalization, and state-aware correction before answering or acting.

papers.title: AdaFlowLite: Scalable and Non-blocking Inference on Asynchronous Mobile Data
papers.abstract:
The rise of mobile devices equipped with numerous sensors, such as LiDAR and cameras, has driven the adoption of multi-modal deep intelligence for distributed sensing tasks, such as smart cabins and driving assistance. However, the arrival time of mobile sensory data vary due to modality size and network dynamics, which can lead to delays (if waiting for slow data) or accuracy decline (if inference proceeds without waiting). Moreover, the diversity and dynamic nature of mobile systems exacerbate this challenge. In response, we present a shift to \textit{opportunistic} inference for asynchronous distributed multi-modal data, enabling inference as soon as partial data arrives. While existing methods focus on optimizing modality consistency and complementarity, known as modal affinity, they lack a \textit{computational} approach to control this affinity in open-world mobile environments. %
\sysname pioneers the formulation of structured cross-modality affinity in mobile contexts using a hierarchical analysis-based normalized matrix. This approach accommodates the diversity and dynamics of modalities, generalizing across different types and numbers of inputs. Employing an multi-modal lightweight Swin Transformer (MMLST), \sysname facilitates real-time and flexible data imputation, adapting to various modalities and downstream tasks without retraining. Experiments show that \sysname significantly reduces inference latency by up to 80.4\% and enhances accuracy by up to 62.1\%, while achieving nearly a 50\% reduction in energy consumption, outperforming status quo approaches. Also, this method can enhance LLM performance to preprocess asynchronous data.
papers.summary: Multi-modal sensor data on mobile systems arrives at different times, forcing a choice between waiting for slow modalities and running inference with missing inputs at lower accuracy. `AdaFlowLite` takes an opportunistic approach, running inference as soon as partial data arrives by modeling cross-modality affinity with a hierarchical analysis-based normalized matrix and imputing missing data with a multi-modal lightweight Swin Transformer (`MMLST`), without retraining for new modalities or tasks. Experiments report **inference latency reduced by up to 80.4%**, accuracy improved by up to 62.1%, and energy consumption cut by nearly 50% compared with existing approaches.

papers.title: TIBECG: Temporal Information Bottleneck for Lead-Specific Demographic Privacy in ECG Waveform Release
papers.abstract: Transmitting an electrocardiogram (ECG) waveform can expose demographic information beyond an intended diagnostic task. We evaluate TIBECG, an architectural temporal information bottleneck, on individual leads extracted from hospital twelve-lead recordings. A 2,302,337-parameter processor varies its latent length while retaining the same nine-score consistency objective, without age or sex labels in protector fitting. Across 6,386 recordings, ten folds, 12 leads and 21 lengths, retrospective selections retained at least 95% of each lead's clean macro-F1. Their weaker age/sex interval gain exceeded the best eligible conventional transformation on all leads, by a median 22.08 percentage points. The implemented sampling-rate comparison shows that direct downsampling usually suppresses demographic inference more strongly but at a larger loss of diagnostic utility, whereas TIBECG favors utility preservation. Selection stability also varies by lead. Lower latent Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence does not reliably rank residual sex leakage at a fixed length. These findings support lead-specific evaluation of waveform processing, not validated consumer deployment or expert-readable reconstruction. When the waveform-input diagnostic classifier is hosted as part of a proprietary cloud service rather than deployed on the device, waveform transmission is required to obtain its scores.
authors: Tsai-Min Chen (Research Center for Information Technology Innovation
RIKEN Center for Interdisciplinary Theoretical and Mathematical Sciences)
Jun Seita (RIKEN Center for Interdisciplinary Theoretical and Mathematical Sciences)
papers.summary: Sending an electrocardiogram (ECG) waveform to a diagnostic service can also reveal the patient's age and sex. `TIBECG` is an architectural temporal information bottleneck that varies its latent length while keeping a diagnostic consistency objective, fitted without age or sex labels and evaluated per lead on 6,386 hospital twelve-lead recordings. Selected configurations retained at least 95% of each lead's clean macro-F1, and their reduction in demographic inference **exceeded the best eligible conventional transformation on all leads by a median 22.08 percentage points**. Direct downsampling usually suppresses demographic inference more strongly but at a larger cost in diagnostic utility, and the authors frame the results as support for lead-specific evaluation, not validated deployment.

papers.title: Stop Early, Stay Simple: Evidence Acquisition for Power System Fault and Attack Diagnosis
papers.abstract: Diagnostic models for cyber-physical power systems usually inspect every telemetry source for every event, although some events are clear from one source and others need several. We ask when a learned policy for choosing that evidence is worth its added complexity. To answer this, we present ActiGrid, a benchmark framework for active evidence acquisition that pairs a classifier trained to tolerate missing modalities with a Double Deep Q-Network (DQN), which either requests another source or stops and diagnoses but never operates grid actuators. On the public TU Delft digital substation and MSU/ORNL power system attack benchmarks, we compare the DQN with fixed subsets and orders, calibrated entropy stopping, a greedy value of information rule, and tree ensembles trained per subset. The learned policy does adapt to what it observes, yet it is statistically indistinguishable from entropy stopping on TU Delft and Pareto dominated by simple controls on MSU/ORNL, while compact subset classifiers outperform it while reading fewer sources on both benchmarks. Entropy stopping run over those subset classifiers reaches the highest mean Macro-F1 on TU Delft (0.928 while reading 57% of the sources) but brings no saving over a static three source subset on MSU/ORNL, where no method exceeds 0.45 Macro-F1. Selective acquisition can pay off, but on these benchmarks it does not need a learned policy.
papers.summary: Diagnostic models for power-system faults and cyberattacks usually read every telemetry source for every event, although some events are clear from a single source. `ActiGrid` is a benchmark framework that pairs a classifier tolerant of missing modalities with a Double Deep Q-Network (DQN) that either requests another source or stops and diagnoses, compared against fixed subsets, calibrated entropy stopping, a greedy value-of-information rule, and per-subset tree ensembles on the TU Delft digital substation and MSU/ORNL attack benchmarks. The learned policy is statistically indistinguishable from entropy stopping on TU Delft and Pareto dominated by simple controls on MSU/ORNL, and **compact subset classifiers outperform it while reading fewer sources on both benchmarks**. Entropy stopping over those subset classifiers reaches 0.928 Macro-F1 on TU Delft while reading 57% of the sources, whereas no method exceeds 0.45 on MSU/ORNL.

papers.title: Layerwise Learning-Rate Scaling in Vision Networks: Effective-Rate Identification, Power-Mean Aggregation, and Budget Dependence
papers.abstract: Layerwise learning-rate scaling assigns different learning rates to different parts of a network. Although established in fine-tuning pretrained models, its effects in vision networks trained from scratch are commonly assessed by training each candidate recipe. We show that, in this setting, the rate-related component of a layerwise strategy is well summarized by an effective learning rate computable directly from its multiplier profile. Across matched-control comparisons, changes in test accuracy closely track changes in training loss (r = -0.996), which supports an optimization-progress explanation of the short-budget rate effect. Increasing the untuned base learning rate tenfold shifts the rate-matched contrast upward in all six tested architectures (p = 0.016) and increases the number of architectures in which a published discriminative schedule, excluded from model fitting, outperforms the uniform control from two to five of six (p = 0.031). Within the evaluated strategy space, a parameter-weighted power mean with exponent 0.35 (95% confidence interval [0.20, 0.50]) accounts for 42.6% of within-architecture variance, compared with 36.4% for the arithmetic mean. Ranking candidates by this scalar without training improves the selected candidate's mean percentile rank from the 26th to the 10th and reduces its mean accuracy shortfall relative to the best candidate from 3.70 to 1.12 points. The rate-related effect decays as the training budget increases; relative to tuned baselines, the overall strategy effect falls within the prespecified practical-equivalence margin in two of three architectures. A separate grouping-related contrast can persist at long budgets, although its direction and magnitude depend on the architecture.
papers.summary: Layerwise learning-rate scaling in vision networks trained from scratch is usually assessed by training every candidate recipe. The authors show that the rate-related part of a layerwise strategy is well summarized by an effective learning rate computed directly from its multiplier profile, with a parameter-weighted power mean of exponent 0.35 explaining 42.6% of within-architecture variance against 36.4% for the arithmetic mean. Ranking candidates by this scalar without training **cuts the selected candidate's mean accuracy shortfall from 3.70 to 1.12 points**. The rate-related effect decays as the training budget grows, and relative to tuned baselines the overall effect falls within a practical-equivalence margin in two of three architectures.

papers.title: FACE: Flow-Guided Angular Channel Estimation Framework for mmWave MIMO Systems
papers.abstract: Acquiring accurate channel state information (CSI) is essential for millimeter-wave (mmWave) multi-input multi-output (MIMO) systems. However, it remains challenging due to high-dimensional channels, limited pilot observations, and measurement noise.
