Examining the learned edge-weight function directly, together with clustering-validity metrics, edge-distance ratios, and a layer-depth ablation across four depths, we find evidence for an alternative account: curvature-weighting sharpens the separation between clusters, which improves intra-cluster predictions at the cost of inter-cluster (bottleneck) ones. We test this account against topologically defined communities rather than the classification labels used elsewhere. Additionally, we offer practical guidance on when to prefer CGCN over standard GCN, depending on whether intra- or inter-cluster predictions matter most.
papers.summary: Curvature-enhanced graph convolutional networks (`CGCN`) add Ollivier-Ricci curvature (ORC) to message passing on the premise that curvature-weighted edges relieve over-squashing at structural bottlenecks. The authors test that premise on four protein-protein interaction (PPI) datasets by comparing `CGCN` with a standard `GCN` edge by edge rather than only through aggregate metrics. `CGCN` improves aggregate AUC, AUPR, and F1 on all four datasets, but **the gain is concentrated on low-degree edges while performance on low-curvature bottleneck edges degrades in three of four datasets**, the opposite of what the over-squashing account predicts. Analysis of the learned edge-weight function, clustering metrics, and a depth ablation supports an alternative explanation in which curvature weighting sharpens cluster separation, helping intra-cluster predictions at the expense of inter-cluster ones.

papers.title: AR-WAM: efficient streaming world-action modeling for autonomous driving
papers.abstract: Autonomous driving requires anticipating how traffic will evolve while responding quickly to new observations. Video foundation models offer the first ability, but repeated history encoding and iterative video generation make them costly to use for driving. We present AR-WAM, an efficient streaming world-action model that combines autoregressive temporal modeling with single-pass future conditioning. Because its video backbone is causal, AR-WAM updates its visual context incrementally, reusing past computation and conditioning future prediction on observed motion. We further hypothesize that future features computed from recent observations can improve generalization in dynamic traffic without iterative video generation. AR-WAM therefore obtains these features in one forward pass and uses them to condition trajectory generation, and reinforcement learning then improves the policy through direct optimization of driving rewards. With a single front camera, AR-WAM achieves 91.5 PDMS after supervised training and 94.0 after reinforcement learning on NAVSIM-v1, outperforming the compared strong end-to-end world-action models. In a dynamic setting of continuous driving, supervised AR-WAM keeps its visual history across decisions and outperforms strong world-action baselines.
papers.summary: Video foundation models can anticipate how traffic will evolve, but repeated history encoding and iterative video generation make them expensive for driving. `AR-WAM` is a streaming world-action model with a causal video backbone that updates its visual context incrementally, reuses past computation, and computes future features in a single forward pass to condition trajectory generation, with reinforcement learning then optimizing driving rewards directly. Using a single front camera, it scores **91.5 PDMS after supervised training and 94.0 after reinforcement learning on `NAVSIM-v1`**, ahead of the end-to-end world-action models it is compared with. In a continuous-driving setting where visual history is kept across decisions, the supervised model also outperforms those baselines.

papers.title: The Hidden Cost of MoE Diffusion Decoding: Profiling and Fixing the Sampler
papers.abstract: Masked diffusion language models (dLLMs) decode by iteratively denoising a full canvas of tokens, so every forward pass runs a per-token sampling and stopping pipeline over the entire canvas-by-vocabulary logits tensor. We profile single-user decoding of a 26B-parameter diffusion Mixture-of-Experts model on a bandwidth-bound edge accelerator (NVIDIA GB10) and report a result that is easy to miss: after weight quantisation, this logits pipeline, not the expert GEMMs, is the single largest consumer of decode time. Unlike autoregressive decoding, where sampling touches one position's logits per committed token, diffusion decoding processes S times as many logit entries per output token, where S is the number of denoising steps. We show this pipeline is largely redundant or fusable and remove it in two lossless tiers: a bit-exact tier whose output is byte-identical to the reference decoder, and an accuracy-parity tier using a fused single-pass entropy kernel and Gumbel-max sampling. Combined with a W4A16 expert kernel, the full stack reaches 2.4-2.7 times end-to-end speedup over bf16 at unchanged benchmark accuracy on GSM8K, HumanEval, and MATH, on a single 273 GB/s device. We confirm the finding on a second, independently built diffusion MoE (LLaDA2.0-mini: pipeline 28.8% of decode, fused W4A16 3.3 times at accuracy parity) and show it disappears on a dense diffusion model (3.6%). The cost is specific to MoE diffusion, where quantisation makes the backbone cheap. Code and quantised weights are released.
papers.summary: Masked diffusion language models decode by repeatedly denoising a full canvas of tokens, so each forward pass runs a per-token sampling and stopping pipeline over the whole canvas-by-vocabulary logits tensor. Profiling a 26B-parameter diffusion Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model on an NVIDIA GB10 edge accelerator shows that, after weight quantisation, this logits pipeline rather than the expert matrix multiplications is the largest consumer of decode time. The authors remove the redundancy in two tiers, one bit-exact and one at accuracy parity using a fused single-pass entropy kernel and Gumbel-max sampling, and combine them with a `W4A16` expert kernel for **2.4-2.7x end-to-end speedup over bf16 at unchanged accuracy on `GSM8K`, `HumanEval`, and `MATH`**. The effect is confirmed on `LLaDA2.0-mini`, where the pipeline is 28.8% of decode time, and is absent on a dense diffusion model at 3.6%; code and quantised weights are released.

papers.title: tmol: a GPU-accelerated implementation of the Rosetta energy function for machine learning
papers.abstract: Physics-inspired forcefields complement generative machine learning models, showing better generalization beyond the training distribution. However, these forcefields are typically slow to evaluate, and their derivatives are difficult to integrate into ML frameworks. We introduce tmol, a GPU-native PyTorch library implementing the state-of-the-art RosettaGenFF forcefield. tmol supports efficient batched differentiable scoring and whole-structure refinement with up to 362-fold throughput increase (batched). Used as a reward in generative protein design, tmol increases hydrogen bonds and water bridges at designed interfaces.
papers.summary: Physics-inspired forcefields generalize beyond the training distribution better than generative models alone, but they are slow to evaluate and their derivatives are hard to integrate into machine learning frameworks. `tmol` is a GPU-native PyTorch library implementing the `RosettaGenFF` forcefield with batched, differentiable scoring and whole-structure refinement, reaching **up to 362-fold higher batched throughput**. When used as a reward in generative protein design, it increases hydrogen bonds and water bridges at designed interfaces.

papers.title: PromptPack: Training-Free Augmentation of Diffusion Editors for Intent-Aligned Spatial and Semantic Control
papers.abstract: Many image-editing tasks require confining changes to intended spatial regions while exactly preserving user-designated source content. Instruction-driven editing pipelines often leave such user-intent underspecified, while inpainting editors condition generation on explicitly defined edit support but not on the spatial assignment of individual edit concepts. PromptPack addresses both limitations by equipping diffusion editors with two explicit 'Edit Guides': an edit-role partition that labels each pixel as 'Keep,' 'Permit,' or 'Modify' to specify where edits may occur, and a regional-prompt assignment that maps spatial regions to text prompts to specify which concepts apply where. These guides may be manually specified or, for source-object edits, automatically derived from a text-grounded SAM 3 mask. Without retraining, PromptPack injects independently embedded regional prompts into the editor's fixed-length text sequence and uses the Edit Guides to spatially mask attention, gate flow updates, and restore protected source pixels. We integrate PromptPack into FlowEdit FLUX, FlowEdit SD3, and FLUX Kontext and demonstrate improved requested-concept placement and protected-content preservation across all three integrations on PIE-Bench++. In a pairwise user study, PromptPack achieves an 87% preference rate over FlowEdit FLUX, establishing PromptPack as a practical, training-free interface for intent-aligned diffusion editing.
papers.summary: Instruction-driven image editors often leave unclear where changes should happen, while inpainting editors know the edit region but not which concept belongs in which part of it. `PromptPack` adds two explicit guides to diffusion editors without retraining: a per-pixel partition into Keep, Permit, and Modify roles, and a mapping from spatial regions to text prompts, either specified by hand or derived from a text-grounded `SAM 3` mask. The guides are used to inject regional prompts into the editor's text sequence, mask attention spatially, gate flow updates, and restore protected source pixels. Integrated into `FlowEdit FLUX`, `FlowEdit SD3`, and `FLUX Kontext`, it improves concept placement and content preservation on `PIE-Bench++`, and reaches an **87% preference rate over `FlowEdit FLUX`** in a pairwise user study.

papers.title: FaceRiff: Data-Efficient Unified Text-to-3D Face Asset Synthesis via Geometric Conditioning
papers.abstract: High-resolution facial datasets with consistent UV-mapped geometry, albedo, and physically based displacement are scarce, yet such assets are essential for photorealistic digital-human rendering. Existing 3D face generation methods are often slow, single-modality, or require large specialized datasets. Meanwhile, large image diffusion models encode strong facial priors but do not natively produce lighting-independent textures, pore-scale displacement, or UV-aligned geometry. We present FaceRiff, a unified, data- and parameter-efficient framework for generating complete 3D face assets (mesh, albedo, and displacement) directly from text in a shared UV space. FaceRiff adapts a pretrained SDXL backbone with task-specific LoRA adapters and uses UV normal maps as geometric conditioning: per-instance normals guide albedo and displacement synthesis, while a dataset-mean normal provides a canonical spatial anchor for mesh generation. Using only 2,049 scans from approximately 350 identities and training on a single GPU, FaceRiff updates less than 3% of the backbone parameters per task and produces render-ready 3D face assets without per-instance optimization. Compared with FaceG2E and DreamFace, FaceRiff produces greater per-prompt diversity while preserving prompt alignment and fixed-topology UV consistency, and additionally generates lighting-independent albedo suitable for PBR relighting and pore-scale displacement absent from prior text-driven baselines. A blind study with 45 industry professionals shows that FaceRiff achieves substantially higher perceived realism than DreamFace, approaching that of real captures. Overall, FaceRiff demonstrates that pretrained diffusion priors can be adapted to unified 3D face asset synthesis under limited data.
papers.summary: High-resolution face datasets with consistent UV-mapped geometry, albedo, and displacement are scarce, and existing 3D face generators tend to be slow, single-modality, or dependent on large specialized datasets. `FaceRiff` generates a complete face asset (mesh, albedo, and displacement) from text in a shared UV space by adapting a pretrained `SDXL` backbone with task-specific LoRA adapters and conditioning on UV normal maps. It is trained on **only 2,049 scans from about 350 identities on a single GPU, updating less than 3% of backbone parameters per task**, and needs no per-instance optimization. Compared with `FaceG2E` and `DreamFace` it shows greater per-prompt diversity with preserved prompt alignment, and a blind study with 45 industry professionals rated its realism substantially above `DreamFace` and close to real captures.

papers.title: Knowing Which, Not How Much: Language Models Order Party Positions They Cannot Place
papers.abstract: Language models are increasingly asked where real actors stand: what a party's platform prioritises, what an institution has committed to. Such judgments are gradable, carrying both an order and a magnitude. Nearly every benchmark that tests them asks about one entity at a time, then reads that score as the model's knowledge of the domain. Order and magnitude, however, need not be acquired together. Text about social entities carries far more comparison than measurement, so a model may hold a dependable ordering with no anchored scale beneath it. We ask whether a model can place a documented social position on a scale or only order the actors it compares, and what that means for how such knowledge is measured. We test this on party positions in Japan and South Korea, where the Comparative Manifesto Project's coded data supplies a rare external answer key. Asked to order four parties, models beat the strongest fixed-answer baseline by more than a factor of two; asked to place one party on the same scale, they fall below it. The ordering survives inside those failed placements, and supplying the coded values lifts placement to near ceiling. Comparative and absolute questions about the same fact therefore measure different things here, and for party issue salience a benchmark built from one cannot speak for the other.
papers.summary: Benchmarks that probe what language models know about where real actors stand usually ask about one entity at a time, yet such judgments have both an order and a magnitude that need not be learned together. The authors test this on party positions in Japan and South Korea, using coded data from the `Comparative Manifesto Project` as an external answer key. **Asked to order four parties, models beat the strongest fixed-answer baseline by more than a factor of two, but asked to place a single party on the same scale they fall below it.** The correct ordering persists inside the failed placements and supplying the coded values lifts placement to near ceiling, so comparative and absolute questions about the same fact measure different things.

papers.title: Adaptive Memory for Online Reinforcement Learning under Sparse Model Changes
papers.abstract: We study the discounted reinforcement learning (RL) problem in a setting where the underlying environment changes between deployments. Each deployment provides $H$ observations from a fixed MDP. The reward function and transition kernel are fixed within each deployment. Across deployments, at most an $\epsilon >0$ fraction of the reward and transition kernel entries may change. In this setting, learning each model to deploy from scratch may discard useful observations from past deployments, whereas pooling all past observations can bias the estimates of entries that have already changed. We then propose an algorithm that for each state and action pair, selects how much history to reuse to estimate the reward and probabilities of the next state. We start with observations from the current deployment and add earlier deployment observations one at a time, the most recent first. After each addition, we check whether a single average reward agrees with the estimates from all histories considered until that point. We apply the same check to the distribution of next states. For each estimate, we leverage the last history that passes these aforementioned checks. The optimal control policy is then computed on top of the fitted MDP. We characterize the average gap between the optimal return and the return of the learner's policies over a finite number of deployments. We demonstrate that when $0< |S|\epsilon \leq 2$, with $|S|$ being the cardinality of the state space, our algorithm needs only the observations from the most recent $O(1/\epsilon)$ deployments, and achieves a long-run average gap of at most $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{\epsilon/H})$.
papers.summary: The setting is discounted reinforcement learning (RL) where the environment is fixed within a deployment of H observations but at most an ε fraction of reward and transition entries may change between deployments, so learning from scratch wastes data while pooling everything biases estimates. The proposed algorithm chooses, for each state-action pair, how much history to reuse by adding earlier deployments one at a time, most recent first, and checking whether a single average reward and next-state distribution remain consistent with all histories considered so far. The optimal policy is then computed on the fitted model. When the state-space size times ε is at most 2, the algorithm needs only the most recent O(1/ε) deployments and achieves a **long-run average optimality gap of at most roughly sqrt(ε/H)**, up to logarithmic factors.

papers.title: Cancellation-Free Constrained SquareCB for Safe Controller Selection
papers.abstract: We study constrained contextual bandits, in which a learner chooses one of $K$ actions in each round to minimize loss while keeping the expected cost of its play below a budget. Existing reductions to online regression weight the cost by a Lagrange multiplier learned from past constraint residuals, so slack in some rounds can offset violations in others. We instead run SquareCB proposed in \citep{foster2020beyond} with a rectified weight on the cost: it is zero when the estimated cost is within the budget, and otherwise just large enough to bring it back to the budget. Under realizability and Slater's condition with margin $\delta$, the algorithm attains regret $O(\sqrt{KT\,\mathrm{Reg}_{\mathsf{Sq}}(T)}/\delta)$ and cancellation-free violation $\sum_t(V_c^{p_t}-b)^+=O(\sqrt{KT\,\mathrm{Reg}_{\mathsf{Sq}}(T)})$, where $\mathrm{Reg}_{\mathsf{Sq}}$ is the error of the regression oracle. The same bounds hold when the budget must be met in every context, potentially adversarially chosen contexts. In controller selection for a safe-control-gym quadrotor and a BOPTEST building, the violation is 6 to 9 times lower than that of primal-dual and virtual-queue baselines, with a lower or comparable regret.
papers.summary: Constrained contextual bandits require choosing one of K actions per round to minimize loss while keeping expected cost under a budget, and existing reductions to online regression use a learned Lagrange multiplier that lets slack in some rounds offset violations in others. This work instead runs `SquareCB` with a rectified weight on the cost that is zero when the estimated cost is within budget and otherwise just large enough to bring it back. Under realizability and Slater's condition, the algorithm attains regret and cancellation-free violation bounds that both scale with the square root of K, T, and the regression oracle's error, and the bounds also hold when the budget must be met in every context. In controller selection for a `safe-control-gym` quadrotor and a `BOPTEST` building, **violation is 6 to 9 times lower than primal-dual and virtual-queue baselines** at lower or comparable regret.

papers.title: WM-Quant: Rollout-Aware Post-Training Quantization for JEPA-Style World Models
papers.abstract: We present WM-Quant, to our knowledge, the first post-training quantization (PTQ) framework designed specifically for JEPA-style world models. Although world models typically feature relatively few parameters, action planning algorithms often require thousands of inferences, which can quickly become computationally expensive. PTQ is a natural way to reduce this cost. However, we show that in world models using autoregressive model predictive control (MPC) rollouts, quantization error can compound with each predictor step, resulting in action rankings from the quantized model becoming near-random. WM-Quant addresses this with three components that build on existing PTQ methods: early-encoder precision, control-path preservation, and rollout-aware scaling. Early-encoder precision protects accurate latent state and goal information to mitigate long-term error propagation. Control-path preservation allows the world model predictor to distinguish between fine-grained actions, significantly improving action rankings and execution. Rollout-aware scaling jointly calibrates encoder and per-step predictor activation ranges with respect to an entire rollout rather than a single prediction, reducing the cumulative rollout error. Across multiple world models, environments, and PTQ methods, WM-Quant substantially improves planning success at low bit-widths, approaching full-precision performance at W4A4.
papers.summary: World models have relatively few parameters, but planning with them can require thousands of inferences, which makes post-training quantization (PTQ) attractive. The authors show that in JEPA-style world models using autoregressive model predictive control (MPC) rollouts, quantization error compounds at each predictor step until the quantized model's action rankings become near-random. `WM-Quant` adds three components on top of existing PTQ methods: higher precision in the early encoder, preservation of the control path so fine-grained actions stay distinguishable, and calibration of activation ranges over a whole rollout rather than a single prediction. Across multiple world models, environments, and PTQ methods, it improves planning success at low bit-widths, **approaching full-precision performance at `W4A4`**.

papers.title: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights
papers.abstract: Language models are trained once, frozen and deployed: improving one again takes another training run, and a prompt, a scaffold or extra computation at inference is gone once the task ends. A frontier model has been shown to edit the weights of a much smaller one. We ask whether a model can rewrite its own weights to make itself better, and find that it can, by its own reasoning, with no gradients and no training; we call this self-rewriting. Given its weights, graded answers and the ability to run itself, a 27B model diagnoses its failure and edits the weights behind it. It surpasses itself: its own edit makes it 6.6 points more accurate on 490 problems it never saw, in a test fixed in advance, and another session's edit also makes it significantly better. It keeps getting better: it submits an edit only when its own tests support it, each edit replacing the last, and over its first eight such sessions its accuracy only rises. Unlike test-time scaling, the gain persists in its weights and adds no cost per answer; unlike training, it needs no pre- or post-training infrastructure, only an open model and hours on one GPU. It repairs a damaged copy of itself: it locates the corrupted matrix and rewrites it with values of its own, never reading the undamaged weights; found on text math problems alone, the repair lifts the copy on six image benchmarks it never saw from 7% to 70% accuracy, 83% of the undamaged model's. And the ability emerges with scale: across four sizes of one family, the 2B model makes no edit and the 4B and 9B models break themselves; only the 27B model works on itself as a human would, comparing its hidden states on answers that finish and on answers that run out of tokens, weakening the direction that separates them. Like a human, a model need not separate training from inference; improving a language model may come to take a conversation rather than a training run.
papers.summary: The question posed is whether a language model can improve itself by directly editing its own weights through reasoning, with no gradients or training, a process the authors call self-rewriting. Given access to its weights, graded answers, and the ability to run itself, a 27B model is reported to diagnose a failure and edit the responsible weights, with **its own edit making it 6.6 points more accurate on 490 unseen problems in a test fixed in advance**, and accuracy only rising over its first eight sessions. The authors also report that it repairs a damaged copy of itself without reading the undamaged weights, lifting accuracy on six unseen image benchmarks from 7% to 70%. Across four sizes of one model family, the 2B model makes no edit and the 4B and 9B models break themselves, while only the 27B model succeeds, by comparing hidden states on answers that finish against answers that run out of tokens and weakening the direction that separates them.
papers.highlight_summary:
The authors test whether a language model can improve itself by directly editing its own weights through reasoning alone, with no gradients or optimizer, and report that a 27B `Qwen3.5` model can do so while smaller models in the same family cannot. The model works in a sandboxed session on its own weights, diagnoses why its answers fail, and keeps only the edits that its own tests support.

- Each session gives the model its graded answers on `DeepScaleR` math practice problems, a CPU-only Python environment that can read and replace weight tensors with gradients and optimizers blocked, and a budget of **20 forward passes** and 200 code runs to read hidden states or run same-seed paired tests of edited against unedited weights.
- In the eight sessions that check an edit on reserved problems before submitting, the model withdrew in five and submitted three edits, two of which were significantly better on 490 held-out problems, by **+6.6** and **+4.0 points** (p < 10⁻⁵ each), with the larger gain coming from raising the time-step bias of every linear-attention layer by 0.5 so that fewer answers run out of tokens.
- The edit the authors trace step by step, which removes 5% of a "finished versus unfinished answer" direction from the two output matrices of layer 8, gave a much smaller held-out gain of **57.2% to 58.3%**.
- Given a copy with eight rows of the layer-30 MLP output matrix overwritten by noise, the model found the 1397×-median outlier and clipped weights at 15× the median, lifting held-out math accuracy from **0% to 33.0%** (base 58.5%) and six unseen image benchmarks from **7.3% to 70.2%**, about 83% of the base model's accuracy, including 0 to 89 of 100 on `ScreenSpot-v2`.
- The evidence is narrow: it covers one model family in which the 2B model made no edit and the 4B and 9B models broke themselves with random perturbations, the gains mostly fix one failure mode (looping until the token limit), every session restarts from the base weights so gains do not compound, and at the 16,384-token budget shared with the smaller models the 27B model withdrew its edit.

papers.title: Domain-Tuned Diffusion Super-Resolution for 4K Facial Asset Maps
papers.abstract: Physically based facial assets require 4K albedo and displacement maps for cinematic close-ups, yet generative pipelines commonly produce them at only 1K. Naively applying photographic super-resolution is a poor fit: facial UV maps have domain-specific statistics, and displacement is a scalar height field whose errors directly distort geometry. We present a domain-tuned diffusion upscaler for 4x (1024 to 4096) facial asset super-resolution. Starting from a bilinearly upsampled map, we adapt a frozen SDXL backbone per modality with lightweight LoRA modules, while a Tile ControlNet preserves input structure as the diffusion prior restores pore- and wrinkle-scale detail. On held-out maps, our method produces sharper, more faithful detail than bilinear and off-the-shelf GAN and diffusion super-resolvers, reducing albedo LPIPS from 0.21 to 0.08 while avoiding misplaced or excessive displacement relief. These results show that lightweight domain adaptation can produce render-ready 4K facial asset maps without a custom super-resolution architecture.
papers.summary: Physically based facial assets need 4K albedo and displacement maps for close-ups, but generative pipelines typically produce 1K maps, and photographic super-resolution fits poorly because UV maps have their own statistics and displacement errors distort geometry. The proposed 4x upscaler starts from a bilinearly upsampled map and adapts a frozen `SDXL` backbone per modality with lightweight LoRA modules, while a `Tile ControlNet` preserves input structure as pore- and wrinkle-scale detail is restored. On held-out maps it yields sharper, more faithful detail than bilinear and off-the-shelf GAN and diffusion super-resolvers, **reducing albedo LPIPS from 0.21 to 0.08** while avoiding misplaced or excessive displacement relief.

papers.title: Call-Efficient ICD-10 Code Prediction via Supervised Candidate Generation and Selective LLM Invocation
papers.abstract: Automatic assignment of ICD-10 codes from short clinical diagnosis text is a practical medical text classification and normalization task. The task is difficult because diagnosis phrases are short and noisy, the ICD-10 label space is hierarchical, and the class distribution is strongly imbalanced. This paper presents a call-efficient ICD-10 code prediction pipeline that combines transformer embeddings, tree-based supervised candidate generation, candidate-level reranking, and a gated LLM assistance. The evaluation uses a leakage-safe validation protocol: model and threshold selection are based on out-of-fold cross-validation predictions, while final reporting is performed on a locked test set with no shared source-file groups. The supervised conditional parent-code candidate generator reaches 74.32% Top-1 accuracy on the locked test set and 93.05% Top-10 candidate coverage. A direct zero-shot GPT-5.6-Sol baseline reaches 81.01% Top-1 accuracy, but requires an invocation of this large model for every diagnosis. The final deployable system, Pre-LLM fusion, reaches 81.24% OOF-CV accuracy and 83.19% locked-test accuracy while calling the LLM for only 31.97% of cases. This improves the locked-test error rate from 25.68% for the supervised parent-code baseline to 16.81%, corresponding to a 34.5% relative error reduction. The results show that the most effective role of the LLM is controlled reranking on uncertain examples rather than unrestricted coding or full-dataset invocation.
papers.summary: Assigning ICD-10 codes to short clinical diagnosis text is hard because the phrases are noisy, the label space is hierarchical, and classes are heavily imbalanced. The pipeline combines transformer embeddings, tree-based supervised candidate generation, candidate-level reranking, and a gated large language model (LLM) step that is invoked only on uncertain cases, with model selection on out-of-fold predictions and final reporting on a locked test set. The supervised generator alone reaches 74.32% Top-1 accuracy and a zero-shot `GPT-5.6-Sol` baseline reaches 81.01% while calling the model on every diagnosis. The final system reaches **83.19% locked-test accuracy while calling the LLM for only 31.97% of cases**, a 34.5% relative error reduction over the supervised baseline.

papers.title: World-Grounded Reinforcement Learning for Pollution-Aware Bird Movement Modeling Using a Multi-Instance DQN Framework
papers.abstract: Birds are modeled as environmentally sensitive agents whose movement reflects real-world air quality conditions, where AQI serves as a measurable world feedback signal representing pollution-driven consequences. Instead of relying on human preference or synthetic rewards, the system uses environmental outcomes as the primary training signal, enabling policy learning grounded in ecological impact. We propose a multi-instance reinforcement learning simulation in which agents navigate a 2D grid representation of India integrated with a precomputed AQI matrix and geographic state boundaries. The framework combines bird call metadata from the Xeno-canto dataset, spatial discretization, and real environmental data to learn adaptive navigation strategies under pollution constraints. To ensure scalability and efficiency, repeated real-time API queries are replaced by a structured AQI mapping that enables fast lookup during training and execution. Multiple baselines, including Monte Carlo, Q-Learning, and Value Iteration, are evaluated for comparison. Deep Q-Network demonstrates stronger stability, adaptability, and cumulative performance across varying environmental conditions, establishing a scalable foundation for world-feedback driven ecological decision modeling.
papers.summary: Bird movement is modeled as a reinforcement learning problem in which agents respond to real air quality index (AQI) data, used as the training signal in place of human preference or synthetic rewards. Multiple agents navigate a 2D grid of India built from a precomputed AQI matrix and state boundaries, combined with bird call metadata from the `Xeno-canto` dataset, with a lookup table replacing repeated real-time API queries. Compared against Monte Carlo, Q-Learning, and Value Iteration baselines, **a Deep Q-Network shows stronger stability, adaptability, and cumulative performance** across varying environmental conditions.

papers.title: A Temporal Algebraic Framework for Data Stream Evaluation Under Delayed Labels and Distribution Shifts
papers.abstract: In data streams, labels often arrive late or only for some instances, class prevalence drifts, and rare classes vanish from short windows. Standard evaluation then confuses a degraded decision boundary with a change in prevalence, and is biased when labels are delayed or selected by the model. We extend an algebraic framework that obtains pooled (micro) and per-class (macro) measures from one confusion matrix to streams, weighting the counts in time by exponential fading or a sliding window; the update costs O(m^2) per step, whatever the stream length, and each pooled measure stays a weighted combination of the per-class ones. Delayed and selective feedback enter as an observation mask: until its label arrives, an instance is counted with the model's calibrated class probabilities, and the bias of this interim estimate is driven by their calibration error. Audited conventions report no value for a class without verified instances. We separate prior shift from concept drift by monitoring prior-free coordinates (recall and specificity) and attribute a change in a measure to the two sources with a first-order Jacobian decomposition. On synthetic streams and four real datasets, a detector on these coordinates with a memory per class raises no excess false alarms under label shift, unlike the Jacobian alarm and error-rate detectors. The correction for delayed labels recovers recall in some real settings and is only partial for precision, specificity and F1. Twenty-five statements are checked in Lean 4, and the code is in the aggmetrics package.
papers.summary: Evaluating classifiers on data streams is distorted when labels arrive late or selectively, class prevalence drifts, and rare classes disappear from short windows, so a prevalence change can be mistaken for a degraded decision boundary. The authors extend an algebraic framework that derives pooled and per-class measures from one confusion matrix to streams, weighting counts by exponential fading or a sliding window at a per-step cost independent of stream length, and counting unlabelled instances with the model's calibrated class probabilities until their labels arrive. Prior shift is separated from concept drift by monitoring recall and specificity, which do not depend on class priors, with a first-order Jacobian decomposition attributing changes to each source. On synthetic streams and four real datasets, **a detector on these coordinates raises no excess false alarms under label shift, unlike error-rate detectors**, while the delayed-label correction recovers recall in some settings and only partially corrects precision, specificity, and F1; twenty-five statements are checked in Lean 4 and the code is in the `aggmetrics` package.

papers.title: Lost in a Few Heads: Diagnosing and Repairing Block Selection in Sparse Attention
papers.abstract: Sparse attention models read a few blocks of keys for every query at a fixed budget and can lose much of their long-context retrieval accuracy at that budget. We ask where this loss is made. Using exact attention mass selection at the shipped budget as an oracle, we show that the selector under-ranks the needle rather than running out of budget. We find attention heads that miss the needle by running a calibration probe that teacher-forces the answer and reads two quantities in every head. The first is the needle attention that the selector forfeits, and the second is the share of the answer's log-probability that fixing the head's selection restores, integrated along the path from the shipped selector to full attention. Four checkpoints of the InfLLM-V2 family and NOSA-8B lose multi-key retrieval in the same three blind heads, which attend to the needle while a mean-pooled key summary dilutes its single decisive token. Full attention in those heads or a 4-bit scorer that keeps the shipped budget recovers most of the loss without training. On MiniCPM4.1-8B at 64K, either fix lifts multi-key retrieval accuracy from 54.1 to 97.5%, level with full attention in every head. In production serving engines, full attention in those heads keeps 84 to 89% of the time to first token (TTFT) that sparse attention saves at 32K to 128K context length. Beyond the InfLLM-V2 selector lineage, one unified rule flags attention heads above a threshold swept on each checkpoint until they close most of the gap to full attention on calibration prompts. A similar small set of blind attention heads carry the loss for the SeerAttention-R gates, NSA, and DashAttention, whereas many such heads exist in MoBA. On Qwen3-8B with the SeerAttention-R gates, full attention in 18 of 288 key-value heads lifts multi-key retrieval accuracy from 29.8 to 97.7%.
papers.summary: Sparse attention models read only a few blocks of keys per query and can lose much of their long-context retrieval accuracy as a result. Using exact attention-mass selection at the same budget as an oracle, the authors show the block selector under-ranks the relevant block rather than running out of budget, and a calibration probe traces the loss to a few attention heads; in the `InfLLM-V2` family and `NOSA-8B` it is the same three heads, where a mean-pooled key summary dilutes the single decisive token. Giving those heads full attention, or using a 4-bit scorer at the same budget, recovers most of the loss without training: on `MiniCPM4.1-8B` at 64K context, **either fix lifts multi-key retrieval accuracy from 54.1 to 97.5%, level with full attention in every head**, while the full-attention fix keeps 84 to 89% of the time to first token (TTFT) savings. A similar small set of heads carries the loss for `SeerAttention-R`, `NSA`, and `DashAttention`, though many such heads exist in `MoBA`.

papers.title: ALOHA Lightning: Learning Fast and Precise Manipulation
papers.abstract: Learning from human demonstrations has enabled robots to acquire a wide range of manipulation skills, but learned policies typically execute far slower than ordinary humans. This speed gap is mainly due to lack of an interface for collecting demonstration data at high speed, and the difficulty in training policies that can robustly execute high-speed motions. In this paper, we present ALOHA Lightning (Flash ALOHA), a system for learning fast and precise robotic manipulation. Our system uses kinesthetic teaching to intuitively collect near-human-speed demonstrations on a backdrivable bimanual platform, yielding natural and fast trajectories. We also present a learning pipeline that enables smooth high-speed execution through test-time action smoothing and aligns the visual data distribution between data collection and deployment with masking. Given 50 demonstrations for each task, ALOHA Lightning autonomously completes bimanual tasks such as ball tossing and catching, folding shorts, battery insertion, and bussing tables for over 80% success rates while close to human speed. Project website: https://flash-aloha.github.io/
papers.summary: Robot policies learned from human demonstrations usually run much slower than people, because fast demonstrations are hard to collect and high-speed motions are hard to execute robustly. `ALOHA Lightning` collects near-human-speed demonstrations by kinesthetic teaching on a backdrivable two-armed platform, then trains with test-time action smoothing and with masking that aligns what the cameras see during collection and deployment. With 50 demonstrations per task, it completes ball tossing and catching, shorts folding, battery insertion and table bussing at **over 80% success while close to human speed**.

papers.title: KVUse: Reusable-KV User Memory for Efficient LLM Recommenders
papers.abstract: Memory-augmented recommenders built on large language models (LLMs) maintain a natural-language profile of each user. These profiles are updated by a user profile update path that revises the profile as new interactions arrive and are consumed by downstream task paths like ranking. Because these user profiles are stored as text in the user memory, every ranking LLM call that consumes them must splice them in the prompt and calculate the KV cache of them during the prefill phase. Given these ranking LLM calls are prefill heavy (long prompt but short decoded output) and repeatedly called, these repeated prefill of user profile text dominates the serving. Prefix caching cannot remove it, because these user profiles are preceded by different text in different calls. We present KVUse, which stores the user profiles as reusable key-value (KV) caches instead of text. KVUse trains lightweight LoRA writers by self-distillation, so that the user profile update call produces the reusable KV of the user profile while decoding it, and the LLM can read these reusable KV at new positions and behind new context without recomputation. KVUse also has a customized KV scheduler that uploads the stored reusable KV of the next batch while the current batch is computed, hiding the KV transfer from host memory behind GPU computation. On four InstructRec datasets with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, KVUse shows no statistically significant difference in ranking quality from full prefill over continuous memory update rounds. Under saturated load, KVUse raises the throughput of the downstream scoring path by 4.0x-4.5x and of the profile update path by 1.4x-1.9x.
papers.summary: Recommenders built on large language models (LLMs) keep a text profile per user, and every ranking call must recompute that profile's key-value (KV) cache during prefill, which prefix caching cannot avoid because the profile follows different text in each call. `KVUse` stores profiles as reusable KV caches instead: LoRA writers trained by self-distillation make the profile-update call emit a KV that the model can read at new positions and behind new context, and a scheduler uploads the next batch's KV from host memory while the current batch computes. On four `InstructRec` datasets with `Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct`, ranking quality shows no statistically significant difference from full prefill, while throughput under saturated load rises by **4.0x-4.5x on the scoring path** and 1.4x-1.9x on the profile-update path.

papers.title: Latent Fact Composition under Next-Token Training
papers.abstract: Controlled studies of latent two-hop reasoning train transformers to predict only the answer, whereas language models are trained to predict every token. We ask whether a model trained on every token learns to answer two-hop questions whose intermediate entity appears in no two-hop training example. We build a synthetic corpus with such questions. On this corpus every term of the loss can be computed exactly. A looped transformer, a standard transformer and DiscoLoop answer almost none of these questions. We therefore introduce the Baton family of looped transformers. They pass the intermediate entity to the second loop as a token embedding. When trained to predict only the answer, two of its three variants answer these questions almost perfectly. We then relate the success and failure of each model to three design conditions. Experiments that change one condition at a time agree with this hypothesis. When Baton is trained on every token, however, its accuracy on these questions rises and then declines. We further split the gradient of the next-token loss into three terms. Removing the two terms that depend on the particular training set raises the peak accuracy but does not remove the decline. The decline arises in the second hop while the model still recalls both facts.
papers.summary: Studies of latent two-hop reasoning usually train transformers to predict only the answer, whereas language models are trained on every token, so the authors test whether every-token training yields answers to two-hop questions whose intermediate entity appears in no two-hop training example. On a synthetic corpus where every loss term can be computed exactly, a looped transformer, a standard transformer and `DiscoLoop` answer almost none of these questions, while the new `Baton` family of looped transformers, which passes the intermediate entity to the second loop as a token embedding, answers them almost perfectly in two of three variants under answer-only training. Under every-token training, however, **`Baton`'s accuracy on these questions rises and then declines**, and removing the two gradient terms that depend on the particular training set raises the peak without removing the decline, which arises in the second hop while both facts are still recalled.

papers.title: Wrong Input, Wrong Threshold: Re-evaluating Adversarial Facial Privacy
papers.abstract: Published face-privacy methods report protection above 90% against black-box recognition models. That number comes from an evaluation protocol with two independent defects, reported in a measure that cannot size either one. The input is wrong: methods published since 2022 feed the network the whole photograph, or a detector's box, where deployed systems detect, align to a landmark template and crop. Re-scoring the same files through a realistic front end costs a standard transfer attack 56% of its dodging protection and a budget-allocating attack 7%, with no image regenerated. The measure is wrong: that loss is a difference of success rates, so it saturates, moving by 8.2x over a budget sweep while the effect beneath it moves by 1.34x. We therefore report the paired cosine shift, in which both thresholds cancel algebraically, so the input defect holds without committing to a calibration. Measured that way it is 2.2x and 10.7x larger on three unseen recognizers, and at matched budget it reverses the L-infinity transfer ranking: the one surveyed method that aligns at evaluation gains 0.18 where MI-FGSM loses 0.05. The cause is a resampling mismatch, not perturbation lost outside the crop; optimising through a differentiable alignment operator largely removes it, adding +24 to +58 points on unseen recognizers and a commercial system, with a residual on one of them. The thresholds are wrong: the four constants inherited since 2021 hold the false-accept rate near its nominal 1% on aligned crops but admit 2.3-5.4% on whole images, with an opposite-signed bias across dodging and impersonation, the two tasks reported side by side. Differentiable alignment and gallery scoring are not new: the first generation of this literature used both, and we show what dropping them cost.
papers.summary: Published adversarial face-privacy methods report over 90% protection against black-box recognition, but the evaluation feeds networks whole photographs or detector boxes instead of the detected, landmark-aligned crops that deployed systems use. Re-scoring the same files through a realistic front end **costs a standard transfer attack 56% of its dodging protection** and a budget-allocating attack 7%, and the authors propose a paired cosine shift measure because success-rate differences saturate. They trace the loss to a resampling mismatch that optimising through a differentiable alignment operator largely removes, adding 24 to 58 points on unseen recognizers and a commercial system. The inherited decision thresholds also admit a 2.3-5.4% false-accept rate on whole images instead of the nominal 1%.

papers.title: DNeo: Your Parallel Draft Model Needs Better Target Feature Encoding
papers.abstract: Speculative-diffusion decoding uses a small parallel drafter model to generate b draft tokens in one forward pass, which then undergo parallel verification via a larger target model. Faster inference can be achieved when multiple draft tokens pass verification simultaneously. Recent parallel draft architectures (DFlash, DSpark) improve draft quality by conditioning on rich features computed by the target, through a mechanism known as feature encoding. However, standard feature encoding mechanisms have three limitations: (1) they are lossy, applying encoding projections that are destructive to the underlying target feature-space via a discovered effect known as residual mixing, (2) they are memory-less, with no record of previously processed proposals, and (3) they utilize features sampled uniformly from across the target layers, omitting important hidden states. To address these issues, we propose Mixture-of-Features Attention (MoFA), a lightweight feature-encoding approach equipped with a working memory that encodes previously rejected proposals. Leveraging MoFA, rejection memory, and a set of further enhancements, including 2-tap causal convolutions, prefix-only cross-attention, and non-uniform target layer selection, the final architecture, DNeo, achieves 1.3x faster generation speed than SoTA (DFlash-2) without impacting drafter footprint or generation quality. DNeo marks a new state of the art in high quality, fast LLM inference.
papers.summary: Speculative-diffusion decoding speeds up language model inference by having a small drafter propose several tokens in one pass for a larger target model to verify in parallel, with the drafter conditioned on features computed by the target. The authors argue that existing feature encoding is lossy, keeps no memory of earlier proposals, and samples target layers uniformly, and they propose Mixture-of-Features Attention (`MoFA`), a lightweight encoder with a working memory of previously rejected proposals. Combined with 2-tap causal convolutions, prefix-only cross-attention and non-uniform layer selection, the resulting `DNeo` architecture is reported to generate **1.3x faster than `DFlash-2`** without changing drafter footprint or generation quality.

papers.title: Polylogarithmic Regret via Certainty Equivalence in Degenerate LQR
papers.abstract: Singular input penalties, as in minimum variance control, can reduce what must be identified to control an unknown linear system. In online linear quadratic control, certainty equivalence can achieve polylogarithmic regret when the optimal controller is identifiable from data collected under optimal feedback. With a positive definite input penalty, however, this condition is restrictive, since for an invertible state matrix it requires all unknown parameters to be identifiable under optimal feedback. We show that singular input penalties relax this requirement, expanding the class of problems in which certainty equivalence achieves polylogarithmic regret. Specifically, we prove that a certainty-equivalence algorithm with a short initial exploration phase achieves $O(\log^2 T)$ expected regret over $T$ interactions whenever controller identifiability holds. We complement this guarantee with an $\Omega(\sqrt{T})$ minimax lower bound for a family containing a system where controller identifiability fails. For minimum variance control, knowing the range of the input matrix suffices for controller identifiability, a weaker requirement than knowing the full input matrix, as assumed in prior work with positive definite input penalties. This condition also covers underactuated systems, as we illustrate with a cart-pole example.
papers.summary: In online linear quadratic control of an unknown system, certainty equivalence achieves polylogarithmic regret only when the optimal controller is identifiable from data gathered under optimal feedback, which is a restrictive condition when the input penalty is positive definite. The authors show that singular input penalties, as in minimum variance control, relax this requirement, and prove that a certainty-equivalence algorithm with a short initial exploration phase achieves **O(log^2 T) expected regret** over T interactions whenever controller identifiability holds. They add a minimax lower bound of order sqrt(T) for a family containing a system where identifiability fails, and show that for minimum variance control it suffices to know the range of the input matrix, a condition that also covers underactuated systems such as a cart-pole.

papers.title: V2V Communications Using Blockchain-Enabled 6G Technology and Federated Learning
papers.abstract: This study proposes an interesting approach for vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V) communication, which integrates blockchain technology, federated learning (FL), and allocation optimization of latency and resources. The research evaluates the proposed system using various performance metrics such as packet delivery ratio (PDR), model accuracy, and latency and demonstrates its superiority over existing techniques. Furthermore, the system provides enhanced security through consensus optimization and k-anonymity for data privacy. Overall, the proposed system is a promising solution for efficient and secure V2V communication in the era of connected and autonomous vehicles. Moreover, the proposed approach achieves higher reliability, lower latency, and better resource utilization compared to traditional 5G.
papers.summary: A vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V) communication system is proposed that combines blockchain, federated learning (FL), and optimization of latency and resource allocation, with consensus optimization and k-anonymity for security and privacy. It is evaluated on packet delivery ratio (PDR), model accuracy and latency. The abstract gives no figures but claims **higher reliability, lower latency and better resource utilization than traditional 5G** and existing techniques.

papers.title: Physics-informed neural networks for spacecraft trajectory optimization with exact boundary conditions
papers.abstract: We use neural networks to optimize trajectories by modeling the position as a function of time and minimizing the thrust with respect to the network parameters. This corresponds to an unsupervised training procedure in which physical laws are incorporated directly into the optimization objective. In standard physics-informed neural networks, initial and terminal states are enforced through additional weighted loss terms, resulting in a multi-objective optimization problem that is highly sensitive to the choice of loss weights and can lead to poor convergence and reduced accuracy. To address this challenge, we construct a simple transformation, exploiting the mathematical structure of trajectory optimization problems, to enforce boundary conditions exactly a-priori. This transformation can be interpreted as a reparameterization of the solution space that embeds the boundary conditions directly into the function. This converts the original constrained optimization problem into an unconstrained one over admissible trajectories. I.e. the transformation eliminates the boundary condition penalty terms and reduces the problem to a single-objective optimization. Crucially, trajectory optimization comes with a low-dimensional boundary, which allows particularly simple and stable constructions of distance functions compared to general domains in partial differential equations. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach meaningfully improves convergence behavior and solution accuracy.
papers.summary: Trajectories are optimized by modelling spacecraft position as a neural network function of time and minimizing thrust, with the physical laws built into the objective. Standard physics-informed neural networks enforce initial and terminal states through weighted penalty terms, which makes training sensitive to loss weights, so the authors instead apply a transformation that **satisfies the boundary conditions exactly by construction**, turning the problem into unconstrained single-objective optimization. Because a trajectory's boundary is low-dimensional, the required distance functions are simple and stable to build, and numerical experiments show improved convergence and accuracy.

papers.title: Higher-Order Interaction Reconstruction via Integral Physics-Informed Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Reconstructing higher-order interactions is a fundamental challenge in complex networked systems, with applications in ecological, social, and biological networks. This inverse problem is inherently difficult due to the combinatorial complexity of higher-order structures, the strong nonlinearity of the underlying dynamics, and the prevalence of noisy and sparse observations. In this article, we propose a novel integral physics-informed neural network (IntegralPINN) framework for higher-order interaction reconstruction. Instead of { penalizing derivative-based physics residuals,} we adopt an integral formulation over temporal intervals, which naturally suppresses high-frequency noise and mitigates derivative-induced instability. We further introduce a continuous parameterization of interaction tensors, enabling tractable identification of higher-order structures via gradient-based optimization. We provide theoretical analysis establishing a noise-robust error bound that is independent of derivative amplification when the integration window satisfies an excitation condition. Extensive experiments on ecological dynamics, social contagion, and neuronal synchronization systems demonstrate that IntegralPINN achieves accurate and robust reconstruction under noisy and sparse observations, outperforming state-of-the-art approaches.
papers.summary: Recovering higher-order interactions in networked systems from observed dynamics is hard because of combinatorial structure, strong nonlinearity, and noisy, sparse data. `IntegralPINN` replaces the derivative-based physics residuals of physics-informed neural networks with an integral formulation over time intervals, which suppresses high-frequency noise, and uses a continuous parameterization of interaction tensors so that structure can be found by gradient-based optimization. The authors prove **a noise-robust error bound that is independent of derivative amplification** when the integration window satisfies an excitation condition, and report better reconstruction than prior methods on ecological, social contagion and neuronal synchronization systems.

papers.title: SLED: Sensor SLicing from Edge to Datacenter
papers.abstract: Modern sensing systems generate large volumes of heterogeneous data streams from multiple sensor modalities, increasing reliance on datacenters for computation, artificial intelligence/superintelligence (AI/SI) inference, and AI/SI training. Each sensor stream may have different network and compute requirements depending on its type and data volume. However, current wireless systems typically allocate resources at the device level, leading to contention among co-located sensor streams, where bulk data transfers may starve latency-critical telemetry. To this end, this paper introduces Sensor Slicing (SL). SL provides deterministic, medium access control (MAC)-level isolation for individual sensors within a single user equipment (UE) in open radio access networks (O-RAN). Using agentic coding techniques, SL is implemented in two O-RAN-compliant packages, reducing development time by 400 times (2 h 40 min [OCUDU] vs. 6.5 weeks [OAI]), 228-fold fewer human prompts (4 vs. 913), and less than half the tokens (0.64B vs. 1.43B). An associated end-to-end framework, SLED, is implemented to establish per-sensor radio and network isolation across edge, campus, and remote high-performance computing (HPC) tiers. Over-the-air wireless experiments demonstrate that while conventional network slicing causes critical delays to increase more than 2,300-fold under high traffic load, SLED maintains stable latency. Scaling evaluations on the two RAN stacks show that throughput remains within 0.9% and 1.4% of expected allocations even as the number of sensor slices increases. The results demonstrate that SLED preserves latency-critical telemetry while effectively utilizing resources across the sensor-to-HPC pipeline. The SLED software and evaluation datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/UNL-CPN-Lab/SLED-Sensor-SLicing-from-Edge-to-Datacenter.
papers.summary: Wireless systems typically allocate resources per device, so co-located sensor streams contend and bulk transfers can starve latency-critical telemetry. Sensor Slicing provides deterministic medium access control (MAC)-level isolation for individual sensors within one user equipment (UE) in open radio access networks (O-RAN), and the `SLED` framework extends that isolation across edge, campus and remote high-performance computing (HPC) tiers. In over-the-air experiments, conventional network slicing lets **critical delays grow more than 2,300-fold under high load while `SLED` keeps latency stable**, and throughput stays within 0.9% and 1.4% of expected allocations as slices are added. The authors implemented it in two O-RAN stacks with agentic coding, reporting 2 hours 40 minutes and 4 human prompts for `OCUDU` against 6.5 weeks and 913 prompts for `OAI`.

papers.title: HubEgo-100K: In-the-Wild Egocentric Video of Skilled Work for Robot Learning
papers.abstract: Robot policies trained by imitation generalize poorly outside the environments and objects seen in training. Published data-scaling studies find that generalization grows with the diversity of training environments and objects rather than with more demonstrations per environment. Robot data is costly to collect across many environments, whereas egocentric human video can be recorded in the wild at scale; existing egocentric video, however, mostly shows daily-life activity and contains little skilled work in real workplaces. We present HubEgo-100K, a dataset built for diversity. This version of the paper covers the first release, v1.0: 10,124 hours of 1080p egocentric video with synchronized 100 Hz inertial (IMU) data from one head-mounted phone camera. In v1.0, 12,227 contributors record their own unscripted work in 15,548 environments (each one contributor's own setting of one type, such as their kitchen or workshop) across 11 setting types, 30 work categories, 56 task types and 35 action families, with 83% of hours in workplace settings. The release comprises 72,754 episodes with machine-generated action and language annotations, in LeRobot and MCAP formats under CC BY 4.0. We measure diversity along each axis, show that inside v1.0, with episodes in random order, new contributors and words keep appearing, and relate the measurements to published evidence on six data properties tied to policy performance, including hand visibility and inertial sensing. We also document collection, curation, privacy measures and data format, and provide a datasheet. Later versions of this paper will add benchmarks and cover further releases toward 100,000 hours.
papers.summary: Imitation-trained robot policies generalize poorly beyond their training environments, and prior scaling studies tie generalization to the diversity of environments and objects, while existing egocentric video shows little skilled work in real workplaces. The first release of `HubEgo-100K` provides **10,124 hours of 1080p egocentric video** with synchronized 100 Hz inertial (IMU) data from a head-mounted phone, recorded by 12,227 contributors doing their own unscripted work in 15,548 environments, with 83% of hours in workplace settings. It comprises 72,754 episodes with machine-generated action and language annotations in `LeRobot` and `MCAP` formats under CC BY 4.0. Benchmarks are deferred to later versions, which aim to reach 100,000 hours.

papers.title: Does the Model Use What It Cites? Counterfactual Tests of Grounded Reasoning Chains in Small Video-Language Models
papers.abstract: A grounded reasoning chain cites a frame span and a box for every step, so a reader can check where the model looked. Whether the answer depends on the cited region is a different question. We test it by intervention: the regions a model cited in its own chain are blacked out, and the share of correct answers that flip is compared with blacking out boxes of the same size elsewhere on the same frames. The paired difference, the cite gap, needs no annotation. We apply it to 2-3B video-language models trained on exact CLEVRER chains and on pseudo-labelled NExT-QA chains. With the same weights, the cite gap is 0.089 on CLEVRER and 0.003 on NExT-QA. Pooled over models, masking the cited boxes flips 2.2 times as many correct answers as the control on CLEVRER and 1.1 times as many on NExT-QA, also among the answers that depend on the video at all, while the boxes pass a grounding check on both. Masking the cited entity on every frame, instead of the cited box, flips 1.9 times as many answers as its control. The NExT-QA chains were supervised to cite two frames of entities that stay visible on most frames, so this outcome is what the supervision predicts; the point is that the usual check on grounded chains cannot see it. A citation can be verifiable and relevant without the answer depending on it, and a test of grounded reasoning should remove what a chain names, not only where it points.
papers.summary: Grounded reasoning chains in video-language models cite a frame span and a box for each step, but that does not establish whether the answer depends on the cited region. The authors black out the regions a model cited and compare how often correct answers flip against blacking out same-sized boxes elsewhere on the same frames, a paired difference they call the cite gap that needs no annotation. For 2-3B models with the same weights, **the cite gap is 0.089 on `CLEVRER` but 0.003 on `NExT-QA`**, even though the cited boxes pass a grounding check on both. The conclusion is that a citation can be verifiable and relevant without the answer depending on it, so tests should remove what a chain names and not only where it points.

papers.title: Benchmarking Deep Learning Models for Wheelchair Configuration Classification in Accessible Automated Vehicle Applications
papers.abstract: Making automated vehicles accessible requires consideration of vulnerable road users, including wheelchair users. To offer a more tailored experience that supports independence for this group, vehicle design needs to accommodate the wide range of wheelchair configurations. However, wheelchairs are individualized, varying in frame geometry, propulsion, and visual appearance. Moreover, occupants or accessories may obscure visual cues. Existing mobility-aid datasets only label the presence of a wheelchair, rather than describing its specific configuration. To fill this gap, this paper introduces the Wheelchair Configuration Image Dataset (WCID), comprising 467 face-blurred images across 192 capture groups solely for evaluation. Each image is annotated with (i) a two-class label of manual or powered, (ii) a chair subtype, (iii) occupancy, viewpoint, setting, lighting, occlusion, propulsion, and control, with a 273-image validation split and 194-image test split. Three convolutional neural network backbones and a frozen vision-language probe are trained on an external image dataset and evaluated on WCID to measure cross-dataset generalization, while also testing robustness using Gaussian blur. Convolutional models do well on clean images, but performance drops under strong blur, leaving a gap before deployment. Code, split assignments, labels, trained weights, and the face-blurred images is available at: https://github.com/Mi3-Lab/MAID
papers.summary: Accessible automated vehicles need to recognize the specific configuration of a wheelchair, but existing mobility-aid datasets only label whether one is present. The Wheelchair Configuration Image Dataset (`WCID`) is an evaluation-only set of **467 face-blurred images across 192 capture groups**, annotated with manual versus powered type, chair subtype, and attributes such as occupancy, viewpoint, lighting and occlusion. Three convolutional backbones and a frozen vision-language probe trained on an external dataset are tested on it for cross-dataset generalization and robustness to Gaussian blur. The convolutional models do well on clean images but degrade under strong blur.

papers.title: Conserved Verdicts, Drifting Commitments: Identifying Harmful Overthinking
papers.abstract: A reasoning model that has reached a correct answer can lose it by continuing to think. Deciding whether to stop means comparing two probabilities at the same point of a chain: that the answer the model would give if stopped now is correct (its commitment), and that the answer it will finish with is correct (its verdict). We show that the verdict alone, which is what final-correctness probes estimate, cannot make this comparison. As a forecast of a fixed outcome it has no predictable drift, whether continuing helps or hurts. The commitment-verdict gap equals the expected remaining change in answer quality and the accuracy gained by stopping. A second identity splits any accuracy-versus-budget curve into answer change within chains and change in which chains are still running. We measure both on MATH-500. At all 379 points where DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B holds a correct answer, selected without regard to how its chain ends, continuing loses 3.6 points on average (95% CI [2.2, 5.2]), and the loss concentrates in a few problems. In six reasoning models from three families, on MATH-500 and OlympiadBench and with budgets up to 16,384 tokens, declining accuracy curves come from which chains remain, while the chains still reasoning keep or improve their answers. An oracle stopping rule gains at most +1.8 and +2.5 points at 1.5B and 7B. The framework says what to measure before building a stopping rule.
papers.summary: A reasoning model can reach a correct answer and then lose it by continuing to think, and deciding when to stop requires comparing the probability that the answer it would give now is correct (its commitment) with the probability that its final answer is correct (its verdict). The authors show that the verdict alone, which final-correctness probes estimate, cannot make this comparison because it has no predictable drift, and that the commitment-verdict gap equals the accuracy gained by stopping. On `MATH-500`, at the 379 points where `DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B` holds a correct answer, **continuing loses 3.6 points on average**, concentrated in a few problems. Across six reasoning models on `MATH-500` and `OlympiadBench`, declining accuracy-versus-budget curves come from which chains are still running and not from answers degrading, and an oracle stopping rule gains at most 1.8 and 2.5 points at 1.5B and 7B.

papers.title: Honest Brokers in AI Regulation: How Public Comments Introduce Evidence to Regulators
papers.abstract: The regulation of Artificial Intelligence is susceptible to various forms of capture by industry actors that hold undue influence over the policymaking process, due in part to their information advantage in developing these technologies. In the following paper, we investigate the roles of public commenters in providing evidence to potential regulation in the USA. We build a corpus of 40 potential regulations, and 2,664 public comments submitted by a variety of stakeholders. We computationally process these texts to extract evidence meant to inform regulators, in the form of formal citations and informal references. We find significant differences in the type and amount of evidence supplied: Holding comment length constant, business commenters introduce altogether less evidence, and government, university, and civil society commenters provide significantly more research and legal sources. The publication status of cited research is nearly evenly split, with preprints and peer-reviewed articles being introduced by commenters of all types. We further explore patterns of self-citation and find that while it is prevalent amongst all groups, a small cluster of organizations account for over half of all self-citations in our corpus. Our findings complicate a narrative that public comments alone are means to information capture. We interpret these results in terms of the role that commenters attempt to play in the policymaking process-being either an Issue Advocate or an Honest Broker. These findings on the supply of evidence in public comments shed light on an often overlooked form of policymaking that has implications for how and through what sources information is made accessible to regulators of AI.
papers.summary: Concerns that industry can capture AI regulation through its information advantage motivate a study of what evidence public commenters supply to United States regulators. From a corpus of 40 potential regulations and 2,664 public comments, the authors computationally extract formal citations and informal references. Holding comment length constant, **business commenters introduce less evidence overall**, while government, university and civil society commenters provide significantly more research and legal sources. Cited research is split nearly evenly between preprints and peer-reviewed articles, and a small cluster of organizations accounts for over half of all self-citations.

papers.title: DiscoveryAgent: A Framework for Scientist-centric Agentic AI
papers.abstract: AI agents can assist scientific research, but balancing autonomous investigation with scientists' ability to inspect and redirect ongoing work remains a central design challenge. We present DiscoveryAgent, a domain-agnostic, scientist-centric system that combines autonomous investigation with scientist-directed hypothesis steering. Scientists select, refine, or replace hypotheses between research rounds, while audit agents interrogate checkpointed records to trace claims, reproduce analyses, and inform subsequent decisions. Across two predictive modeling tasks, DiscoveryAgent produced the best variable-star classifier among evaluated baselines and, with scientist steering, a protein variant-effect predictor surpassed by only one of 106 ProteinGym baselines. We develop a rigorous checkpointing system that enables highly capable audit agents, a scalable form of oversight for agentic research. Audit agents autonomously identify errors at higher rates than previous AI scientist agents, and scientists collaborating with audit agents identify 14x more valid errors versus scientists performing manual review. In three case studies led by domain experts across physical science, social science, and life science, we developed a multimodal photometric-redshift estimator that resolves complementary failures of images and photometry, achieving 0.971 AUROC for low-redshift classification; documented an 83% rise in Florida homeowners-insurance premiums from 2013 to 2023, with a growing, regressive burden; and identified CD4+ T-cell relay genes, which both receive and exert broad transcriptional regulation, enriched for autoimmune disease associations. Together, these results show how autonomous research can expand scientists' empirical reach while centering their authority over research direction and their ability to understand and challenge the evidence.
papers.summary: `DiscoveryAgent` is a domain-agnostic research agent system in which scientists select, refine or replace hypotheses between rounds of autonomous investigation, while audit agents interrogate checkpointed records to trace claims and reproduce analyses. On two predictive modelling tasks it produced the best variable-star classifier among the evaluated baselines and, with scientist steering, a protein variant-effect predictor surpassed by only one of 106 `ProteinGym` baselines. Scientists working with the audit agents identified **14x more valid errors than scientists reviewing manually**. Three expert-led case studies in physical, social and life science are also reported, including a multimodal photometric-redshift estimator reaching 0.971 AUROC for low-redshift classification.

papers.title: A Log-Timescale Perturbation Bound for Selective State Space Models at Every Sequence Length
papers.abstract: Mamba models deployed on streaming data, such as limit order book updates, run far past the sequence lengths they were trained on. A guarantee on how much a small change of input can move the hidden state therefore has to hold at every length. The closest existing bound we know of measures the change of the timescale additively, and it grows linearly with the sequence length unless the timescale is bounded away from zero. In this paper, we measure the change on a log scale instead. The key observation is that the decay factor of each step then moves by at most a fixed fraction of that step's input weight, so the per-step errors cannot pile up. Using this, we prove that two runs of a selective-scan cell from a common start stay within a bound that holds at every length, shrinks to zero with the size of the change and needs no lower bound on the timescale. We give a construction showing that, for small changes, this bound is within a factor of about 2 of the best possible, and we extend it to the update used in Mamba's released code when the timescale is bounded above. We then evaluate block-level bounds built from the theorem on two small models trained on one day of order book data. With a bounded timescale, a bound built on the existing analysis is tighter than ours for at most the first 8 steps. With Mamba's softplus timescale, whose certified lower bound is as small as $10^{-21}$, it is looser at every length. Our bounds hold for every input to a block, but they remain more than five orders of magnitude above the changes that gradient attacks find.
papers.summary: `Mamba` models deployed on streaming data run far past their training sequence lengths, yet the closest existing bound on how much a small input change can move the hidden state grows linearly with length unless the timescale is bounded away from zero. Measuring the timescale change on a log scale, the authors prove **a perturbation bound for a selective-scan cell that holds at every sequence length**, shrinks to zero with the size of the change, needs no lower bound on the timescale, and is within a factor of about 2 of the best possible for small changes.
