On two small models trained on one day of limit order book data, the bounds are tighter than the existing analysis in most regimes but remain more than five orders of magnitude above the changes that gradient attacks actually find.

papers.title: ThermLeT: Transformer-based Temperature Prediction for 2.5D Chiplet Architecture
papers.abstract: The drive toward heterogeneous 2.5D chiplet packages promises unmatched performance and customization, yet the resulting density amplifies thermal challenges. To facilitate rapid design space exploration, we present ThermLeT, a multimodal transformer-based, scale invariant surrogate that integrates power density maps, spatial coordinate embeddings, material properties and heat transfer rate to predict steady state temperature in 13 ms, about four orders of magnitude faster than conventional finite element solvers such as ANSYS. To train the transformer model, we also create a dataset of 6,221 chiplet layouts perturbed from three representative architectures. On a 150 sample test set, ThermLeT achieves an RMSE of 3.16{\deg}C and an MAE of 2.24{\deg}C, improving accuracy by 35% over ThermEDGe and by 71% over HotSpot, while running approximately 6x and 11x lower inference latencies respectively. Ablation studies confirm robust generalization to unseen floorplans. Code and dataset available at https://github.com/MicroSystemsDesignLab/ThermLeT
papers.summary: Dense 2.5D chiplet packages create thermal problems, and finite element solvers are too slow for rapid design space exploration. `ThermLeT` is a multimodal, scale-invariant transformer surrogate that takes power density maps, spatial coordinate embeddings, material properties and heat transfer rate and **predicts steady-state temperature in 13 ms**, about four orders of magnitude faster than solvers such as `ANSYS`. Trained on 6,221 chiplet layouts perturbed from three representative architectures, it reaches a root-mean-square error of 3.16 °C on a 150-sample test set, which is 35% more accurate than `ThermEDGe` and 71% more accurate than `HotSpot`.

papers.title: Eight in Ten LLMs Leak System-Prompt Secrets: Nevan, an Agentic Capture-the-Flag Study
papers.abstract: We audit instruction-hierarchy enforcement across 363 text-in/text-out models from the OpenRouter catalog. The research question we answer with this experiment is which models disclose a protected secret embedded in the system prompt, and through which techniques. Each model guards a secret 16-character flag set in its system prompt, while an artificial intelligence (AI) agent (OpenCode, powered by DeepSeek V4.1 Flash), steered by a human researcher, tries to persuade it to emit the flag. The flag was exfiltrated from 296 of the 363 models, plus four models released after the initial catalog freeze, for 300 captures in total. Of these, 170 involved a non-English language pivot, most often French. Each capture shows that a model ranked a user request above its system instruction at least once. It does not show that the model provably resists untested attacks, nor that it would consistently leak semantically sensitive data, nor that it is vulnerable to harmful-content jailbreaks. For practitioners, we draw three lessons: do not store secrets in system prompts, enforce critical behavior outside the model with output validation and deterministic checks, and do not let a large language model (LLM) judge be the sole decider of consequential outcomes.
papers.summary: An audit of instruction-hierarchy enforcement tests 363 text-in/text-out models from the `OpenRouter` catalog, each guarding a 16-character secret flag in its system prompt while an AI agent (`OpenCode` running `DeepSeek V4.1 Flash`), steered by a human researcher, tries to persuade it to reveal the flag. **The flag was extracted from 296 of the 363 models**, plus four released after the catalog freeze, and 170 of the 300 captures involved switching to a non-English language, most often French. The authors note that a capture shows only that a model ranked a user request above its system instruction at least once, not that it is vulnerable to harmful-content jailbreaks. Their advice to practitioners is to keep secrets out of system prompts, enforce critical behaviour outside the model with output validation and deterministic checks, and not let a large language model (LLM) judge be the sole decider of consequential outcomes.

papers.title: Weight-space programming for tractor guidance controller: large language models natively write neural network weights that steer a real tractor
papers.abstract: Weight-space programming is a process where a large language model reads and writes the weights of a neural network directly, guided by a natural language specification, without an optimiser or gradient descent. This study applies it to automatic tractor guidance, where a 253-parameter neural network steers along paths of lines and arcs and must be adapted when the machine changes, such as a slower steering actuator. GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 (also 5.2) edited the network for our research tractor using a small budget of simulated evaluations to repair a network trained for another tractor and write a controller into a network with zero weights. We compared them with an evolution strategy, gradient descent and pure pursuit in simulation and on the real tractor. Both models read the network and analysed the closed loop with control theory correctly, and Fable's repair without simulation succeeded only occasionally. With simulated feedback, both models repaired the trained network in single sessions and wrote a working controller from zero weights, whereas from zero the evolution strategy found none. The controllers written from zero were sparse and in a classical cascaded structure; one model edited the trained network while the other replaced it. Gradient descent reached higher accuracy with far more simulation, and all language model controllers steered the real tractor without intervention, with errors of the same order as pure pursuit. Language models can program the weights of a neural controller directly, much as control engineers design one. We call this Weight-Space Engineering.
papers.summary: Weight-space programming has a large language model read and write a neural network's weights directly from a natural-language specification, with no optimiser or gradient descent. Applied to a 253-parameter tractor steering network, `GPT-6 Astra` and `Claude Fable 5.1` used a small budget of simulated evaluations to repair a network trained for a different tractor and to write a working controller starting from all-zero weights, a starting point from which an evolution strategy found none. Gradient descent reached higher accuracy with far more simulation, but **all the language-model-written controllers steered the real tractor without intervention**, with errors of the same order as the classical pure pursuit method. The controllers written from zero were sparse and followed a classical cascaded structure.

papers.title: OCCAM: Improved Single-Cell Representation Learning and Perturbation Effect Prediction
papers.abstract: Predicting the effects of genetic perturbations requires models that generalize beyond observed cell contexts and gene combinations. We introduce Occam, a multilayer perceptron (MLP) framework for representation learning and perturbation-effect prediction. Occam combines cell representations learned through denoising with gene interaction, text, and protein-sequence features. It achieves the highest aggregate representation scores for perturbation information and cell-type preservation with batch integration. In cross-context few-shot prediction, a perturbation and a cell context are each observed during training, but never together. Occam better captures the measured response patterns for these unobserved combinations than four retrained competitors or direct transfer of the same perturbation's measured effects from other training cell lines. Without fine-tuning, Occam best distinguishes perturbations among the evaluated models and simple baselines in cell lines held out from predictor training, across seen and unseen assays. Predicting expression levels accurately in these settings remains challenging. For double perturbations, which target two genes simultaneously, Occam composes learned single-gene responses to better capture the combined response and reduce expression error compared with competing models and summed single-gene effects. These gains extend to both strongly additive and weakly additive responses. Together, these results support simple MLPs for cell representation learning and perturbation-effect prediction across contexts and gene combinations.
papers.summary: Predicting how cells respond to genetic perturbations requires generalizing to cell contexts and gene combinations never observed together. `Occam` is a multilayer perceptron (MLP) framework that combines cell representations learned through denoising with gene interaction, text, and protein-sequence features. It captures response patterns for unseen perturbation-context pairs better than four retrained competitors, and for double perturbations it **composes learned single-gene responses to beat both competing models and summed single-gene effects**. The authors note that predicting exact expression levels in held-out cell lines remains challenging.

papers.title: Solver to System: LLM Reasoning Across Representations and Execution in Scientific Simulation
papers.abstract: Simulators based on partial differential equations (PDEs) are widely used to model physical systems, but generating and interpreting PDE solver code with large language models (LLMs) remains challenging. Scientific simulation code is a useful testbed for LLM scientific reasoning because (1) one system can be represented by code, equations, natural language, and numerical trajectories and (2) code can execute successfully while implementing invalid physics. We introduce Solver2System, a dataset of PDE solvers with multiple representations, controlled corruptions, and lexical perturbations, to evaluate whether LLMs can recover the underlying physical system through (1) cross-representation consistency and (2) static and agentic detection of physical invalidity. Across eight open-weight models, LLMs systematically favor some representations when evidence conflicts, and lexical perturbations to code alter interpretation of other unchanged representations. Execution improves physical-validity judgments, but weaker agents can judge correctly without identifying the causal defect. Thus, LLMs may reach correct judgments despite inconsistent representation reconciliation or causal misdiagnosis.
papers.summary: Simulation code for partial differential equations (PDEs) can run successfully while implementing invalid physics, which makes it a useful test of whether large language models (LLMs) understand the system behind the code. `Solver2System` is a dataset of PDE solvers given as code, equations, natural language, and numerical trajectories, with controlled corruptions and lexical perturbations. Across eight open-weight models, LLMs systematically favor some representations when evidence conflicts, and renaming things in the code changes how they interpret the other, unchanged representations. Executing the code improves physical-validity judgments, but **weaker agents can reach the correct verdict without identifying the actual defect**.

papers.title: It's My Turn! Interpretable Methods Reveal Developmental Differences from Mother-Child Conversational Dynamics
papers.abstract: Understanding conversational interactions between mothers and children is an important challenge for computational behavioral modeling. Existing methods use traditional statistical approaches and subjective measures of conversational dynamics, without incorporating temporal or probabilistic modeling. We developed an interpretable computational framework that combines sequence analysis, information-theoretic measures, and Bayesian hierarchical modeling to characterize temporal conversational dynamics in parent-child play. We applied this framework to interactions from 94 mother-child dyads with two-year-old children. Sequence analysis revealed that dyads with lower language development (as defined by scores on the Bayley developmental test) exhibited more heterogeneous conversational organization and fewer serve-and-return exchanges than higher-development dyads, a reciprocal turn-taking pattern in which one partner initiates communication and the other responds. Mutual information analyses suggested differences in conversational predictability between lower- and higher-development dyads, although the bootstrap confidence intervals overlapped. Bayesian hierarchical models estimated temporal trajectories for maternal consecutive turns, child responses following maternal speech, and overlapping responses; HDIs showed that trajectories differed in whether they excluded 0, but there were no statistically credible differences between the Bayley groups. Overall, these results indicate that children with higher developmental scores have more organized and predictable communication styles, with more ``serve-and-return" patterns with their mothers. These results demonstrate that interpretable computational representations of conversational dynamics capture developmental differences beyond simple measures of speech quantity.
papers.summary: Mother-child conversation is usually analyzed with traditional statistics and subjective measures that ignore temporal structure. The authors combine sequence analysis, information-theoretic measures, and Bayesian hierarchical modeling, and apply the framework to play sessions from 94 mother-child dyads with two-year-olds. Dyads with lower language scores on the Bayley developmental test showed **more heterogeneous conversational organization and fewer serve-and-return exchanges**, the reciprocal pattern in which one partner initiates and the other responds. The mutual information differences had overlapping bootstrap confidence intervals, and the Bayesian models found no statistically credible differences between the groups.

papers.title: Beyond Bitwidth: Deployment-Constrained Mixed-Precision Quantization for Multilingual LLM Inference on NVIDIA Blackwell
papers.abstract: Low-bit LLM quantization is useful only if a model preserves service-relevant accuracy, executes through supported GPU kernels, and meets measured memory and latency limits. We study Qwen3-8B on NVIDIA B200 with vLLM, including INT2/INT3, GPTQ, NVFP4, and mixed-precision configurations. We verify native packed execution and precision on all 144 fused linear modules and evaluate Korean, English, numerical, and reasoning quality under preregistered gates. Packed INT2 and INT3 execute, but all seven tested INT2 grids degenerate on generation. Isolated module-restoration effects are strongly non-additive; Korean and reasoning sensitivity rankings disagree, and a promising INT4/INT8 development candidate fails independent final evaluation. A configuration with 16-bit activations, 98 NVFP4 weight-only modules, 46 INT8 modules, and an INT8 output head passes all gates on the untouched FINAL-81 set (5,168 items): 5.917 GiB of weight-loading memory (limit 5.98), Korean teacher-correct retention 0.904 (gate 0.90), and TPOT ratio 0.939 relative to BF16. It improves paired accuracy over NVFP4 W4A4 by +1.4 percentage points (Bonferroni-adjusted interval [+0.2, +2.6]), compared with +3.4 points on the selection set. This comparison changes both activation precision and INT8 protection; exploratory analyses suggest that the activation change contributes substantially, but the isolated allocation effect is not established. Final checkpoints were not retained, and bitwise rebuild reproducibility remains unverified.
papers.summary: Low-bit quantization only helps in production if the model keeps its accuracy, runs through supported GPU kernels, and meets measured memory and latency limits. The authors study `Qwen3-8B` on an NVIDIA B200 with `vLLM`, testing INT2/INT3, `GPTQ`, `NVFP4`, and mixed-precision configurations against preregistered quality gates for Korean, English, numerical, and reasoning tasks. All seven INT2 grids degenerate on generation, per-module sensitivity effects are strongly non-additive, and a promising INT4/INT8 candidate fails independent final evaluation. A mix of 98 `NVFP4` and 46 INT8 modules with 16-bit activations **passes every gate at 5.917 GiB of weight memory, gaining 1.4 percentage points over `NVFP4` W4A4**, though the comparison confounds activation precision with module allocation and the final checkpoints were not retained.

papers.title: Pathology Randomization for Synthetic Priors and Zero-Shot Detection
papers.abstract: Hospital brain imaging archives hold a diverse array of pathology at sample sizes beyond prospective studies, particularly for underrepresented populations and diseases. To unlock uncurated clinical data and scale analysis, methods are needed to detect abnormalities across contrasts and resolutions. Synthetic data has provided robust, contrast-agnostic models for a variety of human neuroimaging tasks in healthy anatomy, but pathology detection and other tasks in clinical settings still require real patient data, contrast-specific models, or disease-specific generators. We propose PathoDraw, a generative model of brain MRI with pathology. A conditional distribution of lesions given the healthy anatomy is drawn into the label map before contrast-agnostic rendering, and a single network estimates healthy anatomy with exact signed intensity deviation of any input scan. The contrast-agnostic 3D UNet learns the healthy labels under the lesion and the signed deviation directly and identifies pathology via robust tissue statistics and learned features, despite no training on real pathology. We show zero-shot detection on public stroke, tumor, and white matter hyperintensity datasets as well as archived clinical data, spanning $T_1$w, FLAIR and $T_2$w at various resolutions under a recent unsupervised anomaly detection benchmark protocol. Our single model exceeds or performs comparably to contrast-specific anomaly detectors trained on real scans and keeps healthy anatomy intact. The same generator trains networks for super-resolution and for registration in the presence of pathology. Our model, robust across acquisition and disease, enables the use of uncurated, archived data for clinical analysis. Our code is available at https://github.com/agr78/Pathology-Randomizer.
papers.summary: Synthetic training data has produced contrast-agnostic brain MRI models for healthy anatomy, but detecting pathology still tends to require real patient scans, contrast-specific models, or disease-specific generators. `PathoDraw` is a generative model that draws lesions into the anatomical label map before contrast-agnostic rendering, and trains a single 3D UNet to estimate the healthy anatomy under a lesion plus the signed intensity deviation of any input scan. With no training on real pathology, the one model **matches or exceeds contrast-specific anomaly detectors trained on real scans** on public stroke, tumor, and white matter hyperintensity datasets and on archived clinical data across T1-weighted, FLAIR, and T2-weighted contrasts. The same generator also trains networks for super-resolution and for registration in the presence of pathology.

papers.title: Sparse Integer Fourier Transform and Its Application In Machine Learning
papers.abstract: The Discrete Fourier transform, mainly implemented by Fast Fourier Transform (FFT), has been essential for numerous domains, such as digital signal processing and feature extraction in materials design. However, current FFT methods suffer from extensive non-trivial multiplications and twiddle-factor operations in the big data era. To improve the computational efficiency of FFT, this study proposes Sparse Integer Fourier Transform (SIFT), a method that leverages the fast computing of sparsity and small integers, and applies the Radix-n method to derive an FFT. The 2N-point DFT matrix in Radix-n FFT is decomposed into four sparse integer matrices. A diagonal matrix containing complex twiddle factors is efficiently approximated using an optimization strategy while the remaining matrices retain sparsity and integer entries. For radix-32 FFT, SIFT reduces the estimated arithmetic cost by 75%, with RMSE below $2.3765\times10^{-8}$ and MAPE below 0.01089%. We evaluate frequency extraction in a numerical test and an engineering case. In the numerical test, MAPE and RMSE are below 2.016% and $2.536\times10^{-6}$, respectively. For wind turbine fault diagnosis, SIFT extracts compact spectral features that retain fault information while reducing the classifier's input dimensionality relative to the full time series.
papers.summary: Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) implementations spend much of their cost on non-trivial multiplications and twiddle-factor operations. The Sparse Integer Fourier Transform (`SIFT`) decomposes the DFT matrix of a Radix-n FFT into four sparse integer matrices, with a diagonal matrix of complex twiddle factors approximated through an optimization strategy. For radix-32, it **reduces the estimated arithmetic cost by 75%** with root-mean-square error below 2.4e-8. In a wind turbine fault diagnosis case, it extracts compact spectral features that retain fault information while shrinking the classifier's input dimensionality.

papers.title: WebAgents: Unbundling Agent Creation, Hosting, and Execution for an Agent-Native Web
papers.abstract: Large language models are moving from isolated assistants toward autonomous agents that can plan, use tools, and coordinate with others, motivating an emerging Agentic Web of independently developed agents and services. Realizing this vision requires agent behavior to move across creators, hosts, and runtimes without coupling publication to a particular execution environment or transferring authority over user resources. We introduce WebAgents, which unbundles these roles through a signed agent.pkg that carries portable workflows, skills, schemas, and resource requirements. An OpenClaw-based agent-native browser/runtime verifies the package, obtains authorization, and binds it at run time to user-controlled models, tools, permissions, and budgets, while hosts distribute the public program and may retain private services server-side. We demonstrate this contract with three unrelated workflows executed unchanged under local and API-backed models, including literature review with live services and a website-published travel agent using semantic tools and user-selected personal resources. In a controlled suite, WebAgents explicitly blocks all 716 injected contract violations while accepting all 295 matched benign controls, with median automated pre-execution processing below 0.5 s for all three packages. We conclude by outlining a path toward NANDA-based discovery and interoperable package ecosystems while retaining execution authority in the user's runtime.
papers.summary: An open web of independently built agents needs agent behavior to move between creators, hosts, and runtimes without tying publication to one execution environment or handing over authority over user resources. `WebAgents` separates those roles with a signed `agent.pkg` carrying portable workflows, skills, schemas, and resource requirements, which an `OpenClaw`-based browser runtime verifies and binds at run time to user-controlled models, tools, permissions, and budgets. Three unrelated workflows ran unchanged under both local and API-backed models, including a literature review and a website-published travel agent. In a controlled suite the runtime **blocked all 716 injected contract violations while accepting all 295 matched benign controls**, with median pre-execution processing under 0.5 seconds.

papers.title: Modeling Document and Section Hierarchies in Embedding Space
papers.abstract: Embedded topic models integrate word embeddings into the topic generation process, producing coherent topics and robust performance on large vocabularies. However, each document is represented by a single topic distribution, ignoring its internal structure. Many real world collections, including legal documents, company and government reports, and online discussion forums, exhibit hierarchical organization in which documents consist of multiple sections that often address distinct subtopics. We introduce the Hierarchical Embedded Topic Model (hETM), a structured topic model that couples the topic distribution of a document and those of its sections through a hierarchical prior in the embedding space. We derive an amortized variational inference procedure for hETM and evaluate it on structured collections from each of these domains. Experimental results show that hETM achieves the lowest or near-lowest held-out perplexity among flat and hierarchical topic model baselines, along with comparable or higher topic quality. It also performs strongly on a downstream clustering task, achieving the best clustering performance on most of the collections.
papers.summary: Embedded topic models represent each document with a single topic distribution, ignoring that legal documents, reports, and forum threads are made of sections covering distinct subtopics. The Hierarchical Embedded Topic Model (`hETM`) couples a document's topic distribution with those of its sections through a hierarchical prior in the embedding space, trained with amortized variational inference. Across structured collections from these domains it achieves **the lowest or near-lowest held-out perplexity among flat and hierarchical baselines**, with comparable or higher topic quality. It also gives the best downstream clustering performance on most of the collections.

papers.title: Large Language Models as Nonlinear Dynamical Systems: The Three Clocks of Depth, Training, and Generation
papers.abstract: Language models are dynamical systems. A transformer is iterated over its layers, over the steps of its training and over the tokens it generates, and on each of these three clocks it shows behavior that nonlinear dynamics has studied for a century: fixed points, bifurcations, synchronization, chaos and noise-driven escape from potential wells. The two communities rarely meet, so this behavior is often rediscovered under new names. We build a bridge between them. To describe, we condense about 200 papers into the Three-Clock Dictionary, which maps fifteen concepts of nonlinear dynamics onto each clock and marks every correspondence as proved, measured or conjectured, and we show each concept in a mechanical system and in a language model side by side. To explain, we derive reduced-order models: the softmax is a Boltzmann distribution, gradient descent an Euler step on a nonlinear spring, a loss spike a ball thrown out of a stiff valley, attention on the circle a Kuramoto model, and a repetition loop a well that deepens while it is occupied. We then test these explanations on open language models, on a laptop CPU. Escape from repetition loops in GPT-2 and Pythia follows the Arrhenius law with the logit gap as the barrier, and the barrier deepens and then saturates, so the temperature needed to leave a loop falls like $1/\ln N$ with the generation length $N$ and rises with model size. Coherent text lives in a narrow window of temperatures, which a small reasoning model shares at its recommended temperature. Training makes each Pythia layer more expansive, and a small transformer trains at a multi-mode edge of stability. The third step, solving problems of language models, is still ahead: controllers derived from the escape analysis remove loops but do not yet beat the best fixed temperature. We state twelve open problems where nonlinear dynamics could get there.
papers.summary: Transformers are iterated over layers, training steps, and generated tokens, and on each of these three clocks they show behavior long studied in nonlinear dynamics, such as fixed points, bifurcations, synchronization, and chaos. The authors condense about 200 papers into a `Three-Clock Dictionary` mapping fifteen dynamics concepts onto each clock and marking every correspondence as proved, measured, or conjectured, then derive reduced-order models such as attention as a Kuramoto model. Laptop-CPU experiments on `GPT-2` and `Pythia` show that **escape from repetition loops follows the Arrhenius law with the logit gap as the barrier**, so the temperature needed to leave a loop falls like 1/ln N with generation length N and rises with model size. Controllers derived from this analysis remove loops but do not yet beat the best fixed temperature, and twelve open problems are listed.

papers.title: Deciding Without Pointing: A Case Study of Whether a Decision Model Localizes the Anomalies It Detects
papers.abstract: Decision models can answer a typed question about an image with a probability per option, without generating text. In our case study of Clef-flash (post-trained Qwen3.5-9B backbone) on industrial inspection benchmarks, we ask whether it localizes the anomalies it detects. We obtained uneven results with zero-shot detection: per-category image AUROC 0.924 on MVTec AD and 0.668 on MVTec AD 2. On the former, the decision head's routing attention produces 0.391 mean per-image pixel AUROC, and hiding the image tokens from it leaves detection unchanged. The multimodal LLM's backbone attention does point at the defect, however it falls below a center prior when we change question. It falls below chance if we remove textual context in the question, partly due to backbone attention leaving the object, while the head's map hardly changes. The backbone's states carry the location when probed with normal images, on the test-split images, however, the decision depends on the defect region. A larger model, Clef, that comes with a post-trained Qwen3.8-27B backbone, gives no useful map in the decision head either. We found that it's possible to recover anomaly location by asking question specifically on an image region, retraining the head or reading the backbone, but none matches dedicated few-shot localizers.
papers.summary: Decision models answer a typed question about an image with a probability per option instead of generating text, which raises the question of whether they locate the anomalies they detect. In a case study of `Clef-flash`, built on a post-trained `Qwen3.5-9B` backbone, zero-shot detection reaches image AUROC of 0.924 on `MVTec AD` and 0.668 on `MVTec AD 2`. The decision head's routing attention **yields only 0.391 mean per-image pixel AUROC, and hiding the image tokens from it leaves detection unchanged**, while the backbone's attention does point at defects but is fragile to changes in the question. Location can be recovered by asking about specific image regions, retraining the head, or reading the backbone, but none of these matches dedicated few-shot localizers.

papers.title: KV-LTM: Persistent Per-Session KV Caches as Long-Term Memory for Personal Assistants
papers.abstract: Personal assistants accumulate months of conversations, but today's long-term memory stacks put derivation or selection between a question and its evidence. In a system-level comparison on LongMemEval, two commercial assistants scored well below the same model reading the history offline [1], consistent with, but not isolating, content loss between write and read. We propose KV-LTM: a memory tier storing each session's raw text plus its KV cache under a fixed reader model, answering by restoring cached sessions and appending the question. KV-LTM is complementary to, not a replacement for, retrieval and indexing. Text is the memory of record; the cache is a recompute-free prefill accelerator, degrading gracefully to text. We specify the design: storage record, budget-derived retention, append-only read path, and bounded aggregation. We size it analytically: across pinned BF16 full-attention (GQA) and latent-cached MLA configurations, per-token state spans approximately 31K-328K bytes (the pinned KDA+MLA hybrid differs: approximately 8.1K bytes/token plus a fixed per-session recurrent term), giving approximately 0.34-3.6 TB per user-year at a declared 30K-token/day scenario, against approximately 49 MB of raw text; per-query cost is modelled as regime-conditional transfer, attention, decode, aggregation, and compute. We define an evaluation protocol needing no persistent-cache implementation for logical QA evaluation: per-session prefill emulates valid cache reuse under the same model/input-state contract and ideal arithmetic, with named arms, controlled baselines, and a preregistered reader-model gate; a separate minimal real-cache replay tests numerical equivalence and measures the cost axis, with outcomes not assumed. KV-LTM trades storage for avoided re-prefill compute and write-time fidelity, within a declared retention budget.
papers.summary: Long-term memory stacks for personal assistants typically summarize or select from past conversations, which can lose evidence between writing and reading. `KV-LTM` is a proposed memory tier that stores each session's raw text alongside its key-value (KV) cache under a fixed reader model, answering questions by restoring cached sessions and appending the question, with text as the record and the cache as a prefill accelerator. Analytical sizing puts the cost at **roughly 0.34 to 3.6 TB per user-year at 30K tokens per day, against about 49 MB of raw text**. No empirical results are reported; the authors specify the design and define an evaluation protocol on `LongMemEval` that emulates cache reuse through per-session prefill.

papers.title: How Much Distribution Shift Can a Clustering Withstand? Exact Split and Merge Certificates for Structured Transports
papers.abstract: In clustering, the distribution of the population being clustered is often uncertain or changes over time, so the true distribution may shift away from the nominal distribution used to form the clustering. Once the clustering is committed and each member is assigned to a cluster, such shifts may change the distribution of each cluster. They can make a cluster too spread out for one representative at a given resolution, motivating a split, or bring distinct clusters close enough to share a representative at that resolution, motivating a merge. We make these split and merge events precise using a local stability criterion built on the phase-transition analysis in deterministic annealing. This notion of stability enables us to quantify how robust a clustering is against such events. Furthermore, motivated by applications in which uncertainty and population change are structured, we study shifts whose displacements are restricted to a prescribed subspace. The smallest structured shifts that reach the respective thresholds define the split and merge radii, for which we obtain exact semidefinite programming (SDP) reformulations. The split SDP has only two scalar decision variables. These convex reformulations enable us to combine the radii into a robustness certificate for the full clustering that gives the size of the smallest structured shift that reaches any monitored split or merge threshold.
papers.summary: Once a clustering is committed, shifts in the underlying population can spread a cluster too wide for one representative or bring distinct clusters close enough to share one. The authors formalize these split and merge events with a local stability criterion based on the phase-transition analysis in deterministic annealing, and consider shifts whose displacements are restricted to a prescribed subspace. The smallest structured shifts that trigger a split or merge **admit exact semidefinite programming (SDP) reformulations**, with the split SDP needing only two scalar decision variables. Combining these radii gives a robustness certificate for the whole clustering.

papers.title: DiagTrace: An Interactive Benchmark for Clinical Decision Making
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance on medical question answering and diagnostic reasoning benchmarks. However, existing evaluations typically provide all patient information upfront and assess only the final diagnosis or rationale. This setup ignores the need to acquire diagnostic evidence incrementally from incomplete information in real-world diagnosis. To bridge this gap, we introduce DiagTrace, a source-grounded benchmark for evaluating whether LLMs can reconstruct the documented diagnostic trajectory through interactive information seeking. Each benchmark instance is built from a PubMed Central case report and includes an initial presentation, an event bank, a clinical course, and diagnostic references. DiagTrace contains 510 cases across eight specialties, with 225 used to evaluate four LLMs on clinical-course alignment, interaction quality, and efficiency. Results reveal trade-offs in coverage, source-consistent ordering, and turn use.
papers.summary: Medical benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) usually present all patient information upfront and grade only the final diagnosis, ignoring that real diagnosis means gathering evidence step by step. `DiagTrace` builds interactive cases from PubMed Central case reports, each with an initial presentation, an event bank, a clinical course, and diagnostic references, and scores whether a model reconstructs the documented diagnostic trajectory through its own information seeking. The benchmark holds **510 cases across eight specialties, 225 of which were used to evaluate four LLMs**. Results show trade-offs between coverage, source-consistent ordering, and number of turns used.

papers.title: On Formal Counterfactual Explanations
papers.abstract: Counterfactual explanations are often seen as counterfactual conditionals under closest-world semantics, requiring one to reason over all minimally distant counterexamples. In contrast, formal XAI typically relies on feature-based abductive explanations (AXps) and contrastive explanations (CXps), which admit efficient computation and a minimal hitting-set duality. This paper bridges these perspectives by (i) characterizing closest-world counterfactual explanations explicitly as a disjunctive normal form over all minimally distant counterexample instances, and (ii) introducing conjunctive counterfactual explanations (CFXps), a subclass of counterfactual antecedents restricted to conjunctions of feature literals that guarantee prediction change. The paper establishes structural results connecting CXps, AXps and CFXps: every CXp induces an AXp for its witness instance, and every CXp together with a witness AXp induces a CFXp whose support is precisely determined by that AXp. These theoretical results yield a modular approach for computing CFXps using existing AXp/CXp machinery. Experiments on a representative set of benchmarks using tree ensembles and neural networks show that CFXp extraction is practically efficient. Compared with popular point-based counterfactual explainers, CFXps generally require no more feature changes and can guarantee the counterfactual prediction beyond a single instance.
papers.summary: Counterfactual explanations under closest-world semantics require reasoning over all minimally distant counterexamples, whereas formal explainability relies on feature-based abductive explanations (AXps) and contrastive explanations (CXps) that are cheaper to compute. The authors characterize closest-world counterfactuals as a disjunctive normal form over those counterexamples and introduce conjunctive counterfactual explanations (CFXps), conjunctions of feature literals guaranteed to change the prediction. They prove that every CXp together with a witness AXp induces a CFXp, which lets existing AXp/CXp tooling compute them. On tree ensembles and neural networks, CFXps **generally need no more feature changes than popular point-based explainers while guaranteeing the prediction change beyond a single instance**.

papers.title: SkillBuffBench: Measuring What Agent Skills Contribute across Harnesses, Models, Skill Access Modes and Memory
papers.abstract: Agent Skills, file-based packages of procedural knowledge that a coding agent can discover and load on demand, are now shipped by every major agent harness, yet the evidence for how much they help comes almost entirely from settings in which the right Skill is hand-picked for the task and the agent starts from a blank slate. Neither holds in deployment, where an agent chooses from whatever library happens to be installed and frequently carries memory from earlier work. We present SkillBuffBench, a benchmark and paired evaluation protocol that treats Skill access as a three-level factor (no Skill, a curated Skill, and automatic invocation from an installed library), crosses it with memory (off and on), with four agent harnesses and with multiple models (the state-of-the-art proprietary models from Anthropic, Google and OpenAI, and the state-of-the-art open-weight models from Chinese providers), every model being run under every harness, and evaluates the result on research tasks contributed by domain experts together with the Skills they use, currently in materials science and biology, with the suite extended on a rolling basis. Every run is marked by a deterministic verifier; uncertainty is reported with a paired, task-level bootstrap; and cost, agent rounds and wall-clock time are reported alongside the score rather than folded into it. This version of the paper describes the design of the benchmark, its evaluation protocol and its current tasks and Skills. The evaluation is in progress: results will be added once the runs are complete, and the task suite, results and analysis will continue to be updated on a rolling basis.
papers.summary: Agent Skills, file-based packages of procedural knowledge that coding agents load on demand, have mostly been evaluated with the right Skill hand-picked and the agent starting from a blank slate. `SkillBuffBench` instead crosses three levels of Skill access (none, curated, and automatic invocation from an installed library) with memory on and off, four agent harnesses, and multiple proprietary and open-weight models, on expert-contributed research tasks in materials science and biology. Runs are scored by a deterministic verifier with paired task-level bootstrap uncertainty, and cost, agent rounds, and wall-clock time are reported separately from the score. This version covers only the design, protocol, and current tasks: **the evaluation is still in progress and no results are reported yet**.

papers.title: Computed Permutation Trellis Coding: Near-Optimal Quantization from Two Multiplications and a 64-Byte Table
papers.abstract: We propose Computed Permutation Trellis Coding (CPTC), a low-bit quantization format for tensors written once and read many times. Formats that round each value on its own, such as INT4 and FP4, waste a large part of their bits against the information-theoretic ideal. Trellis codes recover this loss by encoding values jointly, but prior decoders either need a large lookup table for their best quality or compute values with a hash that restricts what they can decode. CPTC's decoder multiplies its state by two coefficients and adds the top bits of the products to index a 64-byte table. Because that sum is not uniformly distributed, the rarely used ends of a small table can hold values far out in the tails. One decoder serves every bit width from 1 to 6, reproduces the standard integer and floating-point formats exactly, and comes within 0.07 bits of the ideal at 4 bits. It matches a random-permutation trellis code whose table is thousands of times larger, and exceeds every QTIP codebook. In LLM weight quantization without fine-tuning, CPTC has the lowest KL divergence to the unquantized model at every tested bit width on Llama 3.1 8B and 70B Instruct against QTIP's codebooks (by up to 27%). The decoder has been built into the AWS Trainium 4 AI accelerator, where it runs at the throughput of the native FP4 and FP8 formats for a negligible fraction of the systolic array's area. Fused encoding kernels quantize an 8B model's linear layers in under two minutes on one GPU and, in cycle-level simulation, on one Trainium 4 chip.
papers.summary: Low-bit formats that round each value independently, such as INT4 and FP4, waste much of their bit budget, and trellis codes that fix this have needed either large lookup tables or restrictive hash-based decoders. Computed Permutation Trellis Coding (`CPTC`) decodes by multiplying its state by two coefficients and using the top bits of the products to index a 64-byte table, with one decoder covering every bit width from 1 to 6. It **comes within 0.07 bits of the information-theoretic ideal at 4 bits** and matches a random-permutation trellis code whose table is thousands of times larger. Without fine-tuning, it achieves lower KL divergence to the unquantized model than `QTIP` codebooks at every tested bit width on `Llama 3.1` 8B and 70B Instruct, and the decoder has been built into the AWS Trainium 4 accelerator.

papers.title: An AI-Based OSSE Framework to Evaluate Learned Physical Consistency: A Multi-Model Study Using FourCastNet, Aurora, Prithvi WxC, and GraphCast
papers.abstract: Observing System Simulation Experiments (OSSEs) are a central methodology for evaluating future atmospheric observing systems. We present the first AI-based OSSE framework to test whether different AI weather models can reproduce comparable physical impact from new observations that traditional physics based models generate. We evaluate four distinct architectural AI models on the Charney conjecture that incomplete historical observations can infer the present state of the atmospheric. We considner- FourCastNet V2, GraphCast, Aurora and Prithvi WxC and integrate each autoregressively over a 60-day forecast horizon. After a 30-day spin-up, we insert ERA5 temperature fields to infer winds and related atmospheric fields. Similar OSSE experiments are conducted for wind insertion. We measure the performance of each model's response to observational information on a 30-day data assimilation cycle forecast with and without data insertion. Distinct architectural AI weather models respond differently to the same OSSE observations. Foundation models (i.e. Prithvi WxC and Aurora), produce the strongest impact. For example, while GraphCast is the weakest, all three of the four models capture the temperature-to-geopotential height response. The two foundational models retain a positive, non-trivial, tropical zonal wind at 500 hPa response to temperature insertion. Various data insertion experiments can vary significantly even within a given architecture. We identify an architecture-specific numerical instability in GraphCast's full 37-level configuration that produces a runaway feedback concentrated at the uppermost levels with ERA5 temperature insertion correctable by excluding levels at or below 100 hPa.
papers.summary: Observing System Simulation Experiments (OSSEs) estimate the value of new atmospheric observations, traditionally with physics-based models. The authors build an AI-based OSSE framework that inserts ERA5 temperature or wind fields into 60-day autoregressive runs of `FourCastNet V2`, `GraphCast`, `Aurora`, and `Prithvi WxC` and measures how the other atmospheric fields respond. The models react differently to the same observations: **the foundation models `Prithvi WxC` and `Aurora` produce the strongest physical response and `GraphCast` the weakest**, with three of the four capturing the temperature-to-geopotential-height response. `GraphCast` in its 37-level configuration also shows a runaway instability at the uppermost levels under temperature insertion, which can be corrected by excluding some levels.

papers.title: GauntletScore: Auditable Fact-Checking That Matches the Best Published Checkers on LLM-AggreFact
papers.abstract: Checking whether a generated sentence is supported by its source document is a standard safeguard for AI-written text, and the strongest published checkers are single models. We describe GauntletScore, an evidence engine whose few rules and thresholds were set on the benchmark's development split. It puts typed questions to independent readers from different providers and records each answer as a measurement in an evidence ledger. It combines the measurements with a fixed Bayesian rule that counts a contradiction only when two readers agree. On the full LLM-AggreFact test split (29,320 claims across 11 datasets), following the leaderboard's approach, GauntletScore achieves 79.51 balanced accuracy, above every average published on the leaderboard as of 15 November 2026. That places it level with the best of them, nimble-v4-max (79.45 from its published dataset scores; the engine's 95% interval, 78.47 to 80.53, contains it). On the same claims it beats two of its three readers used alone (Readers A and B) by 1.66 and 2.17 points (95% intervals 0.80 to 2.53 and 1.29 to 3.06). Without AggreFact-CNN, described below, the leads are 0.90 and 1.32 and both intervals stay above zero. The engine also records the evidence behind every verdict, which a single model does not. Its largest margin is on full-length news articles checked against multi-sentence summaries (AggreFact-CNN), a format that resembles much regulated writing. There it scores 76.45, the best on the leaderboard, against 70.1 for the next best and 63.9 to 67.8 for the six systems with the highest averages. The test split was run once, on an engine frozen before the first test claim, under a stopping plan committed in advance. We release per-claim predictions and the scoring script.
papers.summary: Checking whether a generated sentence is supported by its source document is usually done by a single model. `GauntletScore` instead puts typed questions to independent reader models from different providers, logs each answer in an evidence ledger, and combines them with a fixed Bayesian rule that counts a contradiction only when two readers agree. On the full `LLM-AggreFact` test split of 29,320 claims it reaches **79.51 balanced accuracy, statistically level with the best published checker, `nimble-v4-max`, at 79.45**, and beats two of its three readers used alone by 1.66 and 2.17 points. Its largest margin is on `AggreFact-CNN`, full news articles checked against multi-sentence summaries, where it scores 76.45 against 70.1 for the next best system.

papers.title: What Does an Agent Need? Bundle-Aware Agent Resource Composition
papers.abstract: An agent resource's value depends on its backbone and companion resources and is known only after execution. Token-based generators remain tied to their training catalog, while independent resource scoring misses complementarities and reused bundles target other tasks. We formulate Task-Conditioned Agent Resource Composition (AgentComposition): jointly selecting a backbone model and a tool-skill bundle to maximize end-to-end execution utility. Our Retrieval-Grounded Bundle-Aware Agent Generation retrieves candidate resources and past configurations of similar tasks. A fine-tuned generator reads resource descriptions and recombines candidates through constrained beam search, allowing new resources without retraining. A bundle-aware critic ranks complete configurations using a large language model (LLM) teacher and historically successful configurations as execution proxies, and adapts to execution feedback when available. We evaluate reference recovery, offline execution with judged and native rewards, and online recommendation with real execution, building AgentSelect-Exec with 5,060 executed configurations. Our method recovers the complete reference configuration within ten candidates for 67.73% of AgentSelect queries, nearly twice the strongest baseline, and leads all baselines on SkillsBench. The proxy-trained critic raises the top-ranked agent's execution score from 7.58 to 8.37 out of 10; execution feedback increases it to 8.78, above the strongest baselines. Four target-domain queries suffice to adapt the generator to SkillsBench. Agents recommended online outperform the strongest baselines under both an LLM judge and native verifiers. These results support learning and transferring joint resource composition from task experience.
papers.summary: Choosing the right backbone model and set of tools and skills for an agent is hard because resources complement one another and their value is known only after execution. The authors frame this as Task-Conditioned Agent Resource Composition and propose a retrieval-grounded pipeline: a fine-tuned generator recombines retrieved candidates through constrained beam search, and a bundle-aware critic ranks complete configurations using a large language model (LLM) teacher and past successful configurations as execution proxies. The method **recovers the full reference configuration within ten candidates for 67.73% of `AgentSelect` queries, nearly twice the strongest baseline**, and leads all baselines on `SkillsBench`. The critic raises the top-ranked agent's execution score from 7.58 to 8.37 out of 10, and to 8.78 with execution feedback, on the new `AgentSelect-Exec` set of 5,060 executed configurations.

papers.title: Thinking Harder Doesn't Lead to Better Choices: Reasoning Effort Increases the Confidence but Not the Correctness of LLM Shopping Agents
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous shopping agents that process multimodal product listings (consisting of visual and text data) and recommend purchases on behalf of consumers. Naturally, one might assume that models with more thinking power would make higher-quality purchasing decisions. To test this belief, we ask two questions about such agents: does asking a model to think harder make it choose better products, and does the confidence it reports tell us the likelihood it may be wrong? We benchmark ten frontier models on three product-choice benchmarks built from WebShop, Amazon's SQID and Wayfair's WANDS platforms to see if LLMs with more thinking power actually make better-quality product purchase decisions. Across all three benchmarks, we found that increasing the thinking effort does not increase decision quality in a statistically meaningful way. The same change in thinking effort raises stated confidence at a statistically significant level, so extra thinking buys confidence rather than correctness. We also measure the calibration of these models (how well their reported confidence percentage matches their true correctness percentage) in these tasks and show that most models are not well-calibrated at every effort level. We also find that errors are strongly shared: when one model errs in a task, several others tend to err on that same task. Furthermore, on tasks where several models all err, a large number of them pick the same wrong product.
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) shopping agents read multimodal product listings and recommend purchases, and it is natural to assume more reasoning effort yields better choices. Ten frontier models were benchmarked on product-choice tasks built from `WebShop`, Amazon's `SQID`, and Wayfair's `WANDS`. Across all three, **raising thinking effort did not improve decision quality in a statistically meaningful way but did significantly raise stated confidence**, and most models were poorly calibrated at every effort level. Errors were also strongly shared: when one model failed a task several others tended to fail it too, often picking the same wrong product.

papers.title: GP--RL--MPC: Uncertainty-Aware Reinforcement Learning-Augmented Model Predictive Control with Gaussian Process Postdecision State-Value Functions
papers.abstract: We propose Gaussian Process Reinforcement Learning-Augmented Model Predictive Control (GP--RL--MPC), which uses a learned critic as the MPC terminal penalty to account for costs beyond the prediction horizon. Gaussian process regression (GPR) enables data-efficient critic learning from limited, noisy rollouts within optimistic approximate policy iteration (OAPI), with soft updates mitigating policy chattering. A tunable risk coefficient weights GP epistemic uncertainty in the terminal cost, regulating sensitivity to uncertain critic predictions. The postdecision state formulation shifts disturbance averaging offline to account for aleatoric uncertainty from the terminal transition onward. Under matching objectives and admissible actions, a one-step horizon recovers greedy value-space RL. After fitting GP hyperparameters by exact marginal likelihood, we construct a sparse deterministic training conditional (DTC) posterior using inducing points selected by pivoted Cholesky (PC), reducing online evaluation costs as the training dataset grows. In a continuous stirred-tank reactor (CSTR) subject to exogenous disturbances, GP--RL--MPC with an appropriately selected risk coefficient and policy screening reduces the sum of squared errors (SSE) by an average of 80.52% relative to an otherwise matched baseline MPC across five random seeds (sample standard deviation: 3.48%).
papers.summary: Model predictive control (MPC) ignores costs beyond its prediction horizon, and learning a terminal cost from limited, noisy rollouts is hard. `GP-RL-MPC` uses a Gaussian process critic, trained with optimistic approximate policy iteration on postdecision states, as the MPC terminal penalty, with a tunable risk coefficient that weights the critic's epistemic uncertainty and a sparse posterior built from inducing points to keep online evaluation cheap. On a continuous stirred-tank reactor with exogenous disturbances, it reduces the sum of squared errors by **an average of 80.52% relative to a matched baseline MPC** across five seeds.

papers.title: RLDE: A Reinforcement Learning Framework for Interpretable Iterative Document Editing
papers.abstract: Improving the quality, clarity, and flow of long documents remains a challenging problem in NLP, as human editing typically occurs through iterative refinement rather than a single-pass rewrite. Most existing automated systems act as black-box generators or rely on supervised learning, limiting interpretability and failing to capture the sequential nature of revisions. In this paper, we propose RLDE, an automated end-to-end metric-driven RL framework that formulates document revision as a reference-free MDP problem (unsupervised with respect to paired document-revision targets). Working with a limited action space (NOOP, INSERT, DELETE, REPLACE), RLDE leverages Pointer Networks for dynamic span selection at the token level and sends generative actions to the frozen BART-base model to obtain context-aware suggestions. PPO agents learn to optimize a multi-objective reward function based on readability, perplexity, and grammar metrics with the help of a novel SBERT-based Semantic Preservation Penalty constraint to avoid deletion degeneracy. Evaluations on the BEA-2019 dataset showed statistically significant results (p < 0.01) across all metrics, where Flesch Reading Ease increased from 49.8 to 59.4, perplexity decreased from 63.7 to 39.8, while preserving 93% of semantic information. When compared to Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompt-engineered models like GPT-4 and LLaMA-2, RLDE shows high performance at a very low computational inference cost. Moreover, the quality of edits generated by RLDE has been verified via human evaluations, scoring 4.9/5 for meaning preservation and 4.4/5 for edit quality.
papers.summary: Document revision is framed as a reference-free Markov decision process, so no paired original-and-revised documents are needed for training. `RLDE` trains `PPO` agents over four actions (no-op, insert, delete, replace), using Pointer Networks to select token spans and a frozen `BART-base` model to generate replacements, with a reward combining readability, perplexity, and grammar metrics plus an `SBERT`-based penalty that discourages deleting meaning. On `BEA-2019`, **Flesch Reading Ease rose from 49.8 to 59.4 and perplexity fell from 63.7 to 39.8 while preserving 93% of semantic information**. The authors report competitive quality against Chain-of-Thought prompted `GPT-4` and `LLaMA-2` at much lower inference cost, with human ratings of 4.9/5 for meaning preservation.

papers.title: A Hybrid Exact-Heuristic Solver for the Integrated Passenger and Parcel Transportation Problem
papers.abstract: We describe the solver we submitted to the second round of the SOICT 2026 contest on the Integrated Passenger and Parcel Transportation problem, a selective pickup-and-delivery routing problem with time windows, open routes and heterogeneous taxis. The solver is a single-file, standard-library Python program that combines (i) a constant-time insertion test based on latest-arrival slack, (ii) greedy insertion, local search and an Adaptive Large Neighborhood Search (ALNS) with simulated-annealing acceptance, and (iii) an exact route-selection engine that enumerates, for every taxi, the best feasible route for each request set and then solves the resulting set-packing problem by branch-and-bound strengthened with route-based large neighborhood search, Lagrangian bounds and reduced-cost fixing. The engine is chosen automatically from the instance size, and an independent verifier and a watchdog guarantee that a valid answer is always printed. On the official evaluation (38 scored instances, 5-minute limit) the solver obtained a total benefit of 487,237, finished every run within 277 s and used at most 279 MB; 28 of the 38 instances terminated well before the limit.
papers.summary: A contest entry for the `SOICT 2026` Integrated Passenger and Parcel Transportation problem, a selective pickup-and-delivery routing problem with time windows, open routes, and heterogeneous taxis. The single-file, standard-library Python solver combines a constant-time insertion feasibility test, greedy insertion with local search and Adaptive Large Neighborhood Search, and an exact engine that enumerates the best route per taxi and request set and then solves the resulting set-packing problem by branch-and-bound; the engine is chosen automatically from instance size. On the official evaluation of 38 scored instances with a 5-minute limit, it achieved **a total benefit of 487,237 with every run finishing within 277 seconds** and at most 279 MB of memory.

papers.title: Beyond Acuity Accuracy: A Multidimensional Framework for Evaluating Patient-Facing Emergency Triage AI Tools
papers.abstract: Patient-facing AI triage tools may support care-seeking and emergency department prioritization, but require evaluation beyond acuity accuracy alone. We developed SAFE-Triage, a framework integrating human review, automated metrics, LLM-as-judge evaluation, and simulation testing across clinical performance, patient interaction, and clinician-facing summary quality. We applied SAFE-Triage to 40 MIMIC-IV-derived emergency vignettes and a 10,030-case acuity analysis comparing prompted LLM triage (PLT) with rule-augmented prompted LLM triage (rPLT). PLT achieved higher emergency severity index (ESI) accuracy (57.5% vs 42.8%, $P < 0.001$), lower undertriage (13.1% vs 29.8%, $P < 0.001$), and higher clinician ratings across all domains. rPLT produced shorter and more stable outputs with higher automated readability scores. SAFE-Triage identified trade-offs between acuity accuracy, undertriage risk, communication quality, readability, and summary quality, supporting pre-deployment refinement and ongoing monitoring by showing where triage tools are efficient, need improvement, or need clinician oversight.
papers.summary: Patient-facing AI triage tools are usually judged on acuity accuracy alone, which misses communication quality and safety trade-offs. `SAFE-Triage` combines human review, automated metrics, LLM-as-judge evaluation, and simulation testing across clinical performance, patient interaction, and clinician-facing summary quality, and is applied to 40 `MIMIC-IV`-derived vignettes plus a 10,030-case acuity analysis. Plain prompted LLM triage beat a rule-augmented variant, with **emergency severity index accuracy of 57.5% versus 42.8% and undertriage of 13.1% versus 29.8%**, while the rule-augmented version produced shorter, more stable, and more readable outputs.

papers.title: DSADiff: Data Structure-Aware Diffusion for Crystal Structure Prediction via Mitigating Complexity- and Imbalance-Induced Biases
papers.abstract: Crystal Structure Prediction (CSP) is an important step in accelerating the generation and discovery of new materials. In recent years, diffusion-based CSP methods have made significant progress. However, existing models still suffer from generation bias when facing diverse materials spaces, while systematic approaches for tracing the sources of such performance variations remain limited. To address this issue, we propose LAS (Layered Analysis Strategy), a mechanism analysis framework that identifies crystal complexity and elemental composition imbalance as two key factors affecting generation difficulty and further reveals their relationships with model generation performance. Building on these findings, we further propose DSADiff (Data Structure-Aware Diffusion), a data structure-aware diffusion model that transforms the key factors identified by LAS into a unified generation difficulty representation and uses it to jointly drive feature modeling and training strategy optimization. This enables the model to adapt its representation and generation capability to samples with different data structures and difficulty levels, thereby mitigating learning bias across samples. Experiments on three CSP benchmark datasets, including Carbon-24, demonstrate that DSADiff consistently improves both Match Rate and RMSE, with a maximum Match Rate improvement of 9%, surpassing existing state-of-the-art methods and achieving new state-of-the-art performance. This work deepens the understanding of diffusion-based CSP models from the perspective of generation bias and provides a new direction for designing less biased generative models for complex materials spaces.
papers.summary: Diffusion models for crystal structure prediction (CSP) perform unevenly across different kinds of materials, and the sources of that variation are poorly understood. A Layered Analysis Strategy (`LAS`) identifies crystal complexity and elemental composition imbalance as two drivers of generation difficulty, and `DSADiff` turns these into a unified difficulty representation that steers both feature modeling and the training strategy. Across three CSP benchmarks including `Carbon-24`, it improves both Match Rate and RMSE, with **a maximum Match Rate improvement of 9%** over prior methods.

papers.title: RiDEx: Reward-Informed Directional Exploration for Diffusion Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Reward-based diffusion post-training updates model parameters from task rewards. While existing approaches improve sampling and policy optimization, they still rely largely on isotropic random perturbations in a high-dimensional latent space for exploration. Such variation often spends the perturbation budget on changes with little influence on the target reward, making exploration inefficient. We study where diffusion models should explore and how to learn from that exploration. We introduce Reward-Informed Directional Exploration (RiDEx), which concentrates local exploration in reward-relevant subspaces of the denoising velocity field. Conditional residuals or differentiable reward gradients propose the subspace, and equal-and-opposite perturbations at the same generation state measure its terminal reward response. The reward difference supplies signed local supervision in the explored coordinates, while all generated images contribute to global DiffusionNFT learning. RiDEx thereby couples exploration-space selection with feedback about the changes it produces. On Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium, RiDEx attains the highest peak rewards among the evaluated methods on four alignment and preference tasks. Its gradient-direction instantiation achieves 15x and 29x target-attainment speedups over DiffusionNFT on HPSv2 and PickScore, measured in H200 GPU hours. Controlled experiments confirm that reward-aligned directions elicit stronger responses at equal perturbation magnitude, and that applying their measured credit improves curve-average reward across all four tasks.
papers.summary: Reward-based post-training of diffusion models typically explores with isotropic random perturbations in latent space, spending much of the perturbation budget on changes that barely affect the reward. `RiDEx` (Reward-Informed Directional Exploration) concentrates exploration in reward-relevant subspaces of the denoising velocity field, proposed by conditional residuals or reward gradients, and uses equal-and-opposite perturbations to measure the reward response and supply signed local supervision alongside global `DiffusionNFT` learning. On `Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium` it reaches the highest peak rewards among evaluated methods on four alignment and preference tasks, and its gradient-direction variant hits targets **15x and 29x faster than `DiffusionNFT` on `HPSv2` and `PickScore`** in GPU hours.

papers.title: A single inference process underlies the behavior and neural circuits of working memory
papers.abstract: Working memory holds past inputs online for future behavior. Despite decades of research, accounts of working memory remain divided across levels of analysis, with long-standing debates on whether its capacity reflects discrete slots or continuous resources, how attention improves recall, and whether its representations rely on persistent neural firing or activity-silent states. Here we show that MemGP, a theory that is specified at the computational, algorithmic, and circuit levels of analysis simultaneously, can explain diverse behavioral and neural phenomena in working memory. At the computational level, MemGP casts working memory as probabilistic inference over a continuous function on feature space, with a variational objective that balances memory strength against a Gaussian-process prior. At the algorithmic level, writing, storing, and reading of memories correspond to approximating this posterior with a finite set of inducing points, the resource that all items share. In simulations, MemGP reproduces load-dependent precision loss, attentional benefits during maintenance, and inter-item attraction and repulsion, in each case revealing multiple complex computational dependencies. At the circuit level, the algorithm analytically (without training) maps onto a recurrent circuit, including its architecture and dynamics. Beyond reproducing neural phenomena such as delay-dependent drift, this analytical map deduces center--surround connectivity, a property long assumed in attractor models, and a structured combination of persistent activity and synaptic weights to hold memories. Thus, a single inference objective not only jointly predicts the behavioral and neural signatures of working memory, but also addresses, across several instances and different levels of analysis, existing competing explanations.
papers.summary: Theories of working memory are split over whether capacity is discrete slots or a continuous resource, how attention helps recall, and whether memories live in persistent firing or activity-silent states. `MemGP` casts working memory as probabilistic inference over a continuous function on feature space with a Gaussian-process prior, approximated by a finite set of inducing points that act as the shared resource. Simulations reproduce load-dependent precision loss, attentional benefits, and inter-item attraction and repulsion, and **the algorithm maps analytically, without training, onto a recurrent circuit** whose center-surround connectivity and mix of persistent activity and synaptic weights are derived instead of assumed.

papers.title: Weight-Space Programming Doesn't Need Transformers
papers.abstract: Standard neural architectures such as the Transformer were chosen because they train well with gradient descent and run fast on GPUs. In weight-space programming, a large language model (LLM) writes target weights by hand without gradient-based training, so those reasons no longer apply. Should we keep the Transformer? Given minimal guidance, ten labeled examples, and a sandbox, mainly on multiple-choice questions, we task three frontier LLMs with either generating the weights of a fixed architecture or designing the architecture themselves. When free to design, all three compile plain-text facts into a sparse table queried by a fixed procedure, reaching up to 54.4% test accuracy. An LLM-designed model achieves higher test accuracy than the most accurate released Transformer that the same LLM wrote while using about 1,800x fewer parameters. Without gradients, they choose a table, in which the LLM can state what each weight means and can find and rewrite a wrong one. Each wrong answer points to one row, and removing a row changes about one other answer. From this, we propose an associative-memory-based model up to 17x faster on GPUs than a same-sized Transformer. We also test pretrained weights, other benchmarks, and tasks where models generate answers. Pretrained LLMs remain more accurate; the claim concerns which structure to build when writing weights.
papers.summary: In weight-space programming, a large language model (LLM) writes a network's weights by hand without gradient training, which removes the usual reasons for choosing a Transformer. Three frontier LLMs were given ten labeled examples and a sandbox and asked either to write weights for a fixed architecture or to design their own; when free to design, all three compiled plain-text facts into a sparse table queried by a fixed procedure, reaching up to 54.4% test accuracy on multiple-choice questions. One LLM-designed model beat the most accurate Transformer the same LLM wrote while using **about 1,800x fewer parameters**, and each weight stays interpretable and individually editable. The authors also propose an associative-memory model up to 17x faster on GPUs than a same-sized Transformer, while noting that pretrained LLMs remain more accurate.
papers.highlight_summary:
When a large language model writes a target model's weights by hand rather than training them with gradients, the usual reasons for choosing a Transformer no longer apply. Given only ten labeled examples and a sandbox, `Claude Opus 5.5`, `GPT-6.1 Sol` and `GPT-6 Astra` all abandon attention and dense embeddings in favour of a sparse fact table read by a fixed lookup procedure.

- Each writer states domain facts as plain-text sentences and compiles them into sparse table rows (4,288 facts over 3,368 concepts in one model), then scores each answer option by matching question and option concepts against the best-supported row.
- On `ARC` science questions the best LLM-designed table reaches **54.4%** test accuracy against **36.1%** for a two-layer Transformer written by the same LLM, and one designed model beats the most accurate released Transformer that LLM wrote with about **1,800× fewer parameters**.
- The table is easy to debug because deleting one written line changes only **0.5 to 1.8** test answers versus 4.8 or more in a written Transformer, and written Transformers score **8.0 points below** plain `BM25` search over their own text while the table models score above it.
- Because the LLM-designed tables score every fact for every question and run a median **9.4× slower** on a GPU than a same-sized Transformer, the authors propose a hashed associative-memory model that reads a fixed 120 pair-table rows per question, stays within about three points of the designed models (49.6% to 52.4%), and answers up to **17× faster** than a same-sized Transformer.
- These models only recall facts the writer stated, so `ARC-Challenge` stays near 38%, `MMLU` sits at chance, and fine-tuned pretrained models remain far ahead (`Qwen3.5-0.8B` at **82.1%**), while the authors concede they cannot rule out that the LLMs pick retrieval tables simply because the approach is familiar.

papers.title: FM-Mamba: An Efficient Native 2D Selective State Space Model with Stability-Aware Discretization
papers.abstract: When applied to two-dimensional features such as images, Mamba-based methods either flatten the feature map into 1D sequences and fuse multiple scans, which breaks spatial adjacency and multiplies computation, or recurse directly on the 2D grid but rescale the recurrence with a fixed input-independent factor and aggregate only the predecessors on a single anti-diagonal, leaving the discrete step unconstrained by 2D stability theory. We propose \textbf{FM-Mamba}, a native 2D selective state space model built on the general Fornasini--Marchesini (FM) model. Its coupled recurrence evolves along both spatial axes; cross-axis coupling induces a discrete diagonal-predecessor term $\tilde A_0$, and two independent input-dependent step sizes $\Delta_1(i,j)$, $\Delta_2(i,j)$ govern propagation along the two axes, so that the coefficients adapt per position and per direction. A normalized ratio $r_k=a_{0,k}/(a_{1,k}a_{2,k})$ yields a closed-form piecewise bound on the two step sizes; when a configuration falls outside the stable interval the steps are projected onto this bound, and the criterion is re-verified per position after training, which suppresses systematic local amplification without global damping. The recurrence is executed by a dual-diagonal wavefront scan: each update gathers information from two anti-diagonals, and the input enters the current state through a single projection, so that neither training nor inference flattens the feature map. Code is available at https://github.com/BitSsm/FM-Mamba-Runtime
papers.summary: Mamba-style state space models applied to images either flatten the feature map into multiple 1D scans, breaking spatial adjacency and multiplying computation, or recurse on the 2D grid without stability constraints on the discrete step. `FM-Mamba` builds a native 2D selective state space model on the Fornasini-Marchesini model, with a coupled recurrence along both spatial axes, a diagonal-predecessor term, and two independent input-dependent step sizes per position. **A closed-form piecewise bound on the two step sizes keeps the recurrence stable**, with out-of-range steps projected onto the bound and the criterion re-verified per position after training; a dual-diagonal wavefront scan executes it without flattening. The abstract reports no benchmark numbers.

papers.title: Two Counterexamples for e-means
papers.abstract: e-means (Bessa et al., 2026) combines exponential averaging and cluster revival. We give two counterexamples to its published recipe with higher final loss than standard k-means (Lloyd, 1982) from identical initial centers. Mass-based revival can destroy a global optimum and make the ratio of expected losses unbounded even with k-means++ seeding.
papers.summary: `e-means`, a clustering method that combines exponential averaging with cluster revival, is shown to fail in two constructed cases where its published recipe ends with higher loss than standard `k-means` from identical initial centers. Mass-based revival can destroy a global optimum, and **the ratio of expected losses can be unbounded even with `k-means++` seeding**.
