papers.title: Addressing Exogenous Variability in Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) often fails under exogenous variability such as shifts in opponents or environment regimes that cannot be controlled by the team but alter the transition dynamics. We formalize this challenge as Exogenous Dec-POMDP (ED-POMDP), in which an episode-level exogenous regime, selected independently of the team, indexes the dynamics, and the global state is partitioned into components that are directly responsive to the current team action and components that are not directly action-responsive at the current step. This formulation exposes mediated influence: while team actions do not directly update the latter at the current step, they can shape their later evolution through induced changes in the former. Based on this, we propose LEICA, a CTDE-compatible algorithm that learns history-conditioned context representations for both components and shapes policy updates using agent-wise, influence-weighted counterfactual intrinsic rewards. Across SMAX benchmarks with opponent strategy shifts, LEICA consistently improves both training performance and generalization to unseen opponents' strategies over existing baselines, supporting the usefulness of influence-weighted shaping under exogenous train-test regime shifts.
papers.summary: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) often breaks when factors outside the team's control, such as opponent strategy or environment regime, change between training and testing. The authors formalize this as an Exogenous Dec-POMDP (`ED-POMDP`), where an episode-level regime indexes the dynamics and the state splits into parts that respond directly to team actions and parts that do not, exposing how actions influence the latter indirectly. Their algorithm `LEICA` learns history-conditioned context representations for both parts and shapes policy updates with agent-wise, influence-weighted counterfactual intrinsic rewards. On `SMAX` benchmarks with opponent strategy shifts, it **improves both training performance and generalization to unseen opponent strategies** over existing baselines.

papers.title: MedGuardBench: A Patient-Oriented Benchmark for Personalized Guardrail Development
papers.abstract: Safety is personal: the same action can be safe for one person but unsafe for another. Yet current guardrails judge content without considering who is affected. Using medication safety, we introduce \textit{patient-conditioned medication guarding}, which predicts a safety verdict and 17 risk categories from a patient profile and prescription. We release \textbf{MedGuardBench}, a drug-disjoint benchmark of 5{,}001 scenarios across 87 medications. We find that standard guardrails rely on surface cues, such as wording and profile presence, rather than patient facts. To address this, we develop \textit{personalized reasoning guardrails} with three components. \textbf{Personalized Reasoning Distillation} links risks to relevant patient fields. \textbf{Context Unrolling (CU)} makes models check each field themselves, reducing false alarms on most backbones; controls show that providing the check does not yield the same benefit. A \textbf{rule-based reward (guided GRPO)} improves unsafe recall and complex-risk detection, including allergies and adverse reactions, on some backbones, but increases false alarms on others. Our models outperform base models and matched no-profile controls in accuracy, while reducing false alarms relative to no-profile controls. Profile removal and swapping confirm that gains come from patient information, not fine-tuning alone.
papers.summary: Content guardrails judge text without considering who is affected, though the same prescription can be safe for one patient and unsafe for another. `MedGuardBench` is a drug-disjoint benchmark of 5,001 scenarios across 87 medications in which a model must predict a safety verdict and 17 risk categories from a patient profile and prescription. Standard guardrails are found to **rely on surface cues such as wording and profile presence instead of patient facts**. The proposed guardrails combine reasoning distillation, a Context Unrolling step in which the model checks each profile field itself, and a rule-based reward with guided `GRPO`; they beat base models and no-profile controls in accuracy, though the reward increases false alarms on some backbones.

papers.title: Can You Undo It? Reversibility Classes for AI Agent Actions
papers.abstract: Tool-using AI agents change files, databases, access rights and public information, yet permission to call a tool does not establish whether a mistake can be undone. We present Reversibility Classes, a declared five-level vocabulary with argument-sensitive rules, conservative defaults and an explicit prior-state capture contract. The pinned implementation and evidence-linked registry cover 536 tools across 20 MCP servers. All 738 rule-case checks conform to declared expectations, while native annotation mapping differs from draft registry labels for 118 of 481 comparable tools. One AI-assisted reviewer approves 148 ratings, 75 matching the registry; this is not independent agreement. On 2,158 recorded runs, the implemented session guard gates the associated action in all 29 attributable attack-positive runs, compared with 18 for a read/write proxy, while adding nine approval points across 1,209 benign runs. Controlled file, Git, SQLite and three-browser experiments show that recovery depends on captured state, later changes, editor storage and recovery route, and expose a Git merge-state exception. The evidence supports making recovery assumptions explicit and testable. It does not establish registry-wide accuracy, reduced production harm or general recovery reliability.
papers.summary: Permission to call a tool says nothing about whether an AI agent's mistake can be undone. Reversibility Classes is a five-level vocabulary with argument-sensitive rules, conservative defaults, and an explicit contract for capturing prior state, implemented with a registry covering 536 tools across 20 Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. On 2,158 recorded runs, a session guard built on it **gated the associated action in all 29 attributable attack-positive runs, versus 18 for a read/write proxy**, while adding nine approval points across 1,209 benign runs. Controlled file, Git, SQLite, and browser experiments show recovery depends on captured state and later changes, and the authors state the evidence does not establish registry-wide accuracy or reduced production harm.

papers.title: Segmentation-Guided Direct Capacity Estimation of Rooftop Photovoltaics from Aerial Imagery
papers.abstract: Distribution planners need installation-level inventories of rooftop photovoltaic (PV) capacity, but interconnection records may be incomplete or spatially aggregated. Conventional image-based estimators segment PV arrays, convert the mask to physical area, and multiply by an estimated power density, coupling capacity prediction to mask-derived area. We propose Direct Head, a segmentation-guided architecture that retains U-Net segmentation and soft-mask pooling while directly regressing nonnegative capacity from PV-region features and area descriptors. We evaluate three independent runs on 7,590 French rooftop installations under the original split and a department-based holdout. Relative to a parameter-matched area-density neural model, Direct Head reduces mean absolute error by 8.7% and 12.5%, and symmetric mean absolute percentage error by 14.0% and 20.7%, respectively. Comparisons with conventional estimators, controlled architecture variants, auxiliary-loss ablations, and representative cases show that segmentation provides useful spatial evidence without requiring capacity to be determined by an area-density product.
papers.summary: Grid planners need per-installation estimates of rooftop photovoltaic (PV) capacity, and conventional image-based methods derive it by segmenting panels, converting the mask to area, and multiplying by an assumed power density. `Direct Head` keeps `U-Net` segmentation and soft-mask pooling but regresses capacity directly from PV-region features and area descriptors. On 7,590 French rooftop installations, under the original split and a department-based holdout, it **reduces mean absolute error by 8.7% and 12.5%** relative to a parameter-matched area-density model, with symmetric mean absolute percentage error down 14.0% and 20.7%.

papers.title: BernBRS: Certified Backward Reachability for Deep Bernstein Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Ensuring the safety of complex neural network systems requires mathematically rigorous verification. While backward reachability analysis is a critical tool for identifying safe initial states, computing tight, formal bounds remains notoriously difficult to scale. Recent advancements have demonstrated that DeepBern-Nets neural networks utilizing Bernstein polynomial activation functions possess advantageous mathematical properties that enable exceptionally fast and tight forward reachability analysis. Building upon this efficiency, this paper introduces BernBRS, a highly accurate and scalable framework for the backward reachability analysis of DeepBern-Nets. BernBRS simultaneously computes certified inner and outer approximations of the Backward Reachable Set (BRS). Rather than relying on single convex bounding, our method intelligently refines a cover of the input space by analyzing activation patterns, splitting the input domain precisely where an exact decomposition of the relaxation gap predicts the most significant reduction in error. This targeted refinement enables high levels of scalability to highly complex and massive architectures that remain intractable for existing certified methods. We demonstrate the efficacy of our framework on high-dimensional models, including a linearized closed-loop approximation of the Half-Cheetah controller and a distilled Bernstein student of a Transformer block and we empirically study how these model-level guarantees relate to the original Half-Cheetah and TinyBERT classifier, respectively.
papers.summary: Backward reachability analysis identifies which initial states of a neural network system lead to a given set of outputs, but computing tight certified bounds scales poorly. `BernBRS` targets `DeepBern-Nets`, networks with Bernstein polynomial activations, and **computes certified inner and outer approximations of the Backward Reachable Set (BRS) simultaneously**, refining a cover of the input space by splitting where an exact decomposition of the relaxation gap predicts the largest error reduction. It is demonstrated on a linearized closed-loop approximation of a `Half-Cheetah` controller and a Bernstein student distilled from a Transformer block, with an empirical study of how those guarantees relate to the original controller and a `TinyBERT` classifier.

papers.title: When Lower Harm Misleads: Auditing Concept Corrections
papers.abstract: An expert who corrects a concept prediction, such as a BI-RADS descriptor in breast ultrasound, expects the diagnosis to improve. Objectives that reduce the harm of such corrections are judged by harm and accuracy, yet harm also falls when a model responds less to every correction or starts from a worse uncorrected prediction, the reference for harm. We propose a correction audit, a reproducible evaluation protocol that separates these explanations: it splits each correction into harm and useful gain on identical events, separates the starting prediction from the correction response, and compares objectives with amplitude baselines matched in source harm. On three breast-ultrasound sources, worst-case correction training, evaluated from the mean-case model's start, lowers harm but gives up more useful gain in all 21 source comparisons pooled over six seeds, raising the corrected negative log-likelihood (NLL); from the same start, selecting between the objectives by harm picks the less helpful model on all three sources. On CUB, a monotonic harm penalty at its reported weight lowers path-level harm in all 80 concept sets while raising the NLL in all 80, almost entirely before any correction. At a fixed start, rescaling both responses to the same source harm reproduces the penalty's mean harm, useful gain and NLL on single-concept corrections within a prespecified margin of 0.0005 nat, although the two responses point in different directions. Lower harm therefore signals better corrections only when it is read together with useful gain, absolute risk and the start it is measured from.
papers.summary: In concept-based models, where an expert can correct an intermediate concept prediction such as a breast-ultrasound descriptor, training objectives are often judged by how much they reduce the harm of such corrections. The proposed correction audit splits each correction into harm and useful gain, separates the uncorrected starting prediction from the response to correction, and compares against amplitude baselines matched in harm. On three breast-ultrasound sources, worst-case correction training **lowers harm but gives up more useful gain in all 21 source comparisons**, raising corrected negative log-likelihood, and on `CUB` a monotonic harm penalty lowers harm in all 80 concept sets while raising negative log-likelihood in all 80. Lower harm therefore indicates better corrections only when read alongside useful gain, absolute risk, and the starting point.

papers.title: ATLAS-Finance: Benchmarking AI Agents in Realistic Banking Environments
papers.abstract: Professional work involves under-specified assignments, where relevant information is spread across workplace applications and may conflict or change over time. To evaluate how well frontier agents can perform economically valuable work in such settings, we introduce ATLAS-Finance, a benchmark of 100 end-to-end investment-banking tasks across 13 simulated firms. As in real banking workflows, agents must search email, chat, calendars, notes, and files to identify requirements, gather information, reconcile conflicts/updates, and then build complex financial models. Tasks were developed by experienced bankers based on their real deal work and take them 15-30 hours to complete. Agent deliverables are evaluated with expert-authored rubrics (median: 124.5 criteria) covering financial rationale and results, spreadsheet construction, completeness, and formatting. Despite completing substantial portions of the requested work, current agents rarely produce correct deliverables. Across today's frontier models, the best ones (Claude Opus and Fable) pass fewer than 11% of tasks.
papers.summary: `ATLAS-Finance` is a benchmark of 100 end-to-end investment-banking tasks across 13 simulated firms, built to test agents on under-specified work where information is scattered across applications and may conflict or change. Agents must search email, chat, calendars, notes, and files to identify requirements and reconcile updates, then build complex financial models; the tasks were written by experienced bankers from real deal work and take them 15 to 30 hours each. Deliverables are graded against expert rubrics with a median of 124.5 criteria. Agents complete substantial portions of the work but rarely get it right: **the best frontier models pass fewer than 11% of tasks**.

papers.title: HyCoInfer: Cloud-Edge Collaborative Inference for Large Language Models on Heterogeneous GPU-FPGA Architectures
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) serving relies predominantly on cloud GPUs, yet autoregressive decoding is memory-bound and often leaves their arithmetic units underutilized. Edge FPGAs offer attractive decoding efficiency, but are ill suited to sustaining a high-concurrency serving workload alone. This paper presents HyCoInfer, a heterogeneous cloud-edge serving system that assigns prefill to cloud GPUs and distributes decoding across cloud GPUs and edge FPGAs. The design addresses three barriers to practical offloading: capacity balancing across heterogeneous accelerators, the large KV cache crossing a constrained wide-area link, and the latency added by heterogeneous execution. HyCoInfer incorporates FPGA decode capacity into GPU prefill/decode role partitioning and places requests according to queue load, prompt length, and network state. It further combines layer-wise pipelined transfer, decoder-side precomputation, and bandwidth-adaptive KV cache compression based on residual vector quantization. We implement HyCoInfer using two NVIDIA V100 GPUs and an AMD Xilinx Alveo U280 and evaluate it over 100-1000 Mbps links. At 500 Mbps, HyCoInfer delivers up to 4.11 times the request goodput of cloud-only vLLM and reduces mean end-to-end latency by up to 61.1%. Across different network conditions and workloads, the system improves overall serving capacity, with the largest gains on communication-intensive tasks, and reduces per-request energy.
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) serving runs mostly on cloud GPUs, although autoregressive decoding is memory-bound and leaves GPU arithmetic units underused. `HyCoInfer` assigns prefill to cloud GPUs and spreads decoding across cloud GPUs and edge FPGAs, placing requests by queue load, prompt length, and network state, and shrinking the KV cache sent over the wide-area link with layer-wise pipelined transfer and bandwidth-adaptive compression based on residual vector quantization. Implemented on two NVIDIA V100 GPUs and an AMD Xilinx Alveo U280, at 500 Mbps it delivers **up to 4.11 times the request goodput of cloud-only `vLLM`** and cuts mean end-to-end latency by up to 61.1%, with lower per-request energy.

papers.title: When AUC Meets Generative Reconstruction: A Unified Principle for Balanced Visual Representation Learning
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) require visual encoders that extract fine-grained visual features while constructing semantically disentangled and discriminative representations. Conventional methodologies encounter a fundamental trade-off: contrastive learning enhances inter-class discrimination by suppressing intra-class variability, whereas generative reconstruction emphasizes perceptual fidelity but lacks explicit comparative supervision. The naive aggregation of these objectives via composite loss functions often induces optimization conflicts and instability due to gradient interference within the shared latent space. To resolve this, we introduce a unified representation-learning paradigm that reformulates generative reconstruction as a discriminative ranking problem within the generative output manifold. Our approach maintains perceptual reconstruction as a supervisory signal and integrates a ranking-based discriminative constraint by systematically ordering matched and mismatched reconstruction outputs. This formulation embeds discriminative information seamlessly into the generative process, alleviating the risk of loss competition. Specifically, we propose AUC Generative Reconstruction (AUCGR), which optimizes the area under the ROC curve (AUC) by ensuring higher scores for matched pairs than for mismatched pairs, and Partial AUC Generative Reconstruction (pAUCGR), which addresses supervision bias by focusing on mismatched comparisons within reliable feature subspaces. The proposed objectives are designed to be plug-and-play, requiring no architectural modifications to existing generative reconstruction frameworks. Theoretical analysis establishes rigorous connections to AUC/pAUC optimization and provides generalization guarantees. Extensive experiments validate that our method advances both discriminative accuracy and fine-grained perceptual representation.
papers.summary: Visual encoders for multimodal large language models need both fine-grained perceptual detail and discriminative semantics, but combining contrastive and generative reconstruction losses tends to cause gradient conflicts and unstable training. The proposed approach **reformulates generative reconstruction as a ranking problem**, scoring matched reconstruction outputs above mismatched ones. `AUCGR` optimizes the area under the ROC curve (AUC) over matched and mismatched pairs, and `pAUCGR` restricts mismatched comparisons to reliable feature subspaces to reduce supervision bias. Both are plug-and-play objectives requiring no architectural changes, backed by generalization guarantees; the abstract reports improvements in discriminative accuracy and perceptual representation without specific numbers.

papers.title: Every Measurement, Every Direction, All at Once: Multimodal Flow Matching for Molecules and Spectra
papers.abstract: Generative modeling in science is often data-limited, where experiments are expensive. However, each experiment may yield several coupled measurements of the same physical entity. Standard generative models often train only on a single direction, discarding supervision from the rest. We argue that each experiment contains more training signal than this asymmetry allows the model to exploit: random masking enables measurements to serve as either conditioning inputs or prediction targets, yielding multiple supervised denoising tasks from a single experiment. We investigate this premise with MOSAIC, a multimodal flow matching transformer over molecular 3D structure and UV, IR, and Raman spectra. MOSAIC is a single model that is capable of any-to-any generation: generating any subset of modalities from any disjoint subset of the others. On QM9S, MOSAIC achieves 88.8% molecular graph recovery, outperforming the strongest spectra-to-structure baseline by 23.2% in structure generation, while simultaneously outperforming a structure-to-spectra specialist model in spectral generation. Ablations show that the any-to-any objective improves structure generation over structure-only training across model sizes. Furthermore, MOSAIC supports arbitrary subsets of available measurements and enables molecular identification by matching generated spectra to experimental references.
papers.summary: Scientific experiments often yield several coupled measurements of the same entity, yet generative models are usually trained in only one direction and discard the rest of the supervision. `MOSAIC` is a multimodal flow matching transformer over molecular 3D structure and UV, IR, and Raman spectra that uses random masking so any measurement can be either a conditioning input or a prediction target, giving a single model for any-to-any generation. On `QM9S` it reaches **88.8% molecular graph recovery, 23.2% above the strongest spectra-to-structure baseline**, while also outperforming a structure-to-spectra specialist on spectral generation. Ablations show the any-to-any objective improves structure generation over structure-only training across model sizes.

papers.title: Semantic Communication via Analog RF Computing: When the Radio Computes the Meaning
papers.abstract: Semantic communication (SC) systems transmit continuous latent representations of meaning, but computing the semantic encoder at resource-constrained edge devices incurs substantial energy and memory costs. To address this challenge, we propose an end-to-end SC framework that executes the semantic encoder in the client's RF receiver front end using analog RF computing. A base station (BS) broadcasts encoder weights as RF waveforms, while each edge device reuses its receiver's passive mixer to compute semantic latents at ultra-low energy. These latents are transmitted over the uplink for network-side task inference. We show that analog computing noise across encoder layers and channel noise affecting transmitted latents admit a unified mathematical model. We define a task-posterior semantic distortion metric and derive its second-order decomposition into per-client, per-stage semantic sensitivities. Using this decomposition, we obtain a closed-form semantic-aware water-filling allocation of the total client energy budget across clients, encoder layers, and uplinks, assigning tighter accuracy targets to semantically sensitive stages. This allocation induces a broadcast beamforming problem that accounts for client-specific, per-layer accuracy requirements. We further refine the allocation through stochastic optimization and jointly design it with multi-task noise-aware training of the shared semantic model. MNIST simulations show that, at matched total client energy, the proposed allocation reduces network semantic distortion by 9.2\%-19.2\% compared with uniform precision and 5.1\%-13.1\% compared with client-blind allocation. Noise-aware co-design yields a further 46\% reduction.
papers.summary: Semantic communication (SC) systems send learned latent representations of meaning, but running the semantic encoder on edge devices costs energy and memory. The proposed framework has a base station (BS) broadcast encoder weights as radio-frequency waveforms so each device can compute latents in its receiver's passive mixer, and it models analog computing noise and channel noise jointly to derive a closed-form, semantic-aware water-filling allocation of energy across clients, encoder layers, and uplinks. In `MNIST` simulations at matched client energy, the allocation **cuts network semantic distortion by 9.2%-19.2% compared with uniform precision**, and noise-aware co-design of the shared model yields a further 46% reduction.

papers.title: EvoDisco: Strategy Discovery for Evolving Agent Memory
papers.abstract: Large language model agents accumulate experience in memory, and how that memory evolves during interaction is as important as what it stores. Recent methods update memory online, yet both the operators that transform memory and the rules that select them remain fixed by design. We propose EvoDisco, which formulates agent memory evolution as evolutionary strategy discovery: the agent must discover which operator to apply, when to apply it, and how to instantiate it, rather than rewriting memory under a static operator schedule. A learnable policy conditions on the current memory state and recent task history, then selects and instantiates one of four semantic operators---Abstract, Refine, Bridge, and Reframe---which respectively compress related memories, decompose overloaded entries, connect weakly linked experiences, and reorganize retrieved reasoning chains. The policy is updated with a bi-level fitness. An inner signal scores each transformation using a retrieval-quality improvement regularized by memory complexity. An outer signal scores strategic efficacy over a window of past decisions, combining historical operator-utility regret, utility-prediction error, and selection diversity. Under a one-pass online plus frozen-transfer protocol on ALFWorld, WebShop, and LifelongAgentBench (OS and DB), EvoDisco improves over strong memory baselines including MemP and MemRL. The largest gains are on ALFWorld ($+8.8$ online / $+12.9$ frozen-transfer points over MemP; $+16.4$ / $+17.9$ over MemRL). Ablations attribute these gains to both fitness levels and the operator library.
papers.summary: Memory systems for large language model agents usually update memory online with a fixed set of operators and fixed rules for choosing them. `EvoDisco` instead learns a policy that looks at the current memory state and recent task history and picks one of four operators (Abstract, Refine, Bridge, Reframe), trained with a bi-level fitness that scores each transformation by retrieval-quality improvement and scores the overall strategy by regret, utility-prediction error, and selection diversity. On `ALFWorld`, `WebShop`, and `LifelongAgentBench`, it beats the `MemP` and `MemRL` baselines, with the largest gains on `ALFWorld` at **+8.8 online and +12.9 frozen-transfer points over `MemP`**.

papers.title: From Sorry to QED: Refining LLM Math Proofs via Angelic Execution
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can now generate Lean proof scripts that capture the high-level structure of many mathematical arguments. However, these scripts frequently fail on complex theorems: a single missing side condition or misapplied lemma can cause the prover to abort early and discard an otherwise viable proof outline. This paper presents MathEye, a framework that converts imperfect LLM-generated proof scripts into fully verified Lean proofs by combining symbolic reasoning with minimal human interaction. At the core of MathEye is angelic proof checking, an optimistic execution model that replaces failing proof fragments with placeholders while preserving the overall structure of the argument. This optimistic check produces an angelic proof that isolates the exact proof obligations that the LLM fails to discharge. Because these unresolved obligations are often logically interdependent, asking a mathematician to address every placeholder directly is inefficient. To minimize human effort, MathEye performs residual analysis over a proof dependence graph that captures symbol-level data flow in the angelic proof. By formulating obligation selection as a MaxSAT optimization problem, MathEye selects a minimal-cost set of essential obligations whose resolution suffices to complete the entire proof. MathEye presents these essential obligations to the mathematician in ordinary mathematical language and uses the mathematician's answers to automatically reconstruct the complete Lean proof. Experiments on 30 real-world benchmarks across analysis and algebra show that MathEye solves 93.3% of the problems while reducing the number of required user interactions by 55%.
papers.summary: Lean proof scripts generated by large language models (LLMs) often capture the right high-level argument but fail outright because of a single missing side condition or misapplied lemma. `MathEye` runs an optimistic, so-called angelic check that replaces failing fragments with placeholders, builds a proof dependence graph over the remaining obligations, and uses a MaxSAT formulation to pick a minimal-cost set of obligations to put to a mathematician in ordinary mathematical language before reconstructing the full Lean proof. On 30 analysis and algebra benchmarks it **solves 93.3% of the problems while reducing required user interactions by 55%**.
papers.highlight_summary:
LLM-generated Lean proofs often capture the right high-level argument but collapse on a single missing side condition, discarding an otherwise viable outline. `MathEye` keeps that outline intact, isolates exactly what the model failed to prove, and asks a mathematician only a minimal set of yes/no questions in ordinary mathematical language before reconstructing the full Lean proof.

- Optimistic ("angelic") checking runs the draft in `Lean 4`, and whenever a tactic fails it backtracks bottom-up over the syntax tree to replace the smallest enclosing block that fixes the error with a `sorry` placeholder, yielding a structurally valid proof plus a list of residual goals.
- Residual analysis builds a proof dependence hypergraph over Lean symbols, adds implicit edges from a library of math inference rules (e.g. FTC, continuity implying integrability), and solves a MaxSAT problem in `Z3` to pick a minimal-cost set of obligations, with cost combining LLM-estimated difficulty, proof-state size, and number of queries.
- On 30 graduate qualifying-exam theorems in analysis and algebra, it fully verifies **28 of 30 (93.3%)**, while the union of five automated baselines (including `DeepSeek-Prover-V2`, `ChatGPT 5.4`, and `Claude Opus 4.6`) solves only **6 (20.0%)** one-shot and **9 (30.0%)** with iterative compiler-feedback repair.
- Human effort is small, with a median of **5 queries and 184 seconds** per problem (max 15 queries, 380 seconds), and the dependence-graph analysis cuts queries by **55%** compared with asking about every residual goal.
- The comparison pits a human-in-the-loop system against fully automated provers on a small, author-curated benchmark, and the approach relies on student yes/no confirmations of intermediate claims and on what appears to be a hand-built rule library covering only analysis, set theory, and algebra.

papers.title: VTT: Reading Vehicle Size and Powertrain Type from Motion Trajectory Across Unseen Car Models
papers.abstract: Vehicle size and powertrain information can enrich trajectory data for traffic analysis and simulation. We present VTT, a dataset and benchmark for identifying these attributes from motion and controller area network (CAN) signals across unseen car models. The dataset contains 9,062 drives, about 3,950 h, from 1,431 vehicles and 174 car models. It provides three footprint-based size classes, powertrain labels, and evaluation on unseen car models and unseen drivers. Using 60-s windows, we compare four sequence architectures, statistical features and physical features proposed by large language models. Training with auxiliary physical targets, data augmentation and task-specific weighting raises drive-level macro-F1 to 92.6-93.0% for battery-electric versus combustion vehicles and from 62.9% to 67.1% for size classification. On public logs from 4,061 additional drivers, the full-input model identifies powertrain correctly for 86 of 88 car models; size accuracy is 63.2%, close to the internal vehicle-level result of 63.5%. Physical-feature analysis links powertrain recognition to deceleration behaviour and size recognition to steering response. Errors near size-class boundaries and limited gains from longer observations highlight the importance of label resolution and training-fleet coverage for cross-model generalisation.
papers.summary: `VTT` is a dataset and benchmark for inferring a vehicle's size class and powertrain type from motion and controller area network (CAN) signals, with evaluation on unseen car models and unseen drivers; it covers 9,062 drives from 1,431 vehicles and 174 car models. The authors compare four sequence architectures, statistical features, and physical features proposed by large language models, and add auxiliary physical targets, augmentation, and task-specific weighting. Drive-level macro-F1 reaches **92.6-93.0% for battery-electric versus combustion vehicles**, while size classification improves only from 62.9% to 67.1%, with errors concentrated near size-class boundaries.

papers.title: RegimeCouncil: Paired-Evidence Routing For Memory Conflict Governance In LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Language agents rely on long-term memory to personalize responses across extended interactions, yet stored facts quietly go stale as the world changes, and an agent often learns that using memory hurt only through delayed feedback after acting on an outdated record. Before the memory store is updated, how far should that negative feedback propagate: should it suppress memory use only on future queries for that same fact (a local policy), or also across other stored facts (a global policy)? Existing memory systems implicitly fix one of these two sharing scopes at design time. We formulate this online scope choice under hidden validity and delayed feedback as memory conflict governance, and prove that neither fixed policy is sufficient on its own. We then propose RegimeCouncil, a lightweight paired-evidence router that retains both scopes as advisors and arbitrates between them online without retraining the LLM. Using revealed comparisons between answering with memory and answering without memory (the no-memory anchor), a Local Advisor tracks the latest outcome on the queried fact alone, while a Global Advisor pools recent outcomes across all stored facts. A Meta Governor follows the Local Advisor by default to avoid cross-fact interference and switches to the Global Advisor only when global pooling accumulates a strictly positive recent utility margin, guaranteeing finite-time switching under delayed feedback. Across LongMemEval update streams and real-world historical drift on TempLAMA and TAQA with Qwen3-30B-A3B and GPT-4o, RegimeCouncil outperforms the better fixed-scope policy by 5.2-7.3 points on primary disagreement episodes and across all 30 held-out settings, while ablations show that removing any of its three modules reduces accuracy by 2-7 points.
papers.summary: When an agent's long-term memory holds a stale fact and it learns this only through delayed negative feedback, it must decide whether to suppress memory use just for that fact or across all stored facts. The authors formalize this as memory conflict governance, prove that neither a fixed local nor a fixed global policy is sufficient, and propose `RegimeCouncil`, a router that follows a Local Advisor by default and switches to a Global Advisor only when pooled recent evidence shows a positive utility margin, without retraining the model. On `LongMemEval` update streams and on `TempLAMA` and `TAQA` with `Qwen3-30B-A3B` and `GPT-4o`, it **outperforms the better fixed-scope policy by 5.2-7.3 points** on primary disagreement episodes.

papers.title: TeleChat to Xing4: Advancing Frontier Agentic Models on Domestic Chips and Frameworks
papers.abstract: We present Xing 4, a series of large language models that extends the TeleChat lineage through coordinated advances in model architecture and training infrastructure on Ascend. This report describes the design principles and systems engineering behind the series, spanning architecture selection, large-scale pretraining, and reasoning and agentic post-training. We study how sparse activation, attention design, model depth and width, and speculative decoding balance model capacity with computation, memory access, and execution overhead. Our pretraining infrastructure builds on MindSpore HyperParallel, combining topology-aware hybrid sharding, efficient distributed optimizer execution, and coordinated management of long-sequence workloads and activation memory. CPU affinity and core isolation further reduce host scheduling interference. Together, these mechanisms support the pretraining of a 285B-parameter model on 8,192 Ascend 910C cards, providing a concrete setting for the architectural and systems studies. For post-training, we introduce TeleGym, a unified agent execution platform that connects execution, evaluation, and trajectory construction to policy optimization. Disaggregated asynchronous execution, bounded oversampling, and partial rollout accommodate heterogeneous task durations while preserving trajectory continuity across policy updates. Together, these advances establish an Ascend-oriented training foundation for the continued development of Xing 4 across model scales and increasingly demanding reasoning and agent workloads.
papers.summary: A technical report on `Xing 4`, a series of large language models continuing the `TeleChat` line, describes the architecture choices and training infrastructure used to build it on Ascend chips. It studies how sparse activation, attention design, depth and width, and speculative decoding trade model capacity against compute and memory, and details a `MindSpore HyperParallel` pretraining stack that supported **pretraining a 285B-parameter model on 8,192 Ascend 910C cards**. For agentic post-training it introduces `TeleGym`, an execution platform using disaggregated asynchronous execution, bounded oversampling, and partial rollouts to handle tasks of very different durations; the report covers design and systems engineering and gives no benchmark results in the abstract.
papers.highlight_summary:
Training frontier-scale models off the GPU/PyTorch stack is mostly a systems problem, and China Telecom's `Xing 4` series tackles it by co-designing mixture-of-experts architectures and a distributed training stack for Huawei Ascend NPUs and `MindSpore`. The report open-sources a **29B** model trained entirely on that stack and uses a **285B** sibling as the testbed for its architecture, pretraining, and agentic post-training studies.

- The open `Xing4.0-29B-A4B` activates **4B** parameters per token with native **256K** context using `mHC`, `MLA`, and `MTP`, while the 285B model (about 17B active, up to 1M-token context, pretrained on **8,192 Ascend 910C** cards) combines `MLA` with `DSA` sparse attention and cross-layer `IndexShare`, and adopts a wider-and-shallower 45-layer topology that improved training throughput by roughly 10% over a 60-layer baseline.
- For inference, simulation at 256K context puts `MLA` + `DSA` + `IndexShare` at **4.68×** prefill throughput and 0.21× time-to-first-token relative to an `MLA`-only baseline, and the block-wise `DSpark` speculative decoder delivers **2.67×–3.77×** decoding throughput over the base configuration (1.48×–2.10× over `MTP3`) across six math and code workloads.
- On the training side, `HSDP` shards parameters within each SuperPoD and replicates them across SuperPoDs to remove pipeline parallelism, cutting step time from 36.4 s to **31.8 s** (1.14×) on a 1,024-NPU profiling cluster, with owner-based `Muon` execution, selective recomputation, and layer-wise indexer backward each trimming a further **9.1%**, **6.9%**, and **15.2%** respectively.
- Post-training runs on `TeleGym`, a unified agent execution platform that decouples generation from optimization on separate device pools and uses bounded oversampling and partial rollout so that long, variable-length trajectories can span multiple policy updates.
- The attention comparisons come from simulation the authors acknowledge may be optimistic versus real serving, the step-time gains are profiling-scale measurements taken independently rather than cumulatively (and the abstract's 16.1% figure for removing pipeline parallelism does not match the 12.6% in the results table), and the reordered `Muon` execution carries no guarantee of bitwise equivalence or unchanged convergence.

papers.title: What MoE Routing Controls: Causal Interventions on Expert Trajectories
papers.abstract: In mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models, a token is routed to a sequence of experts across layers. We investigate how forcing tokens onto chosen expert paths influences model behavior. We build a target path from the experts that a concept's or role's tokens most often use, and we add a fixed bias to each target expert's router logit during generation to steer the token toward this expert path. We study two kinds of targets. Format targets concern the form of the output, and concept targets concern its topic. In Qwen3-30B-A3B, we show that steering a format path changes the text the model writes. We also show that steering a concept path shifts the model's next-token probabilities toward the concept, even when the path is built in another language, yet this shift has little effect on the generated text. We investigate why formats reach the text but concepts do not by steering only part of the generation, and find evidence that a format, once started, reinforces itself. We show that the concepts religion and money steer most strongly, and that the effect is concentrated in the middle layers. We attempt to explain why the strength of the effect varies by concept through an analysis of embedding distinctiveness and word frequency.
papers.summary: In mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models each token passes through a sequence of experts, and the authors test what that routing controls by adding a fixed bias to router logits to push tokens onto a chosen expert path. In `Qwen3-30B-A3B`, **steering a format path changes the text the model writes, whereas steering a concept path shifts next-token probabilities toward the concept but barely changes the generated text**, even though concept paths transfer across languages. Partial-generation experiments suggest a format reinforces itself once started, and concept effects are concentrated in the middle layers and strongest for religion and money.

papers.title: TempQuant: Learning Adaptive Temperatures for Quantized Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed at low precision, yet quantization can degrade their performance. We study how quantization interacts with decoding settings such as the sampling temperature and top-p by examining how it distorts the model's next-token probabilities. Measuring entropy during generation across deployed temperatures, we find that quantization warms the model on average, and that temperature matters much more for the performance of a quantized model than for its full-precision counterpart. Because quantization and temperature both shape the next-token distribution, we investigate how much the sampling settings can undo what quantization changes, through our method TempQuant, which learns the quantized model's temperature and top-p to bring its next-token probabilities closer to the full-precision model's. We learn these settings at two granularities. The first is a single global setting per requested temperature, which finds nearly the same temperatures that tuning on labeled answers would, without any labels. Model cards typically recommend sampling a quantized model with the same settings as its full-precision counterpart, while we find that different settings can substantially improve its accuracy. On 3-bit Qwen3-4B, for example, global TempQuant raises MATH accuracy from 34% under the configuration recommended for Qwen's quantized releases to 51%. The second sets the temperature and top-p for every token, motivated by our finding that tokens whose rankings flip under quantization tend to need warming, while tokens whose rankings are preserved tend to need cooling. When quantization degrades accuracy substantially, TempQuant recovers much of it, and when degradation is lighter, it still brings the quantized model's behavior closer to the full-precision model's.
papers.summary: Quantized language models are usually sampled with the same temperature and top-p as their full-precision versions, yet quantization raises the entropy of the next-token distribution on average and makes accuracy far more sensitive to temperature. `TempQuant` learns the quantized model's temperature and top-p, either as one global setting per requested temperature or per token, so that its next-token probabilities move closer to the full-precision model's, with no labels needed. On 3-bit `Qwen3-4B`, the global variant **raises `MATH` accuracy from 34% under the recommended configuration to 51%**, and the per-token variant builds on the finding that tokens whose rankings flip under quantization need warming while preserved ones need cooling.

papers.title: Bandit Online Submodular Minimisation Using Zeroth-Order Oracles
papers.abstract: We consider online submodular minimisation under bandit feedback, where at each round a decision maker plays a subset and observes only its cost, while the cost functions, and hence their minimiser, change over time. Existing bandit methods only guarantee static regret, which compares against a single fixed subset and is a weak benchmark when the minimiser moves. This paper provides, to the best of our knowledge, the first method with guarantees for tracking a moving minimiser in this setting. We propose a zeroth-order method built on a two-point oracle for the Lov\'asz extension whose two evaluations are both subsets that can be played. The perturbed and base points are rounded by a common random threshold, and drawing the smoothing direction from the unit sphere makes the base evaluation a zero-mean control variate, so the oracle is an unbiased estimator of the smoothed gradient. We establish dynamic regret bounds of order $O\big((1+\sqrt{P^\ast_N})N^{3/4}\big)$ in general and $O\big((1+\sqrt{P^\ast_N})N^{2/3}\big)$ under a sufficiently small drift, where $P^\ast_N$ is the path length of the minimiser sequence, together with the corresponding $O(N^{3/4})$ and $O(N^{2/3})$ static regret bounds. Numerically, the method attains lower regret than the algorithm of (Hazan and Kale (2012)), with the advantage growing with the path length.
papers.summary: Online submodular minimisation under bandit feedback asks a decision maker to play a subset each round and observe only its cost while the cost functions, and their minimiser, drift over time; prior bandit methods only bound regret against a single fixed subset. The proposed zeroth-order method uses a two-point oracle for the Lovasz extension in which both evaluations are playable subsets rounded by a common random threshold, giving an unbiased estimate of the smoothed gradient. It achieves **dynamic regret of order O((1+sqrt(P))N^(3/4)) in general and O((1+sqrt(P))N^(2/3)) under small drift**, where P is the path length of the minimiser sequence, and empirically beats the Hazan and Kale (2012) algorithm by a margin that grows with path length.

papers.title: LoCaR: Localized Canvas Retrieval With Frozen Vision-Language Model
papers.abstract: Whole image embeddings can under represent small objects and local attributes that distinguish relevant images for localized queries. We present LoCaR, a training free framework for localized text to image retrieval with frozen vision language models. LoCaR constructs and utilizes independent proposals (SAM2) focusing on the object so as to get a more localized representation that independently encodes each region using the frozen visual encoder. We further study paired-support adaptation as an optional residual that uses matched text region exemplars without updating the underlying encoders. We also introduce LOCFG, a Visual Genome derived benchmark designed to evaluate localized retrieval for smaller and more challenging referents. Across several vision language backbones, our results show that improving the region representation itself is the main source of gain.
papers.summary: Whole-image embeddings tend to under-represent small objects and local attributes, which hurts text-to-image retrieval for queries about a specific region. `LoCaR` is a training-free framework that generates object proposals with `SAM2` and encodes each region independently with a frozen vision-language encoder, with an optional residual adaptation step that uses matched text-region exemplars without updating the encoders. The authors also introduce `LOCFG`, a benchmark derived from `Visual Genome` for small and difficult referents, and report across several backbones that **improving the region representation itself is the main source of gain**.

papers.title: ReMoE: An Interpretable Mixture-of-Experts Framework for Human Mobility Recovery Forecasting Across Disasters
papers.abstract: Human mobility often declines sharply following disasters and subsequently exhibits complex recovery dynamics. Effective forecasting of this recovery is critical for timely assessment and resource allocation. However, existing approaches are often developed for individual events and operate as black boxes, limiting their transferability and interpretability beyond the events they were trained on. Recent studies have identified recurring post-disaster mobility recovery types across disasters, suggesting that recovery knowledge may be transferable. Motivated by this, we propose ReMoE, an interpretable mixture-of-experts framework for cross-disaster mobility recovery forecasting. ReMoE uses a feature-guided router to adaptively combine specialized experts that learn these heterogeneous yet reusable recovery types, producing a region-specific recovery pattern. It further refines this pattern through residual correction informed by forecasts of future hazard conditions. We evaluate ReMoE on a large-scale mobility dataset covering 18 disaster events spanning hurricanes, floods, winter storms, and wildfires. ReMoE is competitive in-distribution and achieves the strongest performance on unseen events and hazard types, with larger gains under greater distribution shifts. Further analyses show that ReMoE yields interpretable learning outcomes and maintains robust performance under uncertainty. Broadly, ReMoE offers a transferable and traceable forecaster that can support anticipatory post-disaster assessment.
papers.summary: Forecasting how human mobility recovers after a disaster is usually done with event-specific black-box models that transfer poorly to new events. `ReMoE` is a mixture-of-experts forecaster in which a feature-guided router combines experts specialized in recurring recovery types to produce a region-specific pattern, then refines it with a residual correction based on forecasts of future hazard conditions. On a mobility dataset covering 18 hurricanes, floods, winter storms, and wildfires, it is competitive in-distribution and **achieves the strongest performance on unseen events and hazard types**, with larger gains under greater distribution shift.

papers.title: Big Brains, Tiny Board: Pupavision, an Agentic Physical AI Instrument for Monitoring Drosophila Pupariation and Lifecycle Transitions
papers.abstract: Many biology experiments are limited by the availability and ease of use of instruments that monitor and record them. For example, the timing of pupariation in the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster, a widely used model organism, can provide biologically relevant information about growth regulation and is often recorded manually. Here, we present Pupavision, a small physical AI instrument built from a single-board Linux computer and a day/night camera for roughly 45 to 75 US dollars in parts. The key idea is that a frontier coding agent runs its agentic harness directly on the tiny board. The model thinks in the cloud, but the agent works on the device. The agent assists image capture, writes code to repair errors, and checks the experiment every day to keep raw data capture reliable. If recording stops, the researcher gets a ping on their mobile phone. A simple deterministic capture service records one image every ten minutes and never depends on the agent. We report a 26-day pilot in a fly incubator (about 3,580 frames), including eleven days in which the agent was logged out and capture continued, and a 51-hour outage whose cause led to the layered design. A researcher-in-the-loop workflow then produces per-vial pupariation curves by tracing selected pupae backward in time from a late reference frame. Future work will validate the assay for lifecycle tracking accuracy against expert-labeled data and expand real-time computer vision analysis. Pupavision offers a blueprint for do-it-yourself agentic instruments that put frontier intelligence on a tiny board, with deterministic code underneath. We present this as an early case study from a pilot lab deployment and contribute lessons learned toward a future where scientific domain experts are empowered by DIY agentic hardware.
papers.summary: Timing of pupariation in fruit flies is often recorded by hand, so the authors built `Pupavision`, a monitoring instrument made from a single-board Linux computer and a day/night camera for roughly 45 to 75 US dollars in parts. A frontier coding agent runs its harness directly on the board, with the model itself in the cloud, to assist image capture, write code to repair errors, check the experiment daily, and alert the researcher by phone, while a separate deterministic service captures a frame every ten minutes without depending on the agent. In a 26-day incubator pilot of about 3,580 frames, **capture continued through eleven days in which the agent was logged out**, and a 51-hour outage motivated this layered design; accuracy validation against expert labels is left to future work.

papers.title: RoboTeam: Benchmarking Vision-Based Multi-Agent Control of Many Robot Arms in Real Time
papers.abstract: Multimodal agents can now control robot arms by calling tools and writing code. Existing benchmarks fall short in three ways: most test one or two arms on short tasks, many pause the world while the agent thinks, and many give it ground-truth object positions. We present RoboTeam, a simulated benchmark where agents control 4 to 16 robot arms in real time from camera images alone. Its 36 tasks are long jobs that the arms must do together, such as passing timbers or building a picture from hundreds of cubes. We start from the most flexible agent system, the adaptive system, where one agent decides when to fork delegates. With it, gpt-6.1-sol and opus-5.5 complete 28 and 27 tasks, and four other models at most 3. But at a high price: a typical task takes gpt-6.1-sol 3.5 hours and 218 million input tokens, and a third of its steps fail at least once and must be retried. We then compare it with three fixed systems: single-agent, hierarchical, and decentralized. All four complete a similar number of tasks but differ in time and tokens. The hierarchical and decentralized systems are faster but use up to 1.9 times the tokens, and the single agent uses fewer tokens but takes 1.6 times as long, so the adaptive system lies between them. Even so, no model or system is yet fast, cheap, and reliable at once. RoboTeam measures these limits where earlier benchmarks cannot: long multi-arm jobs, camera images only, and a world that never pauses.
papers.summary: `RoboTeam` is a simulated benchmark in which multimodal agents control 4 to 16 robot arms in real time from camera images alone, across 36 long collaborative tasks such as passing timbers or assembling pictures from hundreds of cubes. Using an adaptive system where one agent decides when to fork delegates, **`gpt-6.1-sol` and `opus-5.5` complete 28 and 27 of the 36 tasks while four other models complete at most 3**, but a typical task costs `gpt-6.1-sol` 3.5 hours and 218 million input tokens, with a third of steps needing a retry. Single-agent, hierarchical, and decentralized systems finish a similar number of tasks: the latter two are faster but use up to 1.9 times the tokens, and the single agent uses fewer tokens but takes 1.6 times as long.

papers.title: Synthetic Crystal Data Generation for Diffusion Pretraining in Material Property Prediction
papers.abstract: Diffusion-based pretraining has emerged as a powerful strategy for learning transferable representations in graph neural networks for materials property prediction without requiring quantum-mechanical labels such as energies, forces, and stresses for every pretraining structure. However, the method retains a critical dependency: it requires structures residing near local minima of a potential energy surface, which have traditionally been obtained through costly DFT relaxations of known or physically synthesized compounds. This reliance constrains both the scale and the structural diversity of available pretraining data, leaving large regions of crystal structure space unexplored. In this work, we connect diffusion-based pretraining with synthetic structure generation to reduce this bottleneck. We introduce a synthetic data generation pipeline combining three complementary strategies: perturb-and-relax, generative sampling via MatterGen, and protostructure enumeration. Where structural relaxation is required, we use fast machine-learned interatomic potentials instead of performing a new DFT relaxation for each generated structure. We further compare a coordinate-denoising control with continuous-time variance-preserving (VP) and sub-VP diffusion objectives using a randomly initialized Orb-v2 backbone. The source comparison covers seven MatBench property-prediction tasks, and an eighth task, \texttt{mp\_gap}, is included in the protostructure scaling study. Every synthetic-pretraining condition numerically outperforms random initialization on all seven source-comparison tasks. Scaling the protostructure corpus from 20k to 165k under a fixed 400-epoch schedule numerically matches or exceeds MP-20k pretraining on most tasks; because this protocol increases both data diversity and optimization updates, the result reflects joint data-and-compute scaling.
papers.summary: Diffusion-based pretraining of graph neural networks for materials property prediction needs crystal structures near energy minima, which normally come from costly density functional theory relaxations. The authors generate synthetic pretraining structures through perturb-and-relax, sampling from `MatterGen`, and protostructure enumeration, relaxing with machine-learned interatomic potentials, and compare a coordinate-denoising control with variance-preserving (VP) and sub-VP diffusion objectives on a randomly initialized `Orb-v2` backbone. **Every synthetic-pretraining condition numerically outperforms random initialization on all seven `MatBench` source-comparison tasks**, and scaling the protostructure corpus from 20k to 165k matches or exceeds `MP-20k` pretraining on most tasks, though that result mixes more data with more optimization updates.

papers.title: When does deep reinforcement learning pay off in HVAC supervisory control? Four small Modelica case studies trained directly on FMUs
papers.abstract:
Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) is often proposed for the supervisory control of heating, ventilation and air-conditioning (HVAC) systems. The reported gains are, however, difficult to interpret, because the baselines are often weak and the attainable optimum is seldom known. This paper examines four small, reproducible case studies based on an office building in Brisbane, Australia: pre-cooling under a time-of-use tariff; chiller staging with condenser water reset; chilled water supply temperature reset with a wet cooling coil; and chilled water storage under time-of-use prices and a demand charge. The plants were modelled with the Modelica Buildings library, and in three of the cases a soft actor-critic agent was trained directly on the exported functional mock-up unit (FMU). Each agent was compared with tuned rule-based controllers and, where practicable, with a near-optimal reference from hourly exhaustive search or dynamic programming with perfect foresight.
  In the two cases without storage the agent reached the near-optimal reference, but the margin above a well-chosen rule was small: 1.3% for condenser water reset and 0.18% for chilled water reset. In the latter case two common reset rules consumed more energy than a fixed set point. With a chilled water storage tank the margin was considerably larger. The agent outperformed both rules (-7.8%, compared with -3.9% and -6.3%) and adopted midday charging during the solar off-peak period, yet it obtained only about 45% of the saving achieved by the perfect-foresight schedule and did little to limit the demand peak. In the pre-cooling case a hand-tuned rule remained superior (-12.0% compared with -5.6%). These results suggest that studies of DRL for HVAC control should state the margin between the best rule and a near-optimal reference. Some practical difficulties encountered in training on co-simulation FMUs are also reported.
papers.summary: Reported gains from deep reinforcement learning (DRL) in heating, ventilation and air-conditioning (HVAC) supervisory control are hard to interpret because baselines are often weak and the attainable optimum is unknown. Four small case studies of a Brisbane office building, modelled with the `Modelica Buildings` library, train a soft actor-critic agent directly on exported functional mock-up units (FMUs) and compare it with tuned rule-based controllers and near-optimal references from exhaustive search or dynamic programming. The agent reached the near-optimal reference in two cases without storage, but **its margin over a well-chosen rule was only 1.3% and 0.18%**; with chilled water storage it beat both rules yet captured only about 45% of the perfect-foresight saving, and for pre-cooling a hand-tuned rule remained better. The authors recommend that such studies report the gap between the best rule and a near-optimal reference.

papers.title: Long-Context Generation Is a Sampling Problem (When You Turn Up the Heat)
papers.abstract: Open-weight language models are widely observed to get worse the longer they generate. Often, attempts to fix this involve more training. At high temperature, The sampler, i.e. the rule that picks the next token out of the model's probabilities, decides whether long and agentic generation survives and/or thrives. We test 29 open-weight models from 1B to 122B parameters on ten established benchmarks plus needle retrieval out to one million tokens, covering SWE-bench Verified coding agents, long chain-of-thought reasoning, long-form writing, long structured output and long-context reading. Samplers that keep their pool of candidate tokens small and steady as temperature rises don't lose accuracy. Samplers that let in low-probability tokens fall apart. At temperature 2, coding agents running top-p, top-k or Top-H resolve 0 of 100 GitHub issues, while the same agents running top-nsigma resolve 46 to 62 and win every issue the two samplers disagree on, on three Qwen3.5 models. Over all benchmarks top-nsigma keeps a median 100% of its temperature-1 score where top-p keeps 26%. Counting how many tokens each sampler lets through explains why. In one Llama-3.1-8B story, going from temperature 1 to 2 grows top-p's pool from 4 tokens to 51,845 while top-nsigma stays at 3. Across 133 combinations of sampler setting and temperature, the typical pool size predicts judged quality (Spearman correlation of -0.77), and when we pick the pool at temperature 1 and only apply temperature afterwards, Top-H, min-p and p-less stop collapsing. At the default temperature of 1 most samplers perform about the same, We release all code and data to the public.
papers.summary: Open-weight language models tend to degrade over long generations, and the authors argue that at high temperature the sampler, the rule that picks the next token, determines whether long and agentic generation holds up. They test 29 models from 1B to 122B parameters on ten benchmarks plus needle retrieval out to one million tokens, and find that samplers which keep the candidate pool small and steady as temperature rises retain accuracy while those admitting low-probability tokens collapse. At temperature 2, coding agents on `SWE-bench Verified` using top-p, top-k or `Top-H` resolve 0 of 100 issues while **the same agents using `top-nsigma` resolve 46 to 62**, and overall `top-nsigma` keeps a median 100% of its temperature-1 score versus 26% for top-p. Candidate pool size predicts judged quality (Spearman correlation -0.77), and at the default temperature of 1 most samplers perform about the same.

papers.title: EgoHandWAM: Probing the Role of Hand Motion in Egocentric World Action Modeling
papers.abstract: How much does hand motion tell us about what a first-person camera will see next? EgoHandWAM forecasts three-dimensional wrist and fingertip trajectories and a future visual feature from the current image and recent hand states. We train on 751,065 EgoDex windows using a frozen DINOv2 encoder. On held-out development sessions, the action-only model reduces two-second wrist endpoint error from 60.26 to 56.48~mm relative to a stationary forecast. It still underestimates long reaches. Adding future-feature supervision gives nearly identical trajectory accuracy. With the recorded hand history, the visual head reduces smooth L1 error by 1.32\% relative to copying the current feature. Shuffling histories across sessions erases this gain. In a separate four-task probe, adding recorded future displacements to observed context and future tracking-validity masks reduces visual-feature error by 3.93\%. Masks alone give little improvement. A trajectory predicted from the same observations adds little. On two simulated RoboTwin tasks, substituting aligned human examples for an auxiliary batch of robot examples gives no consistent increase in task success across three training seeds.
papers.summary: `EgoHandWAM` tests how much hand motion predicts what a first-person camera will see next, forecasting 3D wrist and fingertip trajectories and a future visual feature from the current image and recent hand states, trained on 751,065 `EgoDex` windows with a frozen `DINOv2` encoder. The action-only model lowers two-second wrist endpoint error from 60.26 to 56.48 mm against a stationary forecast, and **recorded hand history reduces visual-feature error by just 1.32% relative to copying the current feature**, a gain that vanishes when histories are shuffled across sessions. On two simulated `RoboTwin` tasks, swapping in aligned human examples for a batch of robot examples gave no consistent improvement in task success.

papers.title: Centroid Spectral Coupling: Implicit Alignment and Representation Diversity in Self-Supervised Learning
papers.abstract: Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) aims to align augmented views while preserving representation diversity and preventing collapse. Existing non-contrastive methods often address these goals using multiple weighted loss terms. We introduce Centroid Spectral Coupling (CSC), a single-term SSL objective that implicitly couples view alignment, representation diversity, and collapse resistance. CSC constructs centroids from independently normalized augmented-view pairs and applies a ridge-based spectral objective to their uncentered second-moment matrix. Preserving centroid magnitudes encodes view agreement while encouraging balanced representation energy across spectral directions. We establish an exact decomposition into nonnegative alignment and spectral-imbalance components, characterize the geometry of global optima, and derive finite-loss guarantees for alignment and diversity. We also show that complete constant-output collapse is a strict saddle in normalized representation space. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Imagenette show that CSC achieves the highest linear Top-1 accuracy among the evaluated non-contrastive methods on all three benchmarks, and the highest kNN Top-1 accuracy on both CIFAR datasets. A ridge-parameter sensitivity study reveals an empirical alignment--diversity trade-off: increasing $\kappa$ strengthens view alignment but reduces representation effective rank. These results show that a unified spectral objective yields competitive visual representations without explicit contrastive negatives or separately weighted alignment and diversity penalties.
papers.summary: Non-contrastive self-supervised learning (SSL) methods typically combine several weighted loss terms to align augmented views while keeping representations diverse and avoiding collapse. Centroid Spectral Coupling (`CSC`) replaces these with a single objective that builds centroids from independently normalized view pairs and applies a ridge-based spectral loss to their uncentered second-moment matrix; the authors prove an exact decomposition into alignment and spectral-imbalance components and show that complete collapse is a strict saddle. On `CIFAR-10`, `CIFAR-100`, and `Imagenette`, it **achieves the highest linear top-1 accuracy among the evaluated non-contrastive methods on all three benchmarks**, with the ridge parameter trading view alignment against effective rank.

papers.title: What RL on Expert-Built Tasks Teaches Nemotron 3.5 Super
papers.abstract: We post-train NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Super (120B total, 12B active parameters) with reinforcement learning (RL) on five expert-built task datasets, one at a time: real-world software engineering, complex constraints, long-horizon tool use, professional chart understanding and enterprise document reasoning. Each run trains a fresh rank-32 LoRA adapter with CISPO on Tinker, with no supervised stage, and each adapter is compared with the base model on the same tasks, harness and settings. On twelve headline benchmarks, eight built by other groups and four by Surge AI, the gains range from +4.5 points on IFBench to +13.8 on GDP_pdf, which rises from 10.4% to 24.2%; SWE-bench Pro V2 rises from 86.9% to 92.1%, Terminal-Bench 2.1 from 63.9% to 70.3%, MultiChallenge from 58.3% to 66.6%, AutomationBench from 14.8% to 27.5% and Chartography from 39.4% to 50.6%. The document adapter, trained without API tools, also gains +8.0 points on AutomationBench. In attempts read side by side with the base model's on tasks each adapter newly solves, the base model's failures recur in a few modes, and each adapter does more often what the base model missed: the tool-use adapter finds the data and the rules before acting, the coding adapter writes its own test or scratch files on SWE-bench Pro V2, the constraints adapter carries earlier turns into its answers, the chart adapter measures the marks in code, and the document adapter reads AutomationBench's spreadsheets.
papers.summary: NVIDIA's `Nemotron 3.5 Super` (120B total, 12B active parameters) is post-trained with reinforcement learning (RL) on five expert-built task datasets one at a time, covering software engineering, complex constraints, long-horizon tool use, chart understanding, and enterprise document reasoning. Each run trains a fresh rank-32 LoRA adapter with `CISPO` on `Tinker` with no supervised stage, and is compared with the base model under the same harness. Across twelve benchmarks, **gains range from +4.5 points on `IFBench` to +13.8 on `GDP_pdf`**, including `SWE-bench Pro V2` rising from 86.9% to 92.1% and `Terminal-Bench 2.1` from 63.9% to 70.3%. Side-by-side reading of attempts shows each adapter picking up behaviours the base model missed, such as the coding adapter writing its own tests and the tool-use adapter locating the data and rules before acting.

papers.title: Not All Evidence Is Admissible: Evidence Governance for Tool-Augmented Medical Agents
papers.abstract: Tool-augmented medical agents treat whatever their tools return as evidence. We show that this default is costly: medical tools fail silently, and a frozen reasoner cannot ignore what enters its context, so many cases it would have answered correctly are flipped to wrong once tool outputs are added. We call this evidence hijacking. $\mathcal{V}$-information explains the phenomenon: the reasoner has lost the option to ignore, so a tool output can carry negative usable information, and moving the decision of what to keep outside the reasoner restores that option. The theory further shows that part of any filtering gain comes merely from letting the reasoner see less, and only selection by content lets it see better. Building on this, we recast tool-augmented reasoning as evidence governance, which separates deciding what counts as evidence from the reasoner that answers, and propose context-independent evidence governance (CIEG), the first medical agent framework that rules, after acquisition, on whether each individual tool output may enter as evidence. Every tool output is written as a card that can be checked against the raw input; an independent checker that sees only the input and the cards decides which cards become evidence; and the reasoner answers from the admitted cards alone, with no training anywhere. On medical question answering, fundus glaucoma screening, and chest X-ray pneumonia classification, it achieves the highest accuracy among models of comparable scale, and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art tool-using agents and multi-agent systems built on the same backbone at lower cost.
papers.summary: Tool-augmented medical agents treat every tool output as evidence, and the authors show that silently failing tools can flip answers a frozen reasoner would otherwise have gotten right, an effect they call evidence hijacking and explain using V-information theory. Their context-independent evidence governance (`CIEG`) framework writes each tool output as a card checkable against the raw input, has an independent checker that sees only the input and the cards decide which are admitted, and lets the reasoner answer from admitted cards alone, with no training. On medical question answering, fundus glaucoma screening, and chest X-ray pneumonia classification, it **achieves the highest accuracy among models of comparable scale** and outperforms tool-using agents and multi-agent systems built on the same backbone at lower cost.

papers.title: Readie: Low-Latency Code Sandboxes for AI Agents
papers.abstract:
From quantitative research to personal assistance, AI agents act by iteratively generating and executing code. To decouple the agent harness from code execution, many agents offload execution to dedicated systems called code sandboxes. However, existing code sandboxes suffer from slow startup. Whether they rely on custom snapshots or a single fat image, the root cause is the same: it is hard to build a compact, pre-warmed snapshot that can be shared across diverse agent-generated code while covering nearly all the artifacts (e.g., packages, datasets) it requires.
  In this work, we propose learned startup snapshots for low-latency code sandboxes. Our insight is that while it is hard for a single snapshot to be both compact and cover most workloads, a set of snapshots can achieve both. Each snapshot is small, initializes quickly, and covers a fraction of agent-generated code; together, the set covers most of it. We learn this set from a large training workload by formulating snapshot construction as an optimization problem and solving it with an approximation algorithm. Planned on 15K public and LLM-synthesized scripts, our system, Readie, reduces startup latency by 3-22$\times$ and end-to-end runtime by 1.3-3.3$\times$ compared to existing approaches at the same storage budget.
papers.summary: Code sandboxes used by AI agents start slowly because no single pre-warmed snapshot can be both compact and cover the packages and datasets that diverse agent-generated code needs. `Readie` instead learns a set of small startup snapshots from a large training workload, casting snapshot construction as an optimization problem solved with an approximation algorithm, so that each snapshot covers a fraction of workloads and the set covers most of them. Planned on 15K public and LLM-synthesized scripts, it **cuts startup latency by 3-22x** and end-to-end runtime by 1.3-3.3x against existing approaches at the same storage budget.

papers.title: Towards Optimism-Pessimism Trade-off in Model-based Offline-to-Online Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Model-based offline-to-online reinforcement learning (RL) enables sample-efficient adaptation by leveraging offline pre-training for online fine-tuning. However, the distribution shifts between offline and online stages often hinder fine-tuning performance. Many existing methods encode the optimism-pessimism trade-off through a single-objective formulation. Selecting its trade-off coefficient through online fine-tuning can require costly bi-level optimization. We identify the balance established during offline training as a key challenge: in our motivating experiments, optimistic policies adapt better to novel tasks, whereas pessimistic policies perform better on the same online tasks. To address this challenge, we propose a bi-objective formulation that captures this trade-off, yielding a Pareto policy pool during offline training. This policy pool enables adaptive selection during online fine-tuning across diverse online tasks. To generate the pool, we introduce Multi-Objective Soft Actor-critIC (MOSAIC), which solves bi-objective problems and constructs diverse Pareto policies. After offline training, a contextual bandit algorithm hierarchically selects the most suitable policy for fine-tuning at each online interaction step. Empirically, our pipeline, Hierarchical Pareto Policy Pool (HiP3), achieves the strongest aggregate performance across both same and novel online tasks and maintains its advantage under stronger distribution shifts.
