Comprehensive ablations further clarify the roles of the policy pool, MOSAIC-based pool construction, and the online selection mechanism.
papers.summary: In model-based offline-to-online reinforcement learning, the balance between optimism and pessimism fixed during offline training affects fine-tuning: in the authors' motivating experiments, optimistic policies adapt better to novel tasks while pessimistic ones do better on the same tasks. Rather than a single objective with a tuned trade-off coefficient, the authors pose a bi-objective problem and introduce `MOSAIC` (Multi-Objective Soft Actor-critIC) to build a pool of Pareto policies offline, from which a contextual bandit hierarchically selects a policy at each online interaction step. The full pipeline, `HiP3` (Hierarchical Pareto Policy Pool), is reported to achieve **the strongest aggregate performance across both same and novel online tasks** and to keep its advantage under stronger distribution shifts.

papers.title: Reconfiguring Procedural Knowledge for Compositional Robot Skill Adaptation
papers.abstract: General-purpose behavior models increasingly internalize broad procedural knowledge during training, making their adaptation to new goals and skill interfaces less a problem of learning entirely new behaviors than of reconfiguring existing competence. We study this capability as reconfigurability, the ability to realize new behaviors by cost-efficiently restructuring existing components and relations under sparse governing information, where task specifications provide high-level goals and procedure specifications expose a limited set of reusable factors, leaving the concrete bindings and compositions required for execution underdetermined. We propose RecPo, a framework that represents skills task-agnostically through multiple procedure views and materializes executable skill sequences by composing stored transitions to realize task-specific changes. RecPo maintains a procedure knowledge base of skill-induced transitions, with each view exposing a reusable factor and preserving local skill connectivity. At deployment, it interprets task specifications through the same views and resolves the resulting compositional queries over the stored relations to bind skills for execution. On long-horizon tasks in an extended Franka Kitchen benchmark, RecPo achieves 91.9% ordered completion with 1.0 ms of task inference per episode across varying procedure support and task-record sparsity. Real-robot studies further demonstrate adaptation through local memory edits without task-specific retraining.
papers.summary: Adapting general-purpose robot behavior models to new goals is framed here as reconfiguring skills they already have, under sparse task and procedure specifications that leave the concrete skill bindings underdetermined. `RecPo` keeps a knowledge base of skill-induced transitions organized into multiple procedure views, then interprets a task specification through the same views and composes stored transitions into an executable skill sequence. On long-horizon tasks in an extended `Franka Kitchen` benchmark it reaches **91.9% ordered completion** with 1.0 ms of task inference per episode, and real-robot studies show adaptation through local memory edits without task-specific retraining.

papers.title: The Only Edge Was Memorized in Training: LLM Trading Agents Around Earnings and Bad News
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) trading agents are tested on news, but news reaches stock prices within minutes, and a benchmark that replays headlines at their publication time finds no alpha in trading on them. Money can then remain in two places, before news whose date is known, such as earnings announcements, and after bad news, if the market's fall went too far. However, studies of LLMs and earnings read documents published with or after the announcement, and studies of reversal sort monthly portfolios, so neither tells whether an agent can trade these moments after costs. In this paper, we test LLM agents at both moments on the same look-ahead-free benchmark, before 598 earnings announcements and after 409 bad-news drops of large US stocks. Every input is cut at the decision close, staged agents are compared with single calls, simple rules and a logistic regression, and every decision is made with and without the stock's name. Across five models from four vendors, no agent beat the simple bets. Before earnings, the agents mostly bought and earned what buying before every announcement earned, and after bad news, a Gemini-based agent called almost every fall an overreaction while no agent picked better dips than buying them all. The only gains came from what the models had memorized in training. Given only the ticker and the dates, a GPT-based model called the direction of 59.2% of the announcements before its training cutoff and 53.3% after it. Agent builders should therefore compare an event agent with the simple bet and test it blind after the training cutoff.
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) trading agents are tested at two moments where profit could plausibly remain after news is priced in: before 598 scheduled earnings announcements and after 409 bad-news drops in large US stocks, on a benchmark where every input is cut off at the decision close. Staged agents are compared with single calls, simple rules, and a logistic regression, with and without the stock's name, across five models from four vendors. **No agent beat the simple bets** such as buying before every announcement or buying every dip, and the only gains traced to memorized training data: given only the ticker and dates, a GPT-based model called the direction of 59.2% of announcements before its training cutoff and 53.3% after it. The authors recommend comparing event agents against the simple bet and testing them blind after the training cutoff.

papers.title: CorrectCast: Selective Multimodal Context for Scale-Aware Residual Correction in Precipitation Nowcasting
papers.abstract: Precipitation nowcasting models suffer from errors in intensity, location, and spatial structure. Addressing these errors by retraining nowcaster backbones can be computationally expensive and requires architecture-specific modifications. To overcome these limitations, we propose CorrectCast, a decoupled residual correction framework that refines completed nowcasts while keeping the base nowcaster frozen. By operating on predicted precipitation fields, CorrectCast requires training only a lightweight corrector, reducing computational overhead while providing a unified correction interface across different nowcasting models. Conditioned on the base nowcast and historical quantitative precipitation estimation (QPE) and precipitable water vapor (PWV) observations, the corrector selects multimodal context and employs scale-aware modulation to estimate residual corrections. On the Mississippi River Basin (MRB) and contiguous United States (CONUS) datasets, CorrectCast improves six base nowcasters spanning extrapolation-based, deterministic, and generative approaches, with absolute gains in mean CSI averaging 0.0233 and 0.0290 across the six models, respectively.
papers.summary: Precipitation nowcasting models make errors in intensity, location, and spatial structure, and fixing them by retraining each backbone is expensive and architecture-specific. `CorrectCast` keeps the base nowcaster frozen and trains a lightweight corrector that takes the finished nowcast plus historical quantitative precipitation estimation (QPE) and precipitable water vapor (PWV) observations, selects multimodal context, and applies scale-aware modulation to estimate residual corrections. On the Mississippi River Basin (`MRB`) and contiguous United States (`CONUS`) datasets it improves six base nowcasters spanning extrapolation-based, deterministic, and generative approaches, with **average absolute gains in mean CSI of 0.0233 and 0.0290**, respectively.

papers.title: RAG in a Trenchcoat: When Minimal Memory Is Enough for Agentic Systems, and When It Isn't
papers.abstract: Agentic memory research has accumulated extraction, supersession, reflection, and graph synthesis on top of retrieval-augmented generation. However, we found that almost none of those primitives earn their cost in our tested memory benchmarks: we show this with BRIDGE, a deliberately minimal RAG memory with chained observation notes, hybrid BM25 with cosine retrieval, and chronological rendering, which reaches parity within bootstrap CI with the prior SOTA on LongMemEval-S and BEAM, and beats the best memory baseline on EverMemBench by 5.7-6.3 points at matched reader. It runs at ~5-7K reader-prompt tokens per query, using a single LLM call for each ingestion or query. We argue that this parity is itself the result: standard benchmarks score what memory retrieves, not what memory enables when the agent acts. To test the latter, we introduce five adversarial probes (Rule Application +-, Pattern Induction Style / Procedural, Dynamic Multiturn) judged at generation time by a cross vendor verification chain, where each query can only be solved by applying a remembered rule or pattern it never mentions. Across 5 probes x 20 scenarios, no architecture wins universally: atomic fact extractors (LangMem) win rule application, while BRIDGE's block-summary memory wins pattern induction. This result holds across four domains, three graders, and three reader families. Each design fails where the other wins, for reasons a recall benchmark cannot see: atomic-fact extractors discard the form a demonstrated pattern takes, while block-summary memory retrieves the rule but the reader does not act on it, a gap that presenting the rule more prominently largely closes. What separates memory designs is not what they retrieve but what they enable an agent to do, and that is what agentic memory should be evaluated on.
papers.summary: Agent memory systems have layered extraction, supersession, reflection, and graph synthesis on top of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and the authors test whether those additions pay off. Their deliberately minimal memory, `BRIDGE`, uses chained observation notes, hybrid `BM25` plus cosine retrieval, and chronological rendering with one LLM call per ingestion or query; it matches the prior state of the art on `LongMemEval-S` and `BEAM` and **beats the best memory baseline on `EverMemBench` by 5.7-6.3 points** at a matched reader. Arguing that such benchmarks score retrieval rather than what memory lets an agent do, they add five adversarial probes in which a query can only be solved by applying a remembered rule or pattern it never mentions. No architecture wins across all probes: atomic fact extractors such as `LangMem` win rule application, while `BRIDGE`'s block-summary memory wins pattern induction.

papers.title: CueClash: Frontier Vision-Language Models Judge 3-D Relations Close to the Picture Plane
papers.abstract: A vision-language model (VLM) can judge 3-D relations from the picture or from the ground layout. In photographs the two usually agree. We separate them with CueClash, rendered scenes in which the 2-D cue for each of five relations is right on exactly half the statements. The shortcut gap is accuracy when the cue is right minus accuracy when it is wrong. For Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-5.5 and Gemini 3.6 Flash at low reasoning effort it is +18 to +37 percentage points. It is +7 to +29 without two relations whose cue-wrong items are confounded with borderline cases or occlusion. Given ground coordinates and each relation's definition, they answer 99 to 100% correctly. Pixel measurements with camera depths remove most of the gap for objects fitting through openings. The failure lies in the step from the picture to the layout. The maps that the models draw of the scene from above mostly keep the depth order but, like the picture, shorten depth. GPT-5.5's maps stay close to a copy of the picture. Opus 5.5's and Gemini's maps undo about 0.6 of this shortening. Gemini's then shrink all depths by a further uniform factor. Opus 5.5 follows the picture mainly on fits, and its maps correct depth about as much as human observers of real scenes do. The three models also lose accuracy on CV-Bench photographs where a reliable 2-D cue misleads. In two open models the layout information reaches the language model, but their maps lose much of it.
papers.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) can judge 3-D spatial relations either from 2-D picture cues or from the actual ground layout, and `CueClash` separates the two with rendered scenes in which the 2-D cue for each of five relations is correct on exactly half the statements. For `Claude Opus 5.5`, `GPT-5.5`, and `Gemini 3.6 Flash` at low reasoning effort, **accuracy is 18 to 37 percentage points higher when the 2-D cue is right than when it is wrong**, even though the same models answer 99 to 100% correctly when given ground coordinates and each relation's definition. The failure therefore lies in getting from the picture to the layout: the top-down maps the models draw mostly keep depth order but shorten depth as the picture does, with `GPT-5.5`'s maps staying close to a copy of the picture. The three models also lose accuracy on `CV-Bench` photographs where a reliable 2-D cue misleads.

papers.title: Is 4-Bit Quantization More Than Noise to a Chat Model's Safety Behaviour? Attributing Behavioural Shifts with Matched Perturbations
papers.abstract: Chat models on phones and laptops are usually 4-bit copies of the model that was evaluated, and audits of such copies disagree about what quantization does to refusal. A 4-bit build is one of many weight perturbations of the same size, so a change in its behaviour could come from its specific rounding error or from any perturbation that large. In a pre-registered study of three 3-4B chat models, with paired tests, blind human labels and an 8-bit null, we find two 4-bit shifts of opposite sign: with a compliant reply prefilled, Qwen2.5-3B continues into harmful content more often, and on held-out jailbreaks Llama-3.2-3B complies 10.3 points less often. Matched perturbations separate the two. Shuffled and Gaussian versions of the error average close to zero, while scaling the real error, from its mirror image to twice its size, changes behaviour near-linearly. At half the real error, Llama's likelihood is almost unchanged, yet it already complies 5.8 points less often, and llama.cpp's Q4_K_M, at the same bits per weight, moves neither model. Refusal under 4-bit quantization depends on the specific rounding error, not on bits per weight or likelihood, so each build has to be compared with its original.
papers.summary: Chat models on phones and laptops are usually 4-bit quantized copies of the model that was safety-evaluated, and audits disagree about how quantization affects refusal. A pre-registered study of three 3-4B chat models compares the real 4-bit rounding error against matched weight perturbations of the same size, using paired tests, blind human labels, and an 8-bit null. It finds two shifts of opposite sign: `Qwen2.5-3B` continues into harmful content more often when a compliant reply is prefilled, while **`Llama-3.2-3B` complies 10.3 points less often on held-out jailbreaks**. Shuffled and Gaussian versions of the error average close to zero effect and `llama.cpp`'s `Q4_K_M` build at the same bits per weight moves neither model, so the behaviour depends on the specific rounding error and each build has to be compared with its original.

papers.title: From Imperfective Paradox to Moorean Absurdity: Single-Chain Reasoning Lock-In and Multi-Candidate Verbalization Across Aspectual and Pragmatic Ambiguity
papers.abstract: Natural language entailment and coherence judgments often depend on whether an event merely occurred, reached a telic culmination, satisfied a plan, or was evaluated under multiple pragmatic standards. We test observable consequences of the single-chain premature lock-in hypothesis across four preregistered, sealed formal experiments on Qwen3-8B-Q8_0 (16,640 formal units, temperature=0.0): 15 of 16 hypothesis slots retain confirmatory status (12 rejecting H0 under within-experiment Holm control at alpha_fam=0.05; E3_H3 demoted to descriptive status). In Experiment 1, Direct-CoT vs. MCU differs by 25.00 pp on telic high-confidence completion (Holm p=1.31239e-05), while NLI-CoT collapses by -91.25 pp on uninterrupted atelic items (Holm p=1.81805e-21). Multi-Candidate Verbalization (MCV) elicits K=5 weighted estimates in one call, separating the prompt from unweighted (MCU) and self-weighted (MCW) readouts. Mandarin (E2) and English (E3) expose an Interruption-Anchored Realis Paradox under NLI-CoT. In Experiment 4, MCU-CF raises perceived coherence on implicit Moorean sentences by 26.64 pp over Direct-CoT (Holm p=0.0006), alongside Direct-CF - Direct-CoT = 29.15 pp and MCU-CoT - Direct-CoT = 17.31 pp. A 1,800-call OpenAI ablation and a stage="dev" P16.7 cross-model extension (4,240 planned/collected units across five external models: 4,222 valid, 18 format-missing, 0 transport-missing; <2% missing per slice; OpenAI gpt-4o-mini at top_logprobs=20 achieves 1,000/1,000 valid units) show that discrete NLI-CoT and scalar Direct-CoT judgments dissociate across models. Confirmatory effects concern observable prompt-and-readout protocols; internal premature lock-in remains a hypothesis. All code, stimuli, preregistered analysis plans, and verification tools are available at https://github.com/asj252/llm-judgment-studies.
papers.summary: Entailment and coherence judgments can hinge on whether an event merely occurred, reached its natural endpoint, or is being evaluated under several pragmatic standards, and the authors test whether a single chain of reasoning commits too early to one reading. Four preregistered experiments on a quantized `Qwen3-8B` model compare direct and natural language inference chain-of-thought prompts with Multi-Candidate Verbalization (`MCV`), which elicits five weighted candidate estimates in one call, across aspectual items in English and Mandarin and Moorean sentences. Prompt and readout protocol shift judgments substantially; for example, **a multi-candidate readout raises perceived coherence on implicit Moorean sentences by 26.64 percentage points** over direct chain-of-thought. The authors note that the effects concern observable protocols and that internal premature lock-in remains a hypothesis.

papers.title: RISA: Recoverable Sparse Attention for Block-Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Block-wise diffusion language models (DLMs) refine multiple tokens in parallel, offering an alternative to token-by-token autoregressive decoding. Their long-context inference, however, remains bottlenecked by memory-bound attention: every denoising step repeatedly reads a growing historical key--value (KV) cache. Directly applying sparse attention does not fully solve this problem, because different queries can select different pages, inflating the block's collective read set, while repeated support construction adds overhead and permanent eviction can discard information needed later. We present RISA, a recoverable sparse-attention method with shared read plans for block-wise DLMs. RISA exploits the fact that historical KV remains fixed within a block while queries evolve across denoising steps. Newly generated history is organized into exact priority and recovery tiers; seed queries then build a protected, bounded read plan whose indices are reused across the block while attention is recomputed with fresh queries and current-block KV. This separates history preservation from repeated reading and amortizes sparse-support construction without changing the backbone or decoder. On DreamReasoner-8B, RISA retains comparable task performance. At 32K, the default configuration speeds up attention by $2.67\times$ and fixed-trajectory requests by $1.36\times$ over dense, and attention speedup reaches $5.53\times$ at 128K. Across eight settings on three models, RISA decodes faster than the tested MAGE, QUEST, and LoSA budgets at matched KL.
papers.summary: Block-wise diffusion language models (DLMs) refine many tokens in parallel, but at long context every denoising step re-reads a growing historical key-value (KV) cache, and naive sparse attention helps little because different queries select different pages and eviction can discard information needed later. `RISA` exploits the fact that historical KV stays fixed within a block: it organizes history into priority and recovery tiers and builds a bounded read plan from seed queries whose indices are reused across the block's denoising steps, without changing the backbone or decoder. On `DreamReasoner-8B` task performance stays comparable while **attention speeds up 2.67x at 32K context** and 5.53x at 128K over dense attention, and it decodes faster than the tested `MAGE`, `QUEST`, and `LoSA` budgets at matched KL.

papers.title: An Optimization Framework for Denoising Generation
papers.abstract: Noise-unconditioned denoising learns a single score, so generation can be viewed as gradient ascent on a fixed log-density landscape. This optimization interpretation leaves two questions: do trajectories approach meaningful data, and do different initializations retain diverse outcomes? We establish both phenomena for empirical and population multi-scale Gaussian-mixture objectives. Under explicit posterior and landscape conditions, ascent converges almost surely within $O(m\sigma_{\min}^2/\tau)$ of an $m$-dimensional reference manifold with reach at least $\tau$. We derive a source--sink identity for the same fixed field and use it to prove finite-resolution regional coverage. In an affine construction, we further identify a positive-bandwidth regime where even empirical-score optimization can avoid training-sample memorization while preserving diversity at the training resolution. The same fixed objective naturally supports penalty-guided controllable generation. Experiments support our predicted mechanisms, show improved robustness under large-step guidance, and demonstrate downstream gains consistent with finite-data generative generalization.
papers.summary: When a denoiser is trained without noise conditioning it learns a single score, so generation can be read as gradient ascent on a fixed log-density landscape, raising the questions of whether trajectories reach meaningful data and whether different starting points stay diverse. For multi-scale Gaussian-mixture objectives, the authors prove that under explicit posterior and landscape conditions **ascent converges almost surely to within a bounded distance of a reference data manifold**, and they derive a source-sink identity used to prove finite-resolution regional coverage. In an affine construction they also identify a regime where optimizing the empirical score can avoid memorizing training samples while preserving diversity. Experiments support the predicted mechanisms and show improved robustness under large-step penalty-based guidance.

papers.title: EGS: A Complementary Safety Framework for Educational LLMs
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) offer strong potential for personalized education, but adolescent-facing deployment raises risks of toxic, biased, misleading, or developmentally inappropriate content. We argue that educational safety should move beyond binary refusal: student queries are often ambiguous or curiosity-driven, requiring contextual guidance rather than simple blocking. We introduce the Educational Guardrail System (EGS), a lightweight, model-agnostic runtime framework that complements intrinsic alignment through query moderation, scenario-aware pedagogical guidance, and response moderation. EGS triages inputs by risk level, redirects gray-zone queries with category-specific educational interventions, and audits outputs before delivery. Experiments across general and education-specific benchmarks show that EGS improves moderation performance, refusal quality, and jailbreak robustness across diverse LLMs. These findings suggest that defense-in-depth guardrails can strengthen safety while preserving the pedagogical utility required in educational LLMs. Our code and model weights will be publicly available to support community adoption.
papers.summary: Deploying large language models (LLMs) to adolescents in education carries risks of toxic, biased, misleading, or developmentally inappropriate content, and the authors argue that binary refusal poorly serves ambiguous or curiosity-driven student questions. The Educational Guardrail System (`EGS`) is a lightweight, model-agnostic runtime layer that triages inputs by risk level, redirects gray-zone queries with category-specific pedagogical guidance, and audits responses before delivery. Across general and education-specific benchmarks it is reported to **improve moderation performance, refusal quality, and jailbreak robustness** across diverse LLMs.

papers.title: Flocking Time and Graph Volume in Nonlinear Cucker-Smale Models with Dynamic Networks
papers.abstract: This study proposes a Cucker-Smale model incorporating dynamic networks and the discrete $p$-Laplacian ($p \in (1,2)$) and analyzes the relationship between flocking time constraints and graph connectivity from both theoretical and experimental perspectives. We establish that this model achieves flocking within finite time and derive a quantitative relationship between the lower bound of flocking time and graph volume. Based on these results, we observe that imposing sufficiently small flocking time induces an increase in network volume, and that larger initial velocity variance requires greater volume under the same time constraint. In our experiments, we trained a transformer-based PPO policy to select network structures at each time step. Under the most stringent time constraint, the maximum average number of connections increased sharply, confirming a threshold effect. The negative correlation between convergence time and average number of connections reflects the theoretical results well. This study provides quantitative evidence for the phenomenon that time constraints induce connection mobilization.
papers.summary: A Cucker-Smale flocking model with dynamic networks and the discrete p-Laplacian (p between 1 and 2) is analyzed to relate how fast agents align their velocities to how connected the network is. The authors prove that **the model flocks in finite time and derive a quantitative link between the lower bound on flocking time and graph volume**, implying that tighter time limits and larger initial velocity variance require more connections. In experiments, a transformer-based `PPO` policy chooses the network structure at each step, and under the most stringent time constraint the average number of connections rises sharply, consistent with the predicted threshold effect.

papers.title: Sample-efficient Personalization of Large Language Model Alignment with Multidimensional User Preference Data
papers.abstract: Preference alignment has become a central tool to align large language models (LLMs) with human values and desired behavior, and its online variant can further advance their capabilities beyond what static data alone offer by repeatedly generating and labeling new responses with human feedback. But costly, time-consuming annotations limit its scalability, making sample efficiency essential, and existing methods typically seek to improve it by expanding coverage of the response space or selecting pairs with the highest uncertainty for comparison. Although they are effective, these methods quantify uncertainty from the perspective of the LLM, which may differ from the uncertainty perceived by the user: a pair can appear highly uncertain to the LLM even when past comparisons from the user already imply a clear ordering. In this paper, we propose multidimensional preference-guided online direct preference optimization (MPG-DPO), which leverages low-cost multidimensional evaluations from automated verifiers on the user historical comparisons to construct a personalized preference cone guiding response selection for online preference alignment. Specifically, it first discards responses that are confidently dominated under the estimated user preference, then selects two responses that are competitive under the retained preference cone yet exhibit the strongest unresolved disagreement. Theoretical analysis shows that, with high probability, the fraction of queries spent on cone-dominated responses vanishes as learning progresses. Experiments across multiple LLM families show that MPG-DPO outperforms strong contenders under matched query budgets.
papers.summary: Online preference alignment of large language models (LLMs) needs costly human comparisons, and existing sample-efficient methods choose response pairs by the model's own uncertainty, which can differ from what the user's past choices already imply. `MPG-DPO` (multidimensional preference-guided online direct preference optimization) uses cheap multidimensional scores from automated verifiers on a user's historical comparisons to build a personalized preference cone, discards responses confidently dominated under it, and queries the two competitive responses with the strongest unresolved disagreement. Theory shows that, with high probability, **the fraction of queries spent on cone-dominated responses vanishes as learning progresses**, and experiments across multiple LLM families show it outperforming strong baselines under matched query budgets.

papers.title: Communicate the Change: Efficient Expert Parallelism via Activation Compression
papers.abstract: Scaling has driven the success of large language models (LLM), with sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures enabling greater parameter capacity without a proportional increase in computation. At large scales, MoE models rely on expert parallelism to distribute experts across devices. Each MoE layer requires two synchronous collective communication steps during inference: dispatching hidden states to the activated experts and combining the resulting expert outputs. As compute throughput has outpaced interconnect bandwidth, these synchronous collectives have become a major bottleneck to MoE scaling and efficiency. We address this challenge with EchoMoE, a lightweight architecture modification that retrofits existing MoE models, requiring approximately 8,500x fewer training tokens than full pretraining. Motivated by the observation that transformer blocks update the residual stream incrementally, we use a hidden state from an earlier layer as a reference and communicate only the compressed difference between it and the current state, rather than communicating each hidden state in full. EchoMoE periodically refreshes these reference states and transmits only the compressed differences synchronously, reducing the traffic on latency-critical paths without significant computational overhead. EchoMoE reduces inter-node communication volume by 58% and improves throughput by 22.6%, while preserving average performance within 3.8 percentage points across 18 benchmarks. EchoMoE further improves inference throughput by up to 2.38x over bandwidth-constrained Ethernet, paving the way for wide-area distributed inference. EchoMoE also tolerates quantization of the communicated representations without measurable quality loss. We release an efficient implementation for applying EchoMoE to pretrained MoE models, together with an inference integration for vLLM.
papers.summary: Sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models spread experts across devices, and each MoE layer needs two synchronous communication steps at inference, dispatching hidden states to experts and combining their outputs, which has become a bottleneck as compute outpaces interconnect bandwidth. `EchoMoE` retrofits existing MoE models, with roughly 8,500x fewer training tokens than full pretraining, to send only the compressed difference between the current hidden state and a periodically refreshed reference state from an earlier layer. It **reduces inter-node communication volume by 58% and raises throughput by 22.6%** while keeping average performance within 3.8 percentage points across 18 benchmarks, and it improves throughput by up to 2.38x over bandwidth-constrained Ethernet. An implementation with `vLLM` integration is released.

papers.title: Learning Optimal Transport Plans Via Autoregressive Token Regression
papers.abstract: Optimal Transport (OT) provides a principled framework for finding the minimum cost coupling between probability distributions. Classical solvers remain the gold standard for this task. At the same time, OT is an ideal testbed for studying whether learning-based amortized models can internalize the structure of OT type problems. Here, ground-truth solutions are available and marginal constraints are explicitly defined. Also, exact discrete solutions have well-characterized sparsity. We describe ToR-OT, a transformer-based model that learns to predict discrete OT plans through autoregressive token regression. We reframe OT into a structured sequence generation task. ToR-OT decodes sparse transport plans as sequences instead of solving an optimization task at test time. We focus on three properties: (a) Zero-shot generalization: pretraining on a large synthetic corpus of OT instances allows a single model to generalize to unseen distribution pairs and heterogeneous cost metrics without retraining, (b) Sparse primal decoding: by exploiting the inherent sparsity in exact discrete OT solutions, the decoder predicts only nonzero entries (avoids dense coupling outputs), (c) Amortized inference: on low-dimensional discrete problems, ToR-OT gives accurate approximate plans and compares favorably with per-instance neural OT baselines. Overall, ToR-OT is not yet a replacement for classical solvers, but a step toward understanding how autoregressive transformers can learn structure of constrained optimization problems like OT.
papers.summary: Optimal Transport (OT), which finds the minimum-cost coupling between probability distributions, is used as a testbed for whether a learned model can internalize the structure of a constrained optimization problem with known ground-truth solutions. `ToR-OT` is a transformer pretrained on a large synthetic corpus of OT instances that predicts discrete transport plans by autoregressive token regression, decoding only the nonzero entries of the sparse plan rather than solving an optimization at test time. A single model generalizes zero-shot to unseen distribution pairs and cost metrics and, on low-dimensional discrete problems, gives accurate approximate plans that compare favorably with per-instance neural OT baselines, though the authors state it is **not yet a replacement for classical solvers**.

papers.title: Fine-Grained Japanese Clinical Named Entity Recognition: A Controlled Comparison of BERT and Open-Weight Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Background: Generative large language models (LLMs) offer an alternative to encoder-based clinical named entity recognition (NER), but their performance on fine-grained Japanese extraction tasks and sensitivity to generation settings remain uncertain. Methods: We compared two fine-tuned BERT-CRF baselines with nine open-weight LLMs on iCorpus, which defines 113 entity categories. The evaluation used 433 sentences from 36 test documents; 1,672 sentences were used for training. LLMs were evaluated using zero-shot prompting with and without JSON Schema constraints and three-seed QLoRA fine-tuning. Fine-tuned models were assessed under different output-token limits, including 900 and larger model-specific limits of 2,600 or 4,096 tokens. Performance was measured using sentence-level label-surface matching with relaxed and exact-surface F1. Results: The highest zero-shot relaxed F1 was 0.337, compared with 0.836-0.841 for the BERT baselines. At the larger output limits, all eight fine-tuned LLMs with at least 13B total parameters exceeded both BERT baselines (relaxed F1, 0.882-0.914; exact-surface F1, 0.840-0.880). Across three-seed means, increasing the output limit improved relaxed F1 by 0.052-0.085, alongside higher recall and fewer length-limited outputs. JSON Schema constraints changed relaxed F1 by -0.014 to +0.008 among seven models outside the two reasoning-oriented configurations, while medical-general model pairs showed no consistent advantage for medical specialization. Conclusions: On this historical Japanese case-report benchmark, task-specific fine-tuning combined with adequate generation capacity was associated with stronger LLM extraction performance. Output-token limits materially affected comparisons with BERT, whereas enforcing output structure alone did not overcome low zero-shot accuracy.
papers.summary: Two fine-tuned `BERT-CRF` baselines are compared with nine open-weight large language models (LLMs) on fine-grained Japanese clinical named entity recognition (NER) using `iCorpus`, which defines 113 entity categories. Zero-shot prompting, with or without JSON Schema constraints, peaked at a relaxed F1 of 0.337 against 0.836-0.841 for the BERT baselines, but with `QLoRA` fine-tuning and larger output-token limits **all eight LLMs with at least 13B parameters exceeded both BERT baselines (relaxed F1 0.882-0.914)**. Raising the output limit alone improved relaxed F1 by 0.052-0.085, schema constraints changed it only slightly, and medically specialized models showed no consistent advantage over general ones.

papers.title: SOTA or Luck? The Winner's Curse in LLM Leaderboards
papers.abstract: Public LLM leaderboards guide model evaluation and adoption, yet the reported performance of top-ranked models can be systematically overstated. This leaderboard winner's curse arises because ranking noisy benchmark scores rewards sampling luck alongside genuine ability. The same selection effect can distort scores throughout the leaderboard, a phenomenon we call the rank-induced bias. We develop an $m$-out-of-$N$ bootstrap to correct for this bias. It assumes a fixed model pool with independent, identically distributed bounded tasks while allowing arbitrary within-task correlation among models. Under exact population tiers separated by positive gaps, we prove that the bootstrap reduces $\Theta(N^{-1/2})$ ranking bias to expected residual bias $o(N^{-1/2})$. Across 14 benchmarks from 5 benchmark families, the rank-1 adjustments range from approximately 0.09 to 3.86 percentage points. In our SWE-bench Verified snapshot, the tied leaders receive an adjustment of 0.90 percentage points. Such overstatement is large enough to make the apparent winner statistically fragile. Thus, we use the same bootstrap to further quantify the intervals of plausible rank positions for each model and group models into tiers. We establish sufficient conditions for consistent recovery of population tiers. On SWE-bench Verified, this procedure places 13 of 173 models in the leading tier. We combine the score adjustment and rank intervals in the Rank Uncertainty and Leaderboard Evaluation Report (RULER). We validate its finite-sample performance using sample splitting and calibrated simulations, and advocate publishing RULER alongside raw rankings so readers can assess both reported performance and the precision of the ordering. RULER also provides guidance for benchmark design that accounts for selection effects and ranking uncertainty.
papers.summary: Top scores on public LLM leaderboards are systematically overstated because ranking noisy benchmark results rewards sampling luck along with ability, a winner's curse that also distorts scores further down the list. The authors correct for it with an m-out-of-N bootstrap, prove that it reduces the ranking bias to a lower order in the number of tasks under stated assumptions, and use the same procedure to give each model an interval of plausible ranks and group models into tiers. Across 14 benchmarks from 5 families the adjustment to the top-ranked score ranges from about 0.09 to 3.86 percentage points, and on `SWE-bench Verified` **13 of 173 models fall in the leading tier**. They package the adjusted scores and rank intervals as the Rank Uncertainty and Leaderboard Evaluation Report (`RULER`) and advocate publishing it alongside raw rankings.
papers.highlight_summary:
Ranking noisy benchmark averages rewards sampling luck as well as ability, so top leaderboard scores are systematically overstated and the ordering looks more settled than it is. `RULER` corrects this "rank-induced bias" with an `m`-out-of-`N` bootstrap and reports how firmly each model actually holds its rank.

- The method resamples whole task rows (preserving cross-model correlation) with m = ⌊N^0.9⌋, re-ranks the models in each resample, and rescales the selected model's excess score by √(m/N) to get a per-position adjustment, while the same resamples yield a rank probability matrix, 80% rank intervals, and tiers of statistically unresolved models.
- On `SWE-bench Verified` (173 models, 500 tasks), the two tied leaders drop from 79.2% to 78.3% (**0.90 pp** of inflation), each holds only about **30%** probability of being rank 1, and **13 of 173** models share the leading tier — while 7 of the 13 top-score increases during 2025 were smaller than that inflation.
- Across 14 benchmarks from 5 families, rank-1 adjustments range from **0.09 to 3.86 pp**, exceed 1 pp in 7, and **12 of 14** have a multi-model leading tier, with the largest corrections on 50-task pools such as `LiveBench` instruction following (3.86 pp) and `Tau2 Airline` (3.07 pp).
- Validation supports the correction: in held-out half-splits the magnitude of mean rank-1 error averaged over the 14 benchmarks falls from **2.38 to 0.73 pp**, a simulation calibrated to `SWE-bench Verified` cuts mean winner bias from 1.41 to 0.21 pp, and the theory shows the bias shrinking from order N^(-1/2) to o(N^(-1/2)).
- The guarantees assume i.i.d. tasks and an idealized exact-tie structure, the resample exponent has no principled tuning rule, the correction can overcorrect when gaps are comparable to noise or the winner is well separated, and it addresses only task-sampling noise, not contamination, rerun or judge variance, or adaptive submissions.

papers.title: What Does Weight-Space Programming Add to Diffusion Editing? Program Construction versus Score-Guided Refinement
papers.abstract: Weight-space programming (WSP) lets a language model construct executable weight updates for another network. We study diffusion concept editing through an interface in which programs define training contexts, preservation constraints and update directions, while a shared numerical fitter selects their coefficients. We compare generated programs with published editors, a shared-panel hand-written baseline and budget-matched search over conventional edits on 24 TIMED test edits for Stable Diffusion 1.4. The preregistered rewrite pipeline shows no advantage over the strong baseline. In an exploratory comparison, one-shot Astra programs improve fresh-scene VLM joint success, which requires subject presence together with whole-image target matching, by +10.0 points over the shared-panel baseline, while CLIP relative match shows no detectable change. These programs organise adjustable directions around protected text-state subspaces. Probing and rewriting the Astra programs then raises CLIP by +6.2 points while joint success changes by -9.7. On a fixed 144-image sample, five additional evaluators give point estimates in the same directions under whole-image target matching; checks of subject-local change give less decisive differences. Together, these results identify useful behaviour in complete generated programs and show that score-guided revision need not preserve it: program construction and revision should be evaluated as distinct stages of a WSP pipeline.
papers.summary: Weight-space programming (WSP) has a language model write executable weight updates for another network, studied here for concept editing in `Stable Diffusion 1.4`, where programs define training contexts, preservation constraints, and update directions and a shared numerical fitter picks the coefficients. On 24 `TIMED` test edits, the preregistered rewrite pipeline shows no advantage over a strong hand-written baseline. In an exploratory comparison, **one-shot `Astra` programs raise VLM-judged joint success by 10.0 points** over that baseline with no detectable change in `CLIP` relative match, whereas then probing and rewriting those programs raises `CLIP` by 6.2 points while joint success changes by -9.7. The authors conclude that program construction and score-guided revision should be evaluated as distinct stages.

papers.title: Discovery of new antiviral agents through artificial intelligence: in vitro and in vivo results
papers.abstract: In this research, we employed a deep reinforcement learning (RL)-based molecule design platform to generate a diverse set of compounds targeting the neuraminidase (NA) of influenza A and B viruses. A total of 60291 compounds were generated, of which 86.5% displayed superior physicochemical properties compared to oseltamivir. After narrowing down the selection through computational filters, nine compounds with non-sialic acid-like structures were selected for in vitro experiments. We identified two compounds, DS-22-inf-009 and DS-22-inf-021 that effectively inhibited the NAs of both influenza A and B viruses (IAV and IBV), including H275Y mutant strains at low micromolar concentrations. Molecular dynamics simulations revealed a similar pattern of interaction with amino acid residues as oseltamivir. In cell-based assays, DS-22-inf-009 and DS-22-inf-021 inhibited IAV and IBV in a dose-dependent manner with EC50 values ranging from 0.29 uM to 2.31 uM. Furthermore, animal experiments showed that both DS-22-inf-009 and DS-22-inf-021 exerted antiviral activity in mice, conferring 65% and 85% protection from IAV (H1N1 pdm09), and 65% and 100% protection from IBV (Yamagata lineage), respectively. Thus, these findings demonstrate the potential of RL to generate compounds with promising antiviral properties.
papers.summary: A deep reinforcement learning (RL) molecule design platform was used to generate 60291 candidate compounds targeting the neuraminidase of influenza A and B viruses, which were narrowed by computational filters to nine non-sialic-acid-like compounds for laboratory testing. Two of them, `DS-22-inf-009` and `DS-22-inf-021`, inhibited neuraminidases of both virus types, including H275Y mutant strains, at low micromolar concentrations, and inhibited the viruses in cell-based assays with EC50 values from 0.29 uM to 2.31 uM. In mice, the two compounds conferred **65% and 85% protection from influenza A (H1N1 pdm09) and 65% and 100% protection from influenza B**, respectively.

papers.title: From Temperature-Limited to Battery-Limited Legged Locomotion
papers.abstract: On legged robots, sustained locomotion often ends in thermal shutdown rather than battery depletion: the heat of walking concentrates in a few joint motors, which overheat long before the battery is empty. We train thermally aware locomotion policies by reinforcement learning without ever observing temperature, and demonstrate this on a Unitree Go2 quadruped. We first identify a coupled 13-node lumped RC thermal network, fitted on two runs of a single robot and calibrated against the measured electrical power, that predicts all twelve motor temperatures with a mean RMSE below 1 $^\circ$C across different robot instances, gaits, payloads, and speeds. Under a sustained gait, the temperatures the motors will settle at follow directly from the gait-averaged squared torques and joint speeds. Our core contribution is a reward that drives down the hottest predicted asymptotes: thermal time constants exceed the credit-assignment horizon of reinforcement learning by orders of magnitude, but predicted asymptotes respond to torque and joint speed within a single gait cycle, so the policy learns to lower and spread heat with no temperature input. On the robot, the policy turns sustained locomotion from temperature-limited to battery-limited: with a 5 kg payload at 1 m/s, a learned baseline reaches thermal shutdown after 19 minutes (1.1 km), whereas our policy runs the battery down after 174 minutes (10.0 km) with its hottest motor 14 $^\circ$C below the shutdown threshold in a 26 $^\circ$C room; on an unloaded factory circuit with stairs and ramps, the baseline overheats after 25 laps (6.2 km), while our policy completes 47 (11.2 km) on one battery with 22 $^\circ$C of margin.
papers.summary: Legged robots often stop walking because a few joint motors overheat long before the battery is empty. The authors fit a coupled 13-node lumped thermal network for a `Unitree Go2` quadruped that predicts all twelve motor temperatures with mean error below 1 °C, then train a reinforcement learning policy whose reward lowers the hottest predicted steady-state temperatures, which respond to torque and joint speed within one gait cycle, so the policy needs no temperature input. With a 5 kg payload at 1 m/s, a learned baseline hits thermal shutdown after 19 minutes (1.1 km), while the new policy **runs for 174 minutes (10.0 km) until the battery is depleted**, with its hottest motor 14 °C below the shutdown threshold.

papers.title: The Fragility of Reasoning-Importance Attribution for Pruning Language Models
papers.abstract: Attribution-guided pruning scores components by their causal contribution and protects the important ones, and it is increasingly applied to compress reasoning language models without destroying their chain of thought. Its reliability rests on an unexamined assumption: that reasoning importance can be faithfully measured. Across four small reasoning models, we show this measurement is fragile in three ways, each of which changes pruning decisions. First, scoring final-answer tokens, the natural choice, saturates in every chain-of-thought model we test (answer-token negative log-likelihood, NLL, of $10^{-4}$--$10^{-3}$) because the model states its answer inside its own reasoning; guiding head pruning with this target costs 27.6 and 32.2 accuracy points relative to scoring reasoning tokens on the two models we power with five seeds, while perplexity barely moves and even reverses sign at 7B. Second, causal importance is not localizable to single units: single-neuron effects sit at the measurement floor, their cross-split ranking is noise, and they cancel: a group's ablation effect disagrees in sign with the summed effects of its members in 90\% of groups. Reproducible importance emerges only at groups of $\sim 100$ neurons. Third, contrastively isolated ``reasoning-specific'' importance is not separable from generic importance, and protecting it is worse than protecting raw importance. We additionally pre-registered the hypothesis that distillation-induced concentration of importance predicts the pruning cost; it is not supported, and since our grid confounds concentration with scale, we report it as unresolved rather than reversed. The result is a short set of measurement rules: score reasoning tokens, attribute at coarse granularity, and evaluate with accuracy rather than perplexity.
papers.summary: Attribution-guided pruning compresses reasoning language models by protecting components scored as causally important, which assumes that reasoning importance can be measured faithfully. Across four small reasoning models, the authors find the measurement fragile in three ways: scoring final-answer tokens saturates because the model already states its answer inside its chain of thought, single-neuron effects are noise and only become reproducible at groups of about 100 neurons, and contrastively isolated reasoning-specific importance cannot be separated from generic importance. Guiding head pruning by answer tokens instead of reasoning tokens **costs 27.6 and 32.2 accuracy points** on the two models tested with five seeds, while perplexity barely moves. A pre-registered hypothesis that distillation-induced concentration of importance predicts pruning cost was not supported and is reported as unresolved.

papers.title: Spatially local mini-batching for implicit neural representations
papers.abstract: Neural surrogates based on implicit neural representations (INRs) are typically trained on mini-batches spread over the whole domain, since a generic INR loses accuracy when every point of a batch lies in one small region. We show that low-rank neural representations (LRNRs), INRs whose weight matrices are products of shared bases with coefficients emitted by a small hypernetwork, can be trained with spatially local mini-batches. Each step uses the points of one time snapshot of an adaptive-mesh numerical solution inside one small cell, with snapshots and cells drawn according to the refinement of the mesh. We posit that such training is enabled by the structural property of LRNRs, as a local step reaches the shared bases only through the $r$ coefficients of each layer, and keeps one cell from rewriting the network. By a Kolmogorov-width argument, we show that when restricted to a small cell, the hidden states of LRNRs lie close to a low-dimensional subspace, which suggests the local steps only affect low-rank subspaces of the shared bases. On six hyperbolic-conservation-law problems with solutions computed using adaptive mesh refinement, one local training recipe reaches 1.1-2.3% relative $L^2$ error with a tenth of the parameters of a dense network of the same width. Finally, we provide a comparison by training a hypernetwork-SIREN, a DeepONet, and a Fourier neural operator (FNO) of the same size with the same local batches and training budget. We observe that these baselines reach 16-78% where the LRNR reaches 4.9%. Interestingly, we also observe that local training has a significant effect on the per-cell low-dimensional structure even in a wide generic hypernetwork-SIREN.
papers.summary: Implicit neural representations (INRs) used as surrogates for numerical solutions are normally trained on mini-batches spread over the whole domain, because batches confined to one small region degrade a generic network. The authors show that low-rank neural representations (LRNRs), whose weight matrices are products of shared bases with coefficients from a small hypernetwork, can instead be trained on points from a single cell of one time snapshot of an adaptive-mesh solution, and they give a Kolmogorov-width argument that local steps only affect low-rank subspaces of the shared bases. On six hyperbolic conservation law problems, one local training recipe reaches **1.1-2.3% relative L2 error with a tenth of the parameters** of a dense network of the same width. Under the same local batches and budget, a hypernetwork-`SIREN`, a `DeepONet`, and a Fourier neural operator (FNO) reach 16-78% error where the LRNR reaches 4.9%.

papers.title: Context Has a Price: Adding and Removing Context for LLM Coding Agents under Prefix Caching
papers.abstract: Coding agents repeatedly send their conversation history to a language model. Adding useful code may reduce search, while removing old tool outputs may shorten later prompts. But do these changes reduce the cost of solving a task? We study this as a measurement problem in more than 20,000 runs of open models on SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench and Loc-Bench. We account separately for uncached input, cached input and output tokens. Three findings emerge. First, in our main evidence-package experiments, retrieved code reduces read and search commands by 18--34%, but increases cost by 33--42% when cached input costs one tenth of uncached input, without a measurable improvement in resolution. Second, removing old observations can either save money or increase cost: the same approach saves 19--36% without a cache discount but increases cost by 38--116% with a tenth-price cache. Third, shorter prompts do not guarantee cheaper runs because agents may respond by taking more steps. We also find that concurrent experiments can share cached prefixes and distort cost comparisons. These results show why context-management methods should be evaluated using both token prices and the agent's subsequent behavior.
papers.summary: Coding agents resend their conversation history on every step, so adding retrieved code or removing old tool outputs changes what a task costs in ways that depend on prefix caching. Across more than 20,000 runs of open models on `SWE-bench Verified`, `SWE-bench`, and `Loc-Bench`, the authors account separately for uncached input, cached input, and output tokens. Retrieved code cuts read and search commands by 18-34% but **raises cost by 33-42% when cached input is priced at one tenth of uncached input**, with no measurable gain in resolution rate. Removing old observations saves 19-36% without a cache discount but increases cost by 38-116% with one, and shorter prompts do not guarantee cheaper runs because agents may take more steps.

papers.title: Solver-Free and Cost-Aware Online Scheduling of AI Data Center Tasks
papers.abstract: AI data centers receive computing tasks continuously, whereas solver-based optimization takes time to run and electricity is priced per settlement period. This paper bridges this timing gap through a solver-free online optimization rule inspired by dual decomposition. The rule assigns each task a start period upon arrival to optimize energy cost subject to operational constraints, shifting flexible tasks toward low-price periods while keeping high-priority tasks on schedule. Simulations on the A100 GPU trace (3,456 GPUs, 1,343 tasks) show that the proposed rule keeps GPU and CPU use within capacity while scheduling tasks at low cost. Compared with a multi-timescale optimization benchmark, it achieves a lower cost and, because it needs no solver, much less computation time.
papers.summary: AI data centers receive computing tasks continuously, but solver-based scheduling is slow and electricity is priced per settlement period. The authors propose a solver-free online rule inspired by dual decomposition that assigns each task a start period on arrival, shifting flexible tasks toward low-price periods while keeping high-priority tasks on schedule. In simulations on the `A100` GPU trace (3,456 GPUs, 1,343 tasks), the rule keeps GPU and CPU use within capacity and **achieves lower cost than a multi-timescale optimization benchmark** with much less computation time.

papers.title: Where Does Hindsight Enter Clinical Agent Benchmarks? An Audit of Simulators and Case Construction
papers.abstract: Benchmarks for LLM diagnostic agents are built from retrospective records: the case an agent reads is rewritten from discharge summaries, and unrecorded test results are generated by a simulator that often sees the final diagnosis. HindAudit separates three hindsight channels (the diagnosis given to the simulator, the retrospective context it conditions on, and the agent-facing case text) and measures each with judges trained only on real data. On 27,489 emergency admissions from MIMIC-IV, five registered tests found no leakage into simulated laboratory results: providing the diagnosis to five simulators had a negligible effect, and prompted gatekeepers diluted the diagnostic signal, although exploratory results suggest they can raise agent scores. The largest effect lay in the case text. Against a presentation-time reconstruction from triage records, benchmark-style summaries raised the zero-shot accuracy of four LLMs from 25.4% to 39.7% and discharge histories to 45.3%, and raised six interactive agents' scores while barely changing their ranking. The exploratory gap was reproduced in a registered replication on held-out patients. Masking diagnosis names left it unchanged. Because MIMIC lacks a contemporaneous bedside history, the gap is an upper bound on hindsight. We report all registered outcomes and recommend construction practices.
papers.summary: Benchmarks for large language model (LLM) diagnostic agents are built from retrospective records, so hindsight can leak through the diagnosis given to the result simulator, the retrospective context it conditions on, or the case text the agent reads. `HindAudit` measures each channel separately on 27,489 emergency admissions from `MIMIC-IV`, and five registered tests found no leakage into simulated laboratory results. The largest effect was in the case text: compared with a presentation-time reconstruction from triage records, benchmark-style summaries **raised zero-shot accuracy of four LLMs from 25.4% to 39.7%**, and discharge histories raised it to 45.3%, while agent rankings barely changed. The authors note the gap is an upper bound on hindsight because the dataset lacks a contemporaneous bedside history.

papers.title: Multi-Agent Memory Inconsistency: Where Factual Conflicts Disappear in LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Multi-agent delegation lets LLM systems distribute evidence collection across workers with separate contexts. This creates a consistency challenge: facts retrieved by workers may be missing from the evidence available to the lead for a joint conclusion. We introduce a benchmark and evidence-flow profiler for studying multi-agent memory inconsistency through controlled factual conflicts in Harvey LAB document-review tasks. Pooled across three models with comparable generation spending, requiring delegation increases retrieval of both conflicting claims from 50.2% to 68.7% relative to single-agent execution, yet conflict detection falls from 16.2% to 13.2%. Within this setting, workers report both claims for only 35.2% of retrieved pairs, and pooled matched comparisons show higher detection than single-agent execution when one worker reads both claims but lower detection when the claims are split across workers. Worker-to-lead handoffs are a central target for improving conflict detection in multi-agent LLMs.
papers.summary: When a lead agent delegates evidence collection to workers with separate contexts, facts the workers retrieve may never reach the lead that draws the joint conclusion. The authors build a benchmark and evidence-flow profiler that plants controlled factual conflicts in `Harvey LAB` document-review tasks. Pooled across three models at comparable generation spending, requiring delegation raises retrieval of both conflicting claims from 50.2% to 68.7%, yet **conflict detection falls from 16.2% to 13.2%**. Workers report both claims for only 35.2% of retrieved pairs, and detection drops below single-agent levels when the two claims are split across workers, which points to worker-to-lead handoffs as the weak link.

papers.title: OAK-Mind: Zero-Training Mental Health Change Inference from Passive Sensing via Knowledge-Grounded Multi-Agent LLMs
papers.abstract: Wearable and smartphone sensors capture behavioral signals associated with mental health, yet inferring mental health outcomes from these signals has traditionally relied on supervised models requiring labeled data and offering limited insight into their predictions. Large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities to reason over behavioral evidence, but existing LLM-based approaches to passive sensing have largely continued to rely on task-specific fine-tuning or sensor-specific pretraining. In this paper, we introduce \textbf{OAK-Mind}, a zer\textbf{O}-training, multi-\textbf{A}gent, \textbf{K}nowledge-grounded LLM pipeline for inferring mental health changes from passive sensing data. The pipeline organizes sensing data into behavioral dimensions including sleep, physical activity, location mobility, and smartphone use, and orchestrates specialized agents grounded in mental health literature to interpret longitudinal behavioral changes. It synthesizes their assessments and applies questionnaire-based symptom rating to infer changes relative to an individual's baseline assessment with human-readable rationale grounded in observed behavioral patterns and domain knowledge. Across datasets and prediction tasks, while without task-specific training, OAK-Mind achieves comparable or better performance than the most predictive supervised baselines trained on additional labeled samples. It also demonstrate consistent improvement upon direct prompting across four tested LLM backbones. Ablation analyses support the benefits of combining behavioral interpretation with symptom rating, distributing analysis across domain-specific agents, and incorporating domain knowledge. Our findings highlight the potential of knowledge-grounded, multi-agent LLMs for training-free inference of mental health changes from passive sensing data.
papers.summary: Inferring mental health changes from wearable and smartphone sensor data has usually required supervised models trained on labeled data, and those models offer little insight into their predictions. `OAK-Mind` is a training-free multi-agent large language model (LLM) pipeline that organizes sensing data into sleep, physical activity, location mobility, and smartphone use, has specialized agents grounded in mental health literature interpret longitudinal changes, and then applies questionnaire-based symptom rating relative to an individual's baseline. Without task-specific training, it reportedly **matches or exceeds the most predictive supervised baselines** across datasets and tasks, and improves on direct prompting across four LLM backbones.

papers.title: PCGRL for Complex Platformers: Synthesizing Playable and Diverse Levels via Inflated Envelopes and Forward Curricula
papers.abstract: Procedural Content Generation via Reinforcement Learning (PCGRL) has emerged as a promising paradigm for automated game development. However, existing PCGRL frameworks still suffer from severe exploration bottlenecks and scaling limitations when faced with long-sequence generation tasks governed by strict rigid-body rules and non-linear kinematic boundaries (e.g., platformer constraints). Consequently, traditional approaches frequently fail to maintain reliable level solvability on large-scale canvases. To address these challenges, we present a physics-aware, curriculum-guided PCGRL framework. First, we construct an "Inflated Volume Envelope" mechanism, which provides a physics-constrained representation that incorporates continuous kinematic feasibility into the discrete state space of the MDP. Second, to alleviate the sparse reward challenge induced by extremely long decision sequences, we introduce intermediate state-transition feedback and a multi-stage forward extension curriculum learning framework, enabling informative value estimation and stable credit assignment over long-horizon trajectories. Finally, to resolve the issue where deterministic policies after convergence generate highly monotonous map paths with a lack of diversity, we activate high-entropy stochastic inference during the synthesis phase, regularized by a post-hoc parallel rejection filtering mechanism. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework significantly enhances structural diversity while maintaining high physical playability across multi-scale environments. Comparative evaluations across multi-scale canvases demonstrate that our framework maintains superior convergence stability and dimensional scalability, reliably synthesizing solvable levels where traditional PCGRL baselines degrade.
papers.summary: Procedural Content Generation via Reinforcement Learning (PCGRL) struggles to keep levels solvable on large canvases when generation is long-horizon and bound by platformer physics. The proposed framework encodes continuous kinematic feasibility into the discrete state space through an inflated volume envelope, adds intermediate state-transition feedback with a multi-stage forward extension curriculum to ease sparse rewards, and uses high-entropy stochastic inference with parallel rejection filtering to restore diversity at generation time. The authors report that it **reliably synthesizes solvable levels at scales where traditional PCGRL baselines degrade**, while increasing structural diversity.

papers.title: A Visual Information Extraction System Using Multimodal Large Language Models for Scanned Cognitive and Behavioral Assessments
papers.abstract:
Objective. Paper-based assessments are common in patient care, but handwriting and scanning artifacts make these forms difficult to process at scale. This study proposes a modular, multimodal LLM-based system with human oversight for extracting fields and scores. We conducted a qualitative analysis of the use of LLMs for hand-drawing analysis.
  Materials and Methods. The system processes cognitive assessments (i.e., MMSE, MoCA, Mini-Cog) and the NICHQ Vanderbilt Assessment using two modules: 1) a form classifier that assigns a scanned page to a form type, followed by a corresponding 2) score extractor that extracts fields and scores into a schema. A human-in-the-loop design utilizing dual-model validation engages human annotators when two LLMs disagree, limiting manual review to challenging pages only.
  Results. End-to-end accuracy for cognitive assessments was 88%, with most form types exceeding 90%. For the NICHQ Vanderbilt, overall accuracy reached 97.5%, with all form types above 96%. The human-in-the-loop design further improved cognitive assessment accuracy to 97.5% while reducing manual work by 63.8%. In the Mini-Cog Clock Drawing task, qualitative analysis showed that 62.3% of all extraction errors stemmed from ambiguous drawing, in which cases the LLM provided reasonable readings.
  Discussion. Compared to current manual data extraction, our LLM-based system reduces processing time by 10 to 20 times and costs by over 12 times. The modular design allows seamless expansion to additional form types.
  Conclusion. Our system provides an accurate, scalable, and cost-efficient solution for structuring data trapped in handwritten paper forms for clinical decision support.
papers.summary: Handwritten, scanned clinical assessment forms are hard to process at scale. The system described uses multimodal large language models (LLMs) in two modules, a form classifier and a per-form score extractor that fills a schema, and it covers the `MMSE`, `MoCA`, and `Mini-Cog` cognitive assessments and the `NICHQ Vanderbilt Assessment`. Human annotators are brought in only when two models disagree. End-to-end accuracy was 88% for cognitive assessments and 97.5% for the Vanderbilt forms, and the human-in-the-loop design **raised cognitive assessment accuracy to 97.5% while cutting manual work by 63.8%**. The authors estimate processing is 10 to 20 times faster and over 12 times cheaper than manual extraction.

papers.title: OfficePrism: Benchmarking Agents on Single-Domain Operations Across Enterprise Business Functions
papers.abstract: Broad workplace scores can mix competence within one business function with the extra cost of coordinating across functions and systems, making failures hard to localize. OfficePrism evaluates this prerequisite through 420 single-domain enterprise tasks spanning seven business functions under shared, benchmark-defined L1--L3 task-structure levels. Each task runs in a fresh environment combining a shared synthetic organization with one function-specific domain and yped state access. Our pipeline uses grounded records, business rules, and tool schemas to jointly construct a Chinese-language ticket, a hidden executable reference witness, and an expected response, followed by automated filtering and human curation. The same task set is evaluated through full-schema and search-and-dispatch packages. Across 124 model--harness--package configurations, the per-case joint natural-language-and-database pass rate ranges from 22.6% to 76.4%, with a median of 67.9%. L1 is highest in all 124 configurations, and L2 exceeds L3 in 122. Among 50 configurations sharing the same harness and model labels across both packages, search scores higher in 30, ties in one, and scores lower in 19.
papers.summary: Broad workplace agent scores mix competence within one business function with the cost of coordinating across functions, which makes failures hard to localize. `OfficePrism` isolates the first part with 420 single-domain enterprise tasks across seven business functions at three task-structure levels, each run in a fresh environment with a Chinese-language ticket, a hidden executable reference, and an expected response. Across 124 model, harness, and tool-package configurations, the joint natural-language-and-database pass rate **ranges from 22.6% to 76.4% with a median of 67.9%**. Among 50 matched configurations, a search-and-dispatch tool package scores higher than exposing full tool schemas in 30 and lower in 19.

papers.title: Fidelity Regret: Measuring Simulator Misspecification in Verifiable Design
papers.abstract: RLVF assumes the verifier evaluates the quantity of interest. In genetic-circuit design, a topological verifier can establish that a program is a valid circuit computing the target function, whereas ranking its physical performance requires a simulator. We measure fidelity regret, the reference simple regret incurred when a cheap simulator selects the design, over a 21,362-design combination subspace spanning 5 measured gate libraries and 3 organisms. Exact ordered-assignment checks retain positive regret in every tested cell while shifting magnitudes in both directions. Mean normalized regret is 0.369 over 72 cells and only 6 have zero regret. The discrepancy depends strongly on the reference axis: the yeast library SC1C1G1T1 has mean regret 0.113 for cytometry quality and 0.801 for growth burden, and every evaluated library--circuit-size pair has positive burden regret. Topological verification ties all valid gate assignments, while an oracle whitelist subject to retaining at least 25% of the design space leaves positive regret in 30 of 52 cells. Design-space optimization and feedback-guided search with frozen language models reach the high-regret regions; on a matched zero-regret control, additional optimization instead reduces regret. At a matched modeled-cost budget, mitigation is budget- and library-dependent. An in-sample fixed rule spending $\alpha{=}0.34$ of the budget re-scoring top cheap-simulator designs achieves mean excess regret 0.016, compared with 0.305 for cheap-only and 0.034 for reference-only selection, improving on cheap-only in 330 of 360 cells. More broadly, any workflow optimized through a simulator or digital twin can satisfy its verifier yet perform poorly on the intended physical objective. Fidelity regret provides a transferable template for detecting this gap before optimization and comparing budget-aware remedies across scientific domains.
papers.summary: A verifier can confirm that a design is valid without measuring the quantity that actually matters, as in genetic-circuit design, where a topological check validates a circuit but ranking its physical performance requires a simulator. The authors define fidelity regret as the regret incurred when a cheap simulator picks the design, and measure it over 21,362 designs spanning 5 gate libraries and 3 organisms. They find **mean normalized regret of 0.369 across 72 cells, with only 6 at zero**. Optimization, including feedback-guided search with frozen language models, steers into the high-regret regions. Spending 34% of the budget on re-scoring top cheap-simulator designs with the reference cuts mean excess regret to 0.016, against 0.305 for cheap-only selection.

papers.title: Anticipating or Speculating? Making Futures Pay in AI Ethics
papers.abstract: Philosophers have recently been trying to develop uniform decision rules for instances in which physicians' judgments diverge from the recommendations of medical artificial intelligence (AI) systems. I argue that this effort is fatally flawed because the performance and appropriate use of algorithmic recommendation systems by physicians are highly context-specific, empirical medical matters rather than epistemological ones. In such instances, general decision rules can be stipulated only to the extent that they abstract away from relevant, indeed determinative, contextual circumstances. The alleged problem of physician-AI disagreement, and others like it, play into longstanding disputes in technology ethics about the viability and utility of envisioning possible futures: is this useful "anticipation" or wasteful "speculation"? I suggest that the two may be distinguished. Anticipation explores plausible futures to help inform present actions under irreducible uncertainty. Speculation abstracts away uncertainty, developing formal solutions to stipulated circumstances whose relationship to the real present is often quite unclear. Efforts to develop crisp philosophical solutions to physician-AI disagreement, among other problems, fall into the latter category. Technology ethics should remember that fruitful futures thinking must both begin from and return to the messy, uncertain present.
papers.summary: Philosophers have tried to formulate uniform decision rules for cases where a physician's judgment diverges from a medical AI system's recommendation. The author argues that this effort is **fatally flawed because appropriate use of such systems is a context-specific empirical medical matter**, not an epistemological one, so general rules hold only by abstracting away the circumstances that decide the case. The essay uses this to separate anticipation, which explores plausible futures to inform present action under uncertainty, from speculation, which solves stipulated scenarios whose link to the present is unclear.

papers.title: Teaching Language Models to Narrow Boolean Patent Searches from Search Feedback
papers.abstract: Patent prior-art searchers issue Boolean queries line by line, broadening to find relevant documents and narrowing until candidates can be screened. We distill 38,397 Japan Patent Office search reports into executable expert strategies, re-execute them, and evaluate generated strategies by citation recall and the smallest set containing each citation. Prompted models write valid, high-recall strategies but leave citations in sets too large to screen. We adapt a generator offline from scored rollouts in two forms: strategy-level learning from a screening-aware strategy score, and line-level learning from citation-preserving narrowing credit, which upweights the query lines keeping a found citation in a smaller set. On shared rollouts, line-level credit outperforms strategy-level scores on screening measures; iterated, it cuts the median citation-containing set from 768 to under 50 and places more citations in sets under 100 documents than experts, at lower recall. Strategy-level preference learning reaches near-complete recall; the two forms are complementary.
papers.summary: Patent prior-art searchers build Boolean queries line by line, broadening to find relevant documents and then narrowing until the candidate set is small enough to screen. The authors distill 38,397 `Japan Patent Office` search reports into executable expert strategies and find that prompted language models write valid, high-recall strategies but leave cited documents in sets too large to screen. They adapt a generator offline from scored rollouts, either at the strategy level or with line-level credit that upweights query lines keeping a found citation in a smaller set.
