We report full-context and query-only results for seven general-purpose models and Ant Afu. Across the eight systems, full- query differences range from 11.83 to 31.76 case points and from 10.87 to 38.97 geometric cluster points. GPT-6-Astra leads both full-context metrics at 75.03 and 60.42, followed by Claude-Opus-5-5 and Ant Afu. Cross-condition differences describe score changes under the reported evaluation settings. Response comparisons reveal failures in checking historical information, expressing uncertainty when warranted, and ensuring recommendations respect required conditions. The resource supports model comparison and targeted follow-up evaluation.
papers.summary: `HealthCLBench` is a Chinese-language benchmark for health context learning, meaning a model's ability to acquire, integrate, and apply context at inference time and to respond properly when facts, evidence, or task goals change. It contains 328 controlled clusters, 1,103 cases, and 4,931 rubric criteria, where cases in a cluster share a background but vary in evidence, patient state, or goal, all annotated by a 70-person medical team; human review of 700 responses agreed with the automated judgments 90.5% of the time at the rubric-item level. Among eight systems tested with full context and with the query alone, **`GPT-6-Astra` leads both full-context metrics at 75.03 and 60.42**, followed by `Claude-Opus-5-5` and `Ant Afu`. Observed failures include not checking historical information, not expressing warranted uncertainty, and giving recommendations that ignore required conditions.

papers.title: FailureGen: Scalable Robot Failure Data Generation with World Models
papers.abstract: Robot failures are difficult to collect at scale, limiting the range of failure scenarios represented in robot learning datasets. We present FailureGen, a method for generating synthetic videos with temporal event annotations by reusing action trajectories from recorded failures. The method comprises four stages: (1) fine-tuning an action-conditioned Cosmos world model on successful and failed real executions; (2) annotating source recordings to identify failure-associated donor segments and compatible successful hosts; (3) transferring donor motion into host contexts, with optional spatial offsets, to generate continuous video rollouts; and (4) annotating and filtering the generated samples according to observed events and visual quality. We study two implementations with different tasks and robot configurations, with visual failure detection serving as one downstream application. In a preliminary comparison, a detector trained on real and generated data achieves an average precision of 0.51, compared with 0.41 using real data alone, and detects 33 of 36 failure intervals, compared with 28 of 36. By reusing observed failures in additional contexts, FailureGen expands the data available for studying robot failures and developing downstream learning methods.
papers.summary: Robot failures are hard to collect at scale, which limits the failure scenarios available in robot learning datasets. `FailureGen` fine-tunes an action-conditioned `Cosmos` world model on real successful and failed executions, then transplants failure-associated motion segments from recorded failures into compatible successful recordings to generate annotated synthetic videos, which are filtered for observed events and visual quality. In a preliminary comparison, a failure detector trained on real plus generated data reaches **an average precision of 0.51 versus 0.41 with real data alone**, and detects 33 of 36 failure intervals instead of 28.

papers.title: Seeing What Still Holds: How Waiting Control Changes Cooperative Recovery
papers.abstract: Changing the holding reference during a fixed-duration wait can reverse the ranking of visual recovery methods. We introduce AuditEmbodied, a paired execution and trajectory evaluation framework that independently varies holding references and waiting duration while keeping recovery executors frozen. A 960-execution factorial on 20 initialization seeds compares CAD-feedback and landmark-based recovery from identical post-wait physical states within each holding and waiting condition. Protected completion requires successful recovery under the declared execution constraints. At a 1 s wait with registered wrist references, their protected completion counts change from 6/40 versus 19/40 under registered holding to 34/40 versus 22/40 under position-only holding. Trajectory analysis localizes the main separation to grasp formation: small observation-time target residuals precede large tracking errors. Joint diagnostics and controlled interventions characterize persistent tracking constraints. On fresh seeds, gradual position reanchoring improves CAD recovery's long-wait completion by 42.5 percentage points and reduces mean complete recovery time by 6.06 s relative to registered holding. Additional evaluations with pretrained policies, handover, and a mass-matched geometry characterize holding-reference sensitivity across executors and physical regimes. These findings establish holding reference as an explicit evaluation condition for comparing visual recovery performance.
papers.summary: How a robot holds an object during a fixed-duration wait turns out to affect which visual recovery method looks better in cooperative manipulation. `AuditEmbodied` is a paired evaluation framework that varies the holding reference and waiting duration independently while keeping the recovery executors frozen, and a 960-execution factorial study compares CAD-feedback and landmark-based recovery from identical post-wait states. At a 1 second wait, **completion counts flip from 6/40 versus 19/40 under registered holding to 34/40 versus 22/40 under position-only holding**. Trajectory analysis traces the gap to grasp formation, and gradual position reanchoring improves CAD-based recovery after long waits by 42.5 percentage points on fresh seeds.

papers.title: AutoE2E: Don't speak - Language free end-to-end autonomy A Real-Time Driving Model for L2++ ADAS and L4 Robotaxis
papers.abstract: AutoE2E is an open-source end-to-end driving model developed by the Autoware Foundation Robotaxi Working Group. It introduces a temporal bird's-eye-view (BEV) architecture that combines multi-camera perception, HD-map information and route conditioning to predict future vehicle motion. The evaluated model uses a pretrained camera-BEV backbone, temporal feature fusion and a lightweight recurrent trajectory planner. It contains approximately 79.9 million parameters, of which approximately 1.45 million are trainable in the evaluated configuration. The v1.0 release provides model checkpoints, training and evaluation code, and DataModelConsole, a dashboard for visualizing and inspecting model experiments. On the KITScenes validation benchmark, the fine-tuned checkpoint achieves an average displacement error (ADE) of 0.745 m and a final displacement error (FDE) of 2.020 m at a three-second prediction horizon. The paper also reports preliminary real-vehicle research conducted with the Technical University of Munich's EDGAR platform, alongside ongoing collaboration with the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology. AutoE2E v1.0 is an early open research release. Its quantitative evaluation is open-loop, and the model has not yet demonstrated validated closed-loop autonomous driving. The release is intended to provide the autonomous-driving community with an inspectable baseline for further research, experimentation and collaborative development.
papers.summary: `AutoE2E` is an open-source end-to-end driving model from the Autoware Foundation that predicts future vehicle motion without any language component. It combines multi-camera perception, HD-map information and route conditioning in a temporal bird's-eye-view architecture with a pretrained backbone and a lightweight recurrent trajectory planner, totaling about 79.9 million parameters of which roughly 1.45 million are trainable. On the `KITScenes` validation benchmark the fine-tuned checkpoint achieves **an average displacement error of 0.745 m and a final displacement error of 2.020 m at a three-second horizon**. The evaluation is open-loop only, and the authors state that validated closed-loop autonomous driving has not yet been demonstrated.

papers.title: Leveraging Segmentation Representations for Efficient Classification: A Self-Configuring Framework Based on nnU-Net
papers.abstract: We propose a self-configuring framework that extends the nnU-Net workflow to both segmentation and classification in 3D medical imaging. Building on nnU-Net's self-configuring method, the framework reuses representations learned by a segmentation model for image-level classification. Its encoder features and predicted segmentation probabilities are used by a lightweight classifier. Two information-sharing strategies are investigated. In the frozen-backbone branch, features are augmented with region-of-interest information, predicted foreground volume, and segmentation confidence. In the adaptation branch, the final encoder stage is partially fine-tuned for classification, with an auxiliary segmentation loss to preserve segmentation-related information. Additional five-fold experiments showed that more complex configurations did not consistently improve classification performance. On the public validation leaderboard, our selected framework achieved an Overall score of 0.8056. In the official FLARE 2026 Task 2 final evaluation, our framework ranked first overall, achieving the highest DSC, NSD, and AUROC across all four testing tasks, including two hidden testing tasks. Local inference measurements also remained below the challenge limits of $60 \mathrm{s}$ per case and $4 \mathrm{GB}$ GPU memory. These results demonstrate the practical value of reusing segmentation representations for classification while maintaining a simple and efficient framework.
papers.summary: A self-configuring framework extends the `nnU-Net` workflow from segmentation to image-level classification in 3D medical imaging by feeding the segmentation model's encoder features and predicted probabilities into a lightweight classifier. Two variants are studied: a frozen backbone augmented with region-of-interest information, predicted foreground volume, and segmentation confidence, and a partially fine-tuned final encoder stage with an auxiliary segmentation loss. More complex configurations did not consistently improve classification in five-fold experiments. The selected framework **ranked first overall in the official `FLARE 2026` Task 2 final evaluation**, with inference staying under the challenge limits of 60 s per case and 4 GB of GPU memory.

papers.title: RICoT: Recurrent Interleaved Chain-of-Thought for Page Stream Segmentation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have renewed interest in Page Stream Segmentation (PSS), splitting a multi-page file into its constituent documents. Yet published LLM methods still frame the task as boundary classification over one or a few neighboring pages, and commercial document-splitting APIs do not disclose their methods. We reimagine PSS for LLMs as a sequential process over the whole stream and propose RICoT (Recurrent Interleaved Chain-of-Thought), a prompting framework that works through the pages as a reader would: within a sliding window it reasons about each page and commits its boundary decision before moving on, and across windows it carries forward a compact record of what it has read, keeping per-call cost bounded. We also introduce FinancePSS-205, a benchmark of 205 real-world, de-identified financial page streams, to be released publicly. On FinancePSS-205, RICoT matches or outperforms pairwise and windowed prompting with the same backbone for each of three open-weight LLMs; on a TABME test subset, RICoT with GLM-5 reaches document F1 0.847 and boundary F1 0.915, above published zero-shot results. A 2B-parameter student, trained on a larger teacher's decisions with and without the page-level reasoning, performs comparably in both modes and comes within 0.05 document F1 of the strongest prompted model on FinancePSS-205.
papers.summary: Page stream segmentation, the task of splitting a multi-page file into its constituent documents, is typically handled by large language models as boundary classification over one or a few neighboring pages. `RICoT` (Recurrent Interleaved Chain-of-Thought) instead prompts the model to read the stream sequentially, reasoning about each page in a sliding window and committing a boundary decision before moving on, while carrying a compact record across windows to bound per-call cost. On the new `FinancePSS-205` benchmark of 205 real financial page streams it matches or beats pairwise and windowed prompting for three open-weight models, and on a `TABME` test subset with `GLM-5` it reaches **document F1 of 0.847 and boundary F1 of 0.915**, above published zero-shot results. A 2B-parameter student distilled from a larger teacher comes within 0.05 document F1 of the strongest prompted model.

papers.title: Deal With It: On Better Schedules for Listwise Reranking
papers.abstract: Listwise LLM rerankers cannot reliably rank hundreds of documents in a single call, and rely on schedules to orchestrate their calls. Parallel schedules split candidates into groups and advance a fixed quota from each. When a group holds more of the top passages than its quota, some are cut, and expensive repair calls become required. We show that the way candidates are split matters where such a quota can bind, and that, in expected cuts, the best split there deals them round-robin by retriever rank, like cards. Although not conceptually new, dealing has remained unanalyzed. We prove that, under a simple retriever model, no split with equal quotas cuts fewer of the true top ten on average, and that contiguous chunks cut more as the retriever improves. DealRank, the simplest schedule our analysis allows, is on average within 0.1 nDCG@10 points of the best schedules over six LLMs, in two rounds. It is consistently 1.1 to 1.4 times faster than BlitzRank with concurrent first calls up to a thousand candidates. There, it needs three rounds and is eleven times faster than the sliding window. In existing schedules such as BlitzRank, dealing reduces repair calls from 59% of queries to 14%, improving latency with no significant change in quality. Random partitioning appears equivalent at a quota of four, as predicted, but ties results to the seed and trails by 1.3 nDCG@10 points at a quota of one over a dense retriever.
papers.summary: Listwise rerankers based on large language models cannot rank hundreds of documents in one call, so parallel schedules split candidates into groups and advance a fixed quota from each, which cuts relevant passages when a group holds more than its quota. The authors prove that, under a simple retriever model, dealing candidates round-robin by retriever rank cuts the fewest of the true top ten on average among equal-quota splits, and that contiguous chunks get worse as the retriever improves. Their schedule `DealRank` averages within 0.1 nDCG@10 points of the best schedules across six models in two rounds and is 1.1 to 1.4 times faster than `BlitzRank`. Applying dealing inside `BlitzRank` **reduces repair calls from 59% of queries to 14%** with no significant change in quality.

papers.title: From Constraints to Causality: Petri net Encodings for Explaining Binary Neural Network Inference
papers.abstract: Binary Neural Networks (BNNs) are attractive for resource-constrained hardware and on-device components in autonomous systems. However, their discrete, non-linear behaviour makes them difficult to analyse and trust in safety-relevant settings. Existing approaches based on SAT and Satisfiability Modulo Theories can verify a BNN's input-output properties, but treat it as a monolithic constraint system, which reveal only whether a property holds and not how the computation reaches its result. In this paper, we present an early work that provides a complementary, discrete-event view. We give a compositional translation from the inference semantics of a fixed, trained BNN to a 1-safe Petri net (PN), where each computation step is an explicit transition, so that a firing sequence is a causal trace of the BNN's decision. On a worked example, we establish faithfulness via exhaustive input-output equivalence against a reference implementation, and show how contrasting firing sequences localises where a single-feature change alters the prediction. Finally, we outline two directions this opens: a correctness-of-translation theorem, and a causal-trace analysis of where two trained BNNs diverge in their decisions, a structural question that constraint-based verifiers cannot express.
papers.summary: Binary neural networks suit resource-constrained hardware, but verification based on satisfiability solvers treats them as a monolithic constraint system and reveals only whether a property holds, not how the computation reaches its result. This early-stage work gives a compositional translation from the inference semantics of a fixed, trained binary network to a 1-safe Petri net, so that **each firing sequence is a causal trace of the network's decision**. On a worked example, the authors confirm exhaustive input-output equivalence with a reference implementation and show that contrasting firing sequences localizes where a single-feature change alters the prediction. A correctness theorem and a causal comparison of two trained networks are outlined as future directions.

papers.title: Symbolic Abstraction Refinement
papers.abstract: Autonomous systems choose actions whose outcomes are uncertain and are subject to time constraints. Probabilistic timed automata (PTAs) model exactly this, and verifying one answers a question about the system's decision-making: the maximum probability of reaching a goal, or the minimum probability of reaching a hazard, that a controller can guarantee. Verification normally works over symbolic states, each pairing a discrete location with a region of clock values, and its difficulty is that the best behavior generally varies within such a region. The PRISM verifier's most capable PTA method responds by splitting regions until each is uniform, rebuilding the transitions that reach them and propagating the split backward through the state graph of a stochastic game, a cascade of graph reconstruction that partitions regions the property never depends on. We present SYMAR, which instead makes the value function symbolic: each symbolic state carries a function from sub-regions of its clock region to probability bounds, so refinement is the appearance of new sub-regions in that function, and previously generated states are never split nor their incoming transitions reconstructed. Both sources of PTA nondeterminism, the timing and the choice of actions, are captured implicitly by the preimage computation that produces those sub-regions. Heuristic forward search then bounds how much refinement is done at all, expanding an And-Or graph from the initial state along the most promising behaviors so that effort is confined to the property-relevant fragment, guided by bounds and preferred actions from a single unrefined run of the existing method; a partial-refinement backup keeps the otherwise combinatorial sub-region count lean, and every stored interval provably contains the true probability. On the PRISM PTA benchmarks, whose subproblems recur in autonomous systems (distributed agreement under contention, leader election, and self-configuration without central coordination), SYMAR is up to 108x faster, solves an instance on which the existing method exhausts the time limit, and is markedly less sensitive to the deadline constant, resolving one instance in a 37-node search graph, unchanged as the deadline triples, where the existing method needs 86,380 abstract states and 73 refinement rounds.
authors: Robert P. Goldman (Smart Information Flow Technologies
David J. Musliner (Smart Information Flow Technologies
papers.summary: Probabilistic timed automata model systems whose actions have uncertain outcomes and timing constraints, and verifying them yields the maximum or minimum probability of reaching a goal or hazard that a controller can guarantee. The most capable existing method in the `PRISM` verifier repeatedly splits clock regions and rebuilds the state graph, whereas `SYMAR` attaches to each symbolic state a function from sub-regions to probability bounds, so refinement never splits existing states or reconstructs their transitions. A heuristic forward search over an And-Or graph confines effort to the property-relevant fragment, and every stored interval provably contains the true probability. On the `PRISM` benchmarks, `SYMAR` is **up to 108x faster** and solves an instance on which the existing method times out.

papers.title: ROSMonitoring in Action: Runtime Monitoring and Enforcement for ROS 2 Actions
papers.abstract: Robotic applications often rely on long-running operations, such as navigation, manipulation, and inspection, which in ROS~2 are commonly implemented as actions. Unlike topics and services, actions involve a structured lifecycle comprising goal submission and acceptance, feedback, status updates, result retrieval, and cancellation. Existing versions of ROSMonitoring support topics and services, but do not reconstruct this lifecycle or expose action-level events to a runtime-verification oracle. In this paper, we extend ROSMonitoring with runtime monitoring and enforcement for ROS~2 actions. Actions are declared directly in the monitoring configuration and automatically instrumented through the underlying ROS~2 communication endpoints. The generated monitor reconstructs action-level events, correlates them through goal identifiers, maintains the state of active goals, and translates violations into protocol-aware enforcement operations. These include goal rejection, cancellation, message suppression, and protocol-compliant responses generated directly by the monitor when the original communication cannot be forwarded. We evaluate the implementation through controlled stress tests that vary the number of action invocations, workload size, and clientâ€“server topology. The results show approximately linear growth in monitoring cost with repeated action invocations under a fixed workload, while larger action workloads and a greater number of configured clientâ€“server pairs introduce additional overhead. These results characterise the scaling behaviour of the current implementation under the tested sequential workloads while highlighting the main performance limitations of the current synchronous implementation.
papers.summary: Long-running robot operations in `ROS 2` are implemented as actions, which have a structured lifecycle of goal submission, acceptance, feedback, status, result, and cancellation that the `ROSMonitoring` runtime-verification framework previously could not track. The extension lets actions be declared in the monitoring configuration and instrumented automatically, with the generated monitor reconstructing action-level events, correlating them by goal identifier, and enforcing properties through goal rejection, cancellation, message suppression, or protocol-compliant responses. Stress tests show **approximately linear growth in monitoring cost with repeated action invocations** under a fixed workload. Larger workloads and more client-server pairs add overhead, which the authors attribute to the current synchronous implementation.

papers.title: SignAligner: Dual-Granularity Span Generation for Sign Language Alignment
papers.abstract: Large sign-language corpora benefit from temporal labels at two scales: subtitle spans for subtitle alignment and word spans for sign spotting. Sign spottings already locate words in time at corpus scale, but training subtitle alignment jointly on subtitle and word spans remains underexplored. We present SignAligner, a prompt-conditioned visual-language span generator that maps a sign-language video and a subtitle-sentence or target-word query to a textual start/end frame interval. It is first trained jointly on subtitle spans and word spans from sign spottings, then refined with overlap-based rewards while retaining auxiliary word examples. On the subtitle test set of the British Broadcasting Corporation-Oxford British Sign Language (BOBSL) corpus, the refined model reaches 66.68 F1@0.50 (F1 with a temporal intersection-over-union threshold of one half), the best among compared systems without external sign-video resources. This overlap-reward refinement outperforms cross-entropy continuation from the same jointly trained model. Joint training with word spans improves subtitle alignment in a pair of our generators matched in code, labels and maximum update budget. The advantage remains after both models of the pair are refined with overlap rewards. For word queries, the refined model follows the queried word, not a fixed position in the video: when the word's sign lies away from the video centre, it is far more accurate than predictions that use position alone. Together, these findings support one shared span generator refined with overlap rewards, aligning subtitles and producing word spans for human review.
papers.summary: Sign-language corpora need temporal labels at two scales, subtitle spans and individual word spans, yet training subtitle alignment jointly on both has been little explored. `SignAligner` is a prompt-conditioned visual-language model that takes a sign-language video plus a subtitle sentence or target word and generates the start and end frame interval as text; it is trained jointly on both span types and then refined with overlap-based rewards. On the subtitle test set of the `BOBSL` British Sign Language corpus it reaches **66.68 F1 at a temporal intersection-over-union threshold of 0.50**, the best among compared systems that use no external sign-video resources. Joint training with word spans improves subtitle alignment, and reward-based refinement outperforms continued cross-entropy training from the same model.

papers.title: Proceedings of the 2026 XCSP3 Competition
papers.abstract: This document constitutes the proceedings of the 2026 XCSP3 Competition. The results of this competition of constraint solvers were presented at FLOC (Federated Logic Conference) 2026 Olympic Games, held in Lisbon, Portugal from 20th to 29th July, 2026.
papers.summary: These are the proceedings of the 2026 `XCSP3` Competition, a competition of constraint solvers. The results were presented at the **Federated Logic Conference (FLOC) 2026 Olympic Games in Lisbon, Portugal**, held from 20 to 29 July 2026.

papers.title: LMMR: Learned Multigranular Memory Retrieval for Small Language Model Agents
papers.abstract: Small language model agents have limited space to read the memory needed for multi-hop questions. Relevant facts are often scattered across records whose surrounding text consumes much of that space. We propose LMMR, a learned multigranular memory retrieval method that selects both the next source and how much of it to read. LMMR links paragraphs and sentence fragments to their original sources and pairs views that supply the same missing support during training. Relevant distractors and repeated information provide contrasting examples. At inference, the reranker scores what each candidate adds to an anchor passage, and a selector chooses the evidence within a token budget. On 22,398 official validation questions from HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, and MuSiQue, a frozen 2B answer model reaches 61.47, 43.26, and 30.58 F1 under a 400-token budget. The gains over query expansion are 3.06, 2.14, and 4.55 points, while memory input decreases by 23.1-26.9%. LMMR also uses 23.5-27.7% fewer input tokens than a coarse retriever trained on the same questions. Against that retriever followed by LLMLingua-2 at comparable input lengths, F1 gains reach 3.99 points and are significant on HotpotQA and 2WikiMultihopQA after Holm correction. All eight small answer models evaluated on HotpotQA improve over query expansion and MMR in both F1 and exact match.
papers.summary: Agents built on small language models have little context room for the memory that multi-hop questions require, and relevant facts are often buried in records full of surrounding text. `LMMR` is a learned retrieval method that chooses both which source to read next and how much of it, linking paragraphs and sentence fragments to their sources, scoring what each candidate adds to an anchor passage, and selecting evidence within a token budget. With a frozen 2B answer model and a 400-token budget it reaches 61.47, 43.26, and 30.58 F1 on `HotpotQA`, `2WikiMultihopQA`, and `MuSiQue`, **gaining 3.06, 2.14, and 4.55 points over query expansion while cutting memory input by 23.1-26.9%**. All eight small answer models tested on `HotpotQA` improve over query expansion and maximal marginal relevance baselines.

papers.title: InfuseLoop: Cross-Trajectory Latent Injection for Scalable Parallel Looped Transformers
papers.abstract: Parallel Looped Transformers (PLTs) use otherwise idle decoding compute by overlapping recurrent iterations. However, vanilla PLTs scale poorly with depth: they exhibit training-loss spikes, and their quality gains shrink as more loops are added. The benefit of additional loops depends on the information available to each iteration, so we examine whether the existing computational dependencies limit effective depth scaling. We find that only the preceding in-trajectory state is passed across loop boundaries, even though completed cross-trajectory representations are already available. Based on this finding, we propose InfuseLoop, a cross-trajectory latent injection mechanism. It aggregates causally available hidden states from later prediction trajectories through lightweight attention residuals. This design preserves token-parallel training and concurrent loop execution, and requires only $O(Rd)$ additional hidden-state storage. Experiments show that InfuseLoop eliminates training-loss spikes and improves validation-loss scaling up to eight loops. At eight loops, InfuseLoop reduces perplexity by 3.4--17.1% relative to vanilla PLTs and by 10.5--37.3% relative to the non-looped baseline. It also improves average downstream accuracy by 0.84 and 1.99 percentage points over these two baselines. InfuseLoop incurs only 0.3% decoding time over vanilla PLTs and 23.3% over the non-looped baseline, while keeping the same logical KV-cache footprint as vanilla PLTs.
papers.summary: Parallel Looped Transformers reuse otherwise idle decoding compute by overlapping recurrent iterations, but they suffer training-loss spikes and diminishing gains as loops are added. The authors trace this to only the preceding in-trajectory state being passed across loop boundaries, and propose `InfuseLoop`, which injects causally available hidden states from later prediction trajectories through lightweight attention residuals while preserving token-parallel training and concurrent loop execution. It eliminates the loss spikes and improves validation-loss scaling up to eight loops, where it **reduces perplexity by 3.4-17.1% relative to vanilla looped models and by 10.5-37.3% relative to a non-looped baseline**. The decoding-time overhead is 0.3% over vanilla looped models and 23.3% over the non-looped baseline.

papers.title: Do Diffusion Models Learn to Generalize Basic Visual Skills?
papers.abstract: Diffusion models generate high-quality images, but how well they generalize is hard to measure. Current evaluations rely on human preference and prompt-following benchmarks for text-to-image models and on distribution-level metrics such as Fr\'echet Inception Distance (FID) and Inception Score (IS) for class-conditional models, but these cannot tell whether models learn basic visual skills or largely match training patterns. To address this gap, we introduce the Visual Generative Lab (VGL), a controlled experimental framework for studying how diffusion models learn and generalize basic visual skills, including size, position, rotation, count, color, shape, and their compositions. By generating synthetic training data for each skill from explicit rules, VGL allows precise measurement of generalization with task-specific, rule-based metrics. Training models from scratch on these data reveals three patterns in this controlled setting: (1) with our default design, extrapolation is limited: size and position degrade within a few pixels of the training range, count reaches only about 50% accuracy on out-of-range counts, and rotation extrapolation accuracy varies widely across seeds; (2) for compositional generalization, the number of distinct basic visual skill combinations matters more than dataset size; (3) skills mostly fail independently, except position. Code and data-generation scripts: https://github.com/AmishSethi/visual-generative-lab.
papers.summary: Standard metrics such as Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) and prompt-following benchmarks cannot show whether diffusion models learn basic visual skills or merely match training patterns. The `Visual Generative Lab` (`VGL`) trains models from scratch on rule-generated synthetic data for size, position, rotation, count, color, shape, and their compositions, then scores generalization with rule-based metrics. Extrapolation is limited: size and position degrade within a few pixels of the training range and **count reaches only about 50% accuracy on out-of-range counts**. For compositional generalization, the number of distinct skill combinations matters more than dataset size, and skills mostly fail independently, except position.

papers.title: Think Once, Act Fast: Cost-Effective Recursive Self-Improvement for Decision Model Harness
papers.abstract: Fast System-1 models enable responsive actions but struggle with complex or unfamiliar tasks. Large language model (LLM)-based System-2 provides strong reasoning capabilities, yet repeated invocation incurs substantial latency and computational costs. To bridge this gap, we propose JevRSI, a System-1/System-2 collaboration framework that transforms LLM reasoning into transferable decision support through recursive harness improvement. A Jev-style System-1 model enables low-latency action selection, while an asynchronous System-2 LLM develops a modular harness. The harness integrates procedures, state memory, and world models to provide decision contexts spanning the past, present, and future. Utility-driven retrieval selects modules based on both contextual relevance and their utility on previous tasks. Environmental feedback guides targeted revisions and enables recursive self-improvement. Experiments across three datasets show that JevRSI consistently improves decision quality, matching or surpassing LLM agents in several settings. It preserves low-latency execution with favorable performance-cost trade-offs. Moreover, System-2 development interventions decrease as the harness evolves, amortizing System-2 costs through continuous improvement. Our project is available at https://github.com/usail-hkust/JevRSI.
papers.summary: Fast decision models respond quickly but struggle on unfamiliar tasks, while calling a large language model (LLM) at every step is slow and costly. `JevRSI` pairs a low-latency System-1 model with an asynchronous System-2 LLM that builds and revises a modular harness of procedures, state memory, and world models, retrieved according to contextual relevance and past utility and updated from environmental feedback. Across three datasets it **matches or surpasses LLM agents in several settings while keeping low-latency execution**, and the number of System-2 interventions falls as the harness matures.

papers.title: Encoding, Decodability, and Use: A Five-Layer Framework for Benchmark Measurement Audits with Evidence from UAV Intent Recognition
papers.abstract: Benchmark accuracy is routinely read as evidence that a model understands the construct the benchmark measures. We propose and instantiate on AeroIntent a five-layer framework that decomposes that reading into observation, representation, decoding, use, and behaviour. The framework separates encoding, decodability, and use as distinct levels. In the instantiation, the observation layer is unreliable on 7 of the 20 Drone programs and floors the direct visual correlate of radial velocity at a 0.26\% scale change. The representation layer exposes two task-designed RGB features with nominal signals. RAFT flow radial bias reaches $r=+0.257$ ($p=0.030$), and bounding-box optical-flow divergence reaches $r=+0.203$ ($p=0.029$). No multi-feature readout gives a fold-mean test correlation above the cluster minimum detectable effect (MDE), and the largest positive global out-of-sample correlation is $r=+0.080$. The decoding layer sets the MDE at $|r|=0.599$ at the multi-feature Bonferroni threshold ($\alpha=0.00714$, power 0.80), and the observed $r=+0.080$ has power 0.00. Two injection experiments establish the MDE's condition from both sides: aligned injections are detected at or above the simulated power, and orthogonal injections are not detected. The use layer finds accuracy consistent with program memory (program-identity 0.937/0.597/0.210) and multi-region static cues. The behaviour layer is consistent with accuracy not requiring a radial-velocity readout (appearance 0.6552 vs bounding-box trajectory 0.4080, cluster-level paired $\Delta=+0.2471$, $p=0.0132$).
papers.summary: Benchmark accuracy is often taken as evidence that a model understands the construct being measured. A five-layer audit framework separating observation, representation, decoding, use, and behaviour is applied to the `AeroIntent` drone intent recognition benchmark, testing whether models actually read out radial velocity. The observation layer is unreliable on 7 of 20 drone programs, and the largest out-of-sample correlation of any feature readout is **r = +0.080 against a minimum detectable effect (MDE) of |r| = 0.599**, leaving the test with no power. Accuracy is instead consistent with memorized program identity and static appearance cues, with appearance scoring 0.6552 against 0.4080 for bounding-box trajectory.

papers.title: Eyes in the Update? Learning Where Rewards Land in Multimodal Reasoning
papers.abstract: Multimodal post-training has moved from broad instruction tuning toward reinforcement learning for image and video reasoning, where outcome rewards can improve final-answer accuracy. Yet these rewards are assigned to complete generated trajectories, while visual evidence is used only at sparse and uneven positions inside the response. Recent work has begun to make multimodal RL more token-sensitive through grounding signals or external token-level weighting. We ask a more specific question: can the allocation of the same trajectory-level reward be inferred from the model's own multimodal computation, rather than from an auxiliary annotator, perception module, or process label? We propose Gaze-RL, a representation-driven policy optimization method that redistributes completion-level advantage through a latent reward landing field. The field is computed from internal cross-modal geometry and local predictive uncertainty, assigning larger update weight to positions that are both visually anchored and decision-bearing while remaining mean-one, so the total credit of each rollout is preserved and only its positionwise allocation changes. Gaze-RL requires no process supervision, auxiliary perception module, or architectural modification, and improves both Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL3.5 across a broad range of image and video benchmarks.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning for image and video reasoning assigns one outcome reward to a whole generated response, even though visual evidence is used at only a few positions within it. `Gaze-RL` redistributes the trajectory-level advantage across token positions using a latent reward landing field computed from the model's internal cross-modal geometry and local predictive uncertainty, weighting positions that are both visually anchored and decision-bearing. The weights are mean-one, so each rollout's total credit is unchanged, and **no process supervision, auxiliary perception module, or architectural change is required**. The method improves `Qwen2.5-VL` and `InternVL3.5` across a range of image and video benchmarks.

papers.title: Efficient Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
papers.abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) reach an accuracy close to quantum mechanical reference calculations at a small fraction of the cost. Efficiency is the purpose of MLIPs, yet strategies for efficient MLIPs have not been reviewed systematically. This review takes efficiency as its guideline. To compare MLIPs on a common footing, we represent them in a complete basis expansion, the Atomic Cluster Expansion (ACE) and its graph generalization (GRACE). The expansion is canonical, built from products of single-particle functions. Classical interatomic potentials, such as the embedded-atom method, and many modern MLIPs, including equivariant transformers, can be represented within this expansion. Much of the apparent diversity of MLIP architectures therefore reflects how non-linearity, layer coupling and optimization are handled rather than which interactions the models can represent. We show how the cost of an MLIP becomes linear in system size and, at fixed rank of the tensor decomposition, in model complexity, and we discuss the role of machine learning, which provides non-linear parameterizations and optimization. Because efficiency is meaningful only at a given accuracy, we also compare accuracy and cost. On the Matbench Discovery leaderboard, models with three to five layers approach the accuracy of deeper models, and one basis, truncated along the Pareto front of error and speed, spans more than two orders of magnitude in cost. Ultimately, training data determine the quality of any MLIP.
papers.summary: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) approximate quantum mechanical calculations at far lower cost, and this review organizes the field around efficiency. It expresses classical potentials and modern architectures, including equivariant transformers, in a common complete basis, the `Atomic Cluster Expansion` (`ACE`) and its graph generalization `GRACE`, arguing that architectural diversity mostly reflects how non-linearity, layer coupling, and optimization are handled. On the `Matbench Discovery` leaderboard, models with three to five layers approach the accuracy of deeper ones, and **a single basis truncated along the error-speed Pareto front spans more than two orders of magnitude in cost**.

papers.title: As Student Rollouts Continue, Visual Backdoors Keep Growing
papers.abstract:
Conventional knowledge distillation can facilitate the propagation of backdoors from teacher models to student models. However, how this risk manifests in On-Policy Distillation (OPD) remains insufficiently studied. OPD has recently emerged as an important post-training paradigm for Vision-Language Models (VLMs). Unlike traditional offline distillation, OPD does not require teacher-generated responses. Instead, it uses the teacher's probability distributions to supervise response trajectories generated online by the student. Since the initial student model typically generates benign responses and receives no explicit supervision from malicious target responses, OPD appears to offer some inherent resistance to backdoor propagation.
  In this paper, we challenge this intuition and reveal a more subtle risk of visual backdoor propagation in OPD. Through experiments across multiple model families and datasets, together with theoretical analysis, we identify three main findings. First, unlike the relatively gradual propagation observed in traditional offline distillation, backdoors rarely emerge in OPD at low poisoning ratios. However, the attack success rate rapidly approaches 100% once a critical threshold is exceeded. Second, backdoor propagation does not depend on explicit malicious responses. Instead, it is driven by the continuous accumulation of anomalous probability mass assigned by the teacher. Finally, based on these findings, we propose a novel trigger design that enables visual backdoor propagation with zero explicit trigger injection. These findings further reveal an overlooked mechanism of backdoor propagation in OPD and highlight its potential security risks.
papers.summary: On-Policy Distillation (OPD) for vision-language models (VLMs) supervises student-generated responses with the teacher's probability distributions, which seems to resist backdoor transfer because the student never sees malicious target responses. Experiments across several model families and datasets, backed by theoretical analysis, show otherwise: backdoors rarely appear at low poisoning ratios, but **attack success rapidly approaches 100% once a critical threshold is exceeded**. Propagation is driven by accumulating anomalous probability mass from the teacher, not by explicit malicious responses. Building on this, the authors design a trigger that propagates a visual backdoor with zero explicit trigger injection.

papers.title: How Many Training Labels Are Wrong? Auditing a Fitted Model through Gradient Allocation
papers.abstract: How many labels in a training set are wrong, and which ones? The usual answers read a held-out set or the model's outputs. A held-out reading depends on how the held-out set was drawn, and an output-based reading fails once the model has fitted its wrong labels, because the loss of a fitted wrong label is small and the prediction agrees with it. We read the answer from the per-example gradients of a single trained model. Each example, together with its label, asks the network to change in a particular way. We normalise the magnitudes of its gradient into a gradient allocation and compare it with the mean allocation of every class. An example is flagged when relabelling it as its nearest other class makes its allocation fit better than under its own label, and the share of flagged examples is the reading of the noise rate. The rule has no threshold and needs no clean data, no held-out set and no further training. After the model has fitted 99-100% of its wrong labels, the allocation still separates wrong from right labels with an AUC of 0.94-0.96 on the noisiest human labels of CIFAR-10N, where a feature-space margin falls to 0.79-0.84 and the loss, the gradient norm and the self-influence of an example to 0.73-0.76. On such a fitted model, readings of the noise rate from predictions or feature margins fall to 0-6% at true rates of 8-58% on CIFAR-10 with ViT-S, while the audit reads 54-96% of the true rate, and at least 93% of the examples it counts carry wrong labels. On a briefly trained model, before the wrong labels are fitted, the reading lies within 1.7 percentage points of the true noise rate on CIFAR-10 from 0% to 58% noise. Confident learning, which trains four further models, separates wrong labels about as well (AUC 0.925-0.998 against 0.900-0.995) and mostly reads the noise rate more closely, at a lower precision. An audit of 5,000 examples takes 14 to 27 seconds on one GPU.
papers.summary: Estimating how many training labels are wrong usually relies on held-out data or model outputs, which fail once the model has fitted its wrong labels. This audit normalizes each example's per-parameter gradient magnitudes into a gradient allocation and flags an example when relabelling it as its nearest other class fits the class-mean allocation better, with no threshold, clean data, held-out set, or retraining. After a model has fitted 99-100% of its wrong labels, the allocation still separates wrong from right labels with **an AUC of 0.94-0.96 on the noisiest human labels of `CIFAR-10N`**, against 0.73-0.84 for feature margins, loss, gradient norm, and self-influence. `Confident learning`, which trains four further models, separates labels about as well and mostly reads the noise rate more closely, at lower precision.

papers.title: PACD: Provenance-Aware Consensus Decoding for Mitigating Cross-Modal Hallucinations in Omnimodal Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Omnimodal large language models (Omni-LLMs) integrate audio, video, and text for multimodal reasoning, yet remain vulnerable to cross-modal hallucinations, where one modality improperly influences predictions about another. Existing training-free decoding methods mitigate these errors through modality perturbation or relevance-based weighting. However, due to interference from irrelevant modality cues during fusion and difficulty detecting shared errors, these methods may suppress correct unimodal predictions and allow erroneous consensus to persist. To address these limitations, we propose Provenance-Aware Consensus Decoding (PACD), a training-free framework for mitigating cross-modal hallucinations. PACD comprises two complementary paths based on whether the branches reach consensus. For non-consensus cases, Relevance-Guided Candidate Arbitration identifies task-relevant unimodal evidence and selectively arbitrates between predictions using alternative candidates. For consensus cases, Provenance-Based Consensus Recovery leverages the outranking principle to evaluate the consistency and strength of layer-wise modality evidence for alternative answers, selectively resolving erroneous consensus under confidence constraints. Extensive experiments on four Omni-LLMs and five benchmarks across two tasks demonstrate the superiority of PACD. Compared to existing methods, PACD achieves up to 27.6% relative improvement over standard decoding across CMM, AVHBench, and SVHalluc for cross-modal hallucination mitigation, and an average relative improvement of 7.7% over best baseline across OmniVideoBench and FutureOmni for general audio-visual reasoning.
papers.summary: Omnimodal large language models that combine audio, video, and text suffer from cross-modal hallucinations, where one modality improperly influences predictions about another. Provenance-Aware Consensus Decoding (`PACD`) is a training-free decoding method with two paths: when unimodal branches disagree, it arbitrates between candidates using task-relevant unimodal evidence, and when they agree, it checks layer-wise modality evidence to catch erroneous consensus. On four models and five benchmarks it achieves **up to 27.6% relative improvement over standard decoding** on `CMM`, `AVHBench`, and `SVHalluc`, and an average 7.7% relative gain over the best baseline on `OmniVideoBench` and `FutureOmni`.

papers.title: From Ideal to Real: Integrating Language Models into Smart Home for Human-Centric IoT Safety and Security Fuzzing
papers.abstract: Integrating IoT devices into household systems offers enhanced control over living environments. However, as these devices become pervasive in critical sectors such as healthcare, transportation, and home automation, they expose inter-rule vulnerabilities that may lead to privacy breaches, data theft, and physical harm. Traditional fuzz testing methods, which often operate in simulated environments assuming ideal human decisions, fail to account for the complexities of human interactions that can influence device operations in smart homes, potentially leading to unforeseen consequences. To reveal the impact of real human decisions and discover unexpected inter-rule vulnerabilities, we introduce an enhanced version of IoT Fuzz for smart homes by integrating large language models to emulate human decision-making processes. Our novel approach adds a layer of realism and unpredictability to the testing environment, more accurately capturing the diverse and dynamic nature of human interactions in smart home settings.
papers.summary: Smart home devices governed by automation rules can interact in ways that cause privacy breaches or physical harm, and existing fuzz testing assumes ideal human decisions in simulated environments. The authors extend `IoT Fuzz` by **using large language models to emulate human decision-making during fuzzing**, aiming to expose inter-rule vulnerabilities that arise only when realistic, unpredictable human behaviour is in the loop. The abstract reports no quantitative results.

papers.title: Sample-Aligned Decoders for Latent Generative Models
papers.abstract: Latent generative models synthesize images by decoding generated latents, yet their decoder is trained only to reconstruct encoder latents and never sees the latents it decodes at test time, so the residual errors of the generator are rendered directly into the final image. Existing remedies retrain the generator, add cost at every sampling step, or make the decoder robust to perturbed real latents, assuming that generator errors resemble such perturbations. We find that they do not. Generated latents lie on the encoder latent manifold as closely as real ones, yet follow a different distribution. The decoder should therefore be adapted to the distribution of generated latents, which raises two challenges: (1) unpaired supervision, since a generated latent has no ground-truth image, and (2) latent-space drift, since a decoder freed from paired targets forgets the latent space it must decode. We propose Sample-Aligned Decoders (SAD), a post-training framework that fine-tunes only the decoder of a frozen generator at no inference cost. Generated-Sample Distribution Alignment matches decoded generated latents to unpaired real images in a frozen foundation-model feature space, and Encoder Anchor Preservation keeps the decoder close to the original one on encoder latents. Our analysis shows that the alignment is effective only on generated latents, where it corrects each sample in proportion to how much more often the generator produces such latents than the encoder; on encoder latents it can only work against the anchor. SAD improves four state-of-the-art ImageNet generators across three tokenizers, e.g., FID-50K from 1.15 to 0.98 for REPA-E, complements discriminator guidance, and extends to text-to-image generation. Our code and models are available at https://torpedo2003.github.io/SAD/.
papers.summary: Decoders in latent generative models are trained only on encoder latents, so generator errors are rendered directly into the final image. The authors find that generated latents lie on the encoder manifold as closely as real ones but follow a different distribution, which motivates adapting the decoder to that distribution. `Sample-Aligned Decoders` (`SAD`) fine-tune only the decoder of a frozen generator, matching decoded generated latents to unpaired real images in a frozen foundation-model feature space while anchoring behaviour on encoder latents. With no added inference cost it improves four `ImageNet` generators across three tokenizers, for example **FID-50K from 1.15 to 0.98 for `REPA-E`**.

papers.title: Surfacing Disagreement Beats Resolving It: A Gated Ablation Study of Provenance-Weighted Memory for Multi-Agent Debate
papers.abstract: Shared memory for multi-agent debate is usually built to resolve inconsistency: retrieval returns one winning fact and the disagreement disappears before any agent sees it. We ask whether that is correct. In DebateGraph, four backends share one contract (read/write/snapshot), so five mechanisms from the agent-memory literature can be removed independently under a fixed budget, each gated on a pre-declared threshold. Across 39 runs one survives: preserving contradictions and passing the ranked conflict set to the debate, rather than collapsing it to a winner, improves F1 by +0.340 (95% CI [+0.267, +0.414]) and cuts attack success from 22 to 7 of 122 poisoned items (McNemar exact p=0.0003), at equal cost. Reaching it meant fixing a bottleneck in our harness: conflict sets are built only over retrieved edges, and our pre-declared cap left three quarters of planted contradictions unretrievable, first measuring the mechanism at +0.084. The effect replicates on two retrieval substrates and directionally on HotpotQA documents. No other mechanism survives, and two are worse than inert: once contradictions reach the prompt, a write trust-gate and the router's provenance features each cost accuracy (-0.075 and -0.096 F1). The gate fails structurally: poisoned objects are always entities the graph already contains, against 53% of gold, so groundedness scores the lie above a truthful first mention. We release the harness, attack set, and logs, and argue that silently reconciling memory is the assumption worth abandoning.
papers.summary: Shared memory for multi-agent debate usually resolves inconsistencies before agents see them, returning a single winning fact. Using `DebateGraph`, a harness where five memory mechanisms can be removed independently under a fixed budget and pre-declared thresholds, the authors find across 39 runs that only one survives: passing the ranked set of conflicting facts to the debate **improves F1 by +0.340 and cuts attack success from 22 to 7 of 122 poisoned items** at equal cost. The effect replicates on two retrieval substrates and directionally on `HotpotQA`. A write trust-gate and provenance-based routing features each reduce accuracy once contradictions reach the prompt, because poisoned objects are always entities the graph already contains and so score as better grounded than truthful first mentions.

papers.title: MAVE: Reconstructing Editable 3D Blockouts from Film Shots
papers.abstract: Animated 3D blockouts support previsualization and provide structural conditions for video generation, but manually reconstructing them from reference videos is costly. This limits both their use by creators and the production of paired training data. We introduce MAVEBench, a benchmark of 50 film shots and 416 keyframes for evaluating camera motion, spatial layout, and character blocking. We propose MAVE, a video-to-blockout framework combining Metric observation, Agentic modeling, and evidence-based VErification. It first recovers cameras, human motion, and geometric evidence in a shared metric coordinate system. An agent then constructs an editable environment under constraints from these observations, while programmatic checks report inconsistencies to guide refinement. The outputs are editable Blender scenes and frame-aligned blockout videos. On MAVEBench, MAVE improves overall scores by 27.5-41.1 points across three agents over their corresponding vanilla baselines. With DeepSeek-1017, it achieves a score of 73.2 at an average API cost of only USD 0.054 per shot, outperforming the strongest vanilla baseline while reducing total reconstruction time by 53%. We also construct MAVEData-3K, a dataset of 3,000 blockout-video pairs for model training, and will release it publicly. Creators can change viewpoints and character paths, then render the edited scenes to condition video generation. Code is available at https://github.com/yfChang-cv/MAVE.
papers.summary: Animated 3D blockouts used for film previsualization and for conditioning video generation are costly to reconstruct by hand from reference footage. `MAVE` recovers cameras, human motion, and geometry in a shared metric coordinate system, has an agent build an editable Blender scene under those constraints, and uses programmatic checks to guide refinement. On `MAVEBench`, a benchmark of 50 film shots and 416 keyframes, it **improves overall scores by 27.5-41.1 points across three agents** over vanilla baselines, reaching 73.2 with `DeepSeek-1017` at about USD 0.054 per shot. The authors also build `MAVEData-3K`, a dataset of 3,000 blockout-video pairs.

papers.title: Escaping Latent Traps by Remembering: Training-Free Episodic Kernel Repulsion for World-Model Planning
papers.abstract: Latent world models plan towards a goal image by minimising the distance between predicted and goal latents. This distance is not geodesic: it has local minima, latent traps, behind walls, at corners and in dead ends, and memoryless receding-horizon replanning keeps the agent in them, revisiting states far from the goal. We propose Episodic Kernel Repulsion (EKR), a training-free cost term that penalises candidate plans by a top-$k$ Gaussian kernel to a novelty-gated memory of the latents the agent has actually visited, rescaled by the current base cost so that its strength is comparable across models. Across two JEPA world models and four benchmarks, EKR raises average success from 31.8% to 46.7% (LeWM) and from 54.7% to 64.0% (H-JEPA) with the same model, planner and budget. Same-memory counterfactuals show that, in most settings, EKR pushes plans away from visited states, in navigation, often at a higher base cost; stuck episodes and revisits drop accordingly. In seven of eight settings it matches or exceeds $4\times$ samples at $0.8$--$1.5\times$ compute. Without tuning, it transfers to DINO-WM with CEM: $+6.7$ and $+19.3$ points on official and longer-goal Wall tasks, and from 44.7% to 100.0% and from 21.0% to 32.0% on long-horizon PointMaze and Push-T.
papers.summary: Latent world models plan by minimizing distance between predicted and goal latents, but this distance has local minima behind walls and in dead ends where memoryless replanning leaves the agent stuck. Episodic Kernel Repulsion (`EKR`) is a training-free cost term that penalizes candidate plans for being close to a novelty-gated memory of latents the agent has already visited, scaled by the current base cost. Across two JEPA world models and four benchmarks it raises **average success from 31.8% to 46.7% for `LeWM`** and from 54.7% to 64.0% for `H-JEPA` with the same model, planner, and budget. It transfers without tuning to `DINO-WM`, including a rise from 44.7% to 100.0% on long-horizon `PointMaze`.

papers.title: RehearsalBench: Can AI Predict What Happens When You Change a Company?
papers.abstract: Organizations increasingly ask AI systems what will happen if they change how they operate: which work to automate, which team to resize, what a voice agent will do to waiting times. We introduce RehearsalBench, a benchmark that measures whether AI models can diagnose an operation, choose an intervention, and forecast its consequences. Each model is placed in a simulated bank contact center fitted to real call-level records, sees only what a manager would see, and submits a plan and forecasts that are then played out across 200 seeded futures and three plausible versions of the organization. Decisions are scored in dollars at the stakeholders' stated valuations; forecasts are scored on the effect of each change relative to doing nothing. Ten models made 280 attempts across 14 organizations. The best model, GPT-6 Astra, improved on doing nothing by 6.8% of the no-change cost and made 77% less forecast error than a forecaster who always predicts no effect. On average, every model forecast the direction of every specified effect correctly, but models erred on the size of the same effects in the same direction, overstating a voice agent's effect on repeat contacts about five-fold. No model ever recommended holding off when doing nothing was the right choice. To test external validity, twelve models forecast 33 real organizational changes with known outcomes. Under verdict rules fixed in advance, the benchmark's forecast ranking agreed with the real-world ranking (Spearman $\rho = 0.92$, 95% lower bound 0.50). We report the result alongside an inconclusive first test, the analysis choices made after outcomes were seen, and evidence that part of the agreement reflects how well models size their uncertainty.
papers.summary: `RehearsalBench` tests whether AI models can diagnose an operation, choose an intervention, and forecast its consequences, using a simulated bank contact center fitted to real call records and played out over 200 seeded futures. Across ten models and 280 attempts, the best, `GPT-6 Astra`, improved on doing nothing by 6.8% of the no-change cost and made 77% less forecast error than a no-effect forecaster. Models got the direction of effects right on average but shared the same magnitude errors, overstating a voice agent's effect on repeat contacts about five-fold, and **no model ever recommended holding off when doing nothing was the right choice**. On 33 real organizational changes, the benchmark's forecast ranking agreed with the real-world ranking at Spearman rho = 0.92, with caveats the authors report.

papers.title: LeViT-UNet++: Towards Balanced Fine-Grained Details and Context for Efficient Medical Image Segmentation
papers.abstract: Efficient medical image segmentation is essential for clinical applications requiring fast and accurate delineation, such as surgical navigation, radiation therapy, and real-time image-guided intervention. Despite substantial advances in convolutional neural networks and Transformers, attaining high accuracy under limited computational resources remains difficult, because reducing model complexity often sacrifices fine-grained structural details and global context modeling, yielding an unfavorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off. To address this, we propose LeViT-UNet++, an efficient encoder-decoder architecture that better balances local detail preservation and global context modeling. Specifically, we introduce a Haar Wavelet Multi-Scale Downsampling (HWMD) module that decomposes feature representations into low- and high-frequency components to extract multi-scale structural information, thereby mitigating detail loss during downsampling. We further develop a depthwise convolution-based decoder that integrates multi-scale global representations from Transformer blocks with local spatial features, enabling progressive feature refinement while reducing computational overhead. Evaluated on four benchmarks (Synapse, ACDC, LA2018, and MSD Heart) under both 2D and 3D settings, LeViT-UNet++ achieves competitive accuracy with a compact parameter footprint and fast inference. On Synapse, for instance, it attains a DSC of 76.57% with only 8.025M parameters and 241.72 FPS, confirming a favorable accuracy-efficiency balance. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of combining wavelet-based multi-scale feature extraction with lightweight local-global feature fusion for efficient medical segmentation. The source code is available at https://github.com/apple1986/levit_unet_pp.
papers.summary: Medical image segmentation under tight compute budgets tends to lose fine structural detail and global context. `LeViT-UNet++` is an encoder-decoder architecture that adds a Haar Wavelet Multi-Scale Downsampling (`HWMD`) module, which splits features into low- and high-frequency components, and a depthwise-convolution decoder that fuses Transformer global features with local spatial features. Evaluated on `Synapse`, `ACDC`, `LA2018`, and `MSD Heart` in 2D and 3D settings, it reaches **a Dice score of 76.57% on `Synapse` with 8.025M parameters at 241.72 FPS**.

papers.title: Manufacturing Differential Sparsity: Planner-Hardware Co-Design for Efficient World Model Planning
papers.abstract: JEPA-style latent world models let embodied agents plan toward new goals with model predictive control, but they are still too slow for real-life embodied control: sampling-based MPC repeats predictor inference tens of thousands of times per plan, and even on high-end GPUs one planning step can take tens of seconds. We observe substantial latent locality in this repeated-inference workload: the predictor maps close actions to close latents, and inside a quantized predictor this closeness takes a form that hardware can exploit, differential bit-level sparsity. Unlike an input stream, whose temporal similarity is given, a planner itself decides which candidates it evaluates together, so the planner can choose its own references and, with reference forest sampling, manufacture more sparsity: it couples the sampled action sequences of each group to a shared root, with competitive planning quality. We build the accelerator on the insights of the rich line of bit-level sparsity accelerators and design it and the planner tightly coupled as a single co-design: the planner increases sparsity and exposes structure for hardware scheduling, and the bit-exact hardware effectively uses the sparsity that the planner creates. On three JEPA world models, our co-design is 1.28-1.80x faster than a dense accelerator and uses 38-52% less energy, and it is 1.22-1.58x faster than prior bit-sparse design and uses 16-36% less energy, with the same area. To our knowledge, our planner is the first planner that manufactures differential bit-level sparsity across its candidates and exposes its structure for hardware scheduling, and our co-design is the first algorithm-hardware co-design for JEPA-style world-model planning.
papers.summary: Planning with JEPA-style latent world models via sampling-based model predictive control (MPC) repeats predictor inference tens of thousands of times per plan, taking tens of seconds even on high-end GPUs. The authors observe that nearby actions yield nearby latents, which in a quantized predictor appears as differential bit-level sparsity, and they design a planner using reference forest sampling to deliberately create more of it alongside a tightly coupled accelerator that exploits it. On three world models the co-design is **1.28-1.80x faster than a dense accelerator with 38-52% less energy**, and 1.22-1.58x faster than a prior bit-sparse design at the same area.

papers.title: Growing Clusters Lower the Bar: Profile Accretion in LLM-Based Incremental Entity Resolution
papers.abstract: Incremental entity resolution pipelines ask a large language model (LLM) whether a new record belongs to an existing cluster and show it the records already linked. Analyses of matching oracles assume that the answer depends only on the records compared. For the LLM matchers we test, it depends on cluster size, and the model lowers its bar for joining a cluster as the cluster grows. On French procurement suppliers from FOPPA, with SIREN identifiers as ground truth, we hold the new record fixed and vary only the number of verified members shown. Sixteen members instead of one raise the false match rate on similarly named companies by \dfmrMin--\dfmrMax{} percentage points in six open-weight models, while their area under the ROC curve rises by only \aucGainMin--\aucGainMax. In Claude Sonnet~5 and Haiku~5.5 the rise is \clSonD{} and \clHaiD{} points. The shift persists with street addresses, prompt variants and the BatchER and ComEM formats, and one false merge raises acceptance of the intruder's other records in every open model. It does not arise on Czech and Bulgarian TED notices, where one record with its full address already identifies the company. In online linking on confusable blocks, a single threshold set on labelled data raises recall by a factor of \fxRRmin--\fxRRmax{} for five models with no detectable loss of precision and no extra LLM calls.
papers.summary: Incremental entity resolution pipelines ask a large language model (LLM) whether a new record belongs to an existing cluster while showing it the records already linked. Holding the new record fixed on French procurement suppliers from `FOPPA`, the authors show that **showing sixteen verified members instead of one raises the false match rate on similarly named companies** across six open-weight models and in `Claude Sonnet 5` and `Haiku 5.5`, with only a small gain in area under the ROC curve. The shift persists across prompt variants and the `BatchER` and `ComEM` formats, and one false merge makes the intruder's other records more likely to be accepted. A single threshold set on labelled data raises recall for five models with no detectable loss of precision and no extra LLM calls.

papers.title: SciWorkBench: A Benchmark for Real Scientific Workflows
papers.abstract: Language models are increasingly being used as agents capable of planning and executing projects, as well as refining their actions through feedback. This shift raises a question: can current agents complete projects like real scientists? To examine this question, we introduce SciWorkBench, a benchmark for evaluating agents' abilities on real science tasks across biology, chemistry, materials science, and physics. SciWorkBench is built from peer-reviewed literature or expert-contributed research scenarios. We also propose a unified scientific analysis framework validated by domain experts, which can categorize most tasks in SciWorkBench. Each task covers one or more stages of this framework. We evaluate up-to-date models within the Claude Code and Codex agent frameworks under a unified execution and grading protocol. The best-performing agent achieves a mean score of 57.38, indicating that current agents still struggle with realistic scientific workflows. Our failure analysis identifies three recurring weaknesses at the workflow level: difficulty translating scientific knowledge into task-specific procedures, weak integration of evidence across different modalities, and limited capacity for scientific self-correction. These findings highlight the importance of workflow-based evaluation for measuring progress toward reliable AI systems for scientific research.
papers.summary: `SciWorkBench` evaluates whether agents can complete realistic scientific projects in biology, chemistry, materials science, and physics, with tasks drawn from peer-reviewed literature or expert-contributed scenarios and organized by an expert-validated analysis framework. Models are run inside the `Claude Code` and `Codex` agent frameworks under a unified execution and grading protocol, and **the best-performing agent achieves a mean score of 57.38**. Failure analysis points to three recurring weaknesses: translating scientific knowledge into task-specific procedures, integrating evidence across modalities, and scientific self-correction.

papers.title: Motion-Aware Reward Modeling for Instruction-Guided Video Editing
papers.abstract: Reward models for instruction-guided video editing can favor temporal consistency at the expense of motion. We study this failure, termed \emph{motion collapse}, using controlled motion-suppression variants of real edits. On VE-Bench, the evaluated composite reward prefers a motion-suppressed candidate in $97\%$ of cases. Learned video rewards and a VLM judge also struggle with mild suppression, while latent optimization and reward-guided fine-tuning exploit this weakness to increase reward as motion declines. A linear probe of our base reward backbone performs near chance on mild suppression, motivating an explicit inter-frame dynamics input. We propose a motion-aware reward model that combines an RGB frame-difference stream with preference training against motion-suppressed and fabricated-motion negatives. A distillation anchor preserves alignment with human quality judgments. On the VE-Bench motion ladder, our model reduces the rate of selecting motion-suppressed candidates to $0\%$ while achieving a Spearman correlation of $0.57$ with human quality ratings. It also detects unseen suppression variants and preserves motion during reward-guided fine-tuning on two editing pipelines. These results support explicitly modeling motion in rewards for video editing.
papers.summary: Reward models for instruction-guided video editing can favour temporal consistency so strongly that they prefer edits with suppressed motion, a failure the authors call motion collapse. On `VE-Bench`, the evaluated composite reward prefers a motion-suppressed candidate in 97% of cases, and latent optimization and reward-guided fine-tuning exploit the weakness. The proposed motion-aware reward model adds an RGB frame-difference stream and trains against motion-suppressed and fabricated-motion negatives, with a distillation anchor to keep alignment with human quality judgments. It **reduces the rate of selecting motion-suppressed candidates to 0%** while reaching a Spearman correlation of 0.57 with human ratings.

papers.title: DARWIN: a Geospatial Foundation Model for Marine Intelligence
papers.abstract:
We present DARWIN, a geospatial foundation model for marine intelligence. Recent Earth-observation foundation models have concentrated on terrestrial domains. The marine realm poses distinct challenges: missingness, multi-modal physical and biogeochemical variables, sparse labels, and dynamics that are transient, multi-scale, and non stationary over time. DARWIN adapts a masked-autoencoder backbone to these properties through missingness-aware encoding, expanded spatial and temporal masking, and Fourier-style positional embeddings, and is pretrained on 26 years of global Copernicus reanalysis together with GEBCO bathymetry.
  On predicting chlorophyll-a, the pretrained backbone attains the lowest monthly relative error in every month of 2022, outperforming both no-encoder baselines and an identically architected random-init encoder. At 10% of the supervised training data, DARWIN already surpasses the random-init model trained on 100% of the data. Embedding analysis and qualitative reconstructions show that DARWIN captures coherent oceanographic structure rather than memorising input statistics, providing a scalable backbone for downstream marine applications such as anomaly detection, species distribution modelling, and environmental monitoring.
papers.summary: Earth-observation foundation models have concentrated on land, while ocean data brings missing values, many physical and biogeochemical variables, sparse labels, and non-stationary dynamics. `DARWIN` adapts a masked-autoencoder backbone with missingness-aware encoding, expanded spatial and temporal masking, and Fourier-style positional embeddings, pretrained on 26 years of global Copernicus reanalysis plus `GEBCO` bathymetry. On chlorophyll-a prediction it attains the lowest monthly relative error in every month of 2022, and **with 10% of the supervised training data it surpasses a randomly initialized model trained on 100%**.

papers.title: Towards Data-Efficient, Real-Time World Models
papers.abstract: State-of-the-art world models have been used to produce sequences of gameplay that accord with provided user-input actions. However, high quality, consistent gameplay generation often comes at the cost of inference speed, making real-time interactive play and ideation challenging. The substantial quantities of data used to train state-of-the-art models have also made custom training of these models appear impractical, limiting many of their potential uses in creative fields. In this work we demonstrate a major step towards efficient world models: achieving both fast high-quality inference, and improved data efficiency. This is done by replacing the next-token prediction paradigm with a two-stage discrete diffusion-based approach, introducing a lightweight refinement transformer which carries out iterative masked predictions. Building on an autoregressive world model capable of generating highly consistent and complex sequences over minutes (Kanervisto et al., 2025), we achieve substantial model speed-up (79x) with a modest quality trade-off. Additionally, we demonstrate that this model can be trained to reproduce high-quality, consistent gameplay using a dataset containing approximately one day (28 hours) of gameplay data. Our results demonstrate progress towards removing barriers to the use of world models in settings where real-time inference and data efficiency are essential.
