papers.summary: Interactive world models that generate gameplay from user actions are typically too slow for real-time play and need very large training datasets. The authors replace next-token prediction in an existing autoregressive world model (Kanervisto et al., 2025) with a two-stage discrete diffusion approach, adding a lightweight refinement transformer that performs iterative masked predictions. They report a **79x inference speed-up with a modest quality trade-off**, and show the model can reproduce high-quality, consistent gameplay when trained on roughly 28 hours of gameplay data.

papers.title: From syllable representation via gesture generation to articulation: A spiking neural model
papers.abstract:
Speech production requires a transformation from phonological representations into coordinated vocal-tract movements. This paper presents a spiking neural sensorimotor model within the Neural Engineering Framework and Semantic Pointer Architecture. Each syllable occurrence has a neural oscillator whose evolving phase coordinates its gestures and initiates the next syllable. Phase-dependent commands recruit separate neural populations for vocalic, oral-constriction, velopharyngeal, and glottal actions (gestures). Neural ramp integrators shape the rise and fall of gesture activation. Together with articulatory targets, these trajectories determine the extent and time course of articulatory movements. Opponent neural populations provide control signals to a geometric articulatory model.
  Thirty reference recordings cover an input corpus of eight lexical words, an alternative realization of one word, a syllable sequence, and isolated syllables. Two additional paired simulation subcorpora of sixty runs each, covering two words and one syllable sequence, assess activation reliability across neural realizations. Adjusting gesture command amplitudes increased successful realizations from 57/60 to 60/60 under the specified criteria, with ramp rate factors held constant.
  The model demonstrates how neural oscillator and ramp dynamics generate articulatory timing under specified phasing rules. It complements a preceding mental-lexicon model through an ordered syllable interface. Continuous online execution across all components and connection to the acoustic extension remain further integration steps. Accessible code and synchronized visualization support inspection of the neural activation trajectories and resulting vocal-tract movements.
papers.summary: Speech production requires turning phonological representations into coordinated vocal-tract movements, and this work models that transformation with spiking neurons built in the `Neural Engineering Framework` and `Semantic Pointer Architecture`. Each syllable has a neural oscillator whose phase times its gestures and triggers the next syllable, while ramp integrators shape gesture activation and opponent neural populations drive a geometric articulatory model. Across paired simulation runs covering two words and a syllable sequence, adjusting gesture command amplitudes raised successful realizations **from 57/60 to 60/60**. Continuous online execution across all components and connection to an acoustic extension remain future integration steps.

papers.title: Efficient Self-Supervised Adaptation of 3D Abdominal Vision-Language Model for Institution-Specific HCC Classification via Full Fine-Tuning and PEFT
papers.abstract: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) capture cross-modal relationships between image and text, yet their adaptation to institution-specific clinical tasks remains underexplored. In this study, we fine-tuned a pretrained 3D medical VLM for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) classification using paired abdominal CT scans and radiology reports from a different institution with acquisition characteristics that differ from the model's original pretraining corpus. We compared two adaptation strategies: full fine-tuning and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), motivated by the common use of PEFT to reduce computational cost and enable adaptation under limited-data constraints. Both approaches achieve strong downstream HCC classification performance despite the cross-institutional domain shift, with PEFT reaching an AUC of 0.79 and F1 of 0.70, and full fine-tuning achieving an AUC of 0.82 and F1 of 0.71. Although these results remain below the performance reported by supervised HCC classification approaches, our method achieves improvements over the pretrained model through CT-report contrastive learning without requiring lesion-level annotations or HCC classification labels as training targets. Full fine-tuning converges rapidly but overfits within a few epochs, whereas PEFT (ConvLoRA for the image encoder and LoRA for the text encoder) attains comparable performance while updating approximately 1% of the model parameters, although requiring more training steps. We also examine the role of contrastive temperature, observing that temperature initialization significantly affects classification performance. This study demonstrates that a 3D medical VLM can be efficiently adapted to institution-specific HCC classification using self-supervised CT-report contrastive learning, while highlighting the practical trade-offs between full fine-tuning and parameter-efficient fine-tuning.
papers.summary: A pretrained 3D medical vision-language model (VLM) is adapted to hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) classification at a different institution using only paired abdominal CT scans and radiology reports, with contrastive learning and no lesion annotations or classification labels as training targets. The study compares full fine-tuning against parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), using `ConvLoRA` for the image encoder and `LoRA` for the text encoder. **PEFT reaches an AUC of 0.79 while updating about 1% of parameters, versus 0.82 for full fine-tuning**, which converges quickly but overfits within a few epochs. Both remain below supervised HCC classifiers, and the initial contrastive temperature significantly affects results.

papers.title: LMLineage: Content Lineage and Context Governance for LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Interpretability for AI agents should not be confined to understanding the model's internal weights. It must also cover the agent's reasoning and decision-making process over multi-source context. We present LMLineage, an out-of-band system that attributes every output sentence of an agent session to its supporting input spans with calibrated confidences, without requiring white-box access to the model or any additional inference passes. On top of the lineage metadata, we build concept-drift micro compaction: instead of waiting for the context-length limit and summarizing everything, the system detects when previously used input documents have stopped being referenced ("drifted") and surgically compacts only those, preserving user instructions verbatim. We evaluate on a multi-tier corpus: 71 gold annotated sentences from 10 Chinese web-QA cases, plus 90 turns of independently collected multi-turn sessions across three generator models (gpt-4o-mini, qwen3.8-27b, deepseek-v4-flash). Results show that (i) window-level embedding similarity is far better aligned with LLM paraphrasing than whole document or lexical matching; (ii) the greedy-window fast path is both faster and more accurate on average than exhaustive line-matching (a multiple-comparisons bias in the latter inflates web recall at the cost of overall accuracy); (iii) per-turn attribution completes in 1s on a single GPU, remaining stable as context accumulates to 40 turns; and (iv) concept-drift detection is conservative (0% false compaction) with recall bounded by attribution accuracy. We further describe the concept-drift micro compaction design and an interactive incident-tracing/memory-cleaning case study. A companion patent application covers the lineage construction method.
papers.summary: `LMLineage` is an out-of-band system that attributes each output sentence of a large language model (LLM) agent session to the input spans supporting it, with calibrated confidences and without white-box model access or extra inference passes. On top of this lineage data, it performs concept-drift micro compaction: detecting input documents that are no longer being referenced and compacting only those, while keeping user instructions verbatim. Evaluated on 71 annotated sentences from Chinese web question answering and 90 multi-turn turns across `gpt-4o-mini`, `qwen3.8-27b`, and `deepseek-v4-flash`, **per-turn attribution completes in about 1 second on a single GPU and stays stable up to 40 turns**. Window-level embedding similarity tracked LLM paraphrasing better than whole-document or lexical matching, and drift detection produced 0% false compaction with recall bounded by attribution accuracy.

papers.title: MM-ReportBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Multimodal Report Generation from Tables
papers.abstract: The ability to generate multimodal reports integrating fluent narratives with faithful visualizations from tabular data, has become a cornerstone capability for modern vision-language models in practical domains such as finance, healthcare, and policy making. However, existing benchmarks are limited by single-modality focus, simplistic metrics, novelty evaluation, and visualization quality. We address these limitations with MM-ReportBench, a multimodal report evaluation benchmark covering 386 tasks across 185 real-world tables. Each task is paired with an expert-curated reference report featuring standardized chapter structures and verifiable key insight points, constructed through a hybrid pipeline of multimodal reports generation based on Monte Carlo Tree Search and rigorous human quality control. For robust evaluation, we design a dual-judge evaluation framework: Text Judge Model assesses textual quality along structural completeness, grounded insight verification with numerical fact-checking against source tables, and novelty analysis that distinguishes genuine analytical discovery from trivial paraphrasing; Visualization Judge Model evaluates generated visualizations across data fidelity, expressiveness, aesthetics, and technical correctness. They also evaluate cross-modal consistency. Extensive experiments on 20 state-of-the-art models reveal critical weaknesses: even the strongest model achieves only 68.9 overall score, with numerical hallucination affecting 38.5% of reports and genuinely novel insights remaining rare. Our ablation studies further demonstrate that single-judge evaluation consistently inflates scores by 8-12 points compared to dual-judge assessment, confirming that rigorous and reliable benchmarking demands multi-faceted, complementary evaluation probes.
papers.summary: `MM-ReportBench` evaluates how well vision-language models turn tabular data into reports that combine narrative text with visualizations, covering 386 tasks over 185 real-world tables with expert-curated reference reports. Scoring uses two judges: a text judge that checks structure, fact-checks numbers against the source table, and assesses novelty of insights, and a visualization judge that rates data fidelity, expressiveness, aesthetics, and technical correctness. Across 20 models, **the strongest scores only 68.9 overall, and numerical hallucination affects 38.5% of reports**. Ablations indicate that single-judge evaluation inflates scores by 8 to 12 points relative to the dual-judge setup.

papers.title: Right Labels, Wrong Reasons: Signed Feature Attribution for Multi-Label Explainability
papers.abstract: When a multi-label classifier assigns the right labels, it may do so for the wrong reasons. Diffuse feature combinations may vary across classifier families and lack a dominant feature. This paper proposes FLEX (Fisher LDA Explainer), a global surrogate that fits a single direct multi-label Fisher LDA over the full binary label matrix, producing signed feature attribution lists for each label in a single coherent coordinate system. Across the evaluated benchmarks and classifier families, FLEX reproduces the black box's predictions with consistently high fidelity. Pooling covariance across labels outperforms a per-label alternative on most datasets, with the advantage growing largest where labels are numerous and positive examples are scarce. FLEX's fidelity-complexity Pareto curve is monotonically increasing, giving practitioners a predictable path to higher-fidelity explanations as more features are used, and its in-sample fidelity matches or leads Binary Relevance alternatives once a modest feature budget is allowed. The magnitude of each discriminant weight vector bounds its label's separability, flagging labels that may be predicted correctly for the wrong reasons. The evaluated classifiers largely agree on which predictions to make, but reach those decisions through different feature subsets when no single feature dominates.
papers.summary: Multi-label classifiers can assign correct labels while relying on diffuse or weak feature combinations, which per-label explanation methods handle inconsistently. `FLEX` (Fisher LDA Explainer) is a global surrogate that fits a single multi-label Fisher linear discriminant analysis over the full binary label matrix, giving signed feature attributions for every label in one shared coordinate system. It reproduces black-box predictions with high fidelity across the tested benchmarks, and **pooling covariance across labels beats a per-label alternative on most datasets**, especially when labels are numerous and positive examples scarce. The magnitude of each discriminant weight vector bounds that label's separability, which flags labels that may be predicted correctly for the wrong reasons.

papers.title: When Agent Skills Go Stale: Runtime Behavior and Selective Maintenance in Evolving Environments
papers.abstract: Agent skills use past experience and current observations to guide decisions and actions on related tasks. This experience is retained in skill state, whose reuse can amortize inference-time reasoning and environment interaction. When environment changes, parts of this state can become outdated while others remain useful. Across four task settings and two models, we compare skill reuse before and after environment changes. Previously beneficial skills can reduce task performance by over 10 percentage points or increase execution cost by nearly 40% relative to no skill. Task success can also remain unchanged while execution savings decline. These effects depend on which environment-specific details become outdated and the agent's ability to compensate using current observations. We introduce selective maintenance, which replays checks from successful executions without additional model calls. It verifies whether observed differences conflict with skill state, repairs affected content, and validates updates, rebuilding when local repair is insufficient. No description of the change is supplied. Relative to reusing stale state, maintenance improves task accuracy by up to 67pp and reduces execution steps by up to 37%. These results suggest that preserving a skill's inference time value as environments evolve requires selectively maintaining its state.
papers.summary: Agent skills store experience from past tasks so that later runs need less reasoning and environment interaction, but parts of that stored state can become outdated when the environment changes. Across four task settings and two models, previously helpful skills reduced task performance by over 10 percentage points or raised execution cost by nearly 40% compared with using no skill. The authors propose selective maintenance, which replays checks from successful executions without extra model calls, repairs the affected skill content, validates the update, and rebuilds when local repair is insufficient, all without being told what changed. Relative to reusing stale state, it **improves task accuracy by up to 67 percentage points** and cuts execution steps by up to 37%.

papers.title: DGF-Asym: Adaptive Peer Weighting for Collective Estimation under Noisy and Faulty Sensing
papers.abstract: Collective estimation under unreliable sensing requires robots to adaptively balance personal observations and social information from peers. We propose DGF-Asym, a decentralized collective estimation method extending the DeGroot-Friedkin model with asymmetric peer weighting based on retrospective predictive performance. The method supports consensus formation without prior sensor-noise statistics or explicit fault models while keeping inter-robot communication asynchronous. We evaluate DGF-Asym in simulated collective navigation under noisy observations and time-varying sensor faults. Compared with three baselines, it produces more stable estimates and more reliably sustains the decision criterion, at the cost of longer decision times. However, overall performance depends on fault ratio, group size, and influence-threshold selection. Our results demonstrate the potential of adaptive peer weighting for stable model-free collective estimation under unreliable sensing.
papers.summary: Groups of robots estimating a shared quantity must balance their own noisy or faulty sensor readings against information from peers. `DGF-Asym` extends the DeGroot-Friedkin opinion dynamics model with asymmetric peer weights based on how well each peer's past estimates predicted outcomes, requiring no prior sensor-noise statistics or fault models and allowing asynchronous communication. In simulated collective navigation with noisy observations and time-varying sensor faults, it **yields more stable estimates than three baselines at the cost of longer decision times**. Performance depends on the fault ratio, group size, and choice of influence threshold.

papers.title: Testing World Models on Actions They Have Never Seen: Held-Out Plans, Forecast Accuracy and Price Rules in Retail
papers.abstract: A world model is trusted to answer "what if": how its world responds to an action it has never seen. We give a test of that trust for any action-conditioned world model: actions held out of training by design and scored against a known answer; whether forecast accuracy predicts accuracy on those actions; and the same structure given to simpler models. We run it in retail, where the action is a price and promotion plan, across 2,853 fitted models. First, forecast accuracy is a fair guide between kinds of model (rank correlation with error on new plans 0.32 to 0.66) and a poor guide between versions of one world model: where merchants plan into high-demand weeks the link reverses, down to -0.69. Second, training the world model to learn the effect of actions (JEPA pretraining, a latent consistency check, adaptation at the plan date) leaves its error on new plans unchanged. Third, in generated worlds the recorded regular price and three price rules improve it. Given the same rules, a log-linear model is best when its curve can match the truth; in a world whose curve lies outside the rules, the world model with the rules is ahead of the log-linear model with the rules in 36 of 40 worlds, and does as well without its recurrent cell. On real data (Breakfast at the Frat, The Complete Journey and M5) the rules lower the world model's error on pure price cuts deeper than any it saw (0.63 to 0.56 on the Frat; 0.45 to 0.44, within chance, on The Complete Journey), but not on lasting price moves. Fourth, a small share of random test plans helps every model a little. In a generated dosing world, a stress test in a second domain, the first finding repeats, and the built-up drug level lowers the world model's error (2.86 to 1.91) though it still predicts only 0.12 to 0.32 of the true gain. The test carries to any domain where a world model is asked about actions outside its history.
papers.summary: A test is proposed for whether action-conditioned world models can be trusted on actions absent from training: hold out actions by design, score them against a known answer, and check whether ordinary forecast accuracy predicts accuracy on those actions. Applied to retail price and promotion plans across 2,853 fitted models, **forecast accuracy is a fair guide between model families (rank correlation 0.32 to 0.66) but a poor one between versions of the same world model, reversing to as low as -0.69**. Techniques intended to teach action effects, including `JEPA` pretraining, left error on new plans unchanged, whereas supplying the recorded regular price and three price rules reduced it in generated worlds. On real datasets (`Breakfast at the Frat`, `The Complete Journey`, `M5`) the rules helped for deep price cuts, in one case only within chance, but not for lasting price moves.

papers.title: JET: Just-Enough Exploration Tuning for Efficient Tool-Calling Agents in Repository-Level Question Answering
papers.abstract: In repository-level question answering (QA), an agent explores a code repository with tools and should answer a question once enough information is gathered. Nevertheless, we find that LLM agents often continue to invoke tools even after the gathered information is already sufficient to answer. We call this phenomenon over-exploration. Moreover, even though existing methods improve task performance through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on expert trajectories, SFT also propagates the over-exploration in the trajectories to the agent. To mitigate over-exploration, we propose Just-Enough Exploration Tuning (JET), a fine-tuning method that trains the agent to answer once the gathered information is sufficient. JET truncates each training trajectory at the step where the gathered information becomes sufficient, inserts a rationale that explains why the agent can answer at that step, and fine-tunes the agent with a higher loss weight on the rationale. Experiments on two repository-level QA benchmarks with two open-weight 8B models demonstrate that JET reduces tool calls by 11 to 33% on self-generated trajectories while largely preserving the score. On expert trajectories, JET makes 18 to 28% fewer tool calls than SFT while retaining most of the score gain of SFT. In both cases, JET also lowers the inference cost.
papers.summary: In repository-level question answering, tool-using large language model agents often keep calling tools after they have gathered enough information to answer, a behavior the authors call over-exploration, and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on expert trajectories passes this habit on. Just-Enough Exploration Tuning (`JET`) truncates each training trajectory at the step where the information becomes sufficient, inserts a rationale explaining why the agent can answer there, and fine-tunes with a higher loss weight on that rationale. On two benchmarks with two open-weight 8B models, `JET` **cuts tool calls by 11 to 33% on self-generated trajectories while largely preserving the score**. On expert trajectories it makes 18 to 28% fewer tool calls than SFT while keeping most of SFT's score gain, and lowers inference cost in both cases.

papers.title: From Perception to Simulation: Unveiling and Empowering Mental Spatial Dynamics in MLLMs
papers.abstract: Spatial reasoning is a fundamental component of world understanding for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). While existing research has advanced the perception of spatial relations in static scenes, the domain of dynamic spatial simulation remains relatively unexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce MentalGrid, a benchmark focused on spatial reasoning tasks that require models to simulate evolving spatial states without intermediate visual feedback. Extensive evaluation on our benchmark reveals a significant deficiency in the spatial simulation capabilities of existing models. Specifically, we find that performance is constrained by perceptual limitations in simple simulation scenarios and hindered by inadequate multi-step reasoning as complexity increases. To address these challenges, we propose a three-stage curriculum learning framework utilizing 16k specialized spatial reasoning samples. This approach yields SpatialWalker, which achieves a 33.8% average improvement over its base model, surpassing proprietary models like Gemini-3-Flash in spatial simulation. Furthermore, SpatialWalker demonstrates robust generalization, maintaining a 4.9% average gain on out-of-domain benchmarks, demonstrating the pivotal role of spatial simulation as a fundamental building block for broader spatial intelligence.
papers.summary: `MentalGrid` is a benchmark testing whether Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) can mentally simulate spatial states that evolve over several steps without intermediate visual feedback, rather than just perceive relations in a static scene. Evaluations show existing models are limited by perception in simple scenarios and by weak multi-step reasoning as complexity grows. A three-stage curriculum using 16k spatial reasoning samples produces `SpatialWalker`, which **improves on its base model by 33.8% on average** and surpasses proprietary models such as `Gemini-3-Flash` on spatial simulation. It also keeps a 4.9% average gain on out-of-domain benchmarks.

papers.title: JointGV: Structure-Aware Correction of Visual World Models with Parallel Graph Dynamics for Long-Horizon Modeling
papers.abstract: Visual world models predict future visual states conditioned on actions, but recursive errors in entity poses and spatial relations limit their long-horizon prediction for robot planning and control. We ask whether a separately predicted relational state can correct this drift without restructuring the visual model. This is challenging because graph nodes and visual states share neither elements nor a feature space. We propose Joint Graph--Visual Dynamics Correction (JointGV), a plug-in based on a cross-granularity dynamics hypothesis: despite their different representations, graph-node and visual-state changes describe the same physical transition. JointGV rolls out a task-conditioned scene graph alongside the visual world model, couples their predicted changes, and combines the resulting graph-motion context with graph-predicted node positions to compute a bounded residual. Graph-learning and correction gradients do not propagate into the original visual dynamics. We attach JointGV to DINO-WM (spatial tokens) and DreamerV3 (a global latent state), evaluating both on DMC Cheetah Run and Walker Walk across three seeds and extending the evaluation to contact-rich manipulation with DMC Finger Turn Hard. Across 32-step rollouts, JointGV improves structural and visual-prediction accuracy, reducing joint-position error by 11--28\%. For spatial tokens, learned graph--visual change coupling gives lower error than broadcasting the same mean graph-motion context to every token, particularly when non-adjacent parts appear close together in the image. On real-robot inverted-pendulum sequences, JointGV reduces DINO-WM's 32-step pole-angle error from $12.56^\circ$ to $6.69^\circ$ and improves DreamerV3 and LeWorldModel as well. In simulated inverted-pendulum control, an actor trained with JointGV-corrected rollouts completes 46 of 50 episodes, compared with none using the original rollouts.
papers.summary: Visual world models accumulate errors in entity poses and spatial relations over long rollouts, which limits their use for robot planning. Joint Graph-Visual Dynamics Correction (`JointGV`) is a plug-in that rolls out a task-conditioned scene graph alongside the visual model, couples the predicted changes of the two, and applies a bounded residual correction without propagating gradients into the original visual dynamics. Attached to `DINO-WM` and `DreamerV3` on DeepMind Control tasks, it reduces joint-position error by 11 to 28% over 32-step rollouts, and on real-robot inverted-pendulum sequences it lowers `DINO-WM`'s pole-angle error from 12.56° to 6.69°. In simulated pendulum control, an actor trained on corrected rollouts **completes 46 of 50 episodes, compared with none using the original rollouts**.

papers.title: Temporal Diffusion Models for Joint Signal-Channel Estimation under Gaussian and $\alpha$-Stable MIMO Channels
papers.abstract: Diffusion models have emerged as powerful tools for learning complex data distributions and solving inverse problems. However, most diffusion models rely on the Gaussian distribution, which does not accurately represent heavy-tailed data. In this work, we study diffusion-based reconstruction under Gaussian and symmetric $\alpha$-stable fading channels, while also exploring the benefits of using possible temporal dependence in the channel. We consider two variants: pilot-based channel-only estimation and joint image-channel recovery for MIMO systems. Our approach is based on several standard and score-based diffusion models for both Gaussian and $\alpha$-stable distributions. We refine these models by guiding the reverse diffusion process using the observation likelihood and show how a single trained diffusion model can be reused for the location-scale family of distributions without retraining. In blind MIMO recovery, separate diffusion models are used for the image and channel, and their estimates are combined through likelihood guidance. For each setting, we compare independent and temporal reconstruction, where information from previous observations is used to improve the estimation. We show that, under a time-dependent channel model, such a temporal reconstruction improves channel estimation and the quality of the reconstructed image. Finally, we show that, for the same heavy-tailed channel data, using an $\alpha$-stable diffusion prior provides better channel estimation and image reconstruction than using a Gaussian diffusion prior.
papers.summary: Most diffusion models assume Gaussian noise, which poorly represents heavy-tailed data such as some wireless fading channels. This work studies diffusion-based reconstruction for multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems under Gaussian and symmetric α-stable channels, covering both pilot-based channel estimation and blind joint image-channel recovery, with the reverse process guided by the observation likelihood. A single trained model can be reused across a location-scale family of distributions without retraining, and exploiting temporal dependence between observations improves both channel estimates and reconstructed image quality. On heavy-tailed channel data, **an α-stable diffusion prior gives better channel estimation and image reconstruction than a Gaussian prior**.

papers.title: Physically Admissible Generative Flow Matching for Sparse Flow Reconstruction
papers.abstract: Reconstructing full fluid velocity fields from sparse, localized observations is a severely ill-posed inverse problem: most of the spatial domain remains unobserved, discrete conservation laws must hold strictly, and predictive uncertainty must be reliable. Existing generative models typically enforce physical constraints only at the terminal output or via soft penalties, leaving intermediate generative trajectories unconstrained. We introduce Feasible Subspace Consistency (FSC), a framework that preserves physical admissibility as an invariant of continuous generative dynamics: tangent-space matching confines the entire ODE trajectory to the discrete conservation manifold, while mass-orthonormal coordinates preserve the kinetic-energy metric. Sparse reconstruction then reduces to amortized posterior transport in the latent space of a frozen FSC prior, ensuring every posterior sample inherits incompressibility and boundary conditions without per-sample projection loops. We validate FSC on a periodic Kolmogorov flow, where exact spectral projection isolates path tangency and metric isometry, and a wall-bounded cylinder wake with immersed obstacles, realized via matrix-free iterative projection. FSC prevents the mode-coverage collapse induced by terminal projection (increasing mode coverage from $0.000$ to $0.790$) while eliminating high-wavenumber spectral distortion. In sparse reconstruction, amortized FSC reduces global relative error by $50\%$ and $46\%$, and sensor residuals by $63\%$ and $55\%$, relative to the unconditioned prior, while delivering calibrated, spatially heterogeneous uncertainty.
papers.summary: Reconstructing full fluid velocity fields from sparse sensor readings is ill-posed, and generative models usually enforce physical constraints only on the final output or through soft penalties. Feasible Subspace Consistency (`FSC`) is a flow matching framework that keeps the entire generative trajectory on the discrete conservation manifold through tangent-space matching, so every sample satisfies incompressibility and boundary conditions without per-sample projection loops. Sparse reconstruction is then done by amortized posterior transport in the latent space of a frozen prior. On Kolmogorov flow and a cylinder wake, it avoids the mode collapse caused by terminal projection (mode coverage rising from 0.000 to 0.790) and **reduces global relative reconstruction error by 50% and 46%** relative to the unconditioned prior.

papers.title: Balancing Exploration and Exploitation in Constrained Combinatorial Optimization with U(1)-Symmetric Tensor Trains
papers.abstract: Tensor Train (TT) decomposition has emerged as a powerful tool for mitigating the curse of dimensionality in a variety of machine learning and combinatorial optimization tasks. Recent advances show that TT-based generative models can efficiently represent and explore high-dimensional discrete spaces, even when the cost function structure is unknown. However, incorporating hard linear constraints into TT-based optimization remains challenging, as existing interpolation and sampling approaches often fail when feasible points are rare. In this work, we develop a general TT-based framework for constrained combinatorial optimization built upon U(1)-symmetric tensor networks. Our method introduces an expressibility-enhancement mechanism for constructing sparse symmetric tensors and a graph-based diversity measure that guides sample selection during training. On assignment benchmarks, expressibility enhancement and diversity-aware selection improve mean solution quality over their respective baselines. The assignment-selected diversifying strategy also extends to nonpolynomial Set Partitioning, with larger relative gains observed in the higher-tensor-rank data families. Separate runtime benchmarks show substantial speedups over ConstrainTNet and PROTES on non-degenerate assignment workloads; comparisons with simulated annealing depend on constraint information and computational budget, but, overall, support the practicality of the current implementation.
papers.summary: Tensor Train (TT) generative models can explore high-dimensional discrete spaces for combinatorial optimization, but they struggle with hard linear constraints when feasible points are rare. The authors build a constrained optimization framework on U(1)-symmetric tensor networks, adding an expressibility-enhancement mechanism for constructing sparse symmetric tensors and a graph-based diversity measure that guides which samples are kept during training. Both additions **improve mean solution quality over their baselines on assignment benchmarks**, and the diversity strategy carries over to Set Partitioning. Runtime tests show substantial speedups over `ConstrainTNet` and `PROTES` on non-degenerate assignment workloads, while comparisons with simulated annealing depend on constraint information and compute budget.

papers.title: CADMAGEDDON: High-Fidelity CAD Reconstruction with Local Inference
papers.abstract: CAD practitioners often work with proprietary parts that they are unwilling to share with external services. For individuals and small companies, bringing this work in-house also requires computational resources they can afford. We introduce CADMAGEDDON, an open-source agent that reconstructs editable CAD from meshes and can run locally on single-GPU systems and current-generation laptops. The method decomposes this complex task into a chain of simple visual decisions about what to construct and what to correct. Geometric tools support precise construction, allowing the agent to focus on visual reasoning. Using the mid-sized Qwen3.8-27B model, CADMAGEDDON outperforms prior approaches, including systems based on frontier models, in reconstruction quality on all the main benchmarks. CADMAGEDDON integrates with FreeCAD, bringing its reconstructions into practitioners' existing CAD workflows. Code: https://github.com/kulibinai/cadmageddon
papers.summary: `CADMAGEDDON` is an open-source agent that reconstructs editable CAD models from meshes and is designed to run locally on a single GPU or a current laptop, so proprietary parts need not be sent to external services. It breaks reconstruction into a chain of simple visual decisions about what to construct and what to correct, delegating precise construction to geometric tools. Using the mid-sized `Qwen3.8-27B` model, it **outperforms prior approaches, including systems built on frontier models, in reconstruction quality on all the main benchmarks**. The agent integrates with `FreeCAD` so reconstructions fit into existing CAD workflows.

papers.title: MillBill: A Machining Agent with Geometric Feedback
papers.abstract: Turning a CAD model into a machining program requires both process knowledge and geometric precision. Language models can generate such workflows by writing geometry and toolpath code for each part, but this makes numerical execution part of the model's task. We introduce MillBill, an agent that separates machining decisions from their geometric execution and verification. Given a boundary-representation part, stock, and material, a locally hosted, mid-sized open model proposes operations and cutting parameters for indexed three-axis machining. A geometric harness generates toolpaths, simulates material removal, and returns feedback for plan refinement. Setup planning accounts for what the available cutters can physically reach, rather than visibility alone. We evaluate the resulting programs by the fraction of the target surface area within the specified tolerance after simulated machining. With Qwen3.8-27B, MillBill outperforms frontier-model approaches that construct their own geometry and toolpath workflows on the evaluated machining tasks. Code: https://github.com/kulibinai/millbill
papers.summary: `MillBill` is an agent that turns a CAD part, stock, and material into a program for indexed three-axis machining, separating machining decisions from their geometric execution. A locally hosted mid-sized open model proposes operations and cutting parameters, while a geometric harness generates toolpaths, simulates material removal, and returns feedback for refining the plan, with setup planning based on what the available cutters can physically reach. Programs are scored by the fraction of target surface area within tolerance after simulated machining. With `Qwen3.8-27B`, it **outperforms frontier-model approaches that write their own geometry and toolpath code** on the evaluated tasks.

papers.title: Do LLMs Understand Network Traces? A Comparative Study of Reasoning over Raw and Filtered Traffic Data
papers.abstract: The effective delivery and monitoring of ICT services rely heavily on network traffic analysis. However, interpreting complex packet captures remains a challenging task that requires substantial technical expertise. Large language models (LLMs) offer promising opportunities to automate network traffic in- vestigation, yet their reliability in packet-level field extraction and flow-level sequence reconstruction remains an open research question. This study proposes a reproducible, question-answering- based evaluation methodology to assess the capabilities of LLMs in network trace analysis. Using real-world benign traffic from the CICIDS2017 dataset, we evaluate multiple models against a human-generated ground truth, comparing their performance on raw textual traffic dumps and protocol-filtered representations. Model responses are assessed through an automated LLM- as-a-judge pipeline, validated against human evaluations. The results demonstrate that protocol filtering significantly reduces prompt overhead while improving answer accuracy by reducing incorrect responses. These findings highlight the importance of protocol-aware traffic filtering as an effective optimization for improving the efficiency and reliability of LLM-assisted network management.
papers.summary: The study examines how reliably large language models (LLMs) can analyze packet captures, specifically extracting packet-level fields and reconstructing flow-level sequences. It proposes a reproducible question-answering evaluation using benign traffic from the `CICIDS2017` dataset with human-written ground truth, comparing model performance on raw textual traffic dumps against protocol-filtered representations. Answers are graded by an automated LLM-as-a-judge pipeline that was validated against human evaluations. The main result is that **protocol filtering significantly reduces prompt size while improving answer accuracy** by cutting incorrect responses.

papers.title: ReMaRL: Learning to Unmask and Remask in Frozen Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Masked diffusion language models generate tokens in parallel, and the order in which tokens are unmasked affects final-answer accuracy. Several methods learn unmasking policies from task rewards, but these policies cannot remask earlier predictions. Remasking lets the model correct those predictions using newly generated context. Heuristic rules guide both unmasking and remasking, while supervised remaskers learn to detect token errors. Neither approach directly optimizes these decisions for final-answer correctness. To address this gap, we introduce ReMaRL (Remasking with Reinforcement Learning), a lightweight policy that learns which tokens to unmask, retain, or remask. We train this roughly 0.3M-parameter policy with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) from final-answer rewards while keeping the diffusion model frozen. With LLaDA-8B-Instruct, ReMaRL achieves the highest scores among the compared unmasking and remasking policies within the tested inference budgets of 4-32 model calls on math and 8-16 calls on code.
papers.summary: Masked diffusion language models generate tokens in parallel, and both the order of unmasking and the ability to remask earlier predictions affect final-answer accuracy, yet existing learned policies cannot remask and heuristic or supervised remaskers do not optimize for answer correctness. `ReMaRL` (Remasking with Reinforcement Learning) is a policy of roughly 0.3M parameters that decides which tokens to unmask, retain, or remask, trained with Group Relative Policy Optimization (`GRPO`) from final-answer rewards while the diffusion model stays frozen. With `LLaDA-8B-Instruct`, it **achieves the highest scores among the compared unmasking and remasking policies** within the tested budgets of 4 to 32 model calls on math and 8 to 16 calls on code.

papers.title: AfriNORM: An Evaluation Benchmark for Normative Reasoning of LLMs Across African Cultures
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed across various sectors. However, current evaluation benchmarks are insufficient to assess the applicability of these models in local African contexts, as most focus on linguistic fluency (grammar/translation) rather than cultural competence. The few existing benchmarks that measure general knowledge or social conventions do not capture the African deontic modality, i.e., the strict norms and taboos that govern diverse social interactions. In this paper, we introduce AfriNORM, a scenario-based, multiple-choice question dataset designed to measure and diagnose the normative reasoning limitations of LLMs when applied to African sociocultural contexts. We introduce two metrics: a Universal Commonsense Bias Score (UCBS) to quantify commonsense bias in LLM and a Distractor Bias Score (DBS) to quantify an LLM's limited understanding of African cultural norms. We also conduct a case study on the Yor\`ub\'a language, identifying confusion gaps in two closed-source LLMs, "Gemini 2.0 Flash" and "GPT-5", and one open-source LLM, "Llama 3.1 8B Instruct" when prompted in English versus Yor\`ub\'a. While their accuracy in English is high, their performance in Yor\`ub\'a is much lower, attributable to cultural confusion rather than simple bias, indicating that the models exhibit semantic confusion when reasoning about norms in Yor\`ub\'a.
papers.summary: `AfriNORM` is a scenario-based multiple-choice dataset for measuring how well large language models (LLMs) reason about the strict norms and taboos governing social interaction in African cultures, which existing fluency-focused benchmarks do not capture. It introduces two metrics, a Universal Commonsense Bias Score (UCBS) for commonsense bias and a Distractor Bias Score (DBS) for limited understanding of African cultural norms. In a case study with `Gemini 2.0 Flash`, `GPT-5`, and `Llama 3.1 8B Instruct`, **accuracy is high when prompted in English but much lower in Yorùbá**. The authors attribute the gap to cultural and semantic confusion rather than simple bias.

papers.title: Evolution Under Fire: Evolving Agent Safety Harnesses with Adaptive Injection Stressors
papers.abstract: Tool-using language-model agents must act on information from untrusted emails, webpages, and documents. This creates a central security challenge: malicious instructions and legitimate task directives can arrive through the same interaction channel. Existing defenses are largely hand-designed and static, making further improvements dependent on repeated manual redesign. We introduce Evolution Under Fire, a staged framework that couples safety-harness evolution with adaptive stressor evolution. Utility-constrained, Pareto-scheduled tree search evolves complete executable safety harnesses from execution evidence while keeping the task model, benchmark, tools, and evaluator fixed. Adaptive stressor evolution then discovers utility-preserving attacks that guide a subsequent stage of harness evolution. On AgentDyn with GPT-4o-mini, an evolved harness reduces attack success from 50.4% to 3.0%, improves clean and attacked utility over the initial harness, and offers a stronger security-utility trade-off than reproduced defenses. On Agent-SafetyBench with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, harness evolution reduces attack success from 82.6% to 62.0% while retaining helpfulness and runtime validity. Evolved harnesses also transfer without further evolution to Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, reducing attack success from 32.1% to 0.9% while improving attacked-task utility.
papers.summary: Tool-using language-model agents read untrusted emails, webpages, and documents, so injected malicious instructions arrive through the same channel as legitimate task directives, and existing defenses are mostly hand-designed and static. `Evolution Under Fire` uses a utility-constrained, Pareto-scheduled tree search to evolve complete executable safety harnesses from execution evidence, then evolves utility-preserving attacks that drive a further round of harness evolution, keeping the task model, tools, benchmark, and evaluator fixed. On `AgentDyn` with `GPT-4o-mini`, an evolved harness **cuts attack success from 50.4% to 3.0%** while improving clean and attacked utility, whereas on `Agent-SafetyBench` with `Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct` the reduction is smaller, from 82.6% to 62.0%. Evolved harnesses also transfer without further evolution to `Qwen3.5-35B-A3B`, lowering attack success from 32.1% to 0.9%.

papers.title: Adaptive LLM-Driven Honeypots vs. LLM-Driven Attackers: Does Narrative Coherence Improve Deception?
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) enable honeypots to generate responses and deceptive artefacts on demand, yet existing approaches evaluate generated content one reply at a time and leave open whether artefacts that jointly describe a coherent event retain an attacker better than unrelated ones. This question becomes pressing as autonomous LLM-driven offensive agents emerge as realistic adversaries. This paper proposes narrative deception, a reactive strategy in which the defender maps each observed attacker command to a MITRE ATT&CK technique, selects a compatible scenario from a curated catalogue based on MITRE Engage, and deploys mutually referential artefacts (files, processes, services, and logs) on an emulated Ubuntu host while the intrusion is under way. An LLM-powered defender and an autonomous LLM attacker interact through a real SSH session, and the attacker's termination policy distinguishes abandonment due to suspected deception from abandonment due to loss of interest. A campaign of 1,150 sessions compares four conditions of increasing sophistication (Static, Same-TTP, Multi-TTP, and Chain) across four open-weight attacker models, four defender models, and three attacker skill levels. Engagement increases significantly at every step. With the same artefact budget per reaction, coherent scenarios raise the median session length of advanced attackers from 40 to 165 commands and reduce their abandonment from 86% to 52%. The effect grows with attacker skill, holds across all sixteen model pairs, and comes at comparable inference cost. Nearly all sessions ended through loss of interest rather than detection, which suggests that deception should sustain meaningful findings, not only emulator fidelity.
papers.summary: Honeypots driven by large language models (LLMs) can generate deceptive artefacts on demand, but it has been unclear whether artefacts that together describe one coherent event hold an attacker longer than unrelated ones. The proposed narrative deception strategy maps each observed attacker command to a `MITRE ATT&CK` technique, picks a compatible scenario from a catalogue based on `MITRE Engage`, and deploys mutually referential files, processes, services, and logs on an emulated Ubuntu host during a real SSH session with an autonomous LLM attacker. Across 1,150 sessions spanning four conditions, four attacker models, four defender models, and three skill levels, coherent scenarios **raise the median session length of advanced attackers from 40 to 165 commands** and cut their abandonment from 86% to 52% at comparable inference cost. Nearly all sessions ended through loss of interest and not through detection of the deception.

papers.title: PACT: Plan-Action Consistency Training by Preserving Correct Plans and Repairing Actions in GUI Agents
papers.abstract: GUI agents can formulate a correct immediate plan in their reasoning yet emit an action that fails to execute it, creating an execution gap. This recurring mismatch undermines reliable task completion, as a single execution error can derail a multi-step workflow. In outcome-supervised reinforcement learning, broadcasting a negative response-level advantage across all generated tokens risks penalizing valid planning together with erroneous execution. To address this credit-assignment conflict, we introduce PACT (Plan-Action Consistency Training), a training framework that combines reference-aligned plan protection and plan-aligned action repair without altering the original scalar action reward. Using annotated reference actions to identify execution gaps, PACT protects the verified plan by masking negative policy-gradient contributions across its token span. Keeping the generated reasoning unchanged as context, it then favors the reference action over the emitted erroneous action through a preference surrogate with stop-gradient pair weights. Compared with the outcome-only baseline, PACT raises AndroidWorld task success from 60.34% to 68.97% (+8.63 pp), while improving rule-based plan-action consistency on AndroidControl High from 83.71% to 89.74% (+6.03 pp). Adapting PACT to desktop agents also improves task success from 40.92% to 44.17% (+3.25 pp) on the full 369-task OSWorld benchmark. Together, these results establish PACT as an effective credit-assignment framework for bridging execution gaps and improving task completion across mobile and desktop GUI environments.
papers.summary: Agents operating graphical user interfaces (GUIs) often reason their way to a correct next step but then emit an action that does not carry it out, and outcome-supervised reinforcement learning penalizes the valid plan together with the faulty action. `PACT` (Plan-Action Consistency Training) uses annotated reference actions to detect these gaps, masks negative policy-gradient contributions over the verified plan's tokens, and adds a preference term favoring the reference action over the erroneous one, leaving the scalar action reward unchanged. Compared with an outcome-only baseline, it **raises `AndroidWorld` task success from 60.34% to 68.97%** and improves plan-action consistency on `AndroidControl High` from 83.71% to 89.74%. A desktop adaptation lifts success on the full 369-task `OSWorld` benchmark from 40.92% to 44.17%.

papers.title: Lost in the Funnel: Selection-Induced Miscalibration in Ranking and Decision Systems
papers.abstract: Modern ranking and decision systems combine components with divergent objectives, and scores calibrated at the model boundary are used as calibrated probabilities throughout the funnel, across filtering, reranking, business-rule enforcement, and auctions. Yet calibration is typically validated only where the score is produced, so its breakdown where the score is used is routinely overlooked. We ask when calibration survives this selection, how inherited error differs from selection effects, and what can fail for a perfectly calibrated score at a component boundary. We study these questions through a boundary-wise diagnostic framework of residual identities. We target rubric-judged relevance rather than presentation-dependent metrics such as CTR, so calibration is measurable at every funnel layer of interest. We first present an industry-wide case study that applies our diagnosis to settings where calibration deteriorates at decision time, tracing the degradation to selection rather than model error. This diagnosis motivates Funnel-Aware Recalibration (FAR): post-hoc, selection-policy-aware recalibration at the boundary where scores drive decisions. In a live two-region production A/B test, FAR cuts decision-time expected calibration error (ECE) by 60-80% and improves auction efficiency. We further adapt two public datasets to simulate industry settings, providing additional evidence for the mechanism. We plan to release the adapted datasets and their generation pipeline to support further research. Finally, we distill these findings into practical operating principles for calibrating multi-stage scoring systems.
papers.summary: Multi-stage ranking systems treat scores calibrated at the model's output as calibrated probabilities through later filtering, reranking, business rules, and auctions, although calibration is usually checked only where the score is produced. A boundary-wise diagnostic framework built on residual identities separates inherited model error from selection effects, and an industry case study traces decision-time degradation to selection. The resulting `Funnel-Aware Recalibration` (`FAR`) method applies post-hoc, selection-policy-aware recalibration at the boundary where scores drive decisions. In a live two-region production A/B test it **cuts decision-time expected calibration error (ECE) by 60-80%** and improves auction efficiency, with supporting simulations on two adapted public datasets.

papers.title: Propose with the Gradient, Accept with the Loss: One Hedged Attack for Pixel-Sparse Robustness
papers.abstract: A pixel-sparse adversary may change a few pixels of an image to any value. Robustness to such attacks is currently measured with an ensemble, sparse-AutoAttack (sAA), because its members fail in different places: sparse projected gradient descent (sPGD) trusts a first-order model that a full pixel change breaks, and sparse random search (Sparse-RS) ignores the gradient even where it is informative. We show that both attacks are local searches, each a proposal distribution plus an acceptance rule, and ask what such a search can learn from the gradient. A Taylor bound says what to measure, and measurements at the states the search visits give five rules. The sign of the gradient is its most reliable use at a single pixel and sets a new pixel's value. Its ranking of candidate pixels should be followed loosely, and its ranking of the pixels to remove, which is often more reliable, can be followed more closely. A pixel should not be proposed twice before a move is accepted, and acceptance should be decided by the loss alone. These rules define Gradient-guided Random Search (GRS), which runs once and costs one forward and one backward pass per step. On 13 CIFAR-10 configurations and 5 ImageNet models, GRS matches or beats the best single member of sAA and is within one point of sAA itself or stronger on 17 of 18 settings, and it is significantly stronger than sAA on 8. It uses 3 instead of up to 7 forward-pass units, and on CIFAR-10 it runs 3.7 to 5.0 times faster than the members of sAA run in full.
papers.summary: Robustness against adversaries that may set a few image pixels to arbitrary values is currently measured with the ensemble `sparse-AutoAttack` (`sAA`), whose members, sparse projected gradient descent (`sPGD`) and sparse random search (`Sparse-RS`), fail in different places. Both are recast as local searches made of a proposal distribution and an acceptance rule, and measurements along the search yield five rules, including using the gradient sign to set a new pixel's value, following the gradient's pixel ranking only loosely, and accepting moves by the loss alone. The resulting `Gradient-guided Random Search` (`GRS`) runs once at one forward and one backward pass per step. On 13 `CIFAR-10` configurations and 5 `ImageNet` models it is **within one point of `sAA` or stronger on 17 of 18 settings** and significantly stronger on 8, while running 3.7 to 5.0 times faster on `CIFAR-10` than the members of `sAA` run in full.

papers.title: COTTI: Contrastive Training and Time-Aware Inference for Robust Industrial Recommendation under Promotional Drift
papers.abstract: Promotional events shift traffic composition, purchase behavior, and the scale of conversion probabilities on different time horizons. We present \textbf{COTTI} (\textbf{CO}ntrastive \textbf{T}raining and \textbf{T}ime-aware \textbf{I}nference), an industrial recommendation framework that separates historical representation learning from event-time score adjustment. Cross-Period Contrastive Alignment (CPC) regularizes paired histories of the same user with adaptive consistency weights. Active Re-weighting (RW) controls the influence of promotional examples through historical-interest distance. Adaptive Boundary Alignment (ABA) combines stochastic prediction variability with a temporal event kernel to adjust logits while keeping predictor parameters fixed. We analyze the weighted objective and bound ABA-induced probability and ranking changes. On Fliggy data, COTTI attains an offline AUC of 0.8127, compared with 0.8101 for TEN and 0.8123 for TEN with ABA. Cross-category analysis reveals improved discrimination alongside declines in paid-item recall for novel categories. End-to-end measurements give a p99 latency of 38.9\,ms and throughput of 14,700 requests/s; enabling ABA adds 2.2\,ms to p99. A ten-day online experiment against the serving HDR model yields relative gains of 3.14\% in conversion rate and 2.68\% in revenue per mille. Together, these results characterize the trade-off between aggregate prediction, novel-category discovery, and serving cost in promotional recommendation.
papers.summary: Promotional events change traffic mix, purchase behavior, and the scale of conversion probabilities, which destabilizes industrial recommendation models. `COTTI` (Contrastive Training and Time-aware Inference) separates historical representation learning from event-time score adjustment through three parts: Cross-Period Contrastive Alignment over paired histories of the same user, Active Re-weighting of promotional examples, and Adaptive Boundary Alignment, which adjusts logits at inference with predictor parameters fixed. On `Fliggy` data it reaches an offline AUC of 0.8127 against 0.8101 for `TEN`, and a ten-day online experiment shows **relative gains of 3.14% in conversion rate** and 2.68% in revenue per mille. The analysis also reports lower paid-item recall for novel categories and a 2.2 ms increase in p99 latency from the boundary alignment step.

papers.title: Simplicity Goes Far: Auditing Prompt Optimizers with Demonstration-Conditioned Prompt Search
papers.abstract: Automatic prompt optimization is growing more elaborate. Recent methods stack policy-gradient updates, trace reflection, and evolutionary search. These methods share a generate-and-select step; without controlling for it, reported gains may conflate the contributions of optimizer mechanisms and larger sampling budgets. We isolate this step as Demonstration-Conditioned Prompt Search (DCPS), repurposing the Automatic Prompt Engineer (APE) recipe as a mechanism-attribution control: it freezes the generator, conditions it on randomly sampled demonstrations, scores candidates on validation data, and keeps the best---no learned update, reflection, or evolution. Across two optimizer families, DCPS replaces Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) in StablePrompt, matching classification accuracy within 0.5 pp at roughly one-third the measured cost; in DSPy-based compound AI systems, under the reported budgets, it matches GEPA's macro accuracy on GPT-4.1-mini while using 55% fewer rollouts at 32% lower measured API cost on average. The audit reveals a task-dependent pattern: proposal and selection recover much of heavier optimizers' performance on structured and instruction-following tasks, while additional mechanisms retain advantages in some open-ended and reasoning-heavy settings. We recommend benchmarking prompt optimizers against generate-and-select controls and reporting rollout counts, token usage, and dollar costs alongside accuracy. Code and artifacts: https://github.com/bhc6/DCPS.
papers.summary: Automatic prompt optimizers increasingly stack policy-gradient updates, trace reflection, and evolutionary search, yet all share a generate-and-select step whose contribution is rarely isolated from that of a larger sampling budget. `Demonstration-Conditioned Prompt Search` (`DCPS`) repurposes the `Automatic Prompt Engineer` (`APE`) recipe as a control: a frozen generator conditioned on randomly sampled demonstrations proposes prompts, candidates are scored on validation data, and the best is kept, with no learned update, reflection, or evolution. Replacing Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) in `StablePrompt`, it matches classification accuracy within 0.5 percentage points at roughly one-third the cost, and in `DSPy` pipelines it **matches `GEPA`'s macro accuracy on `GPT-4.1-mini` with 55% fewer rollouts** and 32% lower API cost on average. Heavier mechanisms keep an advantage in some open-ended and reasoning-heavy tasks, and the authors recommend reporting rollout counts, token usage, and dollar costs alongside accuracy.

papers.title: DLS: Dual-Logic Graph Neural Networks with Chaos-Fuzzy Residuals for Robust Link Prediction
papers.abstract: Link prediction is a fundamental task in graph mining, critical for applications ranging from biological interaction discovery to recommender systems. While Message Passing Neural Networks (MPNNs) have achieved state-of-the-art results, they are fundamentally limited by the inadvertent suppression of high-frequency signals, as the recursive aggregation that stabilizes structural learning inherently leads to over-smoothing, rendering node representations indistinguishable in deep layers. This limitation is particularly severe in heterophilous graphs, where structural proximity does not imply feature similarity. In this paper, we propose DLS (Dual-Logic SAGE), a novel inductive framework designed to break the over-smoothing barrier via a "controlled instability" mechanism. Unlike conventional methods relying on static structural heuristics, DLS introduces a dynamic residual pipeline. First, a Chaotic Injection Module utilizes the Logistic Map to diversify the feature manifold, exploiting sensitivity to initial conditions to separate topologically similar but semantically distinct nodes. Second, to mitigate the aleatoric uncertainty introduced by chaotic dynamics, a Fuzzy-Logic Gating Mechanism applies soft-thresholding to filter noise and retain only high-confidence signals. Experimental results on diverse benchmarks demonstrate that DLS effectively balances feature discrimination with robustness, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art baselines in heterophilous settings while maintaining competitive efficiency on standard homophilous graphs.
papers.summary: Message Passing Neural Networks (MPNNs) for link prediction suffer from over-smoothing, where repeated aggregation makes node representations indistinguishable, a problem that is worst on heterophilous graphs in which connected nodes have dissimilar features. `DLS` (Dual-Logic SAGE) is an inductive framework with a residual pipeline in which a chaotic injection module based on the logistic map diversifies node features and a fuzzy-logic gate applies soft thresholding to filter the resulting noise. The authors report that it **outperforms prior baselines on heterophilous graphs** while remaining competitive in efficiency on standard homophilous graphs, though the abstract gives no figures.

papers.title: Task Convergent Flow Matching for Generative Robotics
papers.abstract: Successful manipulation requires the manipulated objects to progress toward a desired task outcome. Generative policies can produce plausible robot motions without ensuring this progress, allowing successive action chunks to stall or undo earlier changes to the scene. We introduce a task-centric inference-time refinement framework for flow matching policies that evaluates candidate action chunks through parallel physics-based rollouts and searches for motions satisfying sufficient conditions for task convergence. Task-level performance funnels bound temporary regressions while requiring net progress over each chunk. We establish sufficient conditions under which repeated funnel satisfaction yields convergence throughout execution, and use interval-wise Lipschitz bounds to verify continuous-time funnel satisfaction from sampled rollouts. To accommodate contact-rich hybrid dynamics, we refine the flow's source seeds using derivative-free Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES), constrained to radial quantile bands of the source distribution to help retain the learned motion prior. This formulation supports both Euclidean and pose-valued Riemannian Flow Matching (RMFM) policies. On PushT and three-cube stacking, refinement raises success from 31.3% to 88.5% and from 77.0% to 86.0%. On PushT, whose coverage score responds continuously to the motion of the block, a learned funnel lowers the average maximum loss of achieved progress by 19% relative to constraining the endpoint of each chunk alone, at a similar success rate. With the radial band, 11.3% of the executed motion windows are out of distribution, a rate within the range of held-out demonstrations, compared with 34.1% for an unconstrained search.
papers.summary: Generative robot policies can produce plausible motions whose successive action chunks stall or undo earlier progress on the task. An inference-time refinement framework for flow matching policies scores candidate action chunks with parallel physics-based rollouts and searches for motions that satisfy sufficient conditions for task convergence, expressed as performance funnels that bound temporary regressions while requiring net progress per chunk. The flow's source seeds are refined with the derivative-free Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (`CMA-ES`), restricted to radial quantile bands of the source distribution to stay close to the learned motion prior. Refinement **raises success on `PushT` from 31.3% to 88.5%** and on three-cube stacking from 77.0% to 86.0%, with 11.3% of executed motion windows out of distribution compared with 34.1% for an unconstrained search.

papers.title: EvoSkill-S1: Evolving Reusable Skills with Genetic-Inspired Operators
papers.abstract: Reusable skills allow language-model agents to accumulate and reuse problem-solving experience. However, most existing methods improve a skill bank only indirectly through rollout-driven accumulation and heuristic reflection, often resulting in shallow and weakly controlled updates. We present EvoSkill-S1, an RL-driven framework that instead treats reusable skills themselves as the direct objects of evolution. Given hard-negative failures, EvoSkill-S1 selects parent skills and transforms them into candidate child skills through five genetic-inspired operators: revision, cross-revision, mutation, dual-reflection, and crossover. Downstream task rewards train the skill evolver to generate more effective child skills, while evaluator-guided write-back selectively retains beneficial updates. Complementary Skill Bank Fusion consolidates operator-specific banks to exploit their distinct recovery patterns, while a Procedural Skill Interface supports transfer to unseen problems. Across all reported math and code benchmarks, EvoSkill-S1 improves the corresponding initialized skill banks under both Qwen and GPT-family solvers, with relative gains of up to 12.39%. Compared with the strongest external baseline without direct skill evolution, the largest relative improvement reaches 20.39%.
papers.summary: Language-model agents that store reusable skills usually improve their skill bank only indirectly, through rollout accumulation and heuristic reflection. `EvoSkill-S1` treats the skills themselves as the objects of evolution: starting from hard failures, it selects parent skills and produces child skills with five genetic-inspired operators (revision, cross-revision, mutation, dual-reflection, and crossover), trains the skill evolver with downstream task rewards, and writes back only updates an evaluator judges beneficial. Banks produced by different operators are then fused, and a procedural skill interface supports transfer to unseen problems. Across the reported math and code benchmarks with `Qwen` and GPT-family solvers, it improves on the initialized skill banks by **up to 12.39% relative**, and by up to 20.39% relative over the strongest external baseline without direct skill evolution.

papers.title: DAQ: Decision-Aligned Post-Training Quantization for Spiking Transformers
papers.abstract: Spiking transformers combine attention-based representation learning with sparse spike communication, yet their weights and membrane variables still incur substantial storage and computation overhead. Post-training quantization (PTQ) offers a practical way to reduce these overheads, but preserving neuronal firing under weight and membrane quantization remains challenging. In this paper, we propose Decision-Aligned Post-Training Quantization (DAQ), a method that calibrates the quantizers to align neuronal firing decisions with those of a floating-point reference. We analyze how errors from these quantizers affect firing at decision boundaries and how they propagate over time steps in recurrent neurons. Based on this analysis, we formulate an objective that encourages quantized membrane variables to remain within the reference firing regions along the quantized model's own state trajectory. Experiments across multiple spiking transformer architectures on image classification, semantic segmentation, and event-based tracking demonstrate the effectiveness of DAQ with 4-bit weights and membrane variables. On FE108, DAQ achieves 58.8\% AUC and 90.9\% PR with SDTrack, while reducing energy by 66.2\%.
papers.summary: Spiking transformers pair attention with sparse spike communication, but their weights and membrane variables still carry substantial storage and computation cost, and post-training quantization (PTQ) tends to disturb neuronal firing. `DAQ` (Decision-Aligned Post-Training Quantization) calibrates the quantizers so that firing decisions match those of a floating-point reference, using an analysis of how quantization errors act at decision boundaries and propagate across time steps. Its objective keeps quantized membrane variables inside the reference firing regions along the quantized model's own state trajectory. With 4-bit weights and membrane variables across image classification, semantic segmentation, and event-based tracking, it reaches 58.8% AUC and 90.9% PR on `FE108` with `SDTrack` while **reducing energy by 66.2%**.

papers.title: Right Diagnosis, Unsafe Route: Auditing Clinical AI Decision Trajectories and Corrective Oversight for Validity and Potential Harm
papers.abstract: A clinical AI system can reach a correct final diagnosis through intermediate decisions that could have harmed the patient, and can repair an error while introducing new risks. Most evaluations score final diagnoses; even stepwise benchmarks, which release a case's evidence over time, score whether systems reach the right diagnosis or gather the right information, not whether the decisions a patient passes through are safe. We make patient safety the target of stepwise evaluation. A trajectory audit replays real admissions checkpoint by checkpoint, lets each system decide with only the evidence released so far, and rates every test, treatment and disposition for its potential harm to the patient and, separately, for clinical validity, against the documented final diagnosis and physician-written disease rubrics yet on the evidence available when the decision was made. An LLM judge scores every decision, and a physician reference standard (triple annotation and senior adjudication of a stratified sample) calibrates the rates. An oversight audit branches each trajectory at its first actionable error and measures, on the same branches, whether corrective feedback repairs the error and whether it introduces new harm. Across 300 cases from a hospital cardiology cohort, MIMIC-IV and the public ASCENT benchmark, with up to seven AI systems per source, 55.2% of hospital trajectories reaching an acceptable final diagnosis passed through a decision with moderate or severe potential harm and 24.8% through a clinically unacceptable one; the harm rates were 76.2% on MIMIC-IV and 39.6% on ASCENT. Structured corrections resolved 73.6% of first errors versus 24.8% after bare rejection, yet new potentially unsafe decisions followed 30.2% of corrections versus 19.7% of rejections. A correct final diagnosis does not certify a safe trajectory, and a successful correction does not certify a safe recovery.
papers.summary: Clinical AI evaluations mostly score the final diagnosis, which can hide intermediate tests, treatments, or dispositions that could have harmed the patient. A trajectory audit replays real admissions checkpoint by checkpoint, has each system decide using only the evidence released so far, and rates every decision for potential harm and clinical validity with a large language model judge calibrated against physician annotations, while an oversight audit branches at the first actionable error to test corrective feedback. Across 300 cases from a hospital cardiology cohort, `MIMIC-IV`, and the `ASCENT` benchmark, **55.2% of hospital trajectories that reached an acceptable final diagnosis passed through a decision with moderate or severe potential harm**, with corresponding rates of 76.2% on `MIMIC-IV` and 39.6% on `ASCENT`. Structured corrections resolved 73.6% of first errors against 24.8% for bare rejection, but new potentially unsafe decisions followed 30.2% of corrections against 19.7% of rejections.

papers.title: Understanding Cross-Modal Inconsistency through Representation Subspaces in Omni Models
papers.abstract: Omni Models process audio, vision, and text within a unified language backbone, yet often produce different answers for semantically equivalent inputs across modalities. Existing representation-level analyses do not distinguish between information that predicts whether disagreement will occur and the representation whose perturbation affects the model's answer. In this paper, we estimate a low-dimensional Answer Subspace from answer-position representations and use it to separate answer-related components from the remaining representation. Across three Omni Models and two multimodal reasoning tasks, information predictive of cross-modal inconsistency lies mainly outside the Answer Subspace, concentrating in a reproducible two-dimensional representation that is not explained by a fixed modality offset. Matched interventions reveal distinct behavioral roles: perturbing the Answer Subspace substantially changes the model's predictions, whereas perturbing the disagreement representation, like a random subspace of the same dimensionality, leaves them almost unchanged. Our key finding is that cross-modal disagreement can be induced by misaligning modality-specific answer representations: perturbing the Answer Subspace for only one modality induces disagreement, whereas applying the same perturbation to both largely preserves agreement. Thus, the representation that predicts disagreement is distinct from the answer-level representation through which disagreement can be induced, showing that linear decodability does not imply behavioral efficacy.
papers.summary: Omni models that process audio, vision, and text in one language backbone often give different answers to semantically equivalent inputs presented in different modalities. The analysis estimates a low-dimensional `Answer Subspace` from answer-position representations and separates it from the rest of the representation, across three omni models and two multimodal reasoning tasks. Information that predicts cross-modal inconsistency sits mostly outside that subspace, in a reproducible two-dimensional representation, yet perturbing it leaves predictions almost unchanged. In contrast, **perturbing the Answer Subspace for only one modality induces disagreement**, while applying the same perturbation to both modalities largely preserves agreement, so the representation that predicts disagreement differs from the one through which it can be caused.

papers.title: A Quantum Support Vector Regression Framework for Missing Data Imputation in Ship Performance Data
papers.abstract: The Internet of Ships enables vessels to generate vast amounts of data, yet missing values remain a persistent issue. To the best of the authors' knowledge, existing imputation techniques in this domain rely exclusively on classical machine learning. This study investigates quantum support vector regression (QSVR) for imputing missing values in ship performance data. Classical support vector regression and QSVR models based on different quantum feature maps are compared for estimating marine fuel consumption under varying levels of data availability. The case study uses real-world data from a Panamax bulk carrier, covering 37 variables across six categories.
