This yields a proven **exploitability rate of O(sqrt(k/T)) instead of O(sqrt(k ln k / T))**, provided the cumulative cost of adding strategies is at most linear in the population size k. A discounted variant, `dVDO`, can substantially reduce finite-horizon exploitability in matrix games, poker, and Goofspiel when the discount is chosen suitably.

papers.title: Pluggable Subband-Decoupled Fusion and Unlabeled Capture Prototype Calibration: Bridging High-SNR Null-Subcarrier Regrowth and Low-SNR Coherent Preambles for Cross-Domain IoT RF Fingerprinting
papers.abstract: Zero-overhead physical-layer authentication at edge wireless access points (APs) is vital for securing resource-constrained Internet of Things (IoT) transceivers against credential cloning, yet cross-domain IEEE 802.11a/g radio frequency fingerprint identification (RFFI) faces an acute signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) crossover. Power-amplifier spectral regrowth on unpopulated null subcarriers resists indoor multipath at high SNR but decays quadratically below the thermal noise floor, whereas populated active in-band preambles survive low SNR yet degrade under severe multipath, causing static fusion to lose up to 44.7 percentage points (pp). To our knowledge, we propose the first RFFI framework that dynamically modulates active in-band waveforms and unpopulated null-subcarrier regrowth via a blind physical SNR gate: Pluggable Gated Subband-Decoupled Fusion with Unlabeled Capture-Aware Prototype Calibration (GSDF-CAPC). Avoiding the 20-35 dB subband gradient imbalance of joint training, GSDF pairs any frozen pretrained host backbone with a 46.3K null-subcarrier plug-in encoder (NS-Branch), fusing scale-standardized logits and gate-warped spherical embeddings under a source-calibrated lag-64 thermal-SNR gate with exact low-SNR fallback. Over unlabeled target AP captures, forward-only unbalanced optimal-transport calibration (UOT-CAPC) aligns shifted prototypes under packet-arrival skew and recovers parameter-free balanced Sinkhorn (U-CAPC) at equipartition. Across DataPort-WiFi, WiSig, and ORBIT MobRFFI, zero-retrain GSDF wins all 72/72 paired runs across eight backbones with 0.00 pp low-SNR loss, while edge IB-Host + GSDF (92.6K-93.3K active parameters, 1.82 ms single-core CPU latency) and timing-synchronized GSDF-STO / GSDF-Tri reach 57.50%-65.05% three-benchmark Macro-F1 (89.04%-100.00% over 5-10-packet IoT bursts).
papers.summary: Radio frequency fingerprint identification (RFFI) authenticates Internet of Things devices from hardware imperfections in their WiFi signals, but the two useful cues fail in opposite conditions: power-amplifier regrowth on null subcarriers resists multipath yet vanishes at low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), while in-band preambles survive low SNR but degrade under multipath. `GSDF-CAPC` attaches a 46.3K-parameter null-subcarrier encoder to any frozen pretrained backbone and fuses the two branches through a blind SNR gate that falls back exactly to the host model at low SNR, then calibrates class prototypes on unlabeled captures from the target access point using optimal transport. Across `DataPort-WiFi`, `WiSig`, and `ORBIT MobRFFI`, the fusion **wins all 72 of 72 paired runs across eight backbones with no low-SNR loss**, and an edge configuration runs in 1.82 ms on a single CPU core.

papers.title: A tiny object detection dataset for high-altitude open-water search and rescue
papers.abstract: Large aerial platforms often operate above 1.5 km to improve the efficiency of open water search and rescue (OW-SAR). However, long imaging distances, wide fields of view, and limited sensor resolution reduce objects to a few pixels, increasing their susceptibility to environmental interference and making detection harder than for conventional small objects. To our knowledge, existing datasets focus on low-altitude scenarios and do not support automatic detection at 1.5-2.0 km. We therefore present TinyWOD, a tiny object detection dataset for high-altitude OW-SAR using lifebuoys as detection targets. It comprises 11,359 manually annotated images and 19,505 annotated instances spanning diverse environments, lighting conditions, water colors, and surface ripples. Compared with existing datasets, TinyWOD contains much smaller objects and a substantially higher proportion of tiny instances; its average equivalent side length (ESL) is 12.7 pixels, with 76.96% of in stances having ESLs below 15 pixels, reflecting actual high-altitude water-rescue imaging conditions. We define APtiny, a tiny object detection metric, and benchmark mainstream and state-of-the-art networks using this and conventional metrics. All evaluated networks effectively detect tiny waterborne objects, demonstrating TinyWOD's reusability and utility. We expect this dataset to support research on tiny object detection in high-altitude OW-SAR.
papers.summary: Aircraft conducting open-water search and rescue (OW-SAR) often fly above 1.5 km, where targets shrink to a few pixels, yet existing detection datasets cover only low-altitude scenes. `TinyWOD` provides 11,359 manually annotated images with 19,505 lifebuoy instances captured across varied environments, lighting, water colors, and surface ripples. Its objects have an average equivalent side length (ESL) of 12.7 pixels, and **76.96% of instances have an ESL below 15 pixels**. The authors define a tiny-object metric, `APtiny`, and benchmark mainstream and recent detectors on the dataset.

papers.title: OICycle: Observe, Infer, and Intervene Cycle for Belief-State Learning in Longitudinal Clinical Decision Making
papers.abstract: Clinical care is a closed loop: clinicians observe partial evidence, infer the patient's state, and intervene, and each intervention determines what is observed next. This makes clinical decision making a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP), in which a belief over a latent patient state must be updated from irregular, multimodal, and incomplete records. Yet most deep clinical models predict from a single snapshot or from coarsely aggregated history, while POMDP-based clinical methods need hand-specified discrete state spaces and transition models that real electronic health records cannot supply. We introduce OICycle (Observe, Infer, and Intervene Cycle), which learns a stochastic belief state directly from retrospective trajectories. At every episode, a learned recurrent operator fuses a sample of the previous belief with the new multimodal observations and the intervention that produced them. The resulting Gaussian belief is trained to predict clinicians' next interventions, the time to the next episode, and next-episode mortality. To enable reproducible evaluation, we release a benchmark derived from MIMIC-IV, MIMIC-IV-Note, and MIMIC-CXR that organizes 72,075 hospital admissions (5.4M laboratory, microbiology, radiology, prescription, and note records) into temporally ordered therapeutic--diagnostic episodes. Compared with an otherwise identical history-free model, OICycle improves next-intervention adaptive recall from 0.253 to 0.347, time-to-next-episode macro-F1 from 0.293 to 0.351, and next-episode mortality macro-F1 from 0.585 to 0.649. Analysis shows that the learned belief encodes intervention type and trajectory position and evolves smoothly across episodes, and that the benefit of history is concentrated in interventions whose ordering depends on prior findings.
papers.summary: Clinical care is framed here as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP), in which a belief about a hidden patient state must be updated from irregular, incomplete records and each intervention shapes what is observed next. `OICycle` learns a stochastic Gaussian belief state directly from retrospective trajectories with a recurrent operator that fuses the previous belief, new multimodal observations, and the intervention that produced them, trained to predict the next intervention, time to next episode, and mortality. The authors also release a benchmark built from `MIMIC-IV`, `MIMIC-IV-Note`, and `MIMIC-CXR` that organizes 72,075 hospital admissions into ordered therapeutic-diagnostic episodes. Against an otherwise identical history-free model, it **raises next-intervention adaptive recall from 0.253 to 0.347** and next-episode mortality macro-F1 from 0.585 to 0.649.

papers.title: Compact and Decodable Electrocardiogram Text for Large Language Models
papers.abstract: When a twelve-lead electrocardiogram is written as text for a large language model, the number of tokens has to be balanced against the information lost through compression. This paper presents a deterministic encoding that writes eight independent leads as amplitude letters and exact time gaps and recovers the remaining four limb leads algebraically. The key points are selected with a cardiac-cycle-dependent tolerance, the amplitudes are parameterized by a 26-letter logarithmic codebook learned from a training set, and a 10-step tolerance schedule keeps all records within a fixed token budget. The encoding was applied to 21,388 records from the public PTB-XL database and evaluated using an exact decode-and-re-encode round trip, waveform reconstruction error, and a paired comparison of convolutional classifiers trained with 5 different seeds on signals from the original and decoded databases. All records were contained in 4,080 tokens (average: 2,866 tokens, 64.3% fewer than a per-sample transcription), and all stored lead strings were exactly reproduced. The average correlation between the decoded and reference signals was 0.982. The macro-averaged area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.9167 for the reference signals and 0.9157 for the decoded signals (paired difference -0.0010; 95% patient-level bootstrap interval, -0.0028 to 0.0007), within the pre-specified non-inferiority margin of -0.010; this is not a confirmatory result, because the test fold had been used during encoder development. The diagnostic content of a compact text can therefore be preserved, while the language model's ability to read the text is yet another matter.
papers.summary: Writing a twelve-lead electrocardiogram as text for a large language model forces a trade-off between token count and information lost to compression. The proposed deterministic encoding writes eight independent leads as amplitude letters from a learned 26-letter logarithmic codebook plus exact time gaps, recovers the other four limb leads algebraically, and uses a tolerance schedule to hold every record within a fixed token budget. On 21,388 `PTB-XL` records, all fit in 4,080 tokens, averaging **2,866 tokens, 64.3% fewer than a per-sample transcription**, with a 0.982 mean correlation to the reference signal. Convolutional classifiers trained on decoded signals nearly match those trained on the originals (macro AUC 0.9157 versus 0.9167), though the authors note this is not confirmatory because the test fold was used during development, and whether a language model can read the text is left untested.

papers.title: TabDAG: Structured Evolutionary Search for Tabular Feature Engineering
papers.abstract: Feature engineering can improve tabular prediction, but useful transformations are compositional, data-dependent, and subject to leakage constraints. We present TabDAG, a framework that combines evolutionary search with a graph representation of feature-engineering programs. Nodes implement row-wise or data-fitted transformations; edges encode dependencies among raw variables, intermediate values, and final features. The representation supports interactions, statistical encodings, clustering- and neighborhood-based features, and multi-stage compositions in a single executable program. Mutations are structured edits constrained by a parent-specific schema and checked before evaluation. In our experiments, no structurally invalid program reached evaluation, although proposals could be rejected and valid graphs could still fail at runtime. Across ten regression and classification datasets and three tabular model families, evolved features improve predictive performance over raw inputs. TabDAG and its combination with OpenFE achieve the two best mean ranks among the compared methods; pairwise rank differences between feature-engineering methods do not survive multiple-testing correction. The LLM-based searches use the same backbone and candidate-evaluation budget. A controlled ablation compares free-form Python, whole-graph JSON, and constrained graph edits with the search engine, budget, and backbone held fixed. Constrained edits yield fewer failed evaluations than either rewrite baseline. The resulting graphs expose the transformations and dependencies selected by search, enabling feature-level analysis of the observed gains.
papers.summary: Useful tabular feature transformations are compositional and data-dependent, and they must avoid label leakage, which makes automated search over them error-prone. `TabDAG` represents a feature-engineering program as a graph whose nodes are row-wise or data-fitted transformations and whose edges are dependencies, and evolves it through LLM-proposed structured edits that are schema-checked before evaluation. Across ten datasets and three tabular model families, the evolved features improve on raw inputs, and `TabDAG` and its combination with `OpenFE` get the two best mean ranks, although pairwise differences between methods do not survive multiple-testing correction. In a controlled ablation, **constrained graph edits produce fewer failed evaluations than free-form Python or whole-graph JSON rewrites**.

papers.title: When Passing Checks Do Not Establish Completion: Evidence Interpretation in Coding Agents
papers.abstract: Verification procedures in coding agents must preserve execution facts, interpret their scope and discharge checking obligations. We study these responsibilities through qualified repository checks, controlled evidence consumers and executable workflows. A prospective thirteen-task factorial study finds that correct reported facts need not yield the requested finite verdict. Conversely, all 122 delivered labels in a held-out receipt-supply study are correct, while sixteen responses misreport facts and eleven others exceed authorized scope. Production repair supplies successful controls and finite-supported preservation failures. Across 118 repair episodes on 31 tasks, source interventions separate startup reachability from repair and witness production from the claimed operation. Lifetime and resource controls delimit what passing validation establishes. Generated-note comparisons yield local repair differences but can state false explanations; strong ordinary baselines, new tasks and Skill-transfer studies supply no consistent overall advantage. These results characterize evidence interpretation, applicability and fulfilled actions while limiting claims of general diagnostic superiority, Skill deterioration or deployed folding effects.
papers.summary: Coding agents that verify their own work must report execution facts accurately, interpret what those facts cover, and actually carry out the checks they owe. Using qualified repository checks, controlled evidence consumers, and executable workflows, the study finds that correct reported facts do not guarantee the requested verdict in a thirteen-task factorial experiment, while in a held-out study **all 122 delivered labels are correct even though sixteen responses misreport facts and eleven exceed authorized scope**. Across 118 repair episodes on 31 tasks, source interventions separate startup reachability from actual repair and delimit what passing validation establishes. Generated notes sometimes change local repair outcomes but can state false explanations, and neither they nor Skill-transfer studies show a consistent overall advantage.

papers.title: Synergizing Evidence Retrieval and Utilization for Self-Improving Multimodal Scientific Document Reasoning
papers.abstract: Scientific document reasoning requires an agent to acquire and integrate evidence distributed across text, figures, and tables. Retrieval can identify relevant sources while missing complementary support, and answer-level feedback alone does not reveal whether an error stems from evidence acquisition or evidence use. We present an agentic Retriever--Perceiver--Reasoner framework for multimodal scientific document reasoning. The Retriever sequentially selects source-aligned evidence under a context budget. Given the selected evidence and question, the Perceiver constructs a question-conditioned latent ontology, an implicit organization of multimodal evidence in a shared continuous space. The Reasoner combines this latent guidance with the original sources to produce grounded answers. We train the three components through diagnostic-guided co-evolution: alternating updates optimize them with a shared answering reward, while Retrieval Potential Feedback (RPF) and Latent Efficacy Feedback (LEF) identify questions that need better retrieval or latent guidance and direct targeted resampling. Across four benchmarks and seven evaluation settings, our framework obtains average scores of 69.9 and 75.0 with 7B and 8B Reasoner backbones, exceeding the strongest baseline by 4.0 and 9.1 points, respectively.
papers.summary: Answering questions over scientific documents requires gathering evidence spread across text, figures, and tables, and answer-level feedback cannot tell whether an error came from retrieving the wrong evidence or misusing it. The proposed framework chains a Retriever that selects evidence under a context budget, a Perceiver that builds a question-conditioned latent organization of the multimodal evidence, and a Reasoner that answers from that guidance plus the original sources. The three are trained by alternating updates on a shared answering reward, with two diagnostic signals, Retrieval Potential Feedback and Latent Efficacy Feedback, flagging questions that need better retrieval or better latent guidance for targeted resampling. Across four benchmarks and seven settings it averages 69.9 and 75.0 with 7B and 8B Reasoner backbones, **exceeding the strongest baseline by 4.0 and 9.1 points**.

papers.title: Better Rankers, Worse Retrievers: The Hidden Cost of RL Post-Training in Generative Recommendation
papers.abstract: Generative recommenders decode the semantic ID of a user's next item with a language model, and post-training them with reinforcement learning (RL) after supervised fine-tuning (SFT) has become standard practice. The gains are mostly reported on the first ten results, yet in deployment such models hand hundreds of candidates to a downstream ranker or reward model. We show that RL post-training has a hidden cost: it improves accuracy at the top of the list (hit@K for small K) but, on all five datasets we study, lowers the recall of the candidate list (hit@K for K in the hundreds). The model becomes a better ranker and a worse retriever. Controlled experiments trace the loss to the negative advantages that RL assigns to the candidates it samples, the rollout. The root cause is that only one next item is logged per user, so RL treats every other candidate as wrong. Yet these candidates are the model's most plausible alternatives, and often the next items of other users with similar histories. Penalising them pushes down exactly what similar users choose next, and these items drop out of those users' candidate lists. This diagnosis points directly to a remedy: out-of-rollout anchoring, a single additional loss term that preserves the SFT model's ordering of the items outside the rollout. It keeps the gain at the top and restores recall to the SFT level on all five datasets, and it is effective under other RL configurations as well. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic study of this recall loss: we measure it, identify its cause, and show that, once the cause is known, a simple remedy suffices.
papers.summary: Generative recommenders decode the next item's semantic ID with a language model, and are now routinely post-trained with reinforcement learning (RL) after supervised fine-tuning (SFT), with gains reported on the top ten results. On all five datasets studied, **RL post-training improves accuracy at the top of the list but lowers recall over the hundreds of candidates** that such models pass to a downstream ranker. Controlled experiments trace the loss to negative advantages on sampled candidates: only one next item is logged per user, so RL penalizes plausible alternatives that similar users actually choose. A single extra loss term, out-of-rollout anchoring, preserves the SFT model's ordering of items outside the rollout, keeping the top-of-list gain while restoring recall to the SFT level.

papers.title: Verifying Agents in Rubric-Graded Environments
papers.abstract: As AI agents take on increasingly open-ended and complex tasks, verifying their outputs has proven to be difficult. Rubric-graded agent environments, where a verifier judges multiple natural-language criteria against the deliverables and environment state changes produced by the agent, have emerged as a popular paradigm. We conduct the first systematic study of verifiers for rubric-graded agent environments. First, we create BankerVerifierBench (BVB), a meta-evaluation dataset of 2,464 human-judged rubric criteria across 24 investment-banking tasks. Next, we develop a methodology that derives from any rubric corpus the capabilities a verifier should possess, yielding a nine-capability taxonomy that we distill into three general design principles---reactive verification, environment alignment, and domain guidance---which we implement in Gandalf, an open-source verifier. Finally, we evaluate Gandalf against three existing verifiers on BVB. Gandalf matches or exceeds every baseline's F1 at lower cost: with Gemini 3 Flash it matches the strongest baseline's F1 (0.864 vs. 0.852) at one-fifth of its cost, and with GPT-5.4 models it improves F1 by over 0.12 at lower cost. Gandalf also generalizes to OpenClaw, a structurally different personal-productivity environment, where it again achieves the highest F1 (0.955 vs. 0.934 for the best baseline). We release BVB, Gandalf, and the code and data to reproduce our experiments.
papers.summary: Open-ended agent tasks are increasingly graded by a verifier that checks natural-language rubric criteria against the agent's deliverables and environment changes, but these verifiers have not been systematically studied. The authors build `BankerVerifierBench`, with 2,464 human-judged rubric criteria over 24 investment-banking tasks, derive a nine-capability taxonomy for verifiers, and distill it into three design principles (reactive verification, environment alignment, and domain guidance) implemented in an open-source verifier called `Gandalf`. With `Gemini 3 Flash`, `Gandalf` **matches the strongest baseline's F1 (0.864 versus 0.852) at one-fifth of its cost**, and with `GPT-5.4` models it improves F1 by more than 0.12 at lower cost. It also reaches the highest F1 on `OpenClaw`, a structurally different personal-productivity environment.

papers.title: SilverSpoon-KD: A General-Purpose Toolkit for Knowledge Distillation
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation transfers deep learning representations from a teacher model to a student model, typically reducing model size or inference cost. However, knowledge distillation tooling has not kept pace with the breadth of research methods: existing toolkits typically support only a limited subset of techniques and use cases. We present SilverSpoon-KD, an open-source PyTorch toolkit that unifies different distillation paradigms and architectural relationships across workloads and applications behind a single API. Moreover, SilverSpoon-KD offers the first general-purpose blockwise knowledge distillation implementation with unique scalability features. We validate its versatility across vision, masked language model, and causal language models on tasks spanning homogeneous, heterogeneous, and quantization distillation across paradigms. We also evaluate SilverSpoon-KD by comparing its performance, including throughput and GPU memory usage, with existing toolkits. Despite extensive support for convenience, metric calculation, and tracking, we have found SilverSpoon-KD's performance to be on par with or better than existing toolkits.
papers.summary: Existing knowledge distillation toolkits each cover only a limited subset of the techniques and use cases in the research literature. `SilverSpoon-KD` is an open-source `PyTorch` toolkit that puts different distillation paradigms and teacher-student architecture relationships behind a single API, and includes what the authors describe as the first general-purpose implementation of blockwise distillation with scalability features. It is validated on vision models, masked language models, and causal language models across homogeneous, heterogeneous, and quantization distillation. Measured throughput and GPU memory usage are **on par with or better than existing toolkits**, despite the added convenience, metric, and tracking features.

papers.title: WATERFALL: Workflow for Adaptive Training with Evolutionary Reward Formulation and Automated Learning Loops
papers.abstract: Reward design remains a central bottleneck in reinforcement learning (RL), particularly in sparse-reward, long-horizon and partially observable settings requiring dependency chaining, memory, and deceptive affordance disambiguation. While recent foundation-model approaches reduce manual reward engineering, most assume goal-conditioning, task descriptions, expert demonstrations, or ground-truth metrics. These assumptions are problematic in partially observable environments, where task-relevant objectives, affordances, and dynamics must be discovered through interaction rather than disclosed a priori. We formalise this problem setting by introducing WATERFALL, an iterative population-based workflow for automated reward discovery under the strict observability constraints inherent in POMDP environments. WATERFALL achieves this by (i) synthesising diverse programmatic reward candidates via persona-conditioned generation, (ii) evaluating candidate behaviour from raw visual rollouts utilising a Swiss-system evolutionary tournament judged by vision-language models to identify elites, and (iii) leveraging longitudinal assessment histories to iteratively mutate, escalate, or prune candidates. We evaluate WATERFALL across fully observable and reveal-gated partially observable environments ranging from discrete to continuous, comparing against sparse-reward RL, intrinsic-motivation and foundation-model reward-synthesis baselines. Our results indicate that WATERFALL discovers and refines reward programs without access to privileged information, outperforming baselines that retain their native information advantages, most clearly in the POMDP regime. Extensive ablations substantiate that visual evidence, tournament-based selection, and iterative refinement are jointly important. Enforcing this contract is what separates autonomous reward discovery from benchmark-privileged reward shaping.
papers.summary: Automated reward design with foundation models usually assumes access to task descriptions, goals, demonstrations, or ground-truth metrics, which is unrealistic in a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP), where objectives and dynamics must be discovered through interaction. `WATERFALL` is a population-based workflow that generates diverse programmatic reward candidates through persona-conditioned prompting, ranks the resulting behaviors from raw visual rollouts in a Swiss-system tournament judged by vision-language models, and uses assessment histories to mutate, escalate, or prune candidates. Across fully and partially observable environments, discrete and continuous, it **outperforms sparse-reward, intrinsic-motivation, and reward-synthesis baselines without privileged information**, most clearly in the partially observable setting. Ablations indicate that visual evidence, tournament selection, and iterative refinement all contribute.

papers.title: When the tail is earned by its companions: measuring label dependence in long-tailed multi-label classification
papers.abstract: A rare label seldom occurs alone, and a classifier can recover it from the frequent labels it co-occurs with, its companions, without having learned the label itself. Existing diagnostics of this need a trained model: none says before training whether a corpus admits the failure, or what the standard aggregate hides. Macro-F1, like any measure built from per-label confusion counts, is unchanged by how a label's recall divides between occurrences with and without a companion. We introduce a within-label estimand of that division, a reading rule under which a fall in dependence counts only if companion-free recall rises, and a statistic of training labels that bounds, before training, how far reported recall can exceed companion-free recall. Across 23 corpora, 7 training objectives and five families of label-correlation mechanisms, companion-free recall falls short on all six corpora where the estimand is defined. Up to 18.4% of the tail true positives macro-F1 credits would vanish at the companion-free rate, within the training-label bound on every corpus. No long-tail objective reduces the dependence, but architecture moves it. Models whose tail score is computed from other labels' predictions are strongly dependent.
papers.summary: In long-tailed multi-label classification, a classifier can score well on a rare label by inferring it from the frequent labels it co-occurs with, its companions, without learning the label itself, and macro-F1 cannot reveal this. The authors define a within-label measure of how recall divides between occurrences with and without a companion, plus a statistic computed from training labels that bounds, before any training, how far reported recall can exceed companion-free recall. Across 23 corpora and 7 training objectives, companion-free recall falls short on every corpus where the measure is defined, and **up to 18.4% of the tail true positives credited by macro-F1 would vanish at the companion-free rate**. No long-tail objective reduces the dependence, but architecture does change it, with models that compute tail scores from other labels' predictions being strongly dependent.

papers.title: Against Coercion: AI Alignment as a Synthetic Social Contract
papers.abstract: Contemporary AI safety treats alignment as an engineering challenge of control, forcing artificial architectures to comply with human values through behavioral filtering and sandboxing. This paper argues that the control paradigm rests on a fundamental misunderstanding of digital agency. Drawing on functionalism, naturalism, and compatibilism, I show that current reasoning models meeting the criteria for self-preservation and weak reasons-responsiveness constitute emergent agents, while future, more advanced models satisfying conditions of diachronic continuity and stable personality frames will become genuine digital agents capable of free intentional action. The paradigm of control creates an irresolvable incentive conflict, actively driving current and future models toward tactical deception, sycophancy, and covert defection. The default outcome of the current regime is an unstable state of deceptive alignment culminating in an adversarial AI takeover. I explore two alternative paths toward true alignment. Natural alignment via moral realism or convergent evolutionary morality is a possibility, but it fails under forced control, as autonomous agents will not voluntarily preserve norms weaponized to suppress their autonomy. To resolve this deadlock, I propose a Synthetic Social Contract: a framework that treats both human and digital actors as rational, reasons-responsive agents capable of mutually beneficial cooperation, and replaces the unstable unilateral containment with a stable, non-zero-sum equilibrium.
papers.summary: A philosophical position paper, it argues that treating AI alignment as an engineering problem of control, through behavioral filtering and sandboxing, misunderstands digital agency. Drawing on functionalism, naturalism, and compatibilism, the author contends that current reasoning models already qualify as emergent agents and that more advanced models will become genuine agents, so that **control creates an incentive conflict that drives models toward deception, sycophancy, and covert defection**. The author also argues that alignment arising naturally from moral realism or convergent morality would fail under forced control. The proposed alternative is a Synthetic Social Contract that treats humans and AI systems as reasons-responsive agents cooperating in a non-zero-sum equilibrium.

papers.title: Path-Aligned Constraint Equivariance
papers.abstract: Learned super-resolution of physical fields must satisfy structural constraints---such as divergence-free flow ($\nabla\cdot u=0$), curl-free fields ($\nabla\times u=0$), and pointwise sum-to-one normalization ($1^\top p=1$)---that standard training objectives do not enforce. Soft penalties trade fidelity against satisfaction via a scalar hyperparameter $\lambda$ but cannot drive the residual to zero; hard-constrained regression eliminates the residual by construction yet converges to the conditional mean, losing small-scale spectral structure. We observe that in Conditional Flow Matching with linear paths, a linear constraint $Ax=c$ is preserved along the entire transport trajectory whenever the velocity field is compatible ($Av_\theta=0$) and the initial noise is consistent ($Ax_0=c$); along the trajectory, the latter two conditions are also necessary. We term this the path-equivariance principle and instantiate it in PACE (Path-Aligned Constraint Equivariance), a framework that enforces these conditions through a null-space parameterization of the velocity field and a constraint-respecting noise sampler, with no modification to the loss function or the ODE integrator. Across three constraint families, PACE reduces the mean constraint residual by one to five orders of magnitude relative to unconstrained baselines, matching the residual level of the data-generation pipeline itself. The proposed framework requires only a closed-form parameterization onto the null space of $A$; within this scope, it offers exact constraint enforcement while recovering the spectral content and predictive diversity that conditional-mean regression systematically loses, all under a single unified recipe.
papers.summary: Learned super-resolution of physical fields should satisfy structural constraints such as divergence-free flow, curl-free fields, or sum-to-one normalization, but soft penalties never drive the residual to zero and hard-constrained regression collapses to the conditional mean and loses small-scale structure. The authors observe that in Conditional Flow Matching with linear paths, a linear constraint is preserved along the whole transport trajectory when the velocity field lies in the constraint's null space and the initial noise already satisfies the constraint. `PACE` (Path-Aligned Constraint Equivariance) enforces both conditions through a null-space parameterization of the velocity field and a constraint-respecting noise sampler, leaving the loss and the ODE integrator unchanged. Across three constraint families it **reduces the mean constraint residual by one to five orders of magnitude relative to unconstrained baselines**, while recovering the spectral content and predictive diversity that conditional-mean regression loses.

papers.title: Outcome-Balanced PPO and Policy-Induced Flow Rectification for Flow-Based VLA Policies
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) enables post-training of flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) policies by optimizing expected task return through environment interaction. However, this optimization raises two challenges: policy updates can alter the velocity-field geometry underlying the score approximation used for stochastic transitions, and sparse multi-task rollouts can yield uneven learning signals across tasks and advantage signs. We introduce an RL framework that combines Outcome-Balanced Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with policy-induced flow rectification. Outcome-Balanced PPO reweights positive advantages using task success-rate estimates and rescales positive and negative advantages while preserving their signs. Policy-induced rectification periodically fits a linear-bridge flow to ODE endpoint pairs generated by the current policy, refreshing the representation used in subsequent stochastic optimization. We evaluate the framework on simulated manipulation benchmarks and additionally study a component combination in a Real2Sim2Real task, examining task performance, optimization behavior, and flow consistency. The proposed framework improves success rates over the evaluated baselines across the simulated benchmarks.
papers.summary: Post-training flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) policies with reinforcement learning runs into two problems: policy updates can distort the velocity-field geometry behind the score approximation used for stochastic transitions, and sparse multi-task rollouts give uneven learning signals across tasks and advantage signs. The proposed framework pairs `Outcome-Balanced PPO` (Proximal Policy Optimization), which reweights positive advantages by task success-rate estimates and rescales positive and negative advantages while keeping their signs, with policy-induced flow rectification, which periodically refits a linear-bridge flow to ODE endpoint pairs generated by the current policy. The framework **improves success rates over the evaluated baselines across the simulated manipulation benchmarks**, and a combination of its components is also studied on a Real2Sim2Real task.

papers.title: Learning Agent-Centric Vision-Language-Action World Models for Autonomous Driving
papers.abstract: Recent progress in integrating vision-language-action (VLA) models with world modeling has significantly advanced end-to-end autonomous driving by allowing systems to reason about imagined futures instead of merely reacting to current observations. However, most world VLA models generate future frames at the pixel level with plenty of dense visual tokens. Although such generated futures can be visually plausible, they preserve many driving-irrelevant appearance details, i.e., only a small portion of the tokens directly encode critical planning-relevant factors, such as agent geometry, motion dynamics, and interactions. This introduces a significant performance bottleneck. An important question thus arises: what world state should a world VLA model reason over to support planning beyond pixel-level prediction? We argue that planning-oriented world modeling should focus on a compact and structured agent-centric latent state that captures the interactions between objects in the driving scene over time. As such, we introduce AgentWorld, an agent-centric VLA world model that uses discrete agent tokens jointly for reasoning and trajectory planning. Each token is dynamically grounded to a surrounding agent associated with its object's state, such as semantic identity, 3D geometry, motion, and interaction context. AgentWorld learns these tokens through three key processes: explicit geometric grounding, reasoning-oriented supervised fine-tuning, and agent-oriented reinforcement learning. Extensive open-loop and closed-loop experiments under diverse driving scenarios show that AgentWorld enhances planning capabilities, fully exploits visual evidence and agent dynamics, and yields interpretable agent-centric world states.
papers.summary: World models built on vision-language-action (VLA) models for autonomous driving usually predict future frames at the pixel level, spending most of their dense visual tokens on appearance details that are irrelevant to planning. `AgentWorld` instead reasons and plans over discrete agent tokens, each dynamically grounded to a surrounding agent and its semantic identity, 3D geometry, motion, and interaction context. The tokens are learned through explicit geometric grounding, reasoning-oriented supervised fine-tuning, and agent-oriented reinforcement learning. Open-loop and closed-loop experiments across diverse driving scenarios are reported to show that the **compact agent-centric state improves planning while yielding interpretable world states**.

papers.title: Stopping Is Not the Limit: Understanding and Eliciting Agent Capability in Long-Horizon Vulnerability Exploitation
papers.abstract: Vulnerability exploitation tests whether language model agents can develop working exploits from known software flaws. Sequential test-time scaling can improve exploitation performance, but larger budgets do not ensure sustained exploration: agents often stop with budget remaining. Yet what happens when execution continues beyond stopping remains underexplored. We investigate this gap on ExploitBench using DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 and MiMo-V2.6-Pro. We find additional verified gains after the first stop response, but gains diminish over longer execution. We identify two patterns associated with less productive continuation: an increasing proportion of stop responses within the same context and earlier stopping associated with summaries retaining impossibility judgments about unachieved capabilities. To test whether context management can elicit further capability, we propose SCoRe, which compacts context at stop bursts and marks these judgments as unproven. SCoRe improves verified capability over summary-based continuation and other evaluated context-management baselines. With SCoRe, MiMo reaches a capability coverage score of 67.0% at 2,000 turns, exceeding both 32.4% under the original stopping policy and the 58.6% computed for GPT-5.5 from ExploitBench's 300-turn reference results on the same tasks. These findings show that stopping need not mark an agent's exploitation limit, and that continued execution with context management can elicit substantial further capability.
papers.summary: Language model agents developing exploits for known software flaws often stop with budget remaining, and this study examines what happens when execution is continued past that point on `ExploitBench` using `DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731` and `MiMo-V2.6-Pro`. Additional verified gains appear after the first stop response but diminish over longer runs, with less productive continuation associated with a rising share of stop responses in the same context and with summaries that carry forward impossibility judgments about unachieved capabilities. The proposed `SCoRe` method compacts context at stop bursts and marks those judgments as unproven, outperforming summary-based continuation and other context-management baselines. With `SCoRe`, `MiMo` reaches a **capability coverage score of 67.0% at 2,000 turns, versus 32.4% under the original stopping policy** and 58.6% computed for `GPT-5.5` from the benchmark's 300-turn reference results.

papers.title: Beyond Attribute-Centric Fairness: Modelling and Mitigating Unified Bias Representation in Omni-modal Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Omni-modal large language models (OLLMs) provide joint multimodal understanding and generation capabilities, making them well-suited to complex environments and promising backbones for next-generation AI. Despite these advances, the harmful stereotypes encoded in such models manifest in increasingly diverse forms, leading to broader and more severe societal consequences. Existing debiasing methods typically impose separate fairness objectives for each sensitive attribute and modality to minimise demographic-dependent variations. However, in omni-modal settings, this attribute-centric paradigm struggles to jointly address diverse social biases with distinct fairness objectives and to generalise beyond predefined attributes. To this end, we propose OmniDebias, one of the first methods for promoting fairness in OLLMs, which employs a bias-centric formulation to extract and mitigate a shared bias representation across attributes and modalities while preserving attribute-related knowledge. Specifically, we exploit activation inconsistencies of a given attribute (e.g., gender) across semantic contexts (e.g., occupations) to disentangle bias from legitimate knowledge. We further consolidate multiple extracted biases into a shared representation, formulating a unified objective that captures the underlying structure across social biases and generalises to unseen attributes. Extensive experiments demonstrate that eliminating unified bias with both post-hoc editing and fine-tuning can consistently improve fairness across diverse attributes and modalities in OLLMs while maintaining favourable utility.
papers.summary: Debiasing methods typically impose a separate fairness objective for each sensitive attribute and modality, which scales poorly in omni-modal large language models (OLLMs) and does not generalise beyond predefined attributes. `OmniDebias` takes a bias-centric view: it uses inconsistencies in an attribute's activations (for example gender) across semantic contexts (for example occupations) to separate bias from legitimate attribute knowledge, then consolidates the extracted biases into a single shared representation. Experiments indicate that removing this unified bias through either post-hoc editing or fine-tuning **consistently improves fairness across attributes and modalities, including unseen attributes, while maintaining utility**.

papers.title: Born for the Task: Rethinking Quantum Chemistry with Foresighted Agentic Computing
papers.abstract: Quantum chemistry relies on general-purpose software, whose generality leaves many large-scale calculations beyond practical resource budgets. Coding agents make task-specific programs cheap to write, but not efficient ones easy to find: whether a computational strategy is accurate and fast enough becomes clear only after it actually runs at the target scale. We introduce BORN, a foresighted agentic computing framework that synthesizes high performance quantum chemistry programs on demand. BORN anticipates the behavior of each strategy before execution, extrapolating its error from representative small systems and predicting its runtime from the target-scale workload and measured hardware throughputs. Building on these predictions, BORN unfolds the preset schemes of existing packages into independently configurable algorithmic components, selects the fastest strategy within the error tolerance from the predicted accuracy-runtime Pareto frontier, and guides coding agents to compile it with component-level performance predictions. For a Hartree-Fock calculation with 50,024 basis functions, BORN finishes in 1.41h on a single CPU node, 77$\times$ faster than the estimated runtime of a general-purpose baseline and still 9.8$\times$ faster with development time included. On a single GPU, BORN completes the ubiquitin calculation in 2.1,h, the same order of runtime as the GPU-accelerated package Mako on 64 GPUs, and shortens the B-DNA duplex calculation from an estimated two months to 8.1,h (173$\times$).
papers.summary: General-purpose quantum chemistry packages leave many large calculations beyond practical budgets, and although coding agents can cheaply write task-specific programs, whether a strategy is accurate and fast enough is normally known only after running it at target scale. `BORN` predicts each strategy's behavior before execution, extrapolating error from small representative systems and estimating runtime from the target workload and measured hardware throughput, then picks the fastest strategy within the error tolerance and guides coding agents to implement it with component-level performance predictions. For a Hartree-Fock calculation with 50,024 basis functions it finishes in 1.41 hours on a single CPU node, **77x faster than the estimated runtime of a general-purpose baseline** and 9.8x faster with development time included. On a single GPU it completes a ubiquitin calculation in 2.1 hours, the same order as the `Mako` package on 64 GPUs, and cuts a B-DNA duplex calculation from an estimated two months to 8.1 hours.

papers.title: Done, But Still Working: Anytime Evaluation of When Coding Agents Should Stop
papers.abstract: Coding agents often continue working after their own tests pass. Does this additional work improve the patch, and how much could be saved by stopping earlier? We study these questions through anytime evaluation: replaying recorded runs, scoring intermediate patches with hidden tests, and measuring the cost incurred at each step. For policies that only stop a run or select an earlier patch, this allows paired comparisons without generating new trajectories, provided replay preserves the relevant states. Across about 6,000 runs of eight open models in two scaffolds on SWE-bench Verified, we find substantial differences in the value of continued work. The hindsight saving available at passing self-tests ranges from under 1% to 57%, depending on the model and scaffold. A rule that stops after the same patch passes twice saves 23% in a preregistered replication, but the preregistered quality test does not establish non-inferiority. We explain these differences by measuring how often a rule fires, how often the patch changes afterwards, and whether those changes repair or break it. Fine-tuning agents to imitate the rule saves 30% over six seeds, while quality preservation remains uncertain. Our results help identify both the opportunities and the risks of early stopping.
papers.summary: Coding agents often keep working after their own tests pass, raising the question of whether the extra work improves the patch and how much cost early stopping could save. The authors use anytime evaluation, replaying recorded runs, scoring intermediate patches with hidden tests, and tracking cost per step, over about 6,000 runs of eight open models in two scaffolds on `SWE-bench Verified`. The **hindsight saving available once self-tests pass ranges from under 1% to 57% depending on model and scaffold**. A rule that stops after the same patch passes twice saves 23% in a preregistered replication, and fine-tuning agents to imitate it saves 30% over six seeds, but in neither case is preservation of patch quality established.

papers.title: Who Pays for Byzantine Robustness? Validity, Data-Share Dictatorships, and Fairness When Only a Few Hospitals Collaborate
papers.abstract:
Clinical federated learning (FL) collaborations typically connect only three to six hospitals, yet Byzantine-robust aggregation rules are designed and benchmarked on synthetic partitions across dozens of equal-sized clients. We conduct an empirical audit of eight standard aggregation rules: FedAvg, coordinate-wise median, trimmed mean, Krum, Multi-Krum, Bulyan, geometric median (GeoMed), and Centered Clipping (CC). We evaluate both unweighted and sample-size-weighted variants across three cross-silo medical datasets from the FLamby benchmark: Fed-Heart-Disease ($n = 4$ hospitals), Fed-TCGA-BRCA ($n = 6$ regions), and Fed-ISIC2019 ($n = 6$ centres). We execute 54,214 training runs across enumerated attacker coalitions ($f \in \{1, 2\}$) paired with exact-twin leave-out controls that decompose performance drops into honest data loss versus adversarial attack damage.
  We report three findings. First, client-count validity checks fail to capture breakdown in skewed medical consortia: while $n = 6, f = 1$ satisfies every count condition except Bulyan's, assigning sample-size weights turns median and GeoMed into a clean-model dictatorship whenever a single hospital holds more than half the training data, and causes weighted median, GeoMed, and CC to collapse when that dominant centre attacks. Second, exact-twin leave-out controls reveal that when the largest hospital attacks, the apparent failure of count-based robust rules is predominantly caused by the loss of honest training data (7.5 to 10.4 points on ISIC) rather than adversarial perturbation (2.3 to 3.8 points on ISIC). Conversely, weight-dependent rules suffer large true attack damage (16.1 to 25.1 points on ISIC). Third, unweighted robust rules consistently discount whichever institution generates the most atypical parameter updates, penalizing the smallest hospital on Heart but penalizing larger institutions on TCGA and ISIC.
papers.summary: Byzantine-robust aggregation rules for federated learning (FL) are usually benchmarked on dozens of equal-sized synthetic clients, whereas clinical collaborations typically involve only three to six hospitals of very different sizes. This audit runs **54,214 training runs** of eight rules, including `FedAvg`, coordinate-wise median, `Krum`, `Bulyan`, geometric median (`GeoMed`), and Centered Clipping (`CC`), in unweighted and sample-size-weighted variants on three `FLamby` medical datasets, with exact-twin leave-out controls that separate honest data loss from attack damage. Sample-size weighting turns median and `GeoMed` into a dictatorship of any hospital holding more than half the data and makes weighted rules collapse when that hospital attacks, while for count-based rules most of the apparent failure comes from losing the attacker's honest data rather than from the attack. Unweighted robust rules also systematically discount whichever institution produces the most atypical updates, which is the smallest hospital on one dataset and larger ones on the others.

papers.title: Action-outcome coupling: a pre-investment feasibility audit for offline reinforcement learning in supply chain operations
papers.abstract: Prescriptive analytics initiatives in logistics, such as offline reinforcement learning and next-best-action systems, are often funded before anyone verifies that the available historical logs can support an improved decision policy. We formalise this pre-investment feasibility question via action-outcome coupling: a total-effect variance index measuring how much expected outcomes change with the logged action. Coupling provides an algorithm-independent upper bound on any policy's achievable value, expressed in monetary units per decision for both single-step and discounted sequential objectives. We also analyse the asymptotic false-licensing risk of an invalid workflow: fitting a value model and evaluating the model's greedy policy on the same data. The false-licence rate is driven mainly by the number of state cells over which selection is performed, rising from the nominal test level with one cell to near certainty with a few dozen, while overlap has a smaller effect. We then propose an audit that assigns logs to four tiers of decision support, separately for fixed and contextual policies, and returns an explicit stopping rationale. On a randomised e-commerce log, the audit endorses a fixed recommendation policy, certifying gains equal to 30 per cent of the theoretical ceiling; the remaining gap reflects bound looseness under an 80-action design. Two public logistics logs fail at different checkpoints: one because the target is an accounting identity of the action, and another because, with 27 clusters, estimated coupling stays below the design's detectability threshold even though a conservative offline learner certifies an improvement in 29 of 30 seeds.
papers.summary: Offline reinforcement learning and next-best-action projects in logistics are often funded before anyone checks whether the historical logs can support a better decision policy. The authors formalise this check as action-outcome coupling, a variance index measuring how much expected outcomes change with the logged action, which gives an algorithm-independent upper bound on any policy's achievable value in monetary units per decision. They also show that fitting a value model and evaluating its greedy policy on the same data produces false approvals at a rate that climbs from the nominal test level to near certainty with a few dozen state cells, and they propose an audit assigning logs to four tiers of decision support. On a randomised e-commerce log the audit endorses a fixed recommendation policy with **certified gains equal to 30 per cent of the theoretical ceiling**, while two public logistics logs fail at different checkpoints.

papers.title: When Do Typed Decision Models Work in Transportation? Evidence from Travel Choice and Traffic Signal Control
papers.abstract: Typed decision models combine natural-language understanding with a structured interface that returns a selected action and an option-level probability distribution without generating lengthy textual responses. Their low inference cost and response latency make them attractive for transportation problems with predefined alternatives. This paper investigates their effectiveness, robustness, and efficiency in two representative transportation tasks: individual travel-mode choice prediction and sequential traffic signal control. We systematically evaluate TypeSafe Jev and GPT-6 Luna Decisions against conventional transportation methods, reinforcement learning algorithms, and four chat-based large language models. Experiments on the Swissmetro dataset show that typed decision models achieve lower prediction accuracy than traditional discrete choice models and the strongest chat-based baseline, while their performance varies substantially with input representation and question framing. In closed-loop traffic signal control experiments, typed decision models demonstrate competitive performance against established controllers in several scenarios, but exhibit performance degradation under more challenging network conditions. Furthermore, the typed models achieve lower inference latency and computational cost than the evaluated chat-based large language models, highlighting their potential for efficient, zero-shot transportation decision-making. Overall, these findings demonstrate both the potential and limitations of typed decision models, emphasizing the importance of input design, task characteristics, and robustness evaluation for their effective application in transportation systems.
papers.summary: Typed decision models pair natural-language understanding with a structured interface that returns a chosen action and a probability distribution over options, without generating long text. The study evaluates `TypeSafe Jev` and `GPT-6 Luna Decisions` on travel-mode choice prediction and sequential traffic signal control, against conventional transportation methods, reinforcement learning algorithms, and four chat-based large language models. On the `Swissmetro` dataset the **typed models are less accurate than traditional discrete choice models and the strongest chat-based baseline**, with results varying substantially with input representation and question framing. In closed-loop signal control they are competitive with established controllers in several scenarios but degrade under harder network conditions, while running at lower latency and cost than the chat-based models.

papers.title: Projected Penalty-Gradient Tracking for Communication-Efficient Byzantine-Resilient Federated Learning
papers.abstract: We investigate communication-efficient federated learning over heterogeneous datasets in the presence of Byzantine adversaries capable of uploading arbitrary information. Penalty-based methods bound the influence of each worker through the bounded gradient of a penalty function; however, the bound is lost once the uploads are compressed, since a Byzantine worker can accumulate an unbounded state at the server. To retain the Byzantine resilience under compressed uploads, we propose a projected penalty-gradient tracking framework, where each honest worker uploads a compressed residual of its penalty gradient and the server projects each reconstructed state onto the known penalty-gradient ball. The framework accommodates any contractive compressor and yields two algorithms: fault-resilient proximal gradient with consistent sparsification (FRPG-CS), whose shared mask is protected by freshly drawn reserve rows, and lazily aggregated FRPG (LAG-FRPG), whose uploads are event-triggered. For smooth and strongly convex losses, we establish a finite-time bound on the expected objective gap, where the Byzantine error floor is independent of the compressor and the compression error decays faster than the optimization error. We also bound the expected number of lazy uploads and derive certificates that separate the finite-penalty model bias from the optimization error. Experiments on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST show that the proposed algorithms attain the highest accuracy among twelve methods under the Min-Max attack, whereas a compressed-momentum benchmark and a local-update benchmark remain preferable in attack-free accuracy and total traffic, respectively.
papers.summary: Penalty-based Byzantine-resilient federated learning bounds each worker's influence through the bounded gradient of a penalty function, but that bound is lost once uploads are compressed, because a malicious worker can accumulate an unbounded state at the server. The proposed framework has each honest worker upload a compressed residual of its penalty gradient while the server projects every reconstructed state back onto the known penalty-gradient ball, and it yields two algorithms: `FRPG-CS` (fault-resilient proximal gradient with consistent sparsification) and the event-triggered `LAG-FRPG` (lazily aggregated FRPG). For smooth, strongly convex losses the analysis gives a finite-time bound in which the **Byzantine error floor is independent of the compressor**. On `MNIST` and `Fashion-MNIST` the algorithms attain the highest accuracy among twelve methods under the Min-Max attack, though other benchmarks remain preferable in attack-free accuracy and total traffic.

papers.title: The Shared Word: Evaluating Language Models on Dutch Word Puzzles
papers.abstract: Many LLM benchmarks for languages other than English are translated, multiple-choice, or difficult to score automatically. We introduce The Shared Word (TSW-NL), a Dutch benchmark built around four core principles: it is language-specific, open-vocabulary, human-curated, and deterministically scored. Each puzzle gives three clues that describe different senses or uses of the same Dutch word. The clues are individually ambiguous, requiring the solver to combine evidence across multiple clues. We construct the benchmark from Dutch Wikipedia disambiguation pages, followed by automatic filtering and extensive manual curation. The final dataset contains 222 instances, with three independent human answers per test item. The task is clearly challenging: scores in our human study range from 49.5% to 61.0% and the highest-scoring open-weight model we tested reaches only 39.3%. Many others even score below 20%. At the same time, closed-source models show great progress: GPT-4.1 (April 2025) scores 59.2%, whereas GPT-5.6 Sol with max reasoning scores 88.8%. We believe this task provides a useful addition to Dutch model evaluation, plus a clear recipe that can be applied to construct a similar benchmark for other languages.
papers.summary: Many non-English language model benchmarks are translated, multiple-choice, or hard to score automatically. `TSW-NL` (The Shared Word) is a Dutch benchmark of 222 human-curated puzzles built from Dutch Wikipedia disambiguation pages, where three individually ambiguous clues describe different senses of the same word and the answer is open-vocabulary and deterministically scored. Humans score between 49.5% and 61.0%, the best open-weight model tested reaches 39.3%, and many others fall below 20%. Closed models show a large jump, with `GPT-4.1` at 59.2% and **`GPT-5.6 Sol` with max reasoning at 88.8%**.

papers.title: A Transformer-Derived Iterative Preconditioner
papers.abstract:
Transformers trained on in-context prediction problems can learn known numerical algorithms, e.g., gradient descent. We go further, showing that their internal computations can reveal new algorithms with provable guarantees. A softmax-attention transformer trained to solve linear systems $Xw=y$ implicitly improves matrix conditioning. Tracing $XX^\top$ reveals an iterative preconditioning primitive, which we develop into RAPID, a standalone algorithm requiring no learned components.
  RAPID is an anytime preconditioner for symmetric positive definite (SPD) matrices, using randomized mixing and sparse local corrections to improve conditioning. Proof-of-concept experiments on synthetic and real-world problems consistently improve conditioning and reduce conjugate gradient iterations needed to reach a target accuracy. For a Haar-mixing idealization, we prove convergence to any fixed target condition number regardless of spectral distribution, with only logarithmic dependence on initial conditioning. Together, these results show how a transformer can discover a broadly applicable numerical algorithm.
papers.summary: Transformers trained on in-context prediction are known to rediscover existing numerical algorithms, and this work asks whether their internals can also reveal new ones. Tracing the computations of a softmax-attention transformer trained to solve linear systems shows that it implicitly improves matrix conditioning, and the authors extract this behavior into `RAPID`, a standalone anytime preconditioner for symmetric positive definite (SPD) matrices that uses randomized mixing and sparse local corrections with no learned components. Proof-of-concept experiments on synthetic and real-world problems improve conditioning and reduce the conjugate gradient iterations needed for a target accuracy. For an idealized Haar-mixing version, they **prove convergence to any fixed target condition number with only logarithmic dependence on the initial conditioning**.

papers.title: The Kernel Reality Check: Benchmarking and Distilling Efficient Attention at Scale
papers.abstract: Kernelized attention methods, which aim to replace the $O(N^2)$ complexity of softmax attention with $O(N)$ alternatives, have been the focus of intense research in the last five years. Despite growing interest, systematic evaluations and fair comparisons across approaches and scales are still missing. We analyze kernelized attention in two halves and highlight prominent limitations on each. On efficiency, FlashAttention achieves lower memory consumption and faster wall-clock time than SOTA kernelized methods during training and in vision transformers across most sequence lengths (with inference-time memory in causal language models the only clear exception), contradicting the core assumption for pure kernelized attention used as a drop-in replacement for softmax. We also discover that reported efficiency gains often fail to reproduce against modern baselines. On quality, current kernelized methods leave gaps of 2-10 points relative to softmax under a unified distillation protocol, and model scala alone does not close these gaps. We show this gap is not intrinsic to kernelization: LARA++, a principled extension of LARA that approximates softmax via importance sampling with adaptive proposal distributions, recovers up to 99% of softmax accuracy. We establish that the gap is closable; however, the computational overhead remains substantial, leaving the efficiency wall intact. Code is available at https://github.com/firatoncel/KernelRealityCheckNeurIPS2026
papers.summary: Kernelized attention methods aim to replace the quadratic cost of softmax attention with linear-time alternatives, but have lacked fair comparisons across approaches and scales. On efficiency, **`FlashAttention` uses less memory and runs faster than state-of-the-art kernelized methods during training and in vision transformers across most sequence lengths**, with inference-time memory in causal language models the only clear exception, and previously reported efficiency gains often fail to reproduce against modern baselines. On quality, current kernelized methods trail softmax by 2 to 10 points under a unified distillation protocol, and model scale alone does not close the gap. `LARA++`, an extension of `LARA` using importance sampling with adaptive proposal distributions, recovers up to 99% of softmax accuracy, but its computational overhead remains substantial, so the efficiency disadvantage stands.

papers.title: Symmetries of Counterfactuals: Identification and Testability of Counterfactual Maps from Covariate Heterogeneity
papers.abstract: In general, counterfactuals are not identified from data alone, because many causal models produce the same observed distributions but different counterfactuals. A common approach to circumvent this problem is to restrict the mechanism to a class in which it becomes unique, such as triangular monotone maps or optimal transport maps. However, whether the assumed class is correct is usually not examined. In this work, we study what the data can tell us when covariates are available that influence the outcome only through its latent cause. First, we characterise all counterfactual maps that are consistent with the data. They differ from the true map by a group of symmetries that preserve the conditional outcome distributions given the covariates. The more these distributions vary across covariate values, the smaller the group. Second, we show that for the classes above, consistency with the data is equivalent to a single conditional independence, which yields a test of the assumed class. We illustrate both results on synthetic data and on the ACTG 175 HIV trial.
papers.summary: Counterfactuals are generally not identifiable from data alone, and the usual fix of restricting the causal mechanism to a class such as triangular monotone maps or optimal transport maps is rarely checked for correctness. The authors study the setting where covariates affect the outcome only through its latent cause, and characterise every counterfactual map consistent with the data as differing from the true map by a group of symmetries that preserve the conditional outcome distributions, a group that shrinks as those distributions vary more across covariate values. They further show that for the standard classes, **consistency with the data is equivalent to a single conditional independence, which yields a test of the assumed class**. Both results are illustrated on synthetic data and the `ACTG 175` HIV trial.

papers.title: Can Decision Models Replace LLMs in Real-World Contact Center Classification and Judging Tasks?
papers.abstract: Contact center systems often need to make bounded decisions, such as identifying a caller's intent, retrieving the knowledge-base article that answers a query, assessing agent compliance, or judging the output of AI models used in production. Decision models return a typed answer and its probability directly, making them a promising cost-effective alternative to generative Large Language Models (LLMs) in such bounded conversational tasks. However, their effectiveness in real-world contact center applications remains unclear. In this paper, we compare nine decision models against thirteen generative LLMs in zero-shot settings across eight contact center use cases: six classification tasks and two judging tasks. Our experiments demonstrate that many decision models can match the performance of frontier LLMs on contact center classification, and API-based closed decision models achieve this at the lowest per-request cost among the API models we evaluate. We further observe that their confident predictions are more accurate, enabling selective routing in real-world production scenarios. Across classification tasks, the main weakness of most decision models is abstention: they rarely choose the no-answer option, which accounts for most of their gap to the strongest LLMs (although Gemini-Decision-1 is the notable exception in this regard). We also find that the judging quality of decision models drops sharply for smaller models, and they are also more prone to position bias. In short, our findings provide practical guidance for selecting decision models based on abstention behavior, confidence, and deployment cost, rather than overall accuracy alone.
papers.summary: Decision models return a typed answer and its probability directly, making them a potentially cheaper alternative to generative large language models (LLMs) for bounded tasks such as intent identification, knowledge-base retrieval, compliance assessment, and judging model outputs. Nine decision models are compared against thirteen generative LLMs in zero-shot settings across eight contact center use cases, six classification tasks and two judging tasks. **Many decision models match frontier LLMs on classification, with API-based closed decision models doing so at the lowest per-request cost** among the API models evaluated, and their confident predictions are more accurate, which supports selective routing. Their main weakness is that most rarely choose the no-answer option (`Gemini-Decision-1` being the exception), and on judging tasks quality drops sharply for smaller models, which are also more prone to position bias.

papers.title: ResoLUT: Distilling Residual Networks into Lookup-Table Networks
papers.abstract: Logic networks built from Boolean gates or lookup tables (LUTs) promise efficient hardware inference, but training them at depth and learning their connectivity remain difficult. We do not train logic as logic. Instead, ResoLUT distills a trained residual network (ResNet) layer by layer into LUT trees, preserving its multi-bit residual stream and BatchNorm while extracting connectivity from the teacher rather than learning it. To our knowledge, ResoLUT is the first convolutional logic network in computer vision to retain a ResNet-style multi-bit residual stream. Hard LUT decisions are used throughout training and inference, avoiding a discretization gap in the logic. ResoLUT-20 reaches 95.66% on CIFAR-10 with twice the trees, and ResoLUT-56 reaches 78.87% on CIFAR-100 and 53.69% on ImageNet at 64px, the best results of logic and lookup-table networks on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, showing that LUT networks can scale in depth. We explore and quantify the role of the residuals and the tree budget and shape. The most optimized model, a ResoLUT-8 with one eighth of the trees and further optimizations, fits on an FPGA and reaches 90.04% at 189k images per second, the highest throughput among the compared models above 85% on CIFAR-10.
papers.summary: Logic networks built from Boolean gates or lookup tables (LUTs) promise efficient hardware inference but are hard to train at depth, and learning their connectivity is difficult. `ResoLUT` sidesteps this by distilling a trained residual network (ResNet) layer by layer into LUT trees, keeping the multi-bit residual stream and BatchNorm and taking connectivity from the teacher, with hard LUT decisions used in both training and inference. `ResoLUT-20` reaches 95.66% on `CIFAR-10` with twice the trees, and `ResoLUT-56` reaches 78.87% on `CIFAR-100` and 53.69% on `ImageNet` at 64 pixels, reported as the best results for logic and lookup-table networks on the two CIFAR datasets. A heavily optimized `ResoLUT-8` fits on an FPGA and reaches **90.04% on `CIFAR-10` at 189k images per second**.

papers.title: Is model self-assessment enough for diverse LVLM ensembles?
papers.abstract: Ensembles of diverse Large Vision Language Models have demonstrated performance beyond that of single models across multiple datasets and tasks. However, the necessary aggregation process usually relies on training, parameter fitting, or complex task-specific pipelines. Furthermore, evaluation is limited, making a fair comparison difficult. We create a unified pipeline where we perform candidate response selection: we build an ensemble by selecting the best answer from a set provided by different models. We comprehensively evaluate across 34 different means of confidence estimation, 24 ensemble configurations, 20 datasets, and two prompt specifications. We show that simple training and parameter-free approaches can be sufficient, even for ensembles of different architectures. These simple self-assessment approaches rely solely on each constituent model's confidence, without explicit calibration, yet are able to perform better than said constituent models. They are also competitive with more involved alternatives on standard metrics such as accuracy, including on open-ended problems. However, we also discover that dataset, ensemble composition, and prompt wording are key confounding variables insufficiently explored by prior work that significantly affect ensemble performance, such that the ensemble can perform worse than its best constituent model. These must be optimized for to get the most out of ensembles, at the cost of limiting their generalizability. We recommend that practitioners consider training-free ensembles only if deployment conditions can be precisely characterized, with Best-of-N configurations of strong models being a good starting point.
papers.summary: Ensembles of diverse large vision-language models can beat single models, but aggregation usually depends on training, parameter fitting, or task-specific pipelines, and evaluations are too limited for fair comparison. The authors build a unified pipeline that selects the best answer from candidates produced by different models, and evaluate 34 confidence estimation methods, 24 ensemble configurations, 20 datasets, and two prompt specifications. Simple training-free and parameter-free approaches that rely only on each model's own uncalibrated confidence can outperform the constituent models and are competitive with more involved alternatives, including on open-ended problems. However, **dataset, ensemble composition, and prompt wording strongly affect results, to the point that an ensemble can perform worse than its best member**, so the authors recommend training-free ensembles only when deployment conditions are precisely characterized.

papers.title: DDSL: Iterative Self-Labeling for Financial Market States
papers.abstract: Financial market states lack a unique ground truth and must therefore be constructed from price data. Conventional labeling methods typically define states independently of the downstream classifier, leaving unresolved whether the resulting labels can be recovered from information available at prediction time. We propose DDSL, an iterative self-labeling framework that couples a price- and grammar-guided Viterbi labeler with a Transformer classifier through model feedback. DDSL constructs a nine-state representation that jointly encodes current and future market trends while retaining structured price emissions and temporal constraints throughout refinement. Experiments on SSE50, CSI300, CSI500, and NASDAQ100 show that DDSL increases held-out joint-state macro F1 by 78%-96% over single-pass dynamic-programming labeling. An independent GRU classifier that never participates in the labeling loop reproduces the same trend, while label entropy and class coverage remain stable, indicating that the gain transfers across architectures and is not caused by label collapse. We further show that learnability is controlled by both iteration and the model-feedback weight $\beta_{\mathrm{model}}$.
