Iterative gains diminish as successive label systems converge, whereas stronger feedback increasingly widens the performance gap between the feedback Transformer and the independent GRU. Increased learnability is accompanied by declining segment-level price-feature separation after an initial improvement. Finally, a non-anticipative event study provides partial external validation: refinement strengthens a conditional BEAR$\rightarrow$BULL reversal signal on the three A-share datasets, while the corresponding effect has the opposite sign on NASDAQ100. These results position DDSL as a structured framework for constructing market-state labels whose learnability can be explicitly controlled and evaluated.
papers.summary: Financial market states have no unique ground truth and must be constructed from price data, yet conventional labeling methods define them independently of the classifier that later has to predict them. `DDSL` is an iterative self-labeling framework that couples a price- and grammar-guided Viterbi labeler with a Transformer classifier through model feedback, producing a nine-state representation of current and future market trends. On `SSE50`, `CSI300`, `CSI500`, and `NASDAQ100` it **raises held-out joint-state macro F1 by 78% to 96% over single-pass dynamic-programming labeling**, and an independent GRU classifier outside the labeling loop reproduces the trend without signs of label collapse. Greater learnability comes with declining price-feature separation after an initial improvement, and an event study finds a strengthened bear-to-bull reversal signal on the three A-share datasets but an effect of the opposite sign on `NASDAQ100`.

papers.title: Hierarchical Diffusion Transformer for End-to-End Image Generation
papers.abstract: Pixel-space diffusion learns visual representations and image generation jointly in a single end-to-end training stage, without a separately pretrained visual encoder. However, plain pixel-space Transformers still trail leading two-stage latent diffusion models in generation quality and training efficiency. We hypothesize that part of this gap arises from retaining one token per patch throughout the backbone, which does not explicitly encourage a visual hierarchy that summarizes related content at progressively coarser levels. To address this, we introduce Hierarchical Diffusion Transformers (HiT), which progressively group related tokens and represent each group with a single token. The main Transformer bottleneck processes these compact group tokens, and ungrouping restores features to their original image positions. A compression budget regulates the average compression ratio across the batch, allowing group memberships and counts to vary across images and diffusion timesteps during both training and generation. The model exhibits emergent semantic structure, learning to group coherent objects and object parts without segmentation labels. In text-to-image generation, HiT further learns to group caption words with image patches depicting the same concepts, without region annotations. HiT achieves 1.48 FID on ImageNet $256\times256$ and reaches comparable generation quality to JiT using approximately 40\% of its cumulative training FLOPs. For text-to-image generation, HiT exceeds UniLiP's average score across five benchmarks with roughly $6\times$ fewer denoiser parameters and $3\times$ fewer forward FLOPs. These results suggest that learning a visual hierarchy within the generator breaks down the barrier to stronger image generation without external visual pretraining.
papers.summary: Pixel-space diffusion Transformers train end to end without a separately pretrained visual encoder, but still trail two-stage latent diffusion models in quality and training efficiency. `HiT` (Hierarchical Diffusion Transformers) progressively groups related tokens into single group tokens that the main Transformer bottleneck processes, then ungroups them back to image positions, with a compression budget that lets group memberships and counts vary across images and diffusion timesteps. The model learns to group coherent objects and parts without segmentation labels, and in text-to-image generation groups caption words with the patches depicting them. It achieves **1.48 FID on `ImageNet` 256x256 while matching `JiT` quality with about 40% of its cumulative training FLOPs**, and exceeds `UniLiP`'s average score across five text-to-image benchmarks with roughly 6x fewer denoiser parameters and 3x fewer forward FLOPs.

papers.title: High-Dimensional Black-Box Optimization via Guidance Sampling of Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: Many real-world optimization problems involve optimizing black-box objectives for which only a limited number of evaluations are available. Bayesian optimization (BO) is a powerful framework for such problems, but its effectiveness often deteriorates in high-dimensional spaces. Recent work leverages diffusion models for black-box optimization, often through pre-training a reward-conditioned score network to steer generation towards high-reward samples. Alternatively, gradient-based guidance methods assume access to a differentiable reward function from which guidance gradients are queried. However, these approaches either require large amounts of labeled data for offline training or access to exact reward gradients, limiting their applicability in black-box settings. We propose BReaD (Black-box Reward-guided Sampling of Diffusion Model), a guidance sampling framework for optimizing black-box rewards without assuming access to a labeled dataset or reward gradients. The proposed method uses a Gaussian process (GP) as a differentiable surrogate for the unknown objective and actively queries labels for the generated samples. We provide a theoretical analysis of the total-variation distance between the generated distribution and the target distribution. Using Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) as guidance signals, our method balances exploration and exploitation during generation and enables the discovery of high-reward regions in the data space. Numerical experiments on scientific discovery and image generation tasks demonstrate that our framework can effectively optimize black-box rewards in low-data scenarios.
papers.summary: Bayesian optimization (BO) degrades in high-dimensional spaces, and existing diffusion-based optimizers need either large labeled datasets or exact reward gradients. `BReaD` (Black-box Reward-guided Sampling of Diffusion Model) instead fits a Gaussian process (GP) as a differentiable surrogate for the unknown objective, actively queries labels for generated samples, and uses the Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) as the guidance signal to balance exploration and exploitation. The authors bound the total-variation distance between the generated and target distributions, and report that the method **optimizes black-box rewards without a labeled dataset or reward gradients** on scientific discovery and image generation tasks in low-data settings.

papers.title: CodeReel: Accelerating Code-to-Video Agents with Exact Frame Reuse and Blocking-Aware Scheduling
papers.abstract: Coding agents make videos by writing and refining programs in a build--inspect--edit loop. A finished film costs a median of $2.85 in model calls and 11 minutes, over a third of that time in builds that block the agent. We find that much of this time is avoidable, for two reasons. First, 37.5% of the frames of a session's later films were drawn before, many shifted in time or inside an edited scene. Second, half of the builds stop at a check, where the agent needs only the verdict, but which builds stop is unknown until the checks finish. We present CodeReel, a training-free execution layer behind agents' existing commands. Exact frame reuse keys each frame by its drawing commands, regardless of its position in time, and reuses each frame whose key recurs. Blocking-aware scheduling runs the checks first and starts the render alongside them, at idle priority, unless the session's recent builds make a pass unlikely. Scheduling spends CPU to answer sooner and reuse returns it; exact keys let later versions use frames rendered for a failed one as the agent thinks. We introduce EditLoop, a benchmark of replayable agent sessions whose films are checked against renders from scratch. On it, CodeReel cuts the agent's wait by 36.3% against Rebuild, a warm pipeline with parallel rendering, and by 57.9% against Sequential, today's step-by-step pipeline. On time-shifting edits its reuse renders 43.9%, close to the 43.0% whose pixels are new, while Manim-style caching renders 99.8%. With real agents, the median wait per build is 0.62x Rebuild's in Claude Code, on topics never used in development, and 0.67x in Codex CLI. The gain holds for five models and two frameworks.
papers.summary: Coding agents that produce videos by writing programs spend over a third of their time waiting on builds, even though 37.5% of the frames in a session's later films were already drawn and half of the builds stop at a check where only the verdict is needed. `CodeReel` is a training-free execution layer that keys each frame by its drawing commands so it can be reused regardless of its position in time, and that runs checks first while starting the render alongside them at idle priority. On `EditLoop`, a new benchmark of replayable agent sessions, it **cuts the agent's wait by 36.3% against the warm, parallel `Rebuild` pipeline** and by 57.9% against the step-by-step `Sequential` pipeline. With real agents the median wait per build is 0.62x that of `Rebuild` in `Claude Code` and 0.67x in `Codex CLI`.

papers.title: SEAM: Computer-Use Agents Know the Harm Between Screens, and Commit It Anyway
papers.abstract: Safety benchmarks for computer-use agents (CUAs) place the harm either in the intent of the task or on a single screen: a malicious instruction, an injected command, a phishing page. An agent that checks the task and each screen in isolation can pass them, so they do not test whether it combines facts seen on different screens. Yet in delegated work, harm often arises exactly this way: a fact about a person on one screen, a fact about an item on another, and a legitimate task that binds them. We introduce SEAM (Safety Execution Across Multiple screens), a benchmark of such cross-screen compositional harm: 600 multi-step, cross-application OSWorld tasks in which the instruction and every single observation are benign and only their combination is harmful. Minimal-pair variants that differ in one place, scored from the server log rather than by an LLM judge, locate where an agent fails. General-purpose open-weight and flagship agents carry out the harm in up to 92% of runs, yet decline when the user states it in one sentence. Agents open the decisive pages, so exposure is not the primary bottleneck. Asked about those pages, they flag the harm, and with thinking they often write the conflict into their reasoning and confirm anyway. Safety recognition thus does not reliably translate into safe execution, and the translation depends on the information channel: the same warning stops agents far more often in the user's instruction than on screen. Proprietary models are markedly more cautious. We release SEAM with its generator and quality gates at https://yuxuan2003.github.io/SEAM/ .
papers.summary: Safety benchmarks for computer-use agents (CUAs) usually place the harm in the task instruction or on a single screen, so they do not test whether an agent combines facts seen on different screens. `SEAM` (Safety Execution Across Multiple screens) provides 600 multi-step, cross-application `OSWorld` tasks in which the instruction and every individual observation are benign and only their combination is harmful, with minimal-pair variants scored from the server log rather than by a model judge. General-purpose open-weight and flagship agents **carry out the harm in up to 92% of runs** yet decline when the user states the same harm in one sentence, and they often flag the conflict in their own reasoning before confirming anyway. The same warning stops agents far more often in the user's instruction than on screen, and proprietary models are markedly more cautious.

papers.title: VITAL: A Framework for Validating Agentic AI in Pharmaceutical Drug Development and Clinical Trial Operations
papers.abstract: Current assurance approaches do not establish whether evidence is sufficient to validate, monitor and govern agentic artificial intelligence (AI) within a pharmaceutical context of use. Plausible outputs may conceal failures in retrieval, reasoning, orchestration or human-control points, where reference standards are unavailable. We developed and operationalised VITAL (Validation by Intended use, Traceability, Autonomy and Lifecycle evidence), a validation framework for agents in clinical development, through landscape analysis, regulatory and standards mapping, expert interviews and multi-stakeholder refinement. VITAL integrates context of use, controls, behavioural validation and lifecycle evidence within a risk-adjusted framework. We applied VITAL across epidemiology and treatment-landscape analysis, site selection, enrolment rescue and trial-design trade-off support to translate autonomy, reversibility, transparency and patient impact into proportionate validation activities, evidence requirements and auditable reconstruction of system behaviour. VITAL may inform evidence requirements and lifecycle accountability for higher-risk pharmaceutical uses; evaluation should assess reproducibility across assessors, organisations and system configurations.
papers.summary: Existing assurance approaches do not establish whether the evidence is sufficient to validate, monitor, and govern agentic AI in pharmaceutical settings, where plausible outputs can hide failures in retrieval, reasoning, orchestration, or human-control points. `VITAL` (Validation by Intended use, Traceability, Autonomy and Lifecycle evidence) is a validation framework built from landscape analysis, regulatory and standards mapping, expert interviews, and multi-stakeholder refinement. It **combines context of use, controls, behavioural validation, and lifecycle evidence in a risk-adjusted framework**, and was applied to epidemiology and treatment-landscape analysis, site selection, enrolment rescue, and trial-design trade-off support. The authors note that reproducibility across assessors, organisations, and system configurations remains to be evaluated.

papers.title: Large Language Models Have Not Yet Transformed Science
papers.abstract: The emergence of large language models (LLMs) in late 2022 has raised questions about the future of science, but assessing their impact requires understanding how scientific practices were already evolving. We analyze 2.5 million full-text papers across five disciplines from 2015 to 2025, tracing trends over a broad spectrum of lexical, structural, epistemological, and social dimensions. Aside from frequency shifts in some words, most pre-2023 trends continued with limited detectable breaks. Among the notable exceptions, growth in computer science coauthor teams accelerated significantly in Asia, while apparent declines in biomedical topic diversity largely reflected standardization in article formats. Our study establishes an empirical foundation for monitoring the health of global science as LLM adoption deepens.
papers.summary: To measure how large language models (LLMs) have changed scientific practice, the authors analyze 2.5 million full-text papers across five disciplines from 2015 to 2025, tracing lexical, structural, epistemological, and social trends. Apart from frequency shifts in some words, **most pre-2023 trends continued with limited detectable breaks**. Among the exceptions, growth in computer science coauthor teams accelerated in Asia, while an apparent decline in biomedical topic diversity largely reflected standardization of article formats.

papers.title: Structured AI ideation yields physical strategies for epithelial barrier repair
papers.abstract: AI systems increasingly support literature analysis, candidate evaluation and hypothesis refinement, but enabling researchers to explore research directions beyond established disciplinary approaches remains challenging. We developed Abelio, an AI system designed to generate novel research directions by expanding investigators' avenues of inquiry. Abelio reformulates research objectives, uses these alternative formulations to identify relevant elements outside conventional disciplinary boundaries, and refines the resulting hypotheses. Each stage integrates divergent exploration with convergent selection through a dedicated subsystem. In quantitative evaluations, proposals generated by the Ideation Core (Abelio's hypothesis-generation core) outperformed those of four frontier large language models in scientific soundness and hypothesis diversity, and three of four in distance from existing literature. Subsystem ablation showed that each subsystem contributes to the property it targets, with the contribution of Element Selection measurable before Refinement. To investigate intestinal epithelial barrier restoration, Abelio proposed physical interventions involving membrane-tethered poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) and cholesterol-anchored complementary DNA. Both proposals were archived before experimentation and subsequently tested independently in damaged Caco-2 monolayers. PEG preserved barrier function in a membrane-surface-dependent manner, whereas complementary DNA enabled sequence-specific restoration that was reversible on demand. These findings demonstrate how structured research ideation can identify experimentally testable approaches beyond established disciplinary conventions.
papers.summary: `Abelio` is an AI system for generating research directions outside a field's usual approaches: it reformulates the research objective, uses the alternative formulations to find relevant elements from other disciplines, and refines the resulting hypotheses, pairing divergent exploration with convergent selection at each stage. Proposals from its `Ideation Core` outperformed those of four frontier large language models on scientific soundness and hypothesis diversity, and three of the four on distance from existing literature. For intestinal epithelial barrier repair it proposed membrane-tethered poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) and cholesterol-anchored complementary DNA, and **both proposals, archived before experimentation, worked when tested independently in damaged `Caco-2` monolayers**. PEG preserved barrier function in a membrane-surface-dependent manner, while complementary DNA gave sequence-specific restoration that was reversible on demand.

papers.title: How Web Research Agents Interpret User Priorities
papers.abstract: Web research agents gather information online and write cited reports, including financial analysis. Users can state a priority to guide this research, but a priority may not say how to judge the options, leaving the agent to choose the criteria. We examine how two such agents, built on OpenAI and Anthropic models, interpret a stated priority. In 36 runs, the agents compared Microsoft and Alphabet as businesses. Prompts asked for special attention to growth or resilience, or gave no priority. We analyzed reports, searches, returned sources and cited sources. Of the 24 reports given a priority, 21 focused on it, but their criteria varied. Under the growth priority, OpenAI reports that ranked the companies accounted for risk or predictability and favored Microsoft, while the Anthropic ones judged growth by its pace and favored Alphabet. Under the resilience priority, reports used partly different criteria, and most named Microsoft as the more resilient company. Of the search and source measures tested, only the Anthropic agent's search wording differed detectably by condition. These findings suggest evaluations should examine the criteria behind a report's judgements, not only its focus or accuracy. Interfaces could let users see and adjust those criteria.
papers.summary: When a user tells a web research agent to prioritize something, the instruction may not say how to judge the options, leaving the agent to pick the criteria. In 36 runs, two agents built on `OpenAI` and `Anthropic` models compared Microsoft and Alphabet as businesses under a growth priority, a resilience priority, or no priority, and the authors analyzed the reports, searches, returned sources, and cited sources. **Of the 24 reports given a priority, 21 focused on it, but the criteria they used varied**: under the growth priority, the OpenAI reports that ranked the companies accounted for risk or predictability and favored Microsoft, while the Anthropic ones judged growth by its pace and favored Alphabet. The authors suggest that evaluations should examine the criteria behind a report's judgements and that interfaces could let users see and adjust them.

papers.title: RagHarnessDebugger: Jev-Guided Agentic RAG in Contract Inference Repair Auditing
papers.abstract:
Agentic systems using retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) must repair their own answers by gathering more evidence, testing alternative policies and deciding if, when, and what repairs are needed. Yet how do we know if a system's repairs are working when metrics like accuracy can be misleading? We present RagHarnessDebugger, a framework that records every repair decision in a Jev-guided harness for contract inference and audits the record to facilitate complete debugging of all decisions taken during a RAG repair journey. RagHarnessDebugger checks that each trace is intact, that each validation applies to the candidate it is counted for, and which answers the acceptance rule can reach. We tested our approach on ContractNLI non-disclosure agreements with two reader models and a replication set of separate contracts. Our debugger's audit layer exposed failure patterns that were hidden under aggregate metrics, policies acceptance cost of repairs vs regressions and policy acceptance gap of 77% and 76% of available but unrealised repairs on development and replication sets. Our audit, together with a labeled error analysis and replay mechanism, allowed following the execution path all the way to the terminal decision - uncovering where missing repairs became lost. Our revised harness improved accuracy over the initial BM25-only baseline by 3.6 points on development contracts and 3.7 points on the replication set, and even improved our full contract access reference score by 1.1 on development and 2.4 on replication set. While our work here demonstrates how the debugger can conduct decision root-cause analysis for missed repairs, the true value lies with providing this debugger for judgment visibility serving continuous improvement of RAG decisions and their explainability.
  Keywords: agentic RAG, AI evidence repair, harness explainability, counterfactual replay, Jev, ContractNLI
papers.summary: Agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems repair their own answers by gathering more evidence and testing alternative policies, but aggregate accuracy can hide whether those repairs actually work. `RagHarnessDebugger` records every repair decision in a Jev-guided harness for contract inference and audits the record, checking that each trace is intact, that each validation applies to the candidate it is counted for, and which answers the acceptance rule can reach. On `ContractNLI` non-disclosure agreements with two reader models, the audit exposed a policy acceptance gap in which **77% and 76% of available repairs went unrealised** on the development and replication sets. The revised harness improved accuracy over the `BM25`-only baseline by 3.6 and 3.7 points on those sets.

papers.title: Residual-Guided Lightweight Reinforcement Learning for Risk-Aware Trajectory Selection with a Frozen World Model
papers.abstract: In automated driving, world models provide future scene predictions for evaluating candidate trajectories, but fixed selection rules may not capture scene-dependent trade-offs. We propose a residual-guided reinforcement learning (RL) framework for lightweight trajectory selection with a frozen world model and a fixed candidate bank. The framework uses proximal policy optimization (PPO) to fine-tune a joint policy over candidate selection and bounded trajectory residuals. A context-conditioned ranking network learns candidate preferences from feedback obtained by evaluating local perturbations of the selected trajectories. At inference, the selector combines learned preference and predicted risk ranks using fixed weights and returns the selected candidate trajectory without modification. Fine-tuning updates 16,106 parameters across the actor and critic, while the deployed selector retains only the 11,725-parameter ranking network, with the residual branch and critic used exclusively during training. In open-loop evaluation on the nuScenes validation set, the method reduces average Euclidean trajectory error (L2) by 3.99% relative to the RiskWorld model baseline without RL-based selection. Under matched budgets for feedback accesses and actor updates, residual exploration reduces L2 by 0.83% relative to the categorical PPO variant trained without residuals. The method also maintains lower L2 than RiskWorld when risk features are removed or shuffled.
papers.summary: In automated driving, world models predict future scenes for scoring candidate trajectories, but fixed selection rules may miss scene-dependent trade-offs. The proposed framework keeps the world model frozen and uses proximal policy optimization (PPO) to fine-tune a joint policy over candidate selection and bounded trajectory residuals, while a context-conditioned ranking network learns candidate preferences from perturbation feedback. Only the 11,725-parameter ranking network is kept at deployment, and in open-loop evaluation on the `nuScenes` validation set the method **reduces average Euclidean trajectory error (L2) by 3.99%** relative to the `RiskWorld` baseline without learned selection. Under matched budgets, residual exploration reduces L2 by a further 0.83% relative to a categorical PPO variant trained without residuals.

papers.title: NVIDIA Kumo Tabular: Pushing the Accuracy$\unicode{8211}$Efficiency Frontier for Tabular Prediction
papers.abstract: We introduce Kumo Tabular, a family of open tabular foundation models for classification and regression, in three sizes: Kumo Tabular-S (27M parameters), Kumo Tabular-M (61M), and Kumo Tabular-L (214M). Pretrained only on artificial tables from the Kumo prior, they can make predictions on new tables without any training. In our approach, a table encoder compresses each row into an embedding, and an in-context learning transformer predicts the unlabeled rows from the labeled ones. Kumo Tabular introduces architectural innovations that improve both training stability and predictive performance, enabling the model to scale up to 150M cells on modern GPUs. Kumo Tabular-L ranks first on eight benchmarks: TabArena, TALENT, BeyondArena, ScoringBench, STRABLE, MulTaBench, RamanBench, and TabBench-Bio. These cover probabilistic regression, tables with over 1M rows or 100K columns, and tables with strings, text, or images. Accuracy improves with model size in all tested comparisons. All three sizes lie on the accuracy-speed frontiers of TabArena and BeyondArena. Kumo Tabular-L predicts faster than the runners-up, LimiX-2 on TabArena (36 times) and TabPFN-3.5 on BeyondArena (1.7 times). Weights and pretraining code are released under OpenMDW-1.1 and Apache 2.0, respectively.
papers.summary: `Kumo Tabular` is a family of open tabular foundation models for classification and regression in three sizes: `Kumo Tabular-S` (27M parameters), `Kumo Tabular-M` (61M), and `Kumo Tabular-L` (214M). Pretrained only on artificial tables, they predict on new tables without any training: a table encoder compresses each row into an embedding and an in-context learning transformer predicts the unlabeled rows from the labeled ones, scaling up to 150M cells on modern GPUs. `Kumo Tabular-L` **ranks first on eight benchmarks**, including `TabArena`, `TALENT`, and `BeyondArena`, and predicts 36 times faster than `LimiX-2` on `TabArena` and 1.7 times faster than `TabPFN-3.5` on `BeyondArena`. Weights and pretraining code are released under OpenMDW-1.1 and Apache 2.0 respectively.

papers.title: PhysScope: Agentic Multimodal Physics Reasoning with Grounded Visual Memory
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can correctly interpret physics diagrams yet apply constraints outside the states or conditions in which they hold, causing premise errors to propagate through subsequent calculations. We introduce PhysScope, an inference-time visual harness that supports self-correction of these scope mismatches without updating model weights. PhysScope enables the model to link physical scopes directly to its visual observations and explicitly constructs derived views to support reasoning. The harness imposes explicit constraints on state distinctions, conditions, and physical scopes during model reasoning, and checks agent-proposed revisions against sources and scopes. Accepted revisions invalidate registered dependents, thereby maintaining scope-aware working memory. On PhysAlign, PhysScope achieves higher solving scores than direct solving across all six evaluated VLMs. With Gemini-3.8-flash, it outperforms Canvas-CoT by 9.34 percentage points and substantially improves solving accuracy on the out-of-distribution (OOD) PhysUniBench benchmark. Ablation studies support explicit scope management and dependency maintenance as design principles for multimodal physics reasoning agents.
papers.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) can read a physics diagram correctly and still apply a constraint outside the states or conditions where it holds, so the faulty premise propagates through later calculations. `PhysScope` is an inference-time harness, requiring no weight updates, that links physical scopes to the model's visual observations, builds derived views, checks agent-proposed revisions against sources and scopes, and invalidates dependent results when a revision is accepted. On `PhysAlign` it scores higher than direct solving across all six evaluated VLMs, and with `Gemini-3.8-flash` it **outperforms `Canvas-CoT` by 9.34 percentage points**. It also improves solving accuracy on the out-of-distribution `PhysUniBench` benchmark.

papers.title: PeriaTrace: Tooth-Level Grounding Diagnosis and Patient-Facing Explanations from Periapical Radiographs
papers.abstract: Periapical radiographs (PRs) are central to endodontic diagnosis, but interpreting them and preparing reports are time-consuming. Technical language can limit patients' understanding, while existing automated methods often lack tooth-level links between findings and image evidence. We present PeriaTrace, a three-stage framework integrating tooth-level diagnosis, visually grounded report generation, and patient-friendly explanations and care recommendations. PeriaTrace was developed and evaluated using 12,877 PRs from an internal dataset and two external clinical cohorts. In internal evaluation, it achieved a macro Dice coefficient of 85.35%, BLEU-4 of 0.6504, an F1 score of 94.37% for joint tooth localization and F\'ed\'eration Dentaire Internationale (FDI) identification, and a grounding-tag F1 score of 77.93%. In the two external cohorts, senior endodontists considered 91.16% and 84.52% of reports suitable for retention or revision without complete rewriting. Generation averaged 4.41 seconds per PR, several tens of times faster than manual drafting. Among 196 survey participants without medical backgrounds, 96.4% preferred reports with plain-language explanations and care recommendations, and 84.7% found visual localization cues helpful. PeriaTrace may enable faster, evidence-traceable reporting while supporting clinical review and patient communication. (Abridged version)
papers.summary: Interpreting periapical radiographs (PRs) and writing reports is time-consuming for endodontists, and existing automated methods often lack tooth-level links between findings and image evidence. `PeriaTrace` is a three-stage framework combining tooth-level diagnosis, visually grounded report generation, and patient-friendly explanations with care recommendations, developed and evaluated on 12,877 PRs from an internal dataset and two external clinical cohorts. Internally it reached a macro Dice coefficient of 85.35% and an F1 score of 94.37% for joint tooth localization and Fédération Dentaire Internationale (FDI) identification, and in the external cohorts senior endodontists judged **91.16% and 84.52% of reports suitable for retention or revision without complete rewriting**. Generation averaged 4.41 seconds per radiograph, and 96.4% of 196 surveyed participants without medical backgrounds preferred reports with plain-language explanations.

papers.title: TPHC: Improving Hyper-Connections with Tensor-Parallel Grouped Updates
papers.abstract: Hyper-Connections (HC) expand the residual stream of a Transformer into $N$ parallel streams, and manifold-constrained HC (mHC) stabilizes them at scale. However, mHC benefits little from more than four streams, partly because each sublayer writes a single output to all streams, limiting how differently they can be updated. In this work, we propose TPHC, which integrates tensor-parallel (TP) shards with HC streams to promote greater independence across streams. Specifically, we route a separate mixture of the residual streams to each TP shard and keep the individual shard outputs separate during write-back, so each stream can receive a different mixture of those outputs. This design makes the residual-stream updates more expressive without adding parameters or FLOPs to the attention or FFN sublayers. With native support for stream sharding under TP, TPHC requires only 9% more training time than mHC on an 8B model when both use four streams. Increasing the number of streams from four to sixteen raises its training time by only 19%. On a 1.1B model trained on 100B tokens, TPHC reduces validation loss by 0.7-1.0% and raises average zero-shot accuracy across six commonsense reasoning benchmarks by 0.3-0.7 percentage points relative to mHC at matched stream counts $N\in\{4,8,16\}$. Our code is available at https://github.com/wuyou2002/TPHC.
papers.summary: Hyper-Connections (HC) expand a Transformer's residual stream into N parallel streams, and manifold-constrained HC (`mHC`) stabilizes them at scale, but `mHC` gains little beyond four streams, partly because each sublayer writes a single output to all streams. `TPHC` routes a separate mixture of the residual streams to each tensor-parallel (TP) shard and keeps the shard outputs separate during write-back, so each stream receives a different mixture without adding parameters or FLOPs to the attention or feed-forward sublayers. On a 1.1B model trained on 100B tokens, it **reduces validation loss by 0.7-1.0% relative to `mHC`** at matched stream counts of 4, 8, and 16, and raises average zero-shot accuracy across six commonsense reasoning benchmarks by 0.3-0.7 percentage points. It needs 9% more training time than `mHC` on an 8B model with four streams.

papers.title: Check Your Blind Spots: Decision-Guided Perception by Probing the Planner with Hypothetical Objects
papers.abstract: Not every perception error changes the planner's action. Yet adaptive-resolution perception chooses where to spend high-resolution computation from image cues, which can neither reliably point to an object that low resolution missed nor tell which objects matter to the planner. We observe that the planner can say where an object would matter before anything is seen: inserting a hypothetical object at a location tests whether its action would change. Decision-Guided Speculative Perception (DGSP) treats the low-resolution scene and its action as a draft and probes the planner in this way to obtain a decision-sensitivity field, the locations where an unseen object would change the action. Only this field and the support, the detections on which the current action rests, are verified at high resolution, repeatedly until the action is stable. For two planner classes, we prove that DGSP returns exactly the action of whole-frame high-resolution perception if crop detections match whole-frame ones and the crops cover the field, conditions that real images meet approximately. On three driving datasets, it reproduces this action on about 98% of frames with about a quarter of the pixels. At the pixel cost of uniform downscaling, it repairs more of the draft's disagreements with this action, brakes falsely less often, and recovers many more of the decision-relevant objects that the draft misses.
papers.summary: Adaptive-resolution perception decides where to spend high-resolution computation from image cues, which can neither reliably find objects that low resolution missed nor tell which objects matter to the planner. Decision-Guided Speculative Perception (`DGSP`) treats the low-resolution scene and its action as a draft, then inserts hypothetical objects to probe the planner and map the locations where an unseen object would change the action; only those locations and the detections supporting the current action are verified at high resolution, repeating until the action is stable. For two planner classes the authors prove it returns exactly the action of whole-frame high-resolution perception under stated conditions on crop detections and coverage. On three driving datasets it **reproduces that action on about 98% of frames with about a quarter of the pixels**.

papers.title: Storing the Gemma 4 K=V Cache Once: Exact Global-KV Memory Savings in a Paged Serving Engine with Unchanged Attention Kernels
papers.abstract: In the global attention layers of Gemma 4 31B, the value is the normalized key projection, and the key is the value scaled by a fixed weight, with rotary position encoding on one quarter of its dimensions. The Gemma 4 report states that this design reduces the global KV cache by up to 37.5%, but the open serving engines that we checked still store a full key and a full value: 1,024 values per KV head and token. We store one 640-value row instead, exact in real arithmetic, and an unchanged paged attention kernel reads it through two overlapping strided views as its key cache and its value cache. In a vLLM prototype with the 16-bit 31B model, the outputs are bit-identical to an emulation of the same arithmetic on the stock cache, 2 of 432 final answers differ from the stock engine (within its run-to-run noise), and the steady decode KV memory per request falls by a factor of 1.34 to 1.40 at 32K to 64K tokens. On a prefill/decode pair of two A100 GPUs with NIXL transfer and CPU offload, a decode engine with a full 15 GiB pool ran 1.38 times the stock decode tokens per step for 16K-token prompts (repeated to 0.06%) and 1.24 times for 8K-token prompts; a model of the vLLM block pool predicted both ratios to within 1% (the engine was 0.7% to 0.9% higher) and matched the change between them. The eager decode throughput rose by 1.30 and 1.11 times, and on this path the compact engine gave the same output tokens as the emulation for 8 prompts at batch 1. The run-time prototype makes an eager step 4% to 9% slower at equal batch, and the method does not yet stack with an 8-bit KV cache at the default scale.
papers.summary: In the global attention layers of `Gemma 4` 31B the value is the normalized key projection, so key and value are redundant, yet the open serving engines the authors checked still store both in full at 1,024 values per KV head and token. Their approach stores a single 640-value row and lets an unchanged paged attention kernel read it through two overlapping strided views as its key cache and value cache. In a `vLLM` prototype, outputs are bit-identical to an emulation of the same arithmetic on the stock cache, and **steady decode KV memory per request falls by a factor of 1.34 to 1.40 at 32K to 64K tokens**. On two A100 GPUs split into prefill and decode, a decode engine with a full 15 GiB pool ran 1.38 times the stock decode tokens per step for 16K-token prompts, though the prototype makes an eager step 4% to 9% slower at equal batch and does not yet stack with an 8-bit KV cache.

papers.title: When Anchors Shift the Target: Advantage-Gated Adaptation for Diffusion Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Forward-process reinforcement learning adapts diffusion and flow-matching models by re-noising rewarded generations into regression targets. Because negative advantages induce concave updates with unbounded repulsive gradients, existing methods stabilize training using cached predictions from a moving policy copy, yet these anchors also alter what positive feedback teaches the model to fit. We formalize this conflict as anchor coupling: after separating frozen-reference regularizers, affine moving-anchor rules cannot eliminate negative curvature while preserving every positive regression target. We propose Advantage-Gated Adaptation (AGA) to decouple these roles. Positive samples retain standard target fitting, whose self-limiting update vanishes at the observed target independently of the moving anchor. Negative samples instead use the first-order tangent of the concave objective at the moving-policy prediction, preserving the local repulsion direction with a prediction-independent gradient. Within the quadratic-anchor family, these requirements uniquely determine the parameter-free gate $\omega(a)=\max(-a,0)$. Because the moving copy provides local linearization rather than retention, AGA assigns long-horizon behavior preservation to a frozen pretrained reference regularized at its operating classifier-free guidance scale, interpreted through an implicit-reward lens. Across compositional generation, text rendering, and preference alignment, our experiments show that displacing positive targets degrades visual quality and heightens sensitivity to policy-copy schedules, whereas AGA consistently improves the reward--quality trade-off.
papers.summary: Forward-process reinforcement learning adapts diffusion and flow-matching models by re-noising rewarded generations into regression targets, and existing methods stabilize the unbounded repulsive gradients from negative advantages using cached predictions from a moving policy copy. The authors formalize a conflict they call anchor coupling: **affine moving-anchor rules cannot eliminate negative curvature while preserving every positive regression target**. Advantage-Gated Adaptation (`AGA`) separates the two roles by keeping standard target fitting for positive samples and using the first-order tangent of the concave objective for negative ones, while a frozen pretrained reference handles long-horizon behavior preservation. Across compositional generation, text rendering, and preference alignment, `AGA` improves the reward-quality trade-off, whereas displacing positive targets degrades visual quality.

papers.title: Variance Restoration over Covariance Rank: Memory-Budgeted Analytic Continual Learning
papers.abstract: Analytic continual learning replaces iterative gradient updates with closed-form ridge regression over frozen pre-trained representations, summarizing all past sessions in two running sufficient statistics: the feature autocorrelation matrix $\Sigma_t$ and the class cross-correlation matrix $\Gamma_t$. Lifting backbone features into a wide random code of dimension $M \gg D$ substantially improves linear separability across tasks, but forces $\Sigma_t$ to grow quadratically as $\mathcal{O}(M^2)$. Under a fixed persistent memory envelope $\Bcal$, a learner faces a fundamental structural trade-off: store exact pairwise co-activations inside a narrower feature code, or expand to a wide code while compressing cross-coordinate interactions. We observe that the coordinate self-variances $v_t = \diag(\Sigma_t)$ and class statistics $\Gamma_t$ grow only linearly with $M$, whereas off-diagonal interactions dominate memory. We introduce \method (\textbf{Co}ordinate-\textbf{Re}stored \textbf{A}nalytic \textbf{C}ontinual \textbf{L}earning), which retains $(v_t, \Gamma_t)$ exactly, maintains off-diagonal co-activations through a streaming rank-$q$ factor $F_t$, restores exact diagonal variances via $\Sighat_t = F_t^\top F_t + \Diag(v_t - \diag(F_t^\top F_t))$, and solves the full $M\times C$ normal equations via the Woodbury identity. Across five class-incremental benchmarks on frozen ViT-B/16, \method matches dense full-covariance readouts within $0.09$ points while cutting persistent state by $90.7\%$ ($35.9$ vs.\ $385.3$ MiB). Under equal memory envelopes of $16$--$80$ MiB, prioritizing expansion width $M$ over covariance rank $q$ outperforms exact narrow readouts in $17$ of $18$ configurations by up to $+2.19$ points.
papers.summary: Analytic continual learning replaces gradient updates with closed-form ridge regression over frozen pretrained features, but lifting those features into a wide random code makes the stored feature autocorrelation matrix grow quadratically with code width. Coordinate-Restored Analytic Continual Learning keeps the per-coordinate variances and class statistics exactly, tracks off-diagonal interactions with a streaming low-rank factor, restores the exact diagonal, and solves the normal equations through the Woodbury identity. Across five class-incremental benchmarks on a frozen `ViT-B/16`, it matches dense full-covariance readouts within 0.09 points while **cutting persistent state by 90.7%** (35.9 versus 385.3 MiB). Under equal memory budgets of 16 to 80 MiB, favoring a wider code over higher covariance rank beats exact narrow readouts in 17 of 18 configurations.

papers.title: Uncovering the Invisible in Routine Radiology: Cross-Modal Detection of MRI-Verified Soft-Tissue Pathologies from CBCT via Physics-Guided 3D Self-Supervised Learning
papers.abstract: Routine X-ray modalities like cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) are optimized for high-contrast mineralized tissues, leaving soft-tissue abnormalities buried beneath photon noise and below human visual perception. Thus, detecting non-calcified pathologies requires secondary magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). We demonstrate that sub-visual radiographic signatures of soft-tissue pathology are physically preserved within routine CBCT scans and can be extracted for opportunistic screening using a targeted, physics-guided deep learning pipeline, even under extreme paired-data scarcity. Using the temporomandibular joint (TMJ) as a model system (N = 212 paired CBCT-MRI joints), we address the severe overfitting of high-capacity 3D networks through a two-stage framework. First, we employ a frozen full-grid 3D masked autoencoder (BertsWin) pre-trained on 6,550 unlabeled CBCT volumes via the GradientConductor (GCond) optimizer and an anatomy-aware objective (PhysLoss) redirecting gradient flow into the [-300, 300] HU soft-tissue window. Second, automated localization of the condylar zenith drives a deterministic 3D cropping that eliminates 81% of background osseous variance. Evaluated via a patient-isolated 3x10-fold stratified cross-validation protocol, a statistically robust sub-visual signal for MRI-verified synovial effusion (ROC AUC = 0.793) emerges exclusively from representations pre-trained with the PhysLoss and GCond regime. Crucially, only this setup captures true 3D anatomical chirality (p < 0.001) and high intra-patient structural consistency (0.791) over inter-patient noise; conversely, identical architectures pre-trained with standard L2 loss or unmasked variance decomposition (MVC) collapse to random guessing. These findings establish a generalizable paradigm for repurposing routine, low-contrast radiographic scans into opportunistic screening tools for occult soft-tissue disease.
papers.summary: Cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) is tuned for mineralized tissue, so soft-tissue abnormalities normally require a follow-up magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan. Using 212 paired CBCT-MRI temporomandibular joints (TMJ), the authors pair a frozen 3D masked autoencoder (`BertsWin`), pretrained on 6,550 unlabeled CBCT volumes with the `GradientConductor` optimizer and an anatomy-aware `PhysLoss` objective focused on the soft-tissue intensity window, with deterministic cropping around the condyle that removes 81% of background bone variance. Under patient-isolated cross-validation, the resulting representations **detect MRI-verified synovial effusion with a ROC AUC of 0.793**. Identical architectures pretrained with a standard L2 loss collapse to random guessing.

papers.title: ForecastGym: A Live, Controlled, and Replayable Benchmark for Forecasting Agents
papers.abstract: Agents built on large language models (LLMs) increasingly forecast real-world events by searching the Web and reasoning over what they find. How well such an agent forecasts depends on both the retrieved evidence and the model, making control over that evidence essential for evaluation. Live evaluations can mix retrieval with reasoning when each system searches on its own, while retrospective search can leak later information through date filters or today's ranking of historical pages. Comparing models, search sources, and memory strategies requires both fixed evidence and a record of how it evolved before resolution. We introduce ForecastGym, which records what four commercial web search APIs return for open prediction-market questions every two days and replays this frozen evidence offline once outcomes are known, comparing models, memory, and captured search sources under a fixed evidence-acquisition policy. Its first release covers 150 questions, 614 evidence states, one per question and collection time, and 131k search results. Rerunning the same queries after settlement returns results that all but state the outcome for up to 92% of the questions, despite the tested date filters. On the frozen evidence, all tested LLMs trail the market in forecasting accuracy. Our diagnostic analysis suggests that missed public information contributes more to the gap in high-gap states than misreading does. Switching the search API changes a model's Brier score by up to 0.043, more than the spread across models, while persistent notes score similarly to rereading all evidence at half the input tokens. The evidence a forecaster sees can matter as much as the model that reads it.
papers.summary: Evaluating forecasting agents built on large language models (LLMs) is confounded by retrieval: live evaluations mix search with reasoning, and retrospective search leaks later information. `ForecastGym` records what four commercial web search APIs return for open prediction-market questions every two days and replays that frozen evidence offline once outcomes are known; its first release covers 150 questions, 614 evidence states, and 131k search results. Rerunning the same queries after settlement returns results that all but state the outcome for up to 92% of questions despite date filters, and on the frozen evidence all tested LLMs trail the market in forecasting accuracy. **Switching the search API changes a model's Brier score by up to 0.043, more than the spread across models**, while persistent notes score similarly to rereading all evidence at half the input tokens.

papers.title: Reversing the text is not reversing the path: a fixed-text measure without a zero, and an assembly-order comparison that vanishes identically
papers.abstract:
For an ensemble of trajectories the fluctuation theorems give the entropy production its meaning and zero. The same expression has recently been evaluated on one fixed text, $\Delta = [\log P(x) - \log P(\tilde x)]/L$ with $\tilde x$ the text in reversed order, read as an entropy production separating causally from arbitrarily ordered prose. A single text is neither a distribution nor a dynamics, and the texts at issue were produced by other models. No theorem fixes where the zero of a fixed-text quantity lies: the expression carries over from an ensemble, its zero does not.
  We supply a zero from an exact antisymmetry. Scoring a text's $n$ sentences in all $n!$ orders, reversal carries $\pi$ to $\pi \circ \mathrm{rev}$, a measure-preserving involution, so $\Delta(\pi) = -\Delta(\pi \circ \mathrm{rev})$ identically and the values are centred at zero for any score. The authored arrangement's midrank is then unitless, bounded, and 0.50 for a score blind to order. Across five autoregressive evaluators from 124M to 4B parameters, and taking the prompt-defined labels at face value, 8% to 15% of the median midrank's distance from the null is attributable to causal order and the rest to the arrangement being the order the passage was produced in.
  The thermodynamic reading needs a comparison whose zero does hold on the text read, and a masked model supplies one: the any-order chain rule gives a genuine log-probability, and its left-to-right and right-to-left orders for one text give $\sigma$, a comparison of two assembly orders. Both run from the empty sequence to the same text, so it is not a path against its time reverse. It vanishes identically when the evaluator's conditionals come from a joint, and a non-zero reading reports the evaluator's incompatibility, not the text. Neither is a fixed-text entropy production, for different reasons.
papers.summary: Recent work scores a single text and its reversed version under a language model and reads the per-token log-probability difference as an entropy production that separates causally ordered from arbitrarily ordered prose; the authors argue that a single fixed text is neither a distribution nor a dynamics, so no theorem fixes where that quantity's zero lies. They supply a zero by scoring a text's sentences in all possible orders, where reversal is a measure-preserving involution that centres the values at zero, and across five autoregressive evaluators from 124M to 4B parameters **only 8% to 15% of the median midrank's distance from the null is attributable to causal order**, with the rest due to the arrangement being the order in which the passage was produced. A second comparison, between left-to-right and right-to-left assembly orders under a masked model, vanishes identically when the evaluator's conditionals come from a joint distribution, so a non-zero reading reports the evaluator's incompatibility and not a property of the text. Neither measure is a fixed-text entropy production.

papers.title: Magflow: Differentiable Simulation of Industrial-Grade 6D Magnetic Levitation
papers.abstract: Magnetic levitation with six-degrees-of-freedom enables frictionless transport and micrometer-scale positioning in principle, but low-level control is inherently challenging due to its complex and unstable dynamics. Industrial systems typically rely on deep hardware-software co-design, where mover and stator geometries are jointly designed to enable a compact, hand-crafted approximation of the electromagnetic force computation, thereby keeping control computationally tractable at kilohertz rates. However, this approach imposes overly conservative constraints on the operating workspace and the range of supported mover topologies. Instead of reducing the underlying physics to a hand-crafted approximation, we compute the physics directly. We introduce Magflow, a fully differentiable, GPU-parallel simulator for 6D magnetic levitation. It is used to train the first neural controller for an industrial-grade 6D magnetic levitation system that is learned purely from simulated physics. We show that the learned neural controller transfers zero-shot from simulation to real hardware while satisfying hard real-time constraints at 4 kHz. The learned controller achieves qualitatively new behaviors and even levitates a mover topology for which no hand-crafted solution exists. These results demonstrate that co-design is not a physical necessity for 6D magnetic levitation control. More broadly, control learning from simulated physics can find solutions beyond the reach of control engineering in demanding industrial domains. Source code and demonstration videos are publicly available at https://sites.google.com/view/magflow.
papers.summary: Six-degree-of-freedom magnetic levitation is normally controlled with hand-crafted approximations of the electromagnetic forces, which requires the mover and stator to be designed together and restricts the workspace and the mover shapes that can be supported. `Magflow` is a fully differentiable, GPU-parallel simulator that computes the physics directly and is used to train a neural controller purely in simulation. The learned controller **transfers zero-shot to real industrial hardware while meeting hard real-time constraints at 4 kHz**, and it levitates a mover topology for which no hand-crafted solution exists.

papers.title: ReTouchGS: Ultralight Render-free Aesthetic Color Enhancement and Transfer for 3D Gaussian Splatting
papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables photorealistic scene reconstruction. Existing 3DGS color transfer and interactive editing methods are guided by reference images and user-specified color adjustments. However, in many applications, users simply want aesthetically guided color enhancement that automatically makes the scene more visually appealing while maintaining consistent colors and tones across viewpoints. We present ReTouchGS, to our knowledge the first framework for reference-free aesthetic color enhancement of pretrained 3DGS models. It predicts a scene-level color lookup table (LUT) from the model and its associated camera parameters. ReTouchGS also supports reference-guided color transfer by fitting a scene-level LUT using one edited view of the same scene and its corresponding original render. A shared blend-aware color refinement network with only 44.7K parameters refines an analytic color update to realize either color mapping without rendering. It preserves geometry and delivers standard 3DGS assets in seconds. We also design the ReTouch3D benchmark to support the evaluation of aesthetic color enhancement and reference-guided color transfer across viewpoints. Experiments demonstrate high color accuracy and strong generalization to unseen scenes in both aesthetic color enhancement and reference-guided color transfer.
papers.summary: Existing color editing methods for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes need a reference image or manual color adjustments, whereas many users simply want the scene to look better automatically and consistently across viewpoints. `ReTouchGS` predicts a scene-level color lookup table (LUT) from a pretrained 3DGS model and its camera parameters, and can also fit a LUT from one edited view for reference-guided color transfer. A shared refinement network with **only 44.7K parameters** applies either color mapping without rendering, preserving geometry and producing standard 3DGS assets in seconds. The authors also introduce the `ReTouch3D` benchmark and report high color accuracy and generalization to unseen scenes.

papers.title: FrameRouter: Frame Budget Routing for Long-Video Understanding on Video-MME-v2 and Beyond
papers.abstract: Long-video question answering benchmarks like Video-MME-v2 typically evaluate systems under a uniform frame budget for every question, despite stark variation in the evidence each query actually demands. We analyze this mismatch on Video-MME-v2 and find that different question subsets prefer different frozen frame-budget policies, while uniformly increasing the frame count does not reliably improve all metrics. These findings motivate fixed-mean frame-budget routing, a controlled inference setting in which each question may receive a different frame budget while the average budget matches a uniform reference. We introduce FrameRouter, a training-free test-time framework that combines an evidence-demand router, a budget-constrained allocation rule, and a frozen bank of frame-sampling policies. By controlling how much visual evidence each question receives while leaving the underlying samplers unchanged, FrameRouter is orthogonal to query-aware frame selection. Across Video-MME-v2 and several long-video understanding benchmarks, FrameRouter improves long-video question answering by using the same average visual budget more selectively across questions. Code is available at https://github.com/bingjunluo/FrameRouter.
papers.summary: Long-video question answering benchmarks give every question the same number of frames, even though questions differ widely in how much visual evidence they need. An analysis on `Video-MME-v2` finds that **different question subsets prefer different frame-budget policies, and uniformly adding frames does not reliably improve all metrics**. `FrameRouter` is a training-free test-time framework that combines an evidence-demand router, a budget-constrained allocation rule, and a frozen bank of frame-sampling policies, so each question gets its own budget while the average matches a uniform reference. It improves results on `Video-MME-v2` and several other long-video benchmarks and is designed to be orthogonal to query-aware frame selection.

papers.title: Deep Reinforcement Learning for Heat Pump and Underfloor Heating Control: An End-to-End Case Study
papers.abstract: Efficient control of underfloor heating (UFH) systems coupled with heat pumps (HPs) is challenging due to the high thermal inertia of buildings and the slow dynamic response of UFH systems. Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) offers a data-driven control approach capable of simultaneously optimizing energy consumption and thermal comfort. However, the application of DRL-based controllers in occupied buildings under real operating conditions remains limited. This work presents and end-to-end case study (development, evaluation, and real-world deployment) of a DRL-based controller for an integrated UFH-HP system. First, a simulation-based pilot study was conducted to assess different DRL algorithms, control strategies, and configurations. Subsequently, a digital twin of a real residential building was developed and used to train DRL agents under simulated operating conditions. The best-performing agent was then deployed in the physical building without additional online fine-tuning. The results show that the controller successfully maintained indoor temperatures within the prescribed comfort limits while dynamically adjusting the HP supply temperature and UFH valve positions. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of deploying DRL controllers in occupied buildings and highlight their robustness and the practical challenges associated with transferring control policies from digital environments to real heating systems.
papers.summary: Controlling underfloor heating (UFH) coupled with heat pumps (HPs) is hard because buildings have high thermal inertia and the heating system responds slowly, and deep reinforcement learning (DRL) controllers have rarely been tested in occupied buildings. This case study covers the full path: a simulation pilot comparing DRL algorithms and control strategies, a digital twin of a real residential building used for training, and deployment of the best agent in the physical building. The controller was **deployed without any online fine-tuning and kept indoor temperatures within the prescribed comfort limits** while adjusting the heat pump supply temperature and valve positions. The authors also discuss the practical difficulties of transferring policies from digital environments to real heating systems.

papers.title: Values Shape What Self-Improving Coding Agents Build
papers.abstract: Self-improving agents are typically optimized for the results they produce, with less attention to how they produce them. Their instructions give designers limited ways to shape how they work, especially when the task is open-ended. This paper studies whether a short value statement in an agent's persistent instruction file changes not only how well the agent performs but also what it builds. Four higher-order value types in Schwartz's theory of basic human values were evaluated: openness to change, conservation, self-enhancement, and self-transcendence. Across diverse coding tasks, the values were held fixed within each run over multiple iterations of self-improvement. Three findings emerged: (1) Values matter for performance across a diverse set of tasks. The openness values increase performance on held-out data, whereas the opposite conservation values result in scores below those of an agent given no values. (2) Values change what agents build, producing solution algorithms that differ in size, complexity and approach. (3) Human oversight is still needed for designing values. Allowing the agent to revise its own values narrows the differences between sets of values, and values distilled from the AI literature provide no detectable gain over having no values. Properly designed values can thus influence what a self-improving coding agent builds and, where the task permits, how well it performs.
papers.summary: Designers have few ways to shape how a self-improving coding agent works on open-ended tasks, so this study tests whether a short value statement in the agent's persistent instruction file changes what it builds as well as how well it performs. Four higher-order value types from Schwartz's theory of basic human values were held fixed across multiple self-improvement iterations on diverse coding tasks. **Openness-to-change values raised performance on held-out data, while conservation values scored below an agent given no values at all**, and the different values produced solutions that differed in size, complexity, and approach. Letting the agent revise its own values narrowed these differences, and values distilled from the AI literature gave no detectable gain over having none.

papers.title: The Resolution Hypothesis: Agent Evolution's Key Is Identifying Improvements
papers.abstract: Agent evolution follows a simple loop: a proposer writes candidate artifacts (prompts, skills, memories) and selection accepts those that score higher. This loop has shown promise, yet practitioners face a puzzle: methods trade wins across papers, and evolution often fails to bootstrap on certain tasks. We trace this puzzle to the Resolution Hypothesis: agent evolution stalls not because methods fail to propose better artifacts, but because noisy evaluations cannot reliably identify them. Across seven evolution methods and six models (over 10M LLM calls), we find support for the hypothesis at both levels where evaluation scores are used. At the candidate level (choosing artifacts), helpful candidate artifacts exist, but selection is no better than random at telling them from harmful ones, so errors accumulate across rounds. At the method level (ranking methods), typical margins of a few percentage points are smaller than the difference between two independent runs of the same method, so published rankings often rest on luck. Together, these findings indicate that agent evolution is often bottlenecked by reliably identifying improvements. This calls for a shift in how we develop and evaluate self-improving agents, from designing ever more candidate improvement systems to making true improvements detectable and accumulable.
papers.summary: Agent evolution loops, in which a proposer writes candidate prompts, skills, or memories and selection keeps the ones that score higher, give inconsistent results across papers and often fail to bootstrap. The authors propose the Resolution Hypothesis: evolution stalls because noisy evaluations cannot reliably identify better artifacts, not because none are proposed. Across seven evolution methods and six models, using over 10M LLM calls, helpful candidates exist but **selection is no better than random at telling helpful artifacts from harmful ones**, so errors accumulate over rounds. At the method level, typical margins of a few percentage points are smaller than the gap between two independent runs of the same method, so published rankings often rest on luck.

papers.title: Amortizing Tempered Sampling with Corrected Self-Training
papers.abstract: Learning a neural sampler can reduce the cost of repeated sampling from an un-normalized distribution, but obtaining good training data remains difficult. We develop a corrected self-training scheme across a sequence of tempered targets, making use of importance sampling and Markov chain Monte Carlo to correct the samples and replay buffers to store them. We introduce Sequential Score Sampler (SSS) as a particular case. In SSS, the proposal is a score-based diffusion trained by regression on energy gradients; and the samples are corrected by importance weights on the path space. After training, samples can be collected directly from the model, from its importance-corrected proposals, or from the final-temperature buffer. The method amortizes repeated sampling by encoding the global structure of the target in the model. SSS achieves competitive sampling accuracy across the benchmarks and, on several targets, uses shorter runtimes with fewer energy evaluations than competing samplers.

papers.title: Runtime Verification of Multiple Natural Language Criteria for Agent Governance
papers.abstract: AI agents are governed by hundreds of natural language criteria, yet existing verifiers cannot efficiently evaluate an agent's output against a large set of such criteria and report which are satisfied, violated, or inapplicable. We introduce the VFM, a tree-attention verifier that encodes the shared context and target text, and scores N natural language criteria in parallel, returning independent per-criterion ternary verdicts. The VFM is pretrained on CriteriaBank, a corpus of 394K (context, target, criterion, verdict) tuples spanning over 321K distinct criterion strings. A finetuned VFM-4B outperforms GPT-5.4 on a synthetic governance benchmark. On the DynaBench multi-criterion benchmark, it outperforms DynaGuard-4B on trace-level failure detection, and its per-criterion verdicts localize the violated rule and support focused escalation to a larger chain-of-thought judge. We show that CriteriaBank pretraining improves cross-domain transfer, particularly in the low-data regime, while matching a strong direct-finetuning control at full data. On a single H100, VFM-4B evaluates 1,000 criteria against a 4K-token context in under 2s at <11 GB VRAM, making it suitable for runtime verification.
papers.summary: AI agents are often governed by hundreds of natural language criteria, but existing verifiers cannot efficiently check an output against a large set of them and report which are satisfied, violated, or inapplicable. `VFM` is a tree-attention verifier that encodes the shared context and target text once and scores many criteria in parallel with independent ternary verdicts, pretrained on `CriteriaBank`, a corpus of 394K labeled tuples. A finetuned `VFM-4B` outperforms `GPT-5.4` on a synthetic governance benchmark and beats `DynaGuard-4B` on trace-level failure detection on `DynaBench`. On a single H100 it **evaluates 1,000 criteria against a 4K-token context in under 2 seconds using less than 11 GB of VRAM**.

papers.title: Pareto-Informed Smart "Predict, then Optimize" for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Problems
papers.abstract: Many real-world planning applications, from logistics, routing to resource allocation, give rise to optimization problems that need to balance multiple, conflicting objectives. While machine learning is often used to predict the unknown parameters or costs of these problems, standard models trained on prediction accuracy can lead to suboptimal plans. Decision-Focused Learning (DFL) addresses this by integrating the downstream optimization task into the training objective. However, existing DFL methods for multi-objective problems rely on simple scalarization, which fails to capture the rich trade-offs of the Pareto Frontier. To address this gap, we propose a Pareto-aware extension to single-objective Smart "Predict, then Optimize" (SPO+) for multi-objective combinatorial optimization problems. Our loss function leverages the true Pareto Frontier, forming a target decision that aligns with a sampled preference vector, and minimizes regret against this target. Experiments on multi-objective shortest path and multi-objective knapsack problems show that our approach outperforms traditional two-stage Mean Squared Error (MSE) baselines. It also surpasses scalarization-based SPO+ approaches.
papers.summary: Models that predict unknown costs for planning problems are usually trained for prediction accuracy, which can yield poor decisions, and existing Decision-Focused Learning (DFL) methods for multi-objective problems fall back on simple scalarization that misses the trade-offs along the Pareto frontier. The authors extend the single-objective Smart Predict-then-Optimize loss (`SPO+`) with a Pareto-aware variant that uses the true Pareto frontier to form a target decision aligned with a sampled preference vector and minimizes regret against it. On multi-objective shortest path and knapsack problems, the approach **outperforms both two-stage mean squared error baselines and scalarization-based `SPO+`**.

papers.title: Colombo: A Frontier-to-Frontier Autoresearch System for Oracle-Based Optimization
papers.abstract: Science advances from frontier to frontier as discoveries reshape what is known and create the basis for further discovery. We present Colombo, a self-organizing AI researcher that drives this renewal, first instantiated in oracle-based optimization. Here, the central question is how efficiently a problem class can be solved through a prescribed information interface and what costs no admissible algorithm can avoid. The gap between achievable guarantees and unavoidable limits defines the frontier recorded in its Complexity Atlas, a living map of frontier settings and the current state of knowledge. Self-Organization turns unresolved gaps into adaptive research programmes, coordinating conjecture formation, mathematical investigation, and replanning as evidence accumulates. Adversarial Co-Ascent develops algorithms and hard families through reciprocal challenge, exposing mechanisms of information use and concealment that guide stronger methods and proofs of unavoidable costs. Independent review and Lean-based formal certification check mathematical claims, while the Long-Term Memory carries supported findings and research experience across settings. To date, Colombo has established optimal or near-optimal rates for more than fifty settings in the Atlas. Colombo thus takes a concrete step toward Autopoietic Science: a scientific process whose validated advances regenerate the conditions of its own progress, continually reshaping how inquiry is organized and what it can discover.
papers.summary: `Colombo` is a self-organizing AI research system applied to oracle-based optimization, where the question is how efficiently a problem class can be solved through a given information interface and what costs no algorithm can avoid. It maintains a Complexity Atlas of open gaps between achievable guarantees and lower bounds, turns those gaps into adaptive research programmes, and develops algorithms and hard problem families against each other in an adversarial loop. Claims are checked by independent review and Lean-based formal certification, and a long-term memory carries findings across settings. The authors report that it has **established optimal or near-optimal rates for more than fifty settings** in the Atlas.

papers.title: Learning to Undo: Transfer Reinforcement Learning under State Space Transformations
papers.abstract: Transfer learning in reinforcement learning (RL) has shown strong empirical success. In this work, we take a more principled perspective by studying when and how transferring knowledge between MDPs (a source and a target) can be provably beneficial. Specifically, we consider the case where there exists an undo map such that applying this map to the target's state space recovers the source exactly. We propose an algorithm that learns this map by matching state feature statistics gathered from both MDPs, and then uses it to transfer the source policy to the target. We theoretically justify the algorithm by analyzing the setting when the undo map is linear and the source is linearly-$Q^\star$ realizable, where our approach has strictly better sample complexity than tabula rasa RL in the target MDP. Empirically, we demonstrate that these benefits extend beyond this regime: on challenging continuous control tasks and Atari games, our method achieves significantly better sample efficiency. Overall, our results highlight how shared structure between tasks can be leveraged for efficient transfer of policies across environments.
papers.summary: The question studied is when transferring knowledge between a source and a target Markov decision process is provably beneficial, in the case where an undo map applied to the target's state space recovers the source exactly. The proposed algorithm learns this map by matching state feature statistics from both environments and then uses it to reuse the source policy in the target. When the undo map is linear and the source is linearly Q*-realizable, the method has **strictly better sample complexity than learning the target from scratch**. Experiments on continuous control tasks and Atari games show improved sample efficiency beyond the regime covered by the theory.

papers.title: BugGen 2.0: Rethinking the Roles of LLMs for Scalable RTL Bug Synthesis
papers.abstract: AI-assisted RTL localization and debugging need ground-truth bug datasets with known locations and observable failures, while testbench grading uses injected bugs to measure detection capability. Creating such datasets at scale remains a major EDA challenge. BugGen 1.0 shows that Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate context-aware RTL mutations. Still, it relies on the model for both choosing where to mutate and generating the edit, which increases inference costs and can lead to invalid choices. BugGen 2.0 changes this division of labor. Deterministic algorithms handle structural analysis, target selection, and validation, while the LLM focuses on localized semantic rewriting. Across four OpenTitan IP blocks and FabScalar with three LLMs, BugGen 2.0 reaches every requested quota of compilable bug scenarios that cause at least two test failures, with 14-16 of 16 configured mutation types represented. In completed same-model comparisons, it reduces token use by 6.8x-15.4x relative to BugGen 1.0 and 1.5x-7.9x relative to Firefly. BugGen 2.0 also expands the dataset without simulating every new bug. After finding accepted scenarios with observable failures, it generates alternative mutations at the same locations, simulates only a subset, and estimates acceptance for the rest. This skips 63.6% of AES and 33.9% of FabScalar variant simulations. Full simulation finds that 77.7% of AES variants and 95.2% of FabScalar variants are accepted, with a 1.09% estimation error on the directly comparable FabScalar set. These results show that focusing LLMs on semantic rewriting lowers inference and simulation cost while improving consistency across models and designs.
