For images, they identify the tradeoff the embedding must satisfy, staying stable under content-preserving edits while separating independent generations from the same prompt, and train an image encoder directly for it. The resulting encoder improves separation over off-the-shelf alternatives while keeping stability, and the scheme is demonstrated on both open-source and closed image models.

papers.title: Multimodal Masked Diffusion Autoencoder for Modeling Impaired Driving
papers.abstract: Human cognitive state (e.g., distraction, stress), gaze, and behavior interact with the driving environment in subtle ways that AI could use to assist drivers, but ground-truth labels for human cognitive state levels are costly to obtain at scale. We propose a multimodal masked-diffusion autoencoder, ID-MAE, that adds a self-supervised objective to impairment prediction: alongside predicting the impairment label as a masked token, it reconstructs masked gaze and trajectory. To probe the effects of different modalities and types of impairments on model inference, we introduce DIVERT, a driving-simulator dataset containing 103 hours of driving data (n = 109) with ten impairment inductions spanning cognitive, visual, and emotional states, recorded with gaze, vehicle state, and scene video. We demonstrate how ID-MAE affords significant improvements in impairment inference results on both the DIVERT dataset and existing datasets, and enables strong results in additional tasks, such as trajectory and gaze prediction. For location-matched pairs, our model achieves a paired AUC of 0.706 for impairment detection on DIVERT, compared to 0.590 without reconstruction loss, improving over existing baselines. We probe the design space in terms of input modalities, masking scheme, positional encoding, attention mechanism, and decoding. We also investigate the interaction between various impairments in training and inference, demonstrating that visually demanding distractions are separable from cognitive distractions. Code and data will be available upon acceptance.
papers.summary: Labels for a driver's cognitive state, such as distraction or stress, are expensive to collect at scale. `ID-MAE` is a multimodal masked-diffusion autoencoder that predicts the impairment label as a masked token while also reconstructing masked gaze and trajectory as a self-supervised objective. The authors also introduce `DIVERT`, a driving-simulator dataset with 103 hours from 109 participants under ten cognitive, visual, and emotional impairment inductions, recorded with gaze, vehicle state, and scene video. On location-matched pairs, the model reaches **a paired AUC of 0.706 for impairment detection versus 0.590 without the reconstruction loss**, and the analysis finds that visually demanding distractions are separable from cognitive ones.

papers.title: Higher-Scoring Coding Models Did Not Get More Work Done
papers.abstract: New coding models advertise themselves on score improvements of coding benchmarks. Yet no study has tested if a model that scores higher on these benchmarks gets more real work done. On June 12, 2026, a U.S. export control directive banned access to Claude Fable 5 for 19 days, which forced users to switch to other models. During this time, most former Fable 5 users switched to Opus 4.8 (11 points lower on SWE-Bench Pro compared to Fable 5). We treat this suspension as a natural experiment, where the people and projects stayed the same and only the model changed, so we could isolate the effect of Fable 5 on user productivity. We tracked GitHub pull requests of 297 Fable 5 users before, during, and after the suspension. We used 8,908 developers who stayed on Opus 4.8 all the time as the control group. We also repeated the comparison across five model upgrades before and after the suspension in 2026 (1,208 developers, 15,442 pull requests). Fitting a difference-in-differences model with developer and date fixed effects, we found that having access to Fable 5 increased the 7-day merge rate of pull requests by only 1.4 percentage points [-1.4; +4.3], which was not statistically significant. Similarly, no significant increases of merge rates were found with the upgrades (weighted mean: -0.9 percentage points [-1.9; +0.2]); all five estimates were negative (95% intervals included 0, did not differ from each other). We also did not observe a significant increase in the number of pull requests merged per week (+2.4% [-4.9%; +10.2%]).
papers.summary: Whether a coding model that scores higher on benchmarks actually gets more real work done is tested using a natural experiment: a 19-day suspension of access to `Claude Fable 5` in June 2026, during which most of its users switched to `Opus 4.8`, which scores 11 points lower on `SWE-Bench Pro`. The authors tracked GitHub pull requests from 297 `Fable 5` users before, during, and after the suspension, against a control group of 8,908 developers who stayed on `Opus 4.8`, and fit a difference-in-differences model with developer and date fixed effects. Access to `Fable 5` raised **the 7-day pull request merge rate by only 1.4 percentage points (95% interval -1.4 to +4.3), which was not statistically significant**, and the number of pull requests merged per week also showed no significant change (+2.4%). Repeating the comparison across five other model upgrades in 2026 gave a weighted mean of -0.9 percentage points, again with intervals including zero.

papers.title: What Does a Bias Head Measure? Non-Identifiability in Head-Level Bias Attribution
papers.abstract: Methods that localise social bias in large language models to individual attention heads and remove it by ablation are validated by their effect on a fairness metric, never by evidence that the statistic selecting the heads measures bias. We audit this on Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. The head map correlates at $\rho = -0.950$ and $-0.768$ with a label-blind response-length map, apparently identifying a surface confound. An intervention that breaks the length-label coupling rejects this reading: with the prompt held fixed, response length explains 1% of the statistic's variance. What does explain it is prompt identity, at 64% of variance, in an ordering that is not monotonic in length. Within any fixed prompt the fairness label, response length and the presence of a protected-group token are collinear at $\phi = 0.95$, partly by definition of the labelling rule, so no observational analysis can attribute the map to any of them, and no method in this family performs an experiment that could. The substantive claims fail independently: bias selectivity is not late-layer-concentrated on either model under either reference reading, and no head set we tested reduces the unfairness rate when ablated. Its complement, scored on the opposite label, reliably destroys refusal behaviour ($p = 2.7\times10^{-5}$), demonstrating that the pipeline detects effects at this scale.
papers.summary: Methods that localize social bias in large language models to individual attention heads and ablate them are validated by a fairness metric, not by evidence that the head-selecting statistic measures bias. Auditing this on `Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct` and `Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct`, the authors find the head map correlates strongly with a label-blind response-length map (rho = -0.950 and -0.768), but an intervention that breaks the length-label coupling shows length explains only 1% of the statistic's variance, while prompt identity explains 64%. Within a fixed prompt, the fairness label, response length, and presence of a protected-group token are collinear at phi = 0.95, so no observational analysis can attribute the map to any one of them. Bias selectivity was not concentrated in late layers on either model, and **no tested head set reduced the unfairness rate when ablated**, even though ablating the complementary set reliably destroyed refusal behaviour.

papers.title: Do LLM Agents Still Need to Be Told How to Self-Improve?
papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly drive their own learning. Self-improvement methods delegate various components of model optimization to the models themselves. As models become more capable, this motivates a basic question: do these increasingly capable models still need us to specify how they should self-improve? In this paper we study an autonomous paradigm in which, given basic primitives, resources, and a general goal for self-improvement, agents construct their own self-learning algorithm for context-based optimization. Using the setting of gameplay as a testbed, a frozen LLM agent is given a compute budget and tools for collecting experience and updating text documents, and allowed to freely experiment without an externally imposed loop or access to real-world data. We find that sufficiently capable models do self-improve under these conditions, demonstrating strategies that align with classic cognitive frameworks for self-regulated learning and constructs from machine learning literature on self-generated curricula. Furthermore, we study the extent to which the learned text artifacts transfer to external benchmarks, observing improvement across different game horizons, mechanics, and 3D navigation.
papers.summary: Self-improvement methods for LLM agents usually prescribe the learning loop, and the authors ask whether capable models still need that. In a gameplay testbed, a frozen LLM agent gets a compute budget plus tools for collecting experience and updating text documents, and is left to design its own context-based self-learning procedure with no externally imposed loop and no real-world data. They find that **sufficiently capable models do self-improve under these conditions**, using strategies that resemble self-regulated learning from cognitive science and self-generated curricula from machine learning. The learned text artifacts also transferred to external benchmarks, with gains across different game horizons, mechanics, and 3D navigation.
papers.highlight_summary:
Whether capable LLM agents still need a hand-designed self-improvement loop is tested by giving a frozen model only primitive tools, a budget, and a general goal to get better at puzzle games. The model acts as a teacher that writes its own practice games, watches another instance of itself play them, and edits that player's prompt and skill files, with no real games, validation scores, or prescribed procedure.

- The teacher gets `Read`/`Write`, `Bash`, and a `Gameplay` tool that runs a self-written `PuzzleScript` game in a fresh player session, with a budget of **20 context updates** and **150 gameplays**, and success is measured only on held-out benchmarks.
- On `PuzzleScript-t20`, the newer generation in each family improves over the default-context baseline (**+20%** for `Claude Opus-5`, **+10%** for `GPT 6-Astra`, **+6%** for `GLM 5.3`) while older generations show little or no gain, and `Claude Opus-5` matches `GEPA` hill-climbing on 20 real in-distribution games under the same rollout budget.
- The `Claude Opus-5` artifacts transfer beyond the training setting, gaining **+9%** on longer-horizon `PuzzleScript-t30`, **+21%** on Level 1 of `ARC-AGI-3`, and **+0.15 SPL** on 3D `MazeBench`, and context written by `GPT 6-Astra` lifts an `Opus 5` player from **25.4% to 47.5%** win rate.
- Models that self-improve converge on recognizable strategies without being told to: A/B testing games with and without their notes, generating fewer trivial games, concentrating replays on games with low-to-medium win rates, and scoring higher on a 13-subprocess rubric adapted from Zimmerman's self-regulated learning model.
- The link between these strategies and the gains is correlational and partly scored by an LLM judge, improvement plateaus within the 20-update budget, games are a domain where models have strong priors, and imposing the t20 turn and token budgets on the teacher raises `PuzzleScript-t20` scores while lowering `PuzzleScript-t30` transfer.

papers.title: An inexact stochastic variance-reduced gradient method for constrained convex finite-sum optimization
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study a class of constrained convex finite-sum optimization problems. In many practical applications, all or some of the constraints are hard constraints that represent imperative requirements. Consequently, any desirable approximate solution must (nearly) satisfy these constraints. Motivated by this, we focus on computing an $\epsilon$-$surely\ feasible\ stochastic\ optimal$ ($\epsilon$-SFSO) solution, in which the constraint violation is deterministically bounded by $\epsilon$, and the expected optimality gap is at most $\epsilon$. While a recently proposed stochastic variance-reduced first-order penalty method can compute an $\epsilon$-SFSO solution, there remains a significant gap between its first-order oracle complexity for computing an $\epsilon$-SFSO solution and that for computing an $\epsilon$-$expected\ feasible\ stochastic\ optimal$ solution, where both the expected constraint violation and the expected optimality gap are bounded by $\epsilon$. To narrow this gap, we propose an inexact stochastic variance-reduced gradient (SVRG) method that significantly improves the previously best-known first-order oracle complexity for computing an $\epsilon$-SFSO solution. Furthermore, when the objective consists of a single function, the proposed method reduces to a novel deterministic first-order method for solving standard convex conic optimization. It achieves a significantly lower gradient evaluation complexity with respect to the objective function compared to existing methods, and can outperform them when computing constraint gradients and projections onto the associated cone is cheaper than evaluating the objective gradient. Preliminary numerical results are presented to illustrate the performance of the proposed method.
papers.summary: For constrained convex finite-sum optimization with hard constraints, the target is an epsilon-surely feasible stochastic optimal (SFSO) solution, where constraint violation is deterministically bounded by epsilon and the expected optimality gap is at most epsilon. Existing variance-reduced penalty methods can find such solutions, but at a much higher first-order oracle cost than the weaker case where feasibility only holds in expectation. The authors propose an inexact stochastic variance-reduced gradient (`SVRG`) method that **improves the best-known first-order oracle complexity for computing an epsilon-SFSO solution**. With a single objective function, it reduces to a new deterministic first-order method for convex conic optimization that needs fewer objective-gradient evaluations than existing methods, supported by preliminary numerical results.

papers.title: StringQFT: A Multiuse Textbook Resource for AI-Assisted Theoretical Physics
papers.abstract: We present StringQFT as a textbook collection for string constructions of quantum field theory and as infrastructure for AI-assisted theoretical physics. The collection comprises 18 volumes, 190 chapters and 3,795 pages, covering brane probes, brane webs, geometric engineering, F-theory constructions, wrapped M5-branes and exact worldsheet constructions. Its open-book benchmark inventory contains 1,073 items, including 499 with automatic finite-answer checking. For retrieval-augmented generation, it provides 1,371 section records linked to textbook sources and PDF locations, together with a local lexical retriever. Training-data preparation is illustrated by 21 private, source-linked examples. For agents, it exposes 19 calculation tools with specified inputs and finite domains, connecting tool use to textbook derivations. We illustrate these uses through specific questions, retrieved passages and finite calculations. The textbook collection and accompanying resources are available at https://github.com/xingyang-yu/StringQFT.
papers.summary: `StringQFT` is a textbook collection on string-theoretic constructions of quantum field theory, packaged as infrastructure for AI-assisted theoretical physics. It spans 18 volumes, 190 chapters, and 3,795 pages on topics including brane probes, brane webs, geometric engineering, F-theory, and wrapped M5-branes. Alongside the text it provides **an open-book benchmark of 1,073 items, 499 of which have automatic finite-answer checking**, plus 1,371 source-linked section records with a local lexical retriever for retrieval-augmented generation. It also exposes 19 calculation tools with specified inputs and finite domains for agents, and illustrates training-data preparation with 21 source-linked examples.

papers.title: Spool: Low-Latency Streaming Inference for Hybrid Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Applications such as visual accessibility agents and robotics require answering questions about recent video content promptly, over a bounded window of past frames (e.g., the last two minutes). Hybrid vision-language models (VLMs), which interleave attention with linear recurrent layers such as Gated DeltaNet (GDN), are attractive for this setting, but maintaining a sliding window is expensive. The reason is that recurrent layers combine all past frames into a shared state, so expiring old frames normally requires re-running the entire window through the model. We observe that the recurrent update is affine in the state with input-dependent coefficients, so the effect of each frame can be captured as a transformation that composes associatively. We present Spool, a training-free framework that caches per-frame state transformations and composes them efficiently as the window advances, removing expired frames from each recurrent layer's state without replaying frames through the backbone. Removal is exact within each layer; as with key-value eviction in attention, expired frames can retain residual influence through the cached inputs computed by earlier layers. We design a dedicated data structure and GPU kernels to achieve low caching and composition overhead. Across five open-source hybrid VLMs and four video reasoning benchmarks, Spool achieves the lowest p95 time-to-first-token in all 20 model-benchmark tests, reducing it by a geometric mean of $6.6\times$ over the faster of two recent vLLM baselines, while improving accuracy by 2.3 percentage points on average.
papers.summary: Answering questions about a sliding window of recent video is costly for hybrid vision-language models (VLMs) that interleave attention with linear recurrent layers such as Gated DeltaNet (GDN), because the recurrent state mixes all past frames and expiring old ones normally means re-running the whole window. `Spool` is a training-free framework that exploits the fact that the recurrent update is affine in the state: it caches each frame's state transformation and composes them associatively as the window advances, removing expired frames exactly within each layer without replaying frames through the backbone, using a dedicated data structure and GPU kernels. Across five open-source hybrid VLMs and four video reasoning benchmarks, it had the lowest 95th-percentile time-to-first-token in all 20 tests, **cutting it by a geometric mean of 6.6x over the faster of two recent `vLLM` baselines**, while improving accuracy by 2.3 percentage points on average.

papers.title: Ambient LLMs: Data-Efficient Supervised Fine-tuning via Temperature Matching
papers.abstract: Collecting large-scale, diverse, and high-quality post-training datasets for autoregressive language models is challenging. Consequently, Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) is typically applied to datasets significantly smaller than those used for pre-training, which leads to overfitting and the catastrophic forgetting of the tails of the data distribution. To prevent this collapse, we introduce Ambient SFT, a principled framework for leveraging imperfect predictions to augment the fine-tuning set. In our method, a "frozen" version of the pre-trained model serves as a noisy teacher that the fine-tuned model must match at a coarse level. In particular, we require that the high-temperature versions of the conditional distributions produced by the post-training model should match the high-temperature versions of the pre-training ones. The temperature hyperparameter controls the level of trust in the pre-trained model, with the limit $T\to \infty$ reverting back to regular SFT and $T=1$ to knowledge distillation. We demonstrate that our approach outperforms standard SFT across domain adaptation, instruction-tuning, and reasoning, leading for up to $21\%$ average relative improvement to standard SFT.
papers.summary: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on small post-training datasets causes overfitting and forgetting of the tails of the pre-training distribution. `Ambient SFT` treats a frozen copy of the pre-trained model as a noisy teacher and requires the fine-tuned model's high-temperature conditional distributions to match the teacher's high-temperature ones, so the two agree only at a coarse level. The temperature sets how much the pre-trained model is trusted, recovering standard SFT as it goes to infinity and knowledge distillation at a temperature of 1. Across domain adaptation, instruction tuning, and reasoning tasks, the method gave **up to 21% average relative improvement over standard SFT**.

audio.title: TeleChat to Xing4: Advancing Frontier Agentic Models on Domestic Chips and Frameworks
audio.script: Today's pick from the AI Paper Digest. Training the largest AI models away from the usual graphics chips and software is mostly an engineering problem. A team at China Telecom designed its models and its training system together for Huawei's Ascend chips. They released an open model with twenty-nine billion parameters, trained entirely on that stack. Some reported speed gains come from simulation. The authors admit those may be optimistic. Still, it shows large models can be built on different hardware.
